retrieved_contexts: ['First published on 9th November 2022 Polylactide (PLA) is a biodegradable polyester with wide applications, and it degrades readily into CO2 and H2O. Although PLA paves the way for a circular economy with ‘neutral’ carbon footprint in the ecosystem, its complete degradation and the loss of lactic units are inevitable. Therefore, it is highly desirable to develop an efficient and economical recycling method among end-of-life options. In this work, a novel closed-loop process is constructed: L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C, VC) and sodium L-ascorbate (VCNa), two natural catalysts, were applied for the ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of lactide (LA) to PLA. More importantly, VCNa could catalyze the upcycling of PLA to alkyl lactate. Alkyl lactate could be converted back to LA by VCNa, providing an opportunity for a closed-loop process. The ROP of other lactones and copolymerization of lactide and lactone were also investigated. The relationship between the degradation rate and stereo-regularity of PLA was also explored for the first time. For the closed-loop process, a single catalyst that is versatile for all transformations would be ideal. Our attention has been drawn to the ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of lactides and lactones (Scheme 1c), where metal-based catalysts are frequently used. However, these catalysts suffer from the complicated removal process and toxicity of metal cations.10 Recently, organocatalysts without metal contaminations for polyester-based materials were developed for ROP.33-38 However, some synthesized organocatalysts still have toxicity issues.39 Thus, we considered whether a natural compound could be employed as an efficient catalyst.', 'As the fast solubility of CWAs is the key point to their effective detoxification, an alternative to the hydrolysis of CWA, in terms of speed and applicability, could be the metal-ion catalysed alcoholysis. Alcoholysis has several advantages over the hydrolysis of these organic compounds, such as: (i) the metal-ion catalysed reactions occur much faster in methanol than in water, due to a medium effect which involves better pre-equilibrium binding of the substrate and the metal ion;7,8 (ii) the CWAs are far more soluble in lower polarity alcohol media than in water;9-11 (iii) the reactions occur under mild conditions,12 and (iv) the G-agent alcoholysis produces neutral phosphorus esters which do not inhibit the reaction,13,14 while the phosphoric acids formed during hydrolysis inhibit the catalysis through the anionic products formed during their dissociation process.12 Other alternatives involve the use of biodegradable foams, gels and heterogeneous porous materials which, for instance, could exhibit catalytic activity even if the reaction rate is lower.15-21 In this regard, heterogeneous photocatalysis can perform the decomposition of chemical weapons under benign experimental conditions and has already been applied successfully on real CW blistering,22,23 G,24,25 and V nerve agents.26,27 Taking into account the advantages of both methanolysis and heterogeneous photocatalysis, a combination of these methods could be “the golden key” for the development of an efficient and environmentally benign system for the decomposition of real CWA. Herein, we report for the first time the use of a hybrid system that performs La3+-catalysed methanolysis and photocatalytic degradation of real CWA, both blistering and nerve agents under visible light irradiation.', 'First published on 19th February 2024 Biodegradable plastics, represented by polylactic acid (PLA), are considered suitable alternatives to non-degradable commodity plastics; however, their degradation through microbial decomposition is seen as a waste of carbon resources and inevitably brings about CO2 emission. Alternatively, waste PLA plastics can be utilized as feedstocks for the sustainable production of value-added chemicals, which not only avoids a carbon footprint but also realizes upcycling of plastic waste. Here, we show a cascade system that combines alkali-induced depolymerization, pulsed electrooxidation, and electrochemical reductive amination to produce alanine with an overall yield of 69% under near ambient conditions. Specifically, we first implement an alkali catalyst in an aqueous solution to depolymerize PLA into lactate. This cascade process for alanine production benefits from high efficiencies maintained in three consecutive processes, mild operation conditions, and the use of cost-effective feedstocks (plastic wastes), without suffering harsh conditions and expensive feedstock consumption required by conventional biological and chemical approaches for alanine synthesis, respectively. The interest in open-loop upcycling technologies, compared with the above-mentioned closed-loop recycling approaches, arises from their ability to use PLA waste streams as the carbon source for higher-value chemical production. Understanding the degradation kinetics and the impact of degradation byproducts on cell behavior and tissue homeostasis is crucial.57 PHA degradation occurs through the action of enzymes, either intracellularly by intracellular depolymerases, which primarily degrade amorphous PHAs, or extracellularly by extracellular depolymerases, which mainly target crystalline PHAs.58 These enzymes break down the PHA polymer chains into smaller fragments.59 The degradation rate of PHAs can be influenced by factors such as PHA composition, molecular weight, crystallinity and the presence of specific depolymerase enzymes.60 The degradation products and metabolites released from PHA scaffolds can influence cell behavior and tissue regeneration.49 For example, some metabolites released during PHA degradation have been reported to exhibit signaling properties that can modulate cell activities, including cell proliferation, differentiation and ECM production.61 Understanding the specific effects of PHA degradation products on cell behavior and tissue development is important for optimizing scaffold design and promoting desired tissue outcomes.', 'Plastic materials are essential in our daily lives; however, their mass production and disposal have raised serious environmental concerns. Among these, marine pollution caused by discarded plastics is particularly concerning, with an estimated 360 million tons of plastic produced annually worldwide,1, 2 of which 4.8-12.7 million tons enter the ocean.2, 3 The total mass of plastic waste in the sea is expected to exceed that of the fish population in the near future.3, 4 Most plastics have chemically stable structures that resist environmental degradation. retrieved_contexts: ['Copyright © 2013 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim Poly(L-lactide) (i.e., poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA)) is a biodegradable polymer produced from plant-derived renewable resources and is used for biomedical, pharmaceutical, environmental, industrial, and commodity applications.1-13 In some industrial and commodity applications, the enhancement of mechanical performance and hydrolytic/thermal degradation resistance is required. The stereocomplexation between PLLA and poly (D-lactide) (i.e., poly(D-lactic acid) (PDLA)) has been intensively studied because it can enhance their mechanical properties and hydrolytic/thermal degradation resistance of polylactide (PLA)-based materials.14-19 Stereocomplex crystallization from the melt is a matter of concern in terms of processing the high-performance PLA articles. The effects of molecular weight, polymer mixing ratio, optical purity, and processing conditions on the melt-crystallization of PLLA/PDLA and L-lactide-rich PLA/D-lactide-rich PLA blends were intensively investigated.14-19 Moreover, the synthesis of a wide variety of stereoblock copolymers of PLLA and PDLA has been carried out.20-33 On the other hands, linear 2-arm and branched multi-arm PLLA and L-lactide copolymers have been prepared by the polymerization of L-lactide and comonomers by various procedures using diols and polyols as coinitiators, or spirocyclic initiators.1, 4, 9, 34-42 Tsuji et al. reported that the chain directional change, the incorporation of the coinitiator moiety as an impurity in the middle of the molecule, and their mixed effect disturbed the crystallization (abbreviated as “chain directional effects”) of linear 2-arm PLLA prepared with ethylene glycol compared with that of linear 1-arm PLLA prepared with L-lactic acid or 1-dodecanol, in which the chain direction was unvaried and the coinitiator moiety was incorporated in the chain terminal. This result strongly suggests that the reported low crystallizability of multi-arm PLLA (arm number ≥ 3) compared with that of linear 1-arm PLLA is caused not only by the presence of branching points but also by the chain directional effects.28 Moreover, Sakamoto and Tsuji43 reported that, in comparison between 2-arm PLLA prepared with 1,3-propanediol and 4-arm PLLA prepared with pentaerythritol, the branching architecture of 4-arm PLLA delayed or disturbed non-isothermal crystallization during heating and isothermal crystallization compared with linear architecture of 2-arm PLLA, but did not affect segmental mobility, crystalline thickness, and transition temperature from the δ(α′)- to the α-form. To the best of our knowledge, despite the reported results on the effects of stereocomplexation of linear PLLA with star-shaped D-lactic acid (D-LA) oligomers with different architectures on the thermal transition and hydrolytic degradation and the effects of branching and stereochemistry of PLA on the enzymatic degradation and alkaline hydrolysis, a detailed study on the pure effects of chain directional effects and branching on the stereocomplex crystallization behavior and physical properties of PLLA/PDLA blends have not been reported so far.44-46', 'Differences Between Stereocomplex Spherulites Obtained in Equimolar and Non-Equimolar Poly(L-lactide)/Poly(D-lactide) Blends Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) represents one of the most efficient sustainable alternatives for the substitution of petroleum-based polymers since it can be industrially produced at large quantities from annually renewable resources as sugar beet, corn, or rice.1, 2 PLLA can be synthesized either by polycondensation of L-lactic acid or by ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of L-lactide, where the ROP allows much higher molecular weight to be reached. PLLA is biodegradable semi-crystalline polyester with reasonably good mechanical and optical properties, thermal plasticity, and processability.3 Although its melting temperature (Tm) reaches 170-180 °C depending on the enantiomeric purity (i.e. residual content in D-lactic acid), PLLA suffers from a relatively low crystallization rate (υc). Among the different methods reported so far, stereocomplexation between equimolar amount of PLLA and PDLA represents an interesting way to enhance υc.4, 5 The resulting PLA stereocomplexes, herewith coined as sc-PLA, exhibit a Tm close to 230 °C (about 50 °C higher than Tm of homo-PLLA and homo-PDLA), leading to higher thermo-mechanical properties with respect to pure enantiomeric PLLA.6 Therefore, while PLLA is mainly used for short-term purposes where biodegradability is important (e.g., as biomedical sutures, single-use packaging), sc-PLA-based materials are expected to find applications where high-performance and/or long-term shelf-life are required such as home appliances, automotive parts, computer casings, etc. Stereocomplexation (stereoselective association) between PLLA and PDLA is known to occur in solution, from melt, during polymerization or hydrolytic degradation when optically active L-lactide and D-lactide unit sequences coexist in a system.6 The process solely comprises racemic crystallization and, depending on the PDLA/PLLA ratio, results in the formation of two main types of crystallites (homo-crystallites formed during crystallization of either PDLA or PLLA chains; and stereocomplex (sc) crystallites, where PDLA and PLLA chains are packed together due to strong van der Waals interactions). According to the recent literature, stereocomplexation of enantiomeric homo-polylactides ( ≈ 5 000) is complete for PLLA/PDLA molar ratio from 2.5:7.5 to 7.5:2.5.7 Up to date, it mostly concerns the addition of small amounts of PDLA to PLLA. The in-situ formed sc-crystallites act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for the crystallization of the PLLA chains in excess. Actually, the PLLA homocrystalites are epitaxially formed on the stereocomplex crystallites.4, 5, 8, 9 Several studies4, 5 demonstrated that melt-obtained in-situ sc crystallites are more effective to enhance the crystallinity degree of PLA although they were found to reduce the overall PLLA crystallization by hindering the mobility of the PLLA chains. Yet, in spite of the attractive advantages mentioned above, stereocomplexation evokes significant problems in bulk processability due to the extremely high processing temperatures required (>200 °C) and the low system viscosity. Moreover, with such high processing temperatures, PLA often undergoes thermal degradation, which significantly hampers the mechanical properties of the final materials.', 'Stereocomplexation is physical modification composed of two components with same composition but different stereochemical configuration to form a composite material with superior properties [24], [25]. PLA is categorized into three forms according to its optical activity: poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), poly(D-lactide) (PDLA), and poly(D,L-lactide) (PDLLA). PDLLA is one of them and in an amorphous state and incapable of crystallization. PLLA and PDLA are semi-crystalline polymers that crystallize to form α crystals [26], [27]. For PLLA/PDLA system, the polymer chains can be arranged alternately layer by layer through the strong hydrogen bonds between PLA enantiomer chains and tightly packed to form stereocomplex crystals, which differ from α crystals [28]. Previous studies [29], [30], [31] found that stereocompexed PLA based on stereocomplex crystallization has significantly improved mechanical properties, crystallization rate, melting temperature, and hydrolysis resistance than neat PLLA or PDLA. Therefore, stereocomplexation is considered an effective method to enhance PLA’s properties. However, when PLA has a high molecular weight, the blend PLLA/PDLA tends to homo-crystallize either PLLA or PDLA. As a result, the resulting PLA stereocomplex has a poor melt memory effect and cannot withstand repeated heating [32]. This significantly affects the properties and processing of stereocomplexed PLA, limiting its application. Additionally, stereocomplexation cannot make PLA less brittle, which is another reason for its limited application. The design and synthesis of PLA with different structures through chemical modification have attracted extensive attention [33], [34], [35], [36], [37]. Poly(lactide)-based materials, which are composed of poly(lactide) blocks and flexible polymer blocks with triblock, multiblock, long-chain branching, and crosslinked structures [33], [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], [40], significantly improve the brittleness of poly(lactide). However, it is hard to synthesize high molecular weight PLA with flexible blocks polymers containing hydroxyl groups as macromolecular initiator, by the ring-opening polymerization of lactide. The increased molecular weight of PLA leads to the decrease of end-hydroxyl activity and the formation of PLA homopolymer. The synthesis of high molecular weight PLA-based block copolymers from low molecular weight PLA containing flexible blocks by chain extension has been reported [38], [39], [40]. Pan et al. [39] synthesized alternating supramolecular multiblock copolymers with poly(lactic acid) and poly(ethylene-co-butylene) segments by terminal-functionalizing poly(lactic acid)-poly(ethylene-co-butylene)-poly(lactic acid) (PLA-PEB-PLA) triblock oligomers with the 2-ureido-4[1H]-pyrimidinone self-complementary quadruple hydrogen bonding units. The results showed that compared with the PLA-PEB-PLA precursor, the synthesized supramolecular multiblock copolymer not only had better mechanical strength, modulus, and elongation at break but also exhibited better heat-induced shape memory and light-triggered self-healing properties. A series of poly(lactide)-poly(butadiene) (PLA-PB) multiblock copolymers were synthesized by chain extension of PLA-PB-PLA triblock copolymer with toluene-2,4-diisocyanate terephthaloyl chloride. The mechanical properties of PLA-PB multiblock coploymers (fPLA = 0.6-0.8) demonstrated significant improvement over the PLA-PB-PLA triblock copolymer [40]. Although the presence of flexible blocks improves the brittleness of PLA, it may interfere with PLA homogeneous nucleation during the crystallization. The chain extension disrupted the PLA structure and increases its molecular weight [41], [42]. As a results, these factors may restrict the PLA crystallization. Therefore, it is urgent to search for new methods to improve the overall performance of PLA. The introduction of flexible blocks in PLA chains can improve its movement ability, which is an important factor affecting the stereocomplexation of PLA enantiomers [42], [43], [44]. So, it is an effective way to improve the brittleness, crystallization ability and thermal stability of PLA by designing and synthesizing PLA-based block copolymer with flexible block and studying its stereocomplexed behavior [43], [44], [45], [46]. On the basis of the existing literature, we proposed a new method to improve the properties of PLA-based materials by combining chemical method and stereocomplexation. A series of three-arm branched poly(ε-caprolactone-co-γ-butyrolactone)-b-poly(lactide) block copolymers with different compositions and optical activities were first designed and synthesized. PLA-based polyurethane with cross-linked structure was synthesized by chain extension reaction driven three-arm branched poly(ε-caprolactone-co-γ-butyrolactone)-b-poly(lactide) block copolymers. The effects of molecular weight, optical activities and stereocomplexation of PLA blocks on crystallization, thermal stability, mechanical properties, shape memory performance and hydration ability of the synthesized polyurethanes were discussed. In order to evaluate the potential application of the synthesized PLA-based polyurethanes as the biomaterial, its biocompatibility was also tested by cytotoxicity assay and hemolysis assay.', 'Stereocomplex crystal formation of PLA, first reported by Ikada et al.,10 prepared by blending two PLA enantiomers (poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) and poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA)) can improve PLA performance.11 When these chiral species are mixed, they can co-crystallize and form a stereocomplex with a 31 helical conformation12, 13 due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding from the close packing of enantiomeric chains.14, 15 The stereocomplex formation of PLA is different from the 103 helices formed by their homopolymer crystals. PLA stereocomplex (scPLA) crystal formation subsequently grants higher melting temperature,16 improved thermal resistance,17 enhanced mechanical properties18 and anti-hydrolysis ability,19 thus expanding the potential applications of PLA-based materials.20-27 It is found that the formation of stereocomplex crystals is selective and competitive, largely influenced by many parameters including molecular weight,28, 29 enantiomeric blending ratio,30, 31 preparation routes,32, 33 chain architectures34 and the presence of additives.35, 36 While high molecular weight PLA confers greater mechanical properties, a low molecular weight is more conducive to encouraging stereocomplex crystallization to occur.37 In recent years, a variety of star-shaped and branched PLAs have been reported, allowing an understanding about the effect of chain architecture on scPLA properties.38-40 Shao et al.41 reported how the composition of three-armed enantiomeric PLA impacts the phase separation molecular weight of scPLAs, with a 3sPLLA/3sPDLA blend reaching the lowest value. Moreover, the melting temperature and crystallization behavior of scPLAs can be further controlled by star-shaped chain architectures. The formation of scPLA crystals can be promoted using a mixture of star-shaped PLLA and PDLA through inhibiting homochiral crystallization, attributed to the transformation of crystallite structure during heating, which results in multiple melting behaviors evidenced by their DSC traces.42 Furthermore, branched PLLA with varying branch arms can influence the integrity of stereocomplex crystallites as well as their melting temperature.43 Ma et al.44 reported that the blend of PDLA and comb-like nanocrystalline cellulose grafted PLLA exhibited a high stereocomplexation rate and thermal stability. Star-shaped stereo-block copolymers were observed to exhibit increased nucleation density during crystallization, which can accelerate the rate of crystallization and enhance stereocomplexation efficiency.45-48 Compared to linear PLLA/PDLA blends, star-shaped PLLA/linear PDLA blends have faster crystallization kinetics and a higher degree of crystallinity, which benefit from the flexibility of linear chains and the high nucleation density provided by star-shaped chains.49 In addition to star-shaped architecture, the incorporation of suitable modifiers on polymer backbones is another effective method to promote scPLA crystallization. In particular, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has a flexible backbone and its incorporation into PLA materials can accelerate the rate of PLA crystallization.50 Stereocomplexes of racemic PLA blended with PEG, such as PLLA/PDLA/PEG,51-53 PLLA/PDLA-PEG-PDLA,54-56 PLLA-PEG-PLLA/PDLA57 and PLLA-PEG-PLLA/PDLA-PEG-PDLA have been investigated.58 It was found that the incorporation of PEG could lead to fractionated crystallization kinetics and the formation of unstable β-form homo-crystals of PLLA/PDLA blends.51 Moreover, Xie et al.58 demonstrated that equimolar PLLA-PEG-PLLA/PDLA-PEG-PDLA blends with a high PEG fraction tended to form unique homo-crystalline mesophases at low crystallization temperatures (ca 70-120 °C), while the crystalline structures of blends containing low PEG content were similar to those of PLLA/PDLA blends. In this work, PEG can be completely compatible with PLLA/PDLA blends to promote stereocomplex crystallization while suppressing crystallization of homo-crystals.53 Additionally, the brittleness of scPLA can be improved by PEG incorporation as it imparts material flexibility. Li et al.54 reported increased tensile strength and elongation at break of PDLA-PEG-PDLA/PLLA blends with increasing PEG molecular weight. As demonstrated by these examples, the performance of PLA blends can be greatly improved through the stereocomplexation of enantiomeric PLA blends and the plasticization effect from incorporating PEG segments.', 'Currently, stereocomplexation between enantiomeric poly(L-Latide) and poly(D-lactide) is considered an effective method to improve the properties of PLA-based materials [28,29,30]. After adequate mixing of PLLA and PDLA, multicenter hydrogen-bonding interactions leads to possible alternative arrangements of helical chains between L-lactyl and D-lactyl units with opposite chiral conformation for the formation of PLA stereocomplexation [31, 32]. It has been reported [33, 34] that the stereocomplexed PLA exhibits higher melting temperature, fast crystallization rate, high heat resistance and good mechanical properties with respect to the ordinary poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) and poly(D-lactide) (PDLA), which is assigned to the tight chain packing and hydrogen bond interactions [35, 36]. However, the stereocomplextaion of PLLA and PDLA is usally accompanied by homo-crystallization of PLLA or PDLA. Avoiding homo-crystallization and achieving full stereocomplexation is the focus of current research. The adjustion of molecular weight and movement ability of PLA chain is considered to be an effective method to improve the degree of stereocomplexation of its enantiomer blends [35, 37]. PLA-based copolymers with different structures have been synthesized to promote stereocomplex-crystallization. The stereocomplexed ABCBA pentablock copolymers comprising poly(D-lactide) (A), poly(L-lactide) (B) and poly(propylene succinate) (C) were reported, and it was found that the resulting materials exhibit high crystallinity, high heat resistance, and elastomeric properties [37]. In this research, a novel flexible PLA-based thermoplastic polyurethane based on poly(lactide)-b-poly(hexylene succinate)-b-poly(lactide) (PLA-b-PHS-b-PLA) triblock copolymers was devised. FT-IR, 1H NMR and GPC were used to analyze their chemical structures, compositions and molecular weights. The crystallization behavior, thermal stability and mechanical properties of PLA-based thermoplastic polyurethanes with different compositions and mixing ratios were measured by XRD, DSC, TGA and tensile test. Additionally, the hydrophilicity, biodegradability and biocompatibility were determined to evaluate their potential for use as a tissue engineering material. Experimental section', 'The formation of stereocomplex (SC) crystallites between enantiomeric PLA is an interesting phenomenon, poly (l-lactide) (PLLA) and poly (d-lactide) (PDLA) chains interact with each other through intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which causes the denser chain packing in the crystal lattice of SC crystallites than that in the homocrystallites formed by enantiopure PLLA or PDLA. In the present study, biodegradable PUEs based on PCL and stereoisomeric PLA macrodiols were synthesized separately and a PUE with SC crystallites was obtained by equivalent mixing of the enantiomeric PLLA and PDLA containing polyurethane. (China) and used as received except specification.', 'Copyright © 2012 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim Polylactides (PLAs) are biobased and biodegradable polymers having various applications. Because of the enantiomeric nature of their component lactic acid, two stereo isomers, poly(D-lactide) (PDLA) and poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), are present. Currently, only the latter PLLA consisting of naturally abundant L-lactic acid is manufactured.1-3 Although this PLLA exhibits a broad range of physicochemical properties, its poor thermal and mechanical properties do not make it very attractive for use in ordinary structural materials.4 Another PLA polymer showing highly improved properties is the stereocomplex-type PLA (sc-PLA) that can be formed by simple mixing of PLLA and PDLA in the melt or solution state.5-9 As its melting temperature (Tm) reaches 240 °C, sc-PLA is expected to be a heat-resistant material having excellent mechanical properties. The stereocomplexation, however, depends on the compositions and molecular weights of the PLLA and PDLA used.6 In particular, when high molecular weight PLLA and PDLA are mixed, homochiral (hc) crystals are likely to form together with the desired sc crystals, degrading the properties of the processed materials.10-12 For industrial application of sc-PLA, therefore, there is a need for better sc formation without accompanying hc crystallization. One practical approach for improving the stereocomplexation is to use stereoblock-type polylactides (sb-PLA) consisting of PLLA and PDLA sequences from which sc crystals are preferentially formed because of the intrinsic molecular mixing state of both sequences. Until now, many types of sb-PLA having different PLLA and PDLA block sequences have been synthesized, for example, stereo di, tri, and multiblock types.13-28 Yui et al.29 first synthesized stereo diblock PLAs (d-sb-PLA) with a relatively low molecular weight by the two-step ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of D- and L-lactides and confirmed their excellent stereocomplexibility.29 Afterward, we optimized this ROP process to obtain d-sb-PLAs having molecular weights higher than 100 kDa. Furthermore, we discovered that preferential sc formation can be achieved even for those diblocks consisting of different block lengths of PLLA and PDLA.24, 26, 27 We also demonstrated that the melt/solid-state polycondensation of a mixture of PLLA and PDLA prepolymers can give stereo multiblock sb-PLAs (m-sb-PLA). The resultant m-sb-PLAs having different PLLA and PDLA compositions show high stereocomplexibility and excellent mechanical and thermal properties.19-23 Among these sb-PLA derivatives, d-sb-PLAs having different PLLA/PDLA compositions, that is, consisting of long PLLA and short PDLA sequences, are attractive materials in terms of their easiness of production and properties. It was however revealed that an injection mold of d-sb-PLA having a PLLA/PDLA ratio of 80/20, for example, shows a softening temperature (Tsf) around 75 °C, which is only slightly higher than the glass transition temperature (Tg), although its Tm was as high as 205 °C.27 This lower Tsf may be attributed to the lower stereocrystallinity of the d-sb-PLAs whose abundant PLLA chains are not involved in the sc formation and so retain high segment mobility above Tg. One of the most reliable methods for decreasing the mobility of these abundant enantiomeric chains is to use ABA stereo triblock PLAs (t-sb-PLA) because the enantiomeric A chains in both sides can be shorter at a constant A/B block composition (where A is longer than B), thereby making the sc formation easier.', 'Copyright © 2013 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), a plant-derived polyester, has found applications in the biomedical and packaging fields because of its biodegradability and biocompatibility.1-4 Intensive research is going on to improve the properties of PLLA as an alternative to petro-derived polymers to reduce the environmental impact.5-9 Until now poly(lactic acid) (PLA) has enjoyed little success in replacing petroleum-based plastics in the applications which require high impact strength and thermal stability. The mechanical and thermal properties and biodegradability of a semicrystalline polymer generally depend on the crystalline structure and crystallinity.10 The stereocomplex crystallization between PLLA and poly(D-lactic acid) (PDLA) improves mechanical and thermal properties of PLA-based materials.11-14 However, stereocomplex crystallization is disturbed when high-molecular weight PLLA and PDLA are used because of the difficulty in molecular level mixing. A promising method for obtaining stereocomplexed PLA is to use stereoblock PLA composed of PLLA and PDLA segments. Because of neighboring effects of the PLLA and PDLA blocks, stereoblock PLA readily forms stereocomplex crystallites in a wide range of processing windows. The crystallization behavior of block copolymers has been an active area of research for the past several decades. In 1990, Yui et al.15 first showed that stereocomplex crystallization occurs in diblock copolymers PLLA-b-PDLA. To know the crystallization mechanism in details, stereocomplex crystallization behavior of diblock or triblcok PLA and blend, that is, spherulite formation, isothermal crystallization kinetics, and regime analyses of these polymers16-20 and also the crystallization and morphology of diblock copolymers with one crystallizable block21, 22 have been investigated extensively. Tsuji et al.17 showed that only stereocomplex crystallities as crystalline species were formed in PLLA-b-PDLA copolymers with Mn of 3.9 × 103-1.1 × 104 g mol−1. Also, crystallization and stereocomplexation behavior of diblock copolymers which contained a crystalline block and a amorphous block, that is PLLA- or PDLA-poly(N,N-dimethylamino-2-ethylmethacrylate) (PDMAEMA) has been reported by Michell et al.21 They concluded that the crystallization kinetics of the PLLA or PDLA blocks were retarded by the presence of amorphous PDMAEMA block and PLLA-b-PDMAEMA/PDLA-b-PDMAEMA blend formed stereocomplex crystallites. In a previous study, we have shown that only stereocomplex crystallization also takes place in stereo multiblock PLA copolymers with average block length (νav) higher than 7 lactyl units.23 However, as far as we are aware, stereocomplex crystallization of stereo multiblock PLA copolymers consisting of relatively short PLLA and PDLA segments has not been reported. In this study, crystallization and spherulite growth behavior of stereo multiblock PLAs with various stereoblock lengths were investigated using wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and polarized optical microscopy (POM).', 'The stereocomplex technology is considered to be one of the most effective methods to improve the crystallization rate and heat resistance of PLA, which are important issues in expanding the applications of poly(lactide).20 Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) and its enantiomer poly(D-lactide) (PDLA) have been reported to show a strong tendency to interact with each other to form stereocomplexes via the strong van der Waals forces of the CH3⋯CO interactions between enantiomeric molecular chains.21,22 The melting temperature of PLA-based stereocomplexes (sc-PLA) can reach 230 °C, which is higher than that of PLLA or PDLA (about 170 °C). In addition, sc-PLA also has a high crystallization rate and heat resistance compared to PLLA or PDLA. The stereocomplexation between poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) and poly(D-lactide) (PDLA) significantly enhances the thermal properties of polylactic acid (PLA) through the following effects:  

1. **Increased Melting Temperature (Tm):**  
   Stereocomplex (sc) crystallites formed from PLLA/PDLA blends exhibit a **Tm ~230–240°C**, which is **~50°C higher** than the Tm of homo-crystallites (α-form) of PLLA or PDLA (~170–180°C). This is attributed to denser chain packing and stronger intermolecular interactions (e.g., van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonding) between enantiomeric L- and D-lactide chains in the stereocomplex structure [1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 14].  

2. **Improved Heat Resistance:**  
   The higher Tm of sc-PLA enhances thermal stability, making it suitable for high-temperature applications (e.g., automotive parts, electronics) where conventional PLA would soften or degrade [2, 7, 12].  

3. **Enhanced Crystallization Rate:**  
   Stereocomplexation accelerates the crystallization kinetics of PLA, as sc-crystallites act as **heterogeneous nucleation sites**, promoting epitaxial growth of homocrystallites and increasing overall crystallinity [2, 3, 9]. This is particularly advantageous for industrial processing.  

4. **Thermal Degradation Resistance:**  
   Sc-PLA exhibits slower thermal degradation compared to homo-PLLA/PDLA due to the stable stereocomplex crystalline structure, which hinders chain mobility and delays degradation [1, 4, 12].  

5. **Suppressed Homo-Crystallization:**  
   In equimolar PLLA/PDLA blends, stereocomplexation dominates over homo-crystallization under optimized conditions (e.g., low molecular weight, specific processing temperatures), further stabilizing thermal properties [2, 10, 12].  

**Challenges:**  
- High-molecular-weight PLLA/PDLA blends often form mixed homo- and stereocomplex crystallites, reducing thermal benefits.  
- Processing temperatures >200°C risk thermal degradation, necessitating additives (e.g., PEG) or modified architectures (e.g., star-shaped copolymers) to improve stereocomplexation efficiency [4, 7, 9].  

In summary, stereocomplexation elevates PLA’s thermal performance by increasing Tm, accelerating crystallization, and improving heat resistance, making sc-PLA a viable high-performance alternative to petroleum-based polymers.

Thus, PLA/PBAT 3D filament is great potential to replace the petroleum-based 3D filament in the additive manufacturing (AM) industries.', 'Three-dimensional (3D) printing technology, also known as additive manufacturing, has revolutionized conventional designing and prototyping practices by enabling individuals to create artifacts in a rapid and cost-effective manner. Hydro-peroxide and carbonyl groups are generated, and then, PE molecules that contain carbonyl groups dissociate by Norrish type I or type II reactions [1].', 'From the discussion, the degradation behavior of PBAT/TPS blend can be summarized as shown in Figure 10. Second stage is microorganism catalysis of degradation in which hydrolytic chain scission of ester group convert a low molecular chain into carbon dioxide, water, and humus.', 'A review on degradation mechanisms of polylactic acid: Hydrolytic, photodegradative, microbial, and enzymatic degradation Hydrolytic degradation of poly(l-lactic acid)/poly(methyl methacrylate) blends Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a plant-derived polymer and has been utilized for industrial, commodity, biomedical, pharmaceutical, and environmental applications.1-11 When PLLA materials are released in the environment, they are exposed to photodegradation by sunlight especially ultraviolet (UV) rays. Therefore, it is expected that the structural changes of PLLA articles caused by the UV-irradiation in the environment will affect the design of recycling process by hydrolytic/thermal degradation. In biomedical and pharmaceutical applications, UV irradiation or UV treatment can be utilized for sterilization. In the molecular level, UV-irradiation is known to cause PLLA the structural changes, such as decrease in molecular weight and formation of terminal C\uf8feC double bonds through the Norrish II mechanism and of crosslinks via radical recombination.12 Moreover, the comparison of UV-photodegradation behavior between PLLA and poly(ε-caprolactone) strongly suggested that the chemical structure between the adjacent ester groups than the density of ester group is crucial to determine the photodegradability of biodegradable polyesters.12 Although in the material level, the photodegradation of PLLA films proceeds via a bulk erosion mechanism; this indicates that UV rays penetrate the films with no significant reduction.13, 14 Furthermore, it was found that PLLA chains are photodegradable even in the crystalline regions and their photodegradability is lower than that in the amorphous regions.13, 14 The photodegradation behavior of PLLA by UV-irradiation has been intensively investigated.12-26', 'Products made from natural rubber are often vulcanized during the production to improve their strength and durability. Vulcanization improves the mechanical properties of the rubber at the expense of its biodegradability [4], [5]. Sulfur vulcanization and the presence of certain additives (such as antioxidants) in some of these products extend the duration needed for decomposition in the natural environment [5], [6]. Polyolefin plastics and metal complexes (such as Fe, Co, and Mn stearates) that serve as pro-degradant additives (PDA) or catalysts are frequently used to accelerate the natural degradation process of polymers [7]. The mechanism involved includes the absorption of UV light and oxidation, followed by the generation of unstable hydroperoxide that will subsequently dissociate to form a pair of free radicals responsible for the eventual disintegration of the polymer [8], [9]. The oxidation of the polymer also results in the formation of carbonyl groups in the hydrocarbon chain (Fig. 1A), making it more vulnerable to further degradation since these groups are photolabile and easily undergo photolysis via Norrish I and Norrish II reactions (Fig. 1B) [10], [11]. Given the current enormous volume of rubber usage, there is a need to consider the end-of-life treatment of rubber products, including ways to hasten its biodegradation in the environment. One viable strategy is the enhancement of oxo-biodegradable properties of natural rubber [4]. The introduction of oxo-biodegradable properties has been extensively studied in the plastics industry, evidenced by the high volume of patents and successful commercial products in the market with many positive results [12], [13], [14]. The most common approach to improving oxo-biodegradability is introducing a PDA in the polymers. The oxo-biodegradation of a polymer refers to a two-stage degradation process that begins with the oxidation of the carbon backbone of the polymer to form smaller fragments containing carboxyl, ester, aldehyde, and/or alcohol groups, followed by bio-assimilation of the oxidation products by microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), and biomass. In the first stage of degradation, the oxidative breakdown of polymer to produce smaller and hydrophilic fragments is crucial to improve water wettability of the substrate, and molecules of the material must be sufficiently small for microflora, such as bacteria and fungi to assimilate carbon source in the substrate [15], [16]. This explains why most hydrocarbon thermoplastics, which are hydrophobic and usually produced with very high molecular weight, are bioinert. This could also explain the persistency observed in vulcanized natural rubber which is composed of poly(isoprene) chains connected by sulfur linkages [4], [5]. Over the past ten years, there have been reports of successful improvements in the oxo-biodegradability of plastics, particularly through the use of various PDA [17], [18]. Although a similar approach can be applied to rubber and may work equally well, little research has been done to develop oxo-biodegradable rubber, and its potential impact on plant and soil health remain unclear. The objectives of the present study were to develop and characterize oxo-biodegradable rubber through the incorporation of two metal stearates as PDA, namely iron (III) stearate (FeSt) and cobalt (II) stearate (CoSt), as well as to assess the effects of the oxo-biodegradable rubber on plant and soil health. The development of novel and safe oxo-biodegradable rubbers is vital to ensure sustainable development in the rubber industry, and securing a greener future that supports sustainable living, which is in line with the targets of the global sustainable development goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 12 Responsible Consumption and Production, and SDG 15 Life on Land.', 'Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a plant-derived polymer and has been utilized for industrial, commodity, biomedical, pharmaceutical, and environmental applications.1-11 When PLLA materials are released in the environment, they are exposed to photodegradation by sunlight especially ultraviolet (UV) rays. Therefore, it is expected that the structural changes of PLLA articles caused by the UV-irradiation in the environment will affect the design of recycling process by hydrolytic/thermal degradation. In biomedical and pharmaceutical applications, UV irradiation or UV treatment can be utilized for sterilization. In the molecular level, UV-irradiation is known to cause PLLA the structural changes, such as decrease in molecular weight and formation of terminal C\uf8feC double bonds through the Norrish II mechanism and of crosslinks via radical recombination.12 Moreover, the comparison of UV-photodegradation behavior between PLLA and poly(ε-caprolactone) strongly suggested that the chemical structure between the adjacent ester groups than the density of ester group is crucial to determine the photodegradability of biodegradable polyesters.12 Although in the material level, the photodegradation of PLLA films proceeds via a bulk erosion mechanism; this indicates that UV rays penetrate the films with no significant reduction.13, 14 Furthermore, it was found that PLLA chains are photodegradable even in the crystalline regions and their photodegradability is lower than that in the amorphous regions.13, 14 The photodegradation behavior of PLLA by UV-irradiation has been intensively investigated.12-26 On the other hand, manipulating the hydrolytic degradation behavior and rate of PLLA materials is a matter of concern when it is used in environmental, biomedical, and pharmaceutical applications.27 The representative techniques utilized for controlling hydrolytic degradation behavior and rate of poly(lactic acid) (PLA)-based materials include copolymerization, crystallization, and blending with other polymers and additives.1-11 For neat PLA, altering the crystallinity is effective to manipulate the hydrolytic degradation profiles.27-32 It was found that at least in an early stage, the hydrolytic degradation rates traced by weight loss, molecular weight, and mechanical properties become higher with an increase in crystallinity. However, these techniques of copolymerization, crystallization, and blending cannot be applied in situ after the processing of materials. UV-irradiation can be applied in situ after the processing of PLLA materials. UV-irradiation lowers the molecular weight and forms the terminal C\uf8feC double bonds and crosslinks, which are respectively assumed to enhance and disturb the hydrolytic degradation of PLLA materials.12 The effects of simultaneous photodegradation by UV-irradiation and hydrolytic degradation have been studied and found that the degradation was enhanced by the simultaneous photogradation and hydrolytic degradation.20, 21 In our previous study, we found that proteinase K-catalyzed enzymatic degradation of UV-treated PLLA proceeds rapider than that of UV-nontreated PLLA in an early stage, whereas this trend is reversed in a late stage.22 Chu et al. reported the effects of γ-irradiation on the hydrolytic degradation behavior of poly(glycolide) suture and found that the hydrolytic degradation is accelerated by γ-irradiation.33 However, although the effects of UV-irradiation of PLLA on its (nonenzymatic) pure hydrolytic degradation are crucial in terms of environmental, biomedical, and pharmaceutical applications as well as designing the recycling process, they are not fully understood so far. In this study, photodegradation by UV irradiation (UV treatment) and hydrolytic degradation of PLLA were consecutively performed to elucidate the effects of UV treatment on hydrolytic degradation behavior and rate of PLLA materials. For this purpose, PLLA films with typical highly ordered structures, i.e., amorphous and crystallized PLLA films were prepared and exposed to UV-irradiation and subsequent accelerated hydrolytic degradation at 97°C.32 The hydrolytic degradation was monitored by gravimetry, gel permeation chromatography (GPC), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and the combined effects of UV treatment and crystallization on the hydrolytic degradation of PLLA were studied.', 'Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a plant-derived polymer and has been utilized for industrial, commodity, biomedical, pharmaceutical, and environmental applications.1-11 When PLLA materials are released in the environment, they are exposed to photodegradation by sunlight especially ultraviolet (UV) rays. The ester linkages in PBAT are susceptible to Norrish Type I and II photodegradation under UV exposure, with hydrolysis further accelerating degradation [29, 30]. Previous studies have established that CaCO3 content and particle size significantly influence the photo-oxidative stability of polymer matrices [31,32,33]. Consequently, surface modification of CaCO3 may not only affect interfacial compatibility and mechanical properties but may also substantially alter the aging characteristics of PBAT composites. However, the mechanistic understanding of how modification strategies influence the aging behavior of PBAT/CaCO3 films remains limited. In this work, we present a systematic investigation of KH560 and SA co-modified CaCO3 fillers for PBAT-based composite films prepared via melt blending. Through comprehensive comparison with monolayer-modified (KH560-only or SA-only) systems, we evaluated changes in hydrophobicity, mechanical properties, UV-visible light transmittance, micromorphology, and chemical structure before and after accelerated aging. Experimental details', "The mulching film is essential in crop plantations for weed control, soil temperature regulation, irrigation facilitation, and supplying nutrients and chemicals while preventing erosion [1, 2]. A recent report stated that the global annual use of plastic mulching is 4 million tons and is increasing at a rate of 5.6% annually [2]. However, the use of traditional PE plastic mulches in agriculture is unsustainable, leading to costly disposal and microplastic pollution. Biodegradable plastic mulches (BDMs) are gaining interest, but their durability remains a challenge. Developing BDM formulations with the right balance of materials and additives is crucial for sustainable agriculture. PBAT is a significant alternative for biodegradable mulch films, comprising butylene terephthalate for rigidity and butylene adipate for flexibility. PBAT/TPS-based mulch has gained considerable attention in recent years due to its biodegradability, cost-effectiveness, and potential to reduce plastic pollution in agricultural applications. However, PBAT is highly prone to photodegradation, resulting in chain breakage and polymer restructuring via Norrish I or Norrish II mechanisms [3]. Although PBAT is enzymatically hydrolysable, it shows limited biodegradability in soils [4]. To address this, the incorporation of starch or natural fibers into the PBAT matrix has been shown to improve its biodegradability, particularly in soil and marine conditions. The addition of starch not only enhances biodegradation and reduces cost, but also serves to modify PBAT's degradation behavior for more sustainable use in agricultural films [5]. Upon application, biodegradable mulch film (BDM) undergoes photodegradation and biodegradation pathways [6]. The degradation mechanisms of conventional PE and biodegradable plastics differ and are influenced by environmental factors like heat, light, microorganisms, and soil moisture. Photodegradation, initiated by weathering, results in chain scission and film fragmentation, whereas biodegradation involves microbial activity and moisture-driven breakdown. PBAT, though enzymatically degradable, exhibits limited degradation in soil. Thus, its performance can be enhanced by incorporating natural fillers and polysaccharides. Furthermore, the use of additives such as UV absorbers and stabilizers can help prolong the film's durability during field application.", 'Environmental degradation of polyolefins proceeds through two stages: abiotic oxidation, which breaks down the polymers into low-molecular-weight products, followed by biodegradation [8,16]. As being the rate-determining step, several approaches have emerged to accelerate the abiotic degradation of polyolefins by introducing vulnerable sites such as carbonyl (C=O) groups, unsaturations, or hydrolyzable linkages to the non-reactive carbon-carbon (C-C) backbone or side chains of the polymers [8,23]. A more economically expedient strategy is the use of pro-oxidant additives as they are readily applicable to existing polymer production and processing technologies [6,[16], [17], [18], [19],21]. These additives, usually based on transition metals, can catalyze the oxidation of polyolefins once they are disposed of in the natural environment. Metal carboxylates are typical among pro-oxidants, and the mobility of acids affects the degradation. The effect of iron carboxylates on the photo-oxidation of polypropylene (PP) was reported to decrease with shorter chain lengths of carboxylic acids [24]. Despite the extensive studies on the degradation of polyolefins containing biodegradation-promoting additives [6], consistent evidence of their biodegradability has not been reported. A biodegradation study on polyethylene (PE) films containing different types of pro-oxidant additives has reported that the main factor controlling biodegradability is the nature of the pro-oxidants and, to a lesser extent, that of the PE matrix [18]. Therefore, knowledge and understanding of the catalytic activity of pro-oxidants are very important for the advancement of biodegradable polyolefin development. In this work, we investigated the effects of the commercially available pro-oxidants of the oxo-biodegradable type on the photo-oxidation of polyolefin films: high-density PE (HDPE), low-density PE (LDPE), linear low-density PE (LLDPE), and isotactic PP (itPP) in comparison to their neat counterparts. The oxo-biodegradable additives have been claimed by the manufacturer (P-Life Japan Inc.) to be unequivocally proven 100% biodegradation, and their safety complies with the United States food and drug administration (FDA). These additives decompose to form free radicals upon exposure to heat or light in the presence of oxygen, facilitating the formation of macromolecular hydroperoxides to generate C=O compounds, which subsequently undergo Norrish type I and type II cleavages (Scheme 1) [12]. The resulting products have low molecular weights and are, therefore, subject to mineralization by microorganisms. The ability of transition metals to switch between two oxidation states enables the catalytic decomposition of hydroperoxides, thereby promoting auto-oxidation process. UV exposure test was employed to induce photo-oxidation. The surface morphologies of the polymers before and after UV exposure were monitored by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Infrared (IR) spectroscopy, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS and SAXS) were employed to gain insights into the catalytic degradation behaviors of polyolefin polymers, which are of crucial importance to the subsequent bio-assimilation process.', 'Carbonyl index of films with respect to natural weathering time. The area of the band at 1712 cm−1 increased significantly faster with respect to weathering time for PE/chitosan films, compared with PE films (Figure 3); as displayed by the value of CI, an increase in carbonyl groups produced due to photodegradation of the samples is evident; the values of CI for uncompatibilized and compatibilized films, at 180 days, are 37.5 and 52, respectively (Figure 3). Based solely on the provided context, the Norrish Type II mechanism in polymer photodegradation is described as:

1.  **Involves Chain Scission:** It entails chain scission of the polymer backbone ([4], [5], [13]).
2.  **Leads to Depolymerization:** This chain scission leads to depolymerization ([4], [5]).
3.  **Occurs Especially in Amorphous Regions:** The reaction is particularly significant in the amorphous regions of the polymer due to higher oxygen permeability ([4], [5]).
4.  **Requires Carbonyl Groups:** The mechanism occurs in polymers containing carbonyl (C=O) groups ([3], [7], [10], [13]). These carbonyl groups are photolabile ([7]).
5.  **Produces Vinyl Groups:** In polyethylene (PE) specifically, UV-B photodegradation via Norrish Type II causes chain scission and the formation of vinyl (CH₂=CH-) groups ([1], [2]).
6.  **Enhances Degradability:** Unlike Norrish Type I (which can lead to crosslinking and reduced degradability), Norrish Type II reaction enhances polymer degradability ([4], [5]).
reference: Norrish Type II is a photochemical intramolecular reaction where a gamma-hydrogen is abstracted by an excited carbonyl oxygen. This leads to the cleavage of the C-C bond alpha to the carbonyl group, resulting in the formation of a vinyl end group and a methyl ketone, effectively reducing the polymer's molecular weight.

Moreover, chemical modification of fillers or PLA also may affect the biodegradability of the produced bio-composites. For example, it was reported that starch films and sheets grafted with poly(methacrylic acid) and polycaprolactone only partial biodegraded in the soil burial test whereas ordinary starch film fully biodegraded [25, 26]. Similarly, the grafting of natural flax fiber with polyethylene glycol slowed down flax fiber’s biodegradability [27]. Chitin is a natural biodegradable polysaccharide polymer having hydrophobic acetyl amide groups and therefore should be compatible with hydrophobic PLA. Recently Singh et al. reported that the addition of chitin nanocrystals to the triethyl citrate compatibilized-PLA increased the tensile strength and elongation of the produced PLA/chitin nanocrystal nanocomposite [28]. Mahmoodi et al. reported that the addition of a small weight(%) of organic dye-modified-nanoclay to PLA improved the tensile strength, photo-protection capability, and moisture vapor permeability of PLA [29]. Lertphirun and Srikulkit found that the addition of hydrophobic silane-modified cellulose to PLA reduced the moisture vapor permeability of PLA [30]. However, chitin has not been considered for the reinforcing and increasing the moisture vapor barrier properties of PLA. In this work, PLA/chitin micro-particle biocomposites were successfully prepared by melt blending at 150 °C in a Brabender-type static mixer without using any compatibilizer, plasticizer or processing aid. The prepared composites were characterized by thermal differential scanning calorimetry, thermogravimetric analysis, dynamic mechanical analysis and scanning electron microscopy. To the best of our knowledge, no published literature reported the preparation of PLA/chitin microparticle biocomposites by melt blending without using any compatibilizer and the effect of chitin addition on the physicochemical characteristics of PLA.', "In industry, packaging for food or medicine is an important application of starch. Starch film, almost always as edible coatings, is stronger and more easily extended and is a barrier against oxygen and carbon dioxide than protein. However, because of its hydrophilic properties, starch is a worse barrier to moisture.19 The barrier properties of starch films are probably related to the thickness of their films and the packed structure.20 The more ordered the network in the film is, the better the barrier properties will be. However, it is believed that the hydrophobic nature,21 type, and content22 of added plasticizers affect the barrier properties of starch films. For example, sorbitol is a better water- and gas-barrier properties for starch films than GLY does.23 Hyperbranched polyesters are rich in terminal functional groups and, hence, have many superior properties,24, 25 such as a good liquidity, low viscosity, high solubility, not easily crystallized, difficult tangling, high chemical reactivity, and good weather resistance. Therefore, hyperbranched polyesters are widely used in coatings, polymer blending modification, biological materials, and drug carriers.26-28 For plasticization, the properties of hyperbranched polyesters, such as their larger molecular weights, high number of branches, and more multifunctional groups, make their compatibility with host polymers and resistance to migration better than those of linear and small plasticizers.29 Additionally, hyperbranched polyesters can be synthesized by a simple one-pot method that can be tailored by changing the recipes or procedures to meet certain requirements. As mentioned previously, plasticizers may not only promote the mechanical properties of starch but also change its barrier performance. Accordingly, we prepared a type of hyperbranched polyesters with GLY and citric acid, two popular eatable, low price additives in the food industry. After a series of structural characterizations of the hyperbranched poly(citrate glyceride)s (HBPETs),30 they were used to plasticize starch films. On the basis of the principle mentioned previously, the synthesized HBPETs were expected to modify the retrogradation and water vapor permeability (WVP) of starch films, which is the goal of our research. The blends were prepared using a twin-screw extruder where starch gelatinization, water removal, and dispersion of TPS into a PLA matrix were carried out sequentially. The plasticizers were added to starch in the first stage of the extruder to allow complete starch gelatinization. The PLA was added at mid-extruder and thoroughly mixed with the TPS. J Appl Polym Sci, 2011 Themoplastic starch (TPS) and polylactic acid (PLA) are two biobased and biodegradable polymers that are increasingly being used for the replacement of petrochemically-based polymers. PLA is an aliphatic polyester. It is often compared to PET because of its transparency, good stretchability, and low crystallization rate. It is used to fabricate biaxially oriented films, thermoformed containers, and stretch-blown bottles.1 PLA has good barrier properties to aromas but has higher permeability to carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapor.1, 2 TPS is a material obtained by destroying the crystalline structure of native starch in presence of a plasticizer (i.e., the so-called gelatinization process). In turn, the nature and concentration of this plasticizer governs, to a great extent, the rheological and mechanical properties of the TPS. Water is a strong plasticizer for starch, but for material applications, higher boiling point plasticizers are preferred because they improve the material stability and water resistance. Thermoplastic starch has low oxygen permeability and thus could potentially play an oxygen barrier role in biodegradable packaging.3, 4 Because of its hygroscopic nature however, the TPS must be blended with another polymer to produce useful materials for packaging and industrial applications. The addition of dry-starch to PLA to form composites has been investigated but generally leads to very brittle materials.5-8 The addition of starch in its thermoplastic state is more promising since it can deform under flow leading to much finer dispersions. The first reports on noncompatibilized TPS/PLA blends showed only poor and nonhomogeneous TPS dispersions and poor mechanical properties due to the lack of interfacial compatibility between the PLA and TPS.9 More finely and homogeneously dispersed PLA/TPS blends were achieved by using a compatibilization strategy that involved the use of maleic anhydride grafted PLA.10 This finding has opened the path to the biaxial stretching of compatibilized PLA/TPS blends for the production of biaxially oriented films11 and to the production of low-density foams.12', 'The production of a thermoplastic wheat flour/PLA blend by adding CA was described by Abdillahi and co-workers.184 The authors studied the effects of the addition of water and CA on the thermal and mechanical properties of the blend as well as on the barrier properties and water vapor sorption behavior. In one-step extrusion equipment, increasing the ratio of CA from 0 to 20 parts resulted in superior melt viscosity and suitable compatibilization between the TPS based on wheat starch and the PLA phase. Additional water was found to minimize the depolymerization of both starch and PLA, as well as aid CA penetration into the starch phase, inducing a decrease in specific mechanical energy. Thus, blends with the highest elongation and mechanical strength were obtained at 10 parts of water and 10 parts of CA. Morphological investigations and structural analyses showed that CA played several roles during compounding, including acting as a compatibilizer (esterification, hydrogen bonding) and a depolymerization agent as well as promoting gluten disaggregation. Multifunctional CA and water contributed to improving starch plasticization and PLA depolymerization, resulting in the formation of highly flexible materials with excellent toughness. The authors also used these blends to fabricate an injection-molded packaging film, which showed an 80% reduction in water vapor permeability and a 90% reduction in oxygen permeability with only a small content of CA. The results derived from the water sorption isotherms showed that the water vapor permeability of the film was strongly correlated with the water diffusion coefficient. This behavior was attributed to the decreased interfacial tension between the TPS matrix and the PLA phase, which improved the intermolecular interaction in the blends. Furthermore, the incorporation of CA, MA, and TA can decrease the shear viscosity of TPS and its phase sizes in the PLA matrix, which may increase the disordered state of blends (ΔS > 0) and the thermodynamic compatibility. Other research groups have also fabricated high-performance blends by adding polyacids. Our group showed that the addition of 1% TA changed the micromorphology and properties of TPS blends.185 With the incorporation of TA into TPS, the size of the dispersed particles decreased from 382 to 184 nm, and the corresponding TPS-TA particles exhibited ellipsoidal to salami-like dispersed phase structures (Fig. 13a). Therefore, the properties of poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT)/TPS-TA films, such as elongation at break, optical transmittance, and air permeability, improved significantly. The advantage of this film over conventional petroleum-based films or biodegradable blends is that it provides a renewable source for developing green packaging. In a similar study, corn starch plasticized with a small content of TA (feed ratio: 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 wt%) was investigated to explore the characteristics of thermoplastic gels (TGTPS) (Fig. 13b).186 The TGTPS samples produced by reactive extrusion had an adjustable soft-hard segment structure, which imparted a low modulus, high fluidity, and excellent flexibility. The presence of TA in the TGTPS provided compatibility with PLA and allowed uniform dispersion in the PLA matrix on the micro/nanoscale. Consequently, both a crazing phenomenon and shear yielding could be induced by an external force for energy dissipation. Further, the double folding resistance improved from 0 cycles for neat PLA to over 2000 cycles for PLA/TGTPS (20 wt%). As a result, the comprehensive performance of the blends increases, which indicates the key role of the TPS-TA.', 'The combination of PLA with TPS is an alternative to reducing the cost of PLA-based products. TPS is a hydrophilic4, 5, 7, 8 and ductile material5, 9 that is obtained from starch, which is cheap, renewable, sustainable, biodegradable, and compostable. The poor compatibility between PLA and TPS phases, resulting from their different polarities, is a major problem that brings poor mechanical and barrier properties to the final blends.4, 10, 11 Many approaches have been proposed to improve the compatibility between PLA and TPS phases. A variety of compatibilizers, for example, glycidyl methacrylate and benzoyl peroxide,4 maleic anhydride,12 polycaprolactone grafted with maleic anhydride and/or with glycidyl methacrylate2 were employed to improve the interaction between PLA and TPS phases. In some cases, the reactive blending of PLA and TPS was performed in the presence of chemical substances, which eventually played roles as conjugating agents or compatibilizers, for example, glycidyl methacrylate and benzoyl peroxide4 and epoxidized soybean oil13 due to its economical production, in which simultaneous progression of chemical reaction and extrusion took place. Nevertheless, the toxicity from the remaining of unreacted chemicals and some compatibilizers limited the utilization of the resulting blends as food contact materials. Although the addition of fibers14, 15 or inorganic additives such as clays16, 17 has been reported to facilitate the interfacial adhesion between PLA and TPS phases, the obtained composites lacked extensibility. TPS from acetylated starch has been hence blended with some plastics, including linear low-density polyethylene,25 poly(ethylene-co-vinyl alcohol),27 and PLA.8, 10 The compatibility between those plastics and TPS from acetylated starch was improved as compared with the corresponding blends of TPS from native starch, leading to enhanced elongation at break,8, 25 impact strength,8 and tensile strength.8 Until now, although few articles relevant to the blends of PLA and TPS from acetylated starch have been reported, the materials were prepared using a batch mixer (i.e., internal mixer) followed by a compression molding, and composed of TPS in the range of 10-40%.8, 10 The improvement in the mechanical properties was revealed to be due to the better compatibility between two polymer phases. However, the determination of water vapor and oxygen barrier properties and the intensive study of the interaction between PLA and TPS from starch acetate were not elucidated yet. The significance of the **autocatalytic effect** in the hydrolytic degradation of thick PLA implants lies in its role in accelerating and sustaining the degradation process through **self-amplifying mechanisms**. Key points include:

1. **Bulk Degradation Dominance**:  
   PLA degradation primarily occurs in the **bulk** rather than on the surface. Water penetrates the material, initiating chain scission and generating **low-molecular-weight oligomers** with carboxylic acid end groups. These acidic byproducts accumulate internally, lowering the local pH and catalyzing further ester bond hydrolysis, creating a **self-sustaining cycle** of degradation.

2. **Heterogeneous Degradation in Thick Implants**:  
   In thick implants, diffusion pathways for oligomers and acidic products are longer, leading to their retention within the polymer matrix. This retention intensifies the **autocatalytic environment** in the bulk, causing faster degradation in the core compared to the surface. This heterogeneity can result in abrupt structural failure due to rapid internal degradation.

3. **Impact of Crystallinity**:  
   Crystalline regions resist water penetration, slowing hydrolysis, while amorphous regions degrade more rapidly. The autocatalytic effect is amplified in amorphous domains due to higher water accessibility and accumulation of carboxylic acids, accelerating chain scission and molecular weight loss.

4. **Modulation Strategies**:  
   The autocatalytic effect can be mitigated by additives (e.g., starch, layered double hydroxides) that act as barriers to oligomer diffusion or buffer acidic byproducts. Such strategies reduce the local pH drop, decelerating hydrolysis and improving degradation predictability.

5. **Clinical Implications**:  
   Autocatalysis influences implant lifespan and structural integrity. Uncontrolled autocatalytic degradation can lead to premature mechanical failure or inflammatory responses due to acidic byproducts. Understanding this effect is critical for designing implants with tailored degradation rates and ensuring safe, gradual stress transfer to healing tissues.

In summary, the autocatalytic effect is pivotal in governing the **rate**, **homogeneity**, and **mechanical stability** of thick PLA implants during hydrolytic degradation, necessitating careful material design to balance degradation kinetics with clinical requirements.

retrieved_contexts: ['First published on 18th November 2015 PEEK-based biomaterials have great potential applications as hard tissue substitutes in bone tissue engineering. However, inherent bio-inert properties limited their clinical use. In order to improve the bioactivity, in this work, zirconium ions were implanted into the carbon fiber-reinforced PEEK (CFR-PEEK) using plasma immersion ion implantation (PIII) technology. Surface morphologies and chemical compositions of Zr-PIII treated samples were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), respectively. The results indicated that nanostructures and ZrO2 nanoparticles were formed on the surface of CFR-PEEK after Zr-PIII. Mechanical tests revealed that nanohardness, elastic modulus, and elastic resistance increased after implantation, especially for the elastic modulus with a maximum value of about 14 GPa, which is much close to that of human natural bone. In vitro cellular experiments showed that Zr-PIII treated samples enhanced the initial adhesion of rBMSCs, spreading and proliferation significantly. But commercial inorganic nucleating agents have some disadvantages such as expensive price and poor compatibility with PLA matrix, which hinders the development of important factors.27', 'In general, the crystallization process of polymers consists of two main stages: nucleation and crystal growth. However, the dispersion of hydrophilic talc in the hydrophobic PLA matrix is typically hampered by their low compatibility, which results in weak interfacial and mechanical properties.26 Therefore, coupling agents or compatibilizers is pivotal for promoting the interaction between talc and PLA.', "This work deals with the design and experimental development of formulations based on bioplastic materials optimized for the production processes of high-performance packaging products, suitable for food contact and characterized by high thermo-mechanical stability. An increase in crystallinity can be achieved in different ways, by modifying the formulation of the material using nucleating agents or through process-related strategies such as, for example, post-annealing procedures of pre-formed samples or injection molding in a heated mold. Three different crystalline structures for PLA, α, β and γ, have been identified, according to the preparation conditions. The most common form α is constituted by conventional crystallization processes, both from hot and cold conditions, or by solution techniques and it has a helical chain conformation 103.3-5 In addition to this structure, Zhang et al. highlighted the formation of a slightly different structure called α′ for PLA crystallized below 120°C.6 This so-called “distorted” form, in distinction from the pure form α to which it is similar, refers to a structure with a more open packing and less order, to which correspond lower modulus and less barrier properties. The improvement of the resilience and impact resistance of PLA aimed at reducing its typical fragile behavior is usually obtained through the dispersion of core-shell impact modifiers,26-29 the formation of blends with other polymeric phases such as elastomers30, 31 or ductile and high strength thermoplastic polymers, which circumvent the problem of migration of low molecular weight plasticizers (polymer plasticization). These can be bio-derived and/or compostable32-34 or traditional.35-38 In other cases, to improve the thermal resistance, increase the HDT and the Vicat softening point, a high crystallinity would be of crucial importance, also for the stiffening action that can also exert on the amorphous fraction. When polymeric blends are formed, the secondary phases often behave as immiscible with the PLA matrix, resulting in solid dispersions characterized by various morphologies, among which the most typical are drop-shaped,45-52 complex structures such as co-continuous structures or interconnected phase structures.53-56 As known, the characteristics of immiscibility and formation of structures in separate phases often cause deterioration of the mechanical behavior due to the formation of extensive interfaces between the different materials which do not allow an effective transfer of the applied internal stresses, and sometimes loss of the optical transparency properties. Therefore, in combination, compatibilization strategies are often used which provide for the use of block co-polymers57 or highly reactive species, such as maleate or glycidyl methacrylate groups which are very effective towards polyester matrices, in particular by reaction with the carboxylic or hydroxyl groups, activated by high processing temperatures (reactive extrusion processes). These are commonly supported, through functionalization, by acrylic58-60 or non-acrylic polymers46, 61-66 or by PLA to favor compatibilization.67, 68 These materials, belonging to reactive extrusion techniques, are also essential as process co-adjuvants as they can lower the melt flow-Index of the melt (chain extender action). In fact, they restore the molecular weight loss due to the phenomena of de-polymerization and degradation caused by thermal treatments and mechanical stress, especially if consecutive as occurs in melt processing,69 acting, at the same time, as melt-strength enhancers.70 Furthermore, these additives perform a compatibilizing action between the immiscible polymeric phases and any fillers towards which they demonstrate reactivity at the interface.71-74 On the other side, they can simultaneously determine the reduction of the crystallization rate of the PLA due to the formation of ramifications in the macromolecular structure for the type of reactivity involved during chain extension.75, 76 Another method used extensively to increase thermal stability and stem the phenomena of degradation of the material during hot processing, but also to reduce the production costs of the material, is the dispersion of inorganic mineral fillers.21, 23, 77-79 The use of micro- and nano-metric calcium minerals, such as carbonates, phosphates or sulphates,80, 81 mica or natural micro-lamellar talc82 is widely consolidated. The use of these fillers combines, in addition to reducing costs and increasing thermal stability during the process, due to the dissipative effect linked to their mineral nature, also other effects, such as increased mechanical strength due to the higher Young's modulus and possible increase of the barrier properties. This latter effect, in particular, is connected to the high density of the micro-particles of the filler with respect to the organic polymer phase and their morphology, as in the case of micro-lamellar structures, whereby they, orienting themselves under the force fields of the flow conditions generated during the manufacturing processes, can in principle lead to a composite in which the spatial arrangement of the resulting filler reproduces smectic-like structures in the material. These structures can be connected to an increased tortuosity of the permeants inside the material, therefore causing a possible decrease in permeability.83 In addition, the increase in the crystalline content of the PLA due to the effect of heterogeneous nucleation, is connected to other effects, such as: improvement of the final thermal stability of the product, in terms of increasing the temperature of thermal deflection (HDT) and the Vicat softening point. This also promotes the formation, in the surroundings of the crystalline phase, of a more rigid amorphous phase less sensitive to thermal variations.32 Furthermore, given the nucleating action, a synergistic effect on the gas barrier properties is conceivable for the greater crystalline phase content, which with its greater compactness contributes to increasing the average density of the material and therefore allows to reduce the gas permeation. In some cases, the fillers used to form these composites also perform a nucleating action for the polymeric matrix, to increase the crystallization kinetics. To increase thermal stability by exploiting the increase in crystallinity and to avoid the excessive stiffening and deterioration of the mechanical properties caused by the use of nucleating mineral fillers, other nucleation strategies are widely used, such as the use of different classes of organic nucleating agents.24 These types of nucleating agents act according to different mechanisms, mainly influencing the kinetics of the crystallization process. In any case, the formulation of the material, whatever the strategy adopted, cannot disregard the assessment of both the compostability requirements defined by the international standards (EN 13432 or ASTM D6400) and, where necessary, of the standards for application for direct food or pharmaceutical contact."]
