Based solely on the provided context, nucleating agents like talc and zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn) play the following crucial roles in accelerating the crystallization of PLA, specifically relevant to injection molding:

1.  **Acceleration of Crystallization Rate:** They dramatically decrease the crystallization half-time (t1/2) of PLA. For example:
    *   Talc at 1 wt% reduced PLA's crystallization half-time by more than an order of magnitude to less than 3 minutes [9].
    *   PPZn significantly increased the crystallization rate of PLLA compared to neat PLLA, resulting in a much shorter t1/2 [2, 11, 12].

2.  **Increased Crystallinity:** They promote the formation of a higher degree of crystallinity (Xc) in PLA. For instance:
    *   Zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn) increased the degree of crystallinity of PLLA during cold crystallization [2].
    *   A synergistic nucleating agent combining talc and D-sorbitol increased PLA crystallinity from 3.5% to 43.8% [8].

3.  **Enhancement of Thermal Stability (Heat Resistance):** The increased crystallinity directly leads to higher heat deflection temperature (HDT) and Vicat softening point, improving the thermal deformation resistance of the final molded product [1, 15]. This is critical for applications requiring dimensional stability at elevated temperatures.

4.  **Improved Productivity (Shorter Cycle Times):** The dramatically faster crystallization rate allows for significantly shorter cooling times in the injection molding cycle, leading to higher productivity [1, 9]. This is a major industrial advantage.

5.  **Refined Crystal Morphology:** They increase nucleation density and decrease spherulite size:
    *   Talc enhances spherulite morphology in PLA/PBS blends [1, 4, 5].
    *   PPZn particles influence the nucleation mechanism and crystal growth of PLLA [2].
    *   Nucleating agents like BBP result in a greater number of smaller spherulites compared to talc [6].
    *   PDLA, often used as a nucleating agent, reduces spherulite dimensions in PLLA [7, 15].

**In summary:** Nucleating agents like talc and PPZn act as heterogeneous nuclei, drastically speeding up PLA crystallization during processing (crucial for short injection molding cycle times), increasing the final crystallinity content, improving the heat resistance and dimensional stability of the molded part, and refining the crystalline structure. These effects are essential for making PLA viable for industrial injection molding applications. However, the context notes that excessive talc content (e.g., 10 wt%) can lead to embrittlement, so concentration optimization is important [9].

(100)', 'In conclusion, the benefits of employing smart polymers made from amino acids for drug administration include their stimuli-responsive behavior, controlled release capabilities, possibility for targeted distribution, biocompatibility, adaptability, and compatibility with a range of drug classes.[150] A viable platform for creating cutting-edge drug delivery systems that can increase therapeutic efficacy, enhance patient outcomes, and reduce adverse effects, amino acid-derived smart polymers are a result of these benefits. Biocompatible amphiphilic block and graft copolymers, in particular those comprising biodegradable sequences, have found over the last two decades great attention due to their potential applications as micellar drug delivery systems [1], [2], [3], [4]. Beside their biodegradability, an important feature for the biomedical applications is also represented by their responsiveness to different environmental stimuli, such as: temperature, pH, light, etc, which will trigger their colloidal properties and consequently the drug release [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Among these smart copolymers, the temperature-sensitive polymeric systems are of practical interest as this feature is an important physiological factor in the human body. Moreover, some diseases are manifested by a local temperature change. Two types of thermo-sensitive polymers were reported up to now, ones which become molecularly dispersed in aqueous media only upon heating above a certain temperature, called the upper critical solution temperature (UCST), and others undertake a reversible coil-globule transition when they are heated above a critical temperature, so-called the lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) and the poly(N-vinylcaprolactam) (PNVCL) are among the most studied thermo-sensitive polymers having a LCST, near human body temperature [10], [11]. In comparison to PNIPAM, PNVCL is characterized by a higher biocompatibility as the hydrolysis of the amide group of the NVCL units does not produce toxic low molar mass amines [11]. In fact, PNVCL is a nonionic, water-soluble polymer, with low cytotoxicity and with LCST values in the range of 32-36 °C, as a function of the concentration and molar mass [10]. Thus, these features make PNVCL-based polymers very attractive for different applications in the biomedical field.', 'First published on 28th March 2012 In this paper, a series of biodegradable and pH-sensitive hydrogels from Pluronic, poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and methylacrylic acid (MAA) polymer matrix was successfully prepared via UV-initiated free radical polymerization method. A scanning electron microscope was adopted to detect the internal microstructure of the prepared hydrogels at different pH values (pH 1.2 and pH 7.2). To investigate the pH-responsivity and hydrolytic degradation characterization of the hydrogel, detailed parameters including MAA and PCL polymers content, PEG content, BIS content and molecular weight of Pluronic have been employed in this work. The in vitro release behavior of hydrophobic 5-aminosalicylic acid drug was investigated in this paper, which indicated that this new kind of hydrogel with good pH-responsivity might have great potential applications in smart drug delivery systems, especially in colon targeting therapy. In more recent years, considerable attention has been focused on pH-sensitive hydrogels that are used as site-specific drug delivery carriers to specific regions of the gastro-intestinal tract because of their adjustable swelling rates in a mild manner.1 For that reason, these pH-sensitive hydrogels would exhibit pH sensitivity owing to the alternation of COOH/COO- upon pH changes. However, the conventional chemically cross-linked hydrogels have many limitations in morphology and properties, mechanical weakness, limited swelling to equilibrium, and slow hydrolytic degradation rate.2 In order to overcome the above drawbacks and change the biodegradation of these hydrogels, the objective of the current studies was to investigate novel biodegradable and pH-sensitive hydrogels, which have been shown to be compatible with proteins and living tissue due to their great biodegradability, biocompatibility, and smart responsivity for the potential application of drug delivery system.6,17-22', 'First published on 13th August 2019 Thermo-responsive polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) are emerging as a powerful tool in nanomedicine for the fabrication of advanced drug delivery systems. In addition to their size and biodegradation rate, phase separation of NPs upon application of a thermal stimulus provides an additional switch to control the rate of release of active components. Among the materials currently developed for biomedical applications, NPs stabilized by zwitterionic polymers are gaining increasing interest due to their high stability and ability to escape the body immune response. Yet, biodegradable zwitterionic NPs with temperature response under physiological conditions are currently not available. Here, we develop a new class of biodegradable zwitterionic NPs that exhibit UCST phase transition in the biological temperature range (T = 30-45 °C) and in physiological solution (i.e. 0.9% w/w NaCl). We design a strategy that relies on the self-assembly of block copolymers produced via reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) emulsion polymerization. These copolymers comprise a zwitterionic portion exhibiting an upper critical solution temperature (UCST) and a biodegradable hydrophobic block consisting of oligoesters functionalized with a vinyl group. This modular macromolecular architecture allows us to independently control a variety of NP properties by modifying the individual components of the copolymer. In particular, the zwitterionic block of the copolymers controls the UCST-type phase separation behavior, while the number of the oligoester repeating units governs the size of the NPs and the length of the oligoester dictates the degradation rate. After demonstrating the synthesis of highly controlled degradable NPs, we show the potential of this new class of materials in the context of drug delivery by controlling the release of a drug-mimic molecule upon temperature variations in a broad time range from few minutes to 20 hours. Among conventional stimuli, temperature is one of the most attractive switches due to the fact that temperature signals can be easily operated in vivo7,8 and that thermo-responsive materials are generally less affected by the presence of biological macromolecules and electrolytes.', '“Smart” polymers are materials that react to environment changes. Such polymers can respond to environmental alterations for example temperature, pH, specific ions, pressure, light, CO2, reducing/oxidizing agents, salts and etc. [1,2,3]. The polymers with these properties are also known as stimuli-responsive polymers or “environmentally-sensitive” materials and the potential areas of application of these polymers include molecular sensors, drug-controlled release other fields [4,5,6]. One of the most attractive “smart” polymers is poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm), because this homopolymer is thermoresponsive. The phases separate from aqueous solutions when heated through a narrow temperature range. It is investigated that this synthetic polymer tend to exhibit a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) and its molecules undergo a sharp transition from coil-to-globule in water around 32 °C temperature, changing from a hydrophilic state below this temperature to a hydrophobic state above it [7]. Above this specific temperature PNIPAAm becomes a precipitate and could be dissolved again by lowering the solution temperature [8]. Due to this phenomenon, PNIPAAm is a promising thermosensitive material as its transition temperature can be adjusted near human body temperature [9]. Meanwhile, crosslinked PNIPAAm behaves differently than linear PNIPAAm due to the polymer network formed during crosslinking [10]. Due to its structure, crosslinked PNIPAAm forms a thermosensitive hydrogel in water exhibiting the volume phase transition at approximately 32 °C. Below this temperature, the hydrogel is swollen, hydrated and hydrophilic, whereas above the LCST, the hydrogel become dehydrated and shrinks [11]. In addition, the LCST of this homopolymer can be changed during the copolymerization with hydrophilic or hydrophobic polymers. Usually, the copolymerization reaction with a hydrophobic polymer could help to decrease the LCST, meanwhile the copolymerization with a hydrophilic polymer could help to increase this temperature [12, 13]. Due to thermoresponsive properties of PNIPAAm could be suitable for biomedical applications such as controlled wound dressings, tissue engineering, and drug delivery systems [14]. However, this polymer has some disadvantages, including limited biodegradability [15, 16], low mechanical strength [17], limited drug loading capacity [15], rapid release of active compounds [18] and etc. Regarding to low biodegradability of PNIPAAm, its use in clinical practice is limited. A variety of agents and biodegradable polymers, including poly(amino acids), polysaccharides, proteins and synthetic polymers such as poly(esters), poly(caprolactone), and poly(ethylene glycol) could be perspective materials to improve the properties of PNIPAAm. Biopolymers or synthetic biodegradable compounds can modify the chemical composition of PNIPAAm to effectively increase biodegradability and biocompatibility [11]. Beyond the latter advantages, the combination with some synthetic or natural biopolymers may provide additional responsivity properties, e.g., pH, magnetic, concentration, etc., and allow for the preparation of dual-responsive smart delivery materials. The backbone of the thermoresponsive graft copolymer should be composed of relatively high molecular weight polymer [19]. Natural polysaccharides, due to their highly stability, safety, biodegradability and easily chemical and biochemical modification have received much attention in the various fields. In addition, polysaccharides being soluble in aqueous media are attractive materials for the synthesis of such thermoresponsive graft copolymers. Moreover, polysaccharides are also attractive natural alternatives to synthetic polymers due to non-toxicity, biocompatibility, etc. In the scientific literature polysaccharides such as cellulose [20], carboxymethylcellulose [21], chitosan [9, 22,23,24,25,26,27,28] carboxymethylchitosan [29], dextran [30], and sodium alginate [11, 31, 32] have been successfully used to obtain graft copolymers with thermoresponsive properties. Although, all these graft copolymers have different chemical composition, the behaviour of their aqueous solutions is similar and depends on LCST. Such graft copolymers systems could upgrade technological solutions when improved rheological properties above a given temperature are required in a wide range of biomedical applications, such as tissue engineering [33], drug delivery systems [29] or protein refolding [30].', 'Nanoparticles as carriers can be targeted into tumors passively through enhanced permeation and retention effect (EPR) due to leaky vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage in tumor tissues. In addition, their small size can avoid rapid clearance by phagocytes which lead to long systemic circulation of nanoparticles [1]. In this context, smart or stimuli-responsive polymeric drug delivery systems in which drug is delivered directly to the target site in response to an internal (e.g. pH, glucose, redox potential, and lysosomal enzymes) or external stimulus (e.g. temperature, magnetic field, ultrasound, and light) have been actively developed. In cancer therapy, the knowledge of tumor micro-environment such as vascular abnormalities, oxygenation, perfusion, pH, temperature and metabolic states allows researchers to design new therapies [3]. Rapid growth rate of tumor cells can cause a temperature increase and pH decrease i.e. slightly acidic micro-environments in extracellular (pH 6-7), endosomes (pH 5.5-6.0) and lysosomes (pH 4.5-5.0) as compared to physiological pH of 7.4 in the blood and normal tissues [3, 4]. Chitosan (CS) exhibits pH responsive property due to large number of amino groups on its chains and is useful polymeric biomaterial due to its biological properties such as biocompatibility, biodegradability and nontoxicity [5]. Poly (N- isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm) is most extensively studied thermo-sensitive polymer with lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of 32 °C, below which it is water soluble and above which it becomes water insoluble [6]. In this study, more than 40% of drug was released at physiological temperature [18]. Physicochemical properties remain the challenge in development of platinum based anticancer drug delivery systems. Oxaliplatin (OXA) is third generation platinum based antitumor drug currently used as a drug of choice for treatment of colorectal cancer [19]. Oxaliplatin contains a large carrier ligand 1,2-diaminocyclohexane in its structure and creates DNA adducts which are more cytotoxic than those of cisplatin and carboplatin and also, it has been found to be less toxic and more effective than that of cisplatin against cisplatin-resistant tumours. This necessitates the development of tumor microenvironment responsive novel “smart” drug delivery system for oxaliplatin, as the antitumor activity of OXA-loaded CS-g-PNIPAAm nanoparticles in a model has not yet been reported.', 'A series of pH-dependent thermo-sensitive hydrogels for oral insulin delivery is designed and synthesized. POEs’ structural characteristics make them inherently attractive for these applications, particularly their ability to degrade via hydrolysis into non-toxic components that are easily excreted from the body [70]. This research may provide a solution to the plastic waste problem and is expected to be deployed in various applications requiring high toughness and biodegradability.', 'The goal of the presented study was modification of PLA towards its toughening in order to obtain material suitable for food packaging. The molecular weight (Mn) of PLA significantly influences its transition from ductile to brittle behavior during degradation. Key findings from the context include:

1. **Degradation and Molecular Weight Reduction**:  
   - PLA's Mn decreases during hydrolytic degradation (e.g., in seawater or phosphate buffer), with chain scission reducing polymer chain length. For instance, PLA degraded in seawater retained 71% of its initial Mn (44,000 → 31,300) after 6 months, maintaining structural integrity, while alternating copolymers with lower Mn (52,300 → 5,500) became brittle and fragmented ([1], [10]).  
   - High Mn PLA (>100,000) degrades slowly (over years), but when Mn decreases significantly (e.g., to oligomers <1,500 Da), mechanical properties deteriorate, leading to brittleness ([10], [11]).

2. **Chain Entanglement and Brittleness**:  
   - Longer polymer chains (higher Mn) enable greater entanglement, enhancing ductility. As Mn decreases, reduced chain entanglement limits plastic deformation, promoting brittle failure. Degraded PLA with low Mn exhibits shorter chains, increased polydispersity, and oligomer formation, which disrupt structural cohesion ([10], [11]).

3. **Crystallinity and Phase Morphology**:  
   - While not directly addressed in PLA degradation, context [12] notes that shorter chains (lower Mn) in star-shaped PLA reduce crystallinity and chain folding, potentially influencing brittleness. However, linear PLA’s degradation-induced Mn reduction may similarly affect crystallinity and phase morphology, exacerbating brittleness.

4. **Critical Mn Threshold**:  
   - The transition from ductile to brittle behavior likely occurs when Mn drops below a critical value, where chain entanglements are insufficient to sustain ductile deformation. For example, crazed PLA fibers with Mn reduction from 300% stretching showed accelerated degradation and brittleness within 8 weeks ([10], [11]).

**Conclusion**: PLA transitions from ductile to brittle as Mn decreases during degradation due to reduced chain entanglement and the formation of low-Mn oligomers. Higher initial Mn delays this transition by preserving mechanical integrity, while significant Mn loss accelerates embrittlement.

1.  **Operates under milder conditions:** Lipases catalyze the hydrolysis of ester bonds under non-toxic, mild conditions (e.g., pH 4-9, temperature 20-80 °C) [1], avoiding harsh chemicals and high temperatures typically required in traditional chemical degradation approaches.
2.  **Thermostability allows high-temperature processing:** Certain lipases, like Candida antarctica Lipase B (CALB), are thermostable and can function at temperatures up to 120°C [9]. This enables their use in processes like reactive extrusion, where the polymer must be molten (e.g., PBS melts at 115°C) [9].
3.  **Increased depolymerization rate:** Lipases can significantly accelerate the depolymerization rate of polyesters, even at lower temperatures, compared to abiotic hydrolysis. Studies show lipases can increase the rate by up to 30% [5].
4.  **Potential for closed-loop recycling:** Lipase-catalyzed hydrolysis breaks down polyesters (like PCL) into monomers and/or oligomers [7, 9]. These depolymerization products can then be repolymerized to synthesize new virgin-grade polyester, enabling a closed-loop recycling route [7].
5.  **Avoids toxic solvents:** Lipase-mediated depolymerization can be performed in water or potentially in processes with low water activity (a_w) during extrusion [9], eliminating the need for toxic organic solvents (like toluene, acetonitrile, dichloromethane) used in some solvent-based chemical recycling methods [9].

In this study, enhancements in tensile stress at yield (36%), tensile modulus (16%), and thermomechanical stability were observed at the CNC percolation threshold (3 wt.% CNC). Sheets of styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) reinforced with varying levels of CNC from 0.5 to 8 wt.% (based on rubber weight) were fabricated by a solution casting process.28 The tear strength and maximum work required to tear the sheets increased at CNC loading level above 4 wt.% in the SBR latex, at which point the percolation of CNC occurred. Two CNC percolation thresholds at around 0.8 and 1.5 wt.% in poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) matrix were revealed and the mechanical and hydrolytic properties of CNC-PBS nanocomposites showed significant changes at the threshold.29 As discussed above, CNC particles in solution or latex can building a continuous rigid network through hydrogen bonds at the percolation threshold, thereby dramatically improving the performance of polymer composites.33 However, for SDCNC particles, the particle size (microscale), morphologies, and surface energy differs dramatically from CNC on a nanoscale, which are the factors influencing the threshold.19, 33-37 In addition, hydrogen-bonded SDCNC particle networks cannot be built in the melt compounding process as the networks are established during the solution casting process by the solvent drying process.38 Therefore, the effect of percolation threshold on composite performance is entirely different for SDCNC particles in a thermoplastic matrix manufactured using a melt compounding process. The insulating substrate is transformed into a conductive material through the creation of conductive paths of CNTs on top of the substrate [38, 39] following the Sigmoidal percolation process [40]. Based solely on the provided context, the percolation threshold in conductive biodegradable nanocomposites is:

1.  **Critical Volume Fraction**: The minimum concentration of conductive nanofillers required to transition an insulating biodegradable polymer matrix to a conductor by forming a continuous, connected conductive network spanning the entire composite [[1], [2], [4], [8], [9]].

2.  **Key Characteristics**:
    *   **Insulator-to-Conductor Transition**: Marks the point where electrical conductivity increases dramatically as the filler loading reaches the critical concentration [[4], [9]].
    *   **Low Thresholds in Biodegradables**: Research aims for low percolation thresholds to minimize filler content, preserving biodegradability and mechanical properties. Examples include:
        *   ~0.07 vol% MWCNTs in cellulose/MWCNT aerogel-TPU foams [[4]].
        *   0.47% for MWCNTs/PBS [[6]].
        *   0.049% for MWCNTs/PVB/PBS due to double percolation [[6]].
        *   0.11 wt% for RGO/PLA and 0.80 wt% for CNTs/PLA [[8]].
        *   3 wt% for GNP/PLA [[9]].
        *   0.3 wt% CNTs in PLLA/TPU composites achieved via stereocomplex crystallites [[13], [15]].
    *   **Sensitivity Driver**: Near the percolation threshold, small deformations cause large resistance changes, making it ideal for piezoresistive sensing applications [[4], [5], [8]].

3.  **Reduction Strategies**:
    *   **Structural Control**: Tailoring filler dispersion/distribution networks (e.g., segregated structures [[14]], conductive aerogels [[4]], double percolation in cocontinuous blends [[6], [11], [13]]).
    *   **Filler Selection**: Using high-aspect-ratio fillers like graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) [[9], [11]], carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [[8], [13]], or reduced graphene oxide (RGO) [[8]].
    *   **Processing**: Optimizing processing parameters (e.g., sonication time, centrifugal speed for inks [[3]]; mixing sequence/time for melt blending [[11], [13]]; solution casting vs. melt compounding [[1], [2]]).
    *   **Matrix Modification**: Enhancing continuity of the filler-rich phase using methods like stereocomplex formation in PLLA to alter viscosity [[13], [15]].
reference: The percolation threshold is the critical concentration of conductive fillers (e.g., graphene, carbon nanotubes) within the polymer matrix at which a continuous conductive network is formed. Below this threshold, the material is insulating; above it, electrical conductivity increases by several orders of magnitude.

PLA, while bio-based and compostable, exhibits high stiffness but low elongation at break (<10%), limiting its use in flexible packaging. PBAT, a biodegradable aliphatic-aromatic polyester, contributes high flexibility, processability, and ductility to the blend. The aromatic terephthalate groups in PBAT enhance mechanical properties, while its aliphatic adipate component promotes biodegradability. Blending PBAT with PLA improves toughness, increasing elongation at break significantly (e.g., up to 96% with compatibilizers) while maintaining stiffness. However, PLA/PBAT blends are immiscible, requiring compatibilizers (e.g., maleic anhydride, chain extenders) to mitigate phase separation and enhance interfacial adhesion. This synergy creates a material with balanced mechanical performance, processability, and biodegradability, making it suitable for sustainable packaging applications.

Biodegradable polymers derived from renewable feedstocks have garnered significant attention for their favorable environmental profiles, chiefly their ability to undergo decomposition more readily under natural conditions. For instance, polylactic acid (PLA)-based biopolymers demonstrate approximately 84% biodegradability under aerobic, humid conditions, with typical degradation occurring within 60 days [30]. Similarly, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB)-based biopolymers can achieve complete biodegradation in industrial composting environments within roughly three months. The widespread adoption of such biodegradable bioplastics holds considerable promise for mitigating the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Notably, single-use plastic bags, extensively utilized for packaging and shopping, represent a predominant component of marine litter. Replacing these with biodegradable alternatives could thus play a pivotal role in alleviating oceanic plastic pollution. IntroductionPolylactic acid in various forms (PLA) seems to be one of the most promising biopolymers with potential to become high volume plastics [1]. Another candidate broadly investigated is the first homolog of a group of polyhydroxyalkanoates, namely polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) [2]. Both PLA and PHB alone have excellent strength parameters but low toughness and are relatively brittle at room temperature, which limits their applications. Various approaches were proposed to modify these unfavorable characteristics. Physical modification by various additives belongs to the most frequent ways; from this point of view, a formation of polymer blends was approved to be effective in many cases [3].The blends of PLA and PHB have been described in the literature from various points of view. Mixtures of PLA and PHB exhibit in general higher flexibility compared to both basic components alone, but in spite of this, the maximal strain at break values are relatively low [4,5]. Regarding the blends, PLA is reported to be miscible with PHB. The effect is related to the structural parameters of PLA-PLLA [1], but the previous studies on PLA/PHB blends have shown that the miscibility of PLA with PHB strongly depends on the molecular weight of both components and PLA was found to be miscible only with low-molecular-weight PHB and immiscible with high molecular weight of commercial-grade bacterial PHB [[6], [7], [8]].Properties of PLA/PHB blends depend on the composition, the interactions between components on the phase boundaries, and the conditions of the processing. As an example, PLA/PHB blend (75:25 w/w) exhibits improved mechanical properties and higher heat distortion temperature [9]. Both tensile strength and Young's modulus decrease [10] and the decrease occurs also for the glass transition temperature with the rising amount of PHB in the mixture [11]. PHB in the mixture was reported to crystallize forming very small spherulites, which may further act as nucleating centers for PLA, so that the mixture exhibits higher crystallinity [12]. This was suggested to be a reason for the increase in impact strength (120 kJ/m2) of the mixture (PLA/PHB, 80:20) compared to neat PLA (50 kJ/m2).Another material composed of PLA and PHB (75:25) was designed for food packaging application. The mixture was prepared by melt-mixing and subsequent compression molding, exhibited improved impact resistance and improved barrier properties [9]. However, the films were still rather brittle. The addition of plasticizers results in a decrease of brittleness of the PLA/PHB blends. Suitable plasticizers should be acceptable for the intended application, e.g. food packaging and must be miscible with the polymer, stable at the processing temperatures, and biodegradable. Useful plasticizers for PLA phase comprise polyethylene glycol, citric acid esters and their mixture [12], and dibenzoate or dioctyl phthalate [9] for PHB phase.Besides detailed adjusting the mechanical properties and processing parameters of the final PLA/PHB-based biodegradable material, the changes of properties during biodegradation are of interest as well. Biodegradation of PHB proceeds faster compared to PLA probably because of the higher stability of PLA towards hydrolysis [10,[12], [13], [14]]. Due to degradation, elongation at break decreases dramatically while the tensile strength, Young's modulus, and impact strength do not change substantially at least at the beginning of the process [11].During the primary degradation phase, PLA undergoes chemical hydrolysis, which is both temperature- and humidity-dependent and probably does not involve any biological factors. As the number molecular weight Mn drops down to 10,000-20,000, microorganisms present in the soil begin to digest the low molecular weight oligomers and lactic acid. This two-stage process differs substantially from many other biodegradable polymers, which degrade by a single-step process involving a direct bacterial attack on the polymer. In natural environments such as soil or water, degradation of PLA proceeds slowly but steadily, which is convenient feature for the application of agriculture, horticulture, and geotextiles. For biodegradable applications, the preferred disposal route is composting. At composting temperature, 50-70 °C and high humidity at aerobic or thermophilic anaerobic conditions, PLA undergoes to relatively fast biological decomposition and mineralization to CO2 and water [[15], [16], [17]]. The process is fast enough to meet the requirements of all standards for biodegradable compostable plastics [18]. In most cases the biodegradation of 90% is achieved within one third up to a half of 180 days required by the standard. The degradation involves Zipp-mechanism by splitting off the fragments at the end of the polymeric chain [19].Rate of biodegradation of PHA depends on many factors related to the environment (temperature, moisture level, pH) as well as those related to the material itself (composition, crystallinity, presence of additives, surface area of the sample [20]. Generally the degradation of PHB is considered to proceed faster compared to PLA.In the scientific literature the investigation of changes of properties due to degradation is not frequent. Regarding the changes during biodegradation or composting, the molecular weight is the most often followed parameter. Changes in Mn occurring at 60 °C when compared to evolution of CO2 indicate that at the beginning no CO2 is formed for about the first 3 days while a monotonous decrease in Mn occurs from very beginning. After 3 days Mn decreases from original 70,000 down to 50,000 and the decrease is almost linear with time. After 3 days also a formation of CO2 is registered, the Mn decrease continues in a logarithmic dependence and after 12 days the average Mn is around 20% of the original value before degradation [21].Several reports showed that the crystalline part of PLA was more resistant to degradation than the amorphous part, and that the rate of degradation decreases with an increase in crystallinity [[22], [23], [24], [25]]. The crystallinity and crystallization rate of PLA blended with PHB were reported to be significantly greater than those of pure PLA [26].Various plasticizers, such as poly(ethylene glycol), glycerol triacetate (triacetine, TAC), glycerol and oligomeric lactic acid were tested to adjust PLA properties. The effect of TAC on crystallization, chain mobility, microstructure, and the thermal and mechanical properties of PLA was investigated using wide angle X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, dynamical-mechanical analysis and NMR techniques. Rather detailed investigation of the effect of presence of TAC revealed an increase in the rate of crystallization, which is directly associated with increased free volume and molecular mobility in a plasticized sample deduced from the glass transition temperature decrease determined by DSC measurements [[27], [28], [29]].The effect of plasticizers on the morphology and mechanical properties of biodegradable PLA/PHB blends was also investigated and a significant decrease of the glass transition temperatures accompanied by an increase of ductile properties were observed in PLA/PHB blends plasticized with Lapol 108 and oligomeric lactic acid plasticizers [9,30].Simultaneous effect of biodegradation and abiotic hydrolysis on physical parameters of PLA or its blends with polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (PBAT) under soil conditions was reported by Weng Y-X et al. [31]. The addition of PBAT was aimed to increase the toughness of the material [32]. In the paper rather detailed analysis is published regarding the effect of biodegradation under soil conditions on morphology of PLA mixtures with PBAT investigated by SEM, chemical composition determined by both FTIR and elemental analysis, and thermal properties measured by DSC and TGA.In this contribution we investigated several physical characteristics of PLA-based biodegradable plastics materials during early stage of degradation in compost. Three materials have been selected, namely pure PLA, PLA with addition of triacetin as a plasticizer, and the mixture of triacetine-plasticized PLA with addition of small amount (20 wt% related to the overall polymeric content) of PHB as a polymer with different rate of biodegradation. The selection and the content of PHB are based on several reports mentioned above describing the properties of the PLA/PHB blends. Changes of physical and structural properties initiated due to degradation have been monitored related to the time of composting. Based solely on the provided context, the function of compatibilizers like maleic anhydride-grafted PLA (PLA-g-MA) in starch/PLA blends is as follows:

1.  **Chemical Bridging:** PLA-g-MA acts as a compatibilizer by forming chemical bonds between the anhydride groups of PLA-g-MA and the hydroxyl groups present on the starch molecules. This chemical reaction (condensation) bridges the PLA and starch phases ([1], [3], [4], [7], [12], [13], [14]).
2.  **Improved Interfacial Adhesion:** The chemical bridging significantly enhances the adhesion at the interface between the immiscible PLA and starch phases ([1], [4], [7], [13]).
3.  **Reduced Phase Size:** This improved adhesion and bonding leads to a dramatic reduction in the size of the dispersed starch phase within the PLA matrix (e.g., from 5-30 μm down to 1-3 μm) ([3]).
4.  **Enhanced Mechanical Properties:** The key mechanical improvement observed is a remarkable increase in ductility, specifically the percentage elongation at break of the blends. For example, elongation increased from 5-20% to 100-200% with PLA-g-MA addition ([1], [3]). Improvements in tensile strength and modulus are also reported in some systems ([4], [7], [12]).
5.  **Superiority of Pre-Grafted (Two-Step) Method:** The use of PLA-g-MA that was separately prepared before blending (two-step modification) is more effective than forming it in situ during blending (one-step modification) in improving elongation ([1]).
6.  **Potential Side Effects:** The highly reactive anhydride groups in PLA-g-MA can also induce undesirable side reactions, such as chain scission of the PLA polymer via hydrolysis of its ester bonds. This side reaction can compete with the desired compatibilization reaction between PLA-g-MA and starch, lowering its efficacy ([1], [14]).
reference: Compatibilizers reduce the interfacial tension between the hydrophilic starch and hydrophobic PLA phases. The anhydride group reacts with starch hydroxyls, while the PLA chain entangles with the matrix. This strengthens interfacial adhesion, improves dispersion, and enhances the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) of the blend.

retrieved_contexts: ["Supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) foaming technology is a green, efficient, and controllable method that enables the production of low-density, high-porosity foams with tunable properties through precise control of process parameters.[21-24] By combining the excellent properties of PBST with the advantages of scCO2 foaming, the development of biodegradable foam materials holds significant theoretical and practical value. During the production of PBST microcellular foams using scCO2 technology, dimensional stability remains a critical technical challenge. Although the initial expansion ratio of PBST foams can reach up to 40, the shrinkage rate of pure PBST foams can be as high as 80%.[25] This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the slower rate of air diffusion into the foam compared to the rate at which CO2 escapes from the foam cells, resulting in the development of negative pressure within the cells. Additionally, PBST has a glass transition temperature of −29 °C, and at room temperature, the foam cell walls lack sufficient rigidity, leading to significant shrinkage under negative pressure.[26] To address the dimensional stability issue of polymer foams, researchers have explored various strategies. Among these, the use of mixed gases as blowing agents, chain extension techniques,[27, 28] and polymer blending[29, 30] have become the main approaches. For example, Xue et al[31] incorporated PBS into PBST and used a CO2 and N2 mixed gas system as the foaming agent, achieving foams with an expansion ratio of 10.6 and good dimensional stability. Le Moigne et al[32] employed scCO2-assisted single-screw extrusion to prepare PHBV/nano-clay biocomposite foams with a porosity of 40-50%. Long et al[33] studied the effect of adding PLA and epoxy chain extender ADR4368 to PBAT, producing biodegradable foams with high expansion ratios and improved foam stability. Despite the progress made in these studies, significant challenges remain in practical applications. First, while modifying PBST through chain extension or branching can alter foam morphology and reduce shrinkage, it may negatively impact the material's biodegradability.[34] Second, controlling the gas concentration in mixed gas foaming of PBST foams presents difficulties in achieving precise control.[35] Therefore, polymer blending modification remains the simplest and most practical method to enhance the foamability of PBST. Supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) foaming technology uses environmentally friendly CO2 as a blowing agent [10], and the obtained foams exhibit large cell density with small cell size [11,12], usually leading to excellent properties with safe and easily removable CO2 residues [13,14]. Various methods, including blending [35,41], cross-linking [42], chain extension [[43], [44], [45]], grafting [46,47], and adding fillers [40,48], have been developed to address these limitations.', 'In this work, we present an innovative strategy for the grafting of an antibacterial agent onto nanocellulose materials in supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2). Dense cellulose nanofibril (CNF) nanopapers were prepared and subsequently functionalized in supercritical carbon dioxide with an aminosilane, N-(6-aminohexyl)aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (AHA-P-TMS). This study offers a proof of concept for the covalent grafting of active species on nanocellulose structures and the control of aminosilane orientation using a green and controlled approach. Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) are nanoscale cellulose particles extracted from the biomass by chemical and/or mechanical treatments in the form of semicrystalline, long, and entangled fibers. They have gained tremendous interest in the search for sustainable materials. Their renewable, biodegradable, and bio-based nature provides an attractive alternative to fossil-based resources. Their isolation and characterization methods have been actively investigated and reported in many reviews. (1−3) Moreover, their commercial availability has increased interest from both the academic and industrial communities since CNFs are or could be used in many applications such as cosmetics, healthcare, electronics, (4,5) papermaking, (6,7) or the medical industry. (8−10) As far as biomedical applications are concerned, their cytocompatibility has been studied and no evidence of toxicity has been reported. (9,11,12) Jorfi and Foster (8) have discussed the advances of the use of nanocellulose for medical implants, tissue engineering, wound healing, and drug delivery. Specifically, the major advantages of cellulose, such as good mechanical properties, versatility, biocompatibility, and renewability, can be harnessed for the design of sustainable and bio-based wound dressing materials. However, cellulose does not exhibit intrinsic antimicrobial properties. Strong research efforts were therefore dedicated to the functionalization of nanocellulose to confer new antibacterial and antifungal activities to cellulose-based materials. Impregnation of antimicrobial agents can be performed using fast and simple procedures, as illustrated in a previous study with the impregnation of thymol. (13) However, strategies based on noncovalently bound drugs suffer from some limitations such as the possible release of the drug in the environment and the short lifespan of the material. The activity must be long-term lasting and contact activity, the covalent bonding of antimicrobial agents onto the CNFs, should be favored. For this purpose, antimicrobial properties can be added to the nanocellulose particles through chemical grafting. The biodegradation of photo-degradable polyethylene begins at molecular weight 40,000 Daltons, and it was concluded that photo-initiated peroxidation is the rate determining step in the biodegradation of polyolefins in sunlight.', 'Scheme of the oxo-biodegradation process, showing the abiotic and biotic steps The use of pro-oxidant additives, however, requires addressing an important issue: the formation of micro- and nanoplastics. Although there is a large amount of research, there is considerable evidence on the consequences of exposure to micro- and nanoplastics, including for human health, such as inflammation, genotoxicity, and oxidative stress [35,36,37]. Respirometry chambers with soil were used and CO2 emissions were quantified to assess the rate of aerobic degradation.', 'Synthetic polymeric materials have been widely used because of low density, good processability, and low cost etc. However, the biodegradability is considerably less, and the materials easily accumulate in environment. The PEO was photo-catalytically degraded by the TiO2, and then acid and aldehyde compounds were produced. Respirometric biodegradation test must be a powerful tool for studying the OCPC effect.', 'Benzoin favored the degradation of PP exposed to natural weathering, mainly by photooxidation, caused by the incidence of sunlight containing UVA and UVB radiation. Based solely on the provided context, the differences between hydro-biodegradation and oxo-biodegradation are:

1.  **Chemical Origin & Nature:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Initiated by water and involves materials derived from renewable resources (natural occurring materials) such as starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids, or aliphatic polyesters. These are bio-based polymers [2, 5].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** Involves petroleum-derived (synthetic) polymers like polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), polystyrene (PS). These are made biodegradable by adding pro-oxidant additives (oxo-prodegradants), typically metal complexes (e.g., Mn, Fe, Co stearates) or other chemical additives [2, 3, 8, 9, 12, 13].

2.  **Degradation Mechanism:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Degradation occurs primarily through hydrolysis (chain cleavage initiated by water) in an aqueous environment, followed by bioassimilation by microorganisms. This process is rapid for materials like starch, cellulose, and aliphatic polyesters [4, 5].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** Degradation is a two-stage process:
        1.  *Abiotic Oxidation:* The polymer undergoes oxidative chain scission initiated by light (photooxidation), heat (thermo-oxidation), or oxygen catalyzed by pro-oxidant additives. This produces low molecular weight oxidized products like carboxylic acids, alcohols, ketones, and aldehydes [6, 8, 9, 12, 13].
        2.  *Biotic Oxidation (Bioassimilation):* Microorganisms metabolize the low molecular weight oxidation products generated in the abiotic stage, producing biomass, carbon dioxide (CO₂), and water (H₂O) [4, 8, 12].

3.  **Rate:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Degrades more rapidly than oxo-biodegradation, especially under optimal conditions [4, 5].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** Is a slower process compared to hydro-biodegradation, even at optimal temperatures, and cannot fulfill criteria requiring rapid mineralization [4, 5]. The initial abiotic oxidation step (e.g., photo-initiated peroxidation) is often the rate-determining step [8].

4.  **Output:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Releases methane (CH₄) as a byproduct under anaerobic decomposition conditions [3].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** The microbial action results in the production of biomass and carbon dioxide (CO₂), which transforms into humus [4, 5].

5.  **Typical Materials:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Starch-based polymers, cellulose esters, poly(lactic acid) (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL) [2, 5].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** Polyolefins (PP, PE, PS) modified with pro-oxidant additives [2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13].

6.  **Applications/Considerations:**
    *   **Hydro-biodegradation:** Suitable for composting applications and use as soil amendments due to rapid degradation [3].
    *   **Oxo-biodegradation:** Designed to render otherwise persistent synthetic polymers biodegradable, but faces challenges like opacity hindering photo-oxidation in composites [6] and the potential formation of micro/nanoplastics during the fragmentation stage [9]. Standard biodegradation tests like ASTM D 5988-18 are used to assess mineralization rates [14].

1.  **High Crystallinity:** PHB has a "high degree of crystallinity" ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [7], [12], [15]). This inherently high crystallinity is directly linked to its brittleness and "low elongation at break" ([1], [2], [7], [12]).
2.  **Secondary Crystallization:** Upon storage at ambient temperature, PHB undergoes "progressive embrittlement due to additional crystallization occurring at ambient temperature" ([2], [3]). This "gradual increase in crystallinity" further increases brittleness ([2]).
3.  **Constrained Amorphous Regions (Rigid Amorphous Fraction - RAF):** The growth of secondary crystals creates "constrained amorphous regions located in proximity of the crystals" ([2]). These constrained regions form the "rigid amorphous fraction (RAF)" ([2]). The formation of RAF contributes to "further progressive PHB embrittlement" ([2]).
4.  **Large Spherulites:** The brittleness is also caused by the "large size of crystalline spherulites (diameter > 200 μm)" ([4]). These large spherulites create structural weaknesses.
5.  **Overall Effect:** The combination of high inherent crystallinity, secondary crystallization increasing crystallinity over time, the formation of RAF, and the large spherulite size results in the "stiffness-toughness imbalance" and "brittleness" that limits PHB's applications ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [7], [8], [12], [13], [15]).
reference: PHB forms large, spherulitic crystals with a high degree of crystallinity (50–80%). These large spherulites often contain inter-spherulitic cracks and amorphous regions that are constrained by the rigid crystals. This morphology, combined with a Tg near 0°C (limiting chain mobility), results in high stiffness but very low elongation at break and high brittleness.

user_input: What are 'Triboelectric Nanogenerators' (TENGs) and why are biodegradable polymers suitable for them?
retrieved_contexts: ['First published on 9th November 2020 Cellulose is the most earth-abundant natural polymer resource, which with combined eco-friendly and extraordinary sustainable properties such as renewability, biodegradability, low cost and excellent biocompatibility has been widely used by humans for thousands of years. In the past few years, many novel cellulosic materials and their unique applications have been developed including the recent research focus on energy harvesting. The high crystallization and plentiful polar hydroxyl groups endow cellulose with a large number of dipoles and strong electron donating capacity, resulting in a promising potential of piezoelectric and triboelectric effects. However, there is no review about cellulose-based nanogenerators until now. In this paper, the most recent developments of designing, modification, processing and integration of cellulose-based piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs), triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) and hybrid piezo/triboelectric nanogenerators (PTENGs) for energy harvesting and other applications are reviewed in detail. For cellulose-based PENGs, representative basic piezoelectric cellulose and recent research on PENG devices are discussed. For cellulose-based TENGs, several effective strategies including rough modification of contact surface, addition of electronic functional fillers and chemical modification for improving the output performance are further summarized. Meanwhile, the latest cellulose-based hybrid PTENG is also introduced from the fundamental design to the investigations on enhanced strategies. The opportunities and challenges of these cellulose-based nanogenerator devices are put forward in the final part, which could enable this up-to-date and state-of-the-art review to be an effective guidance for the future research on cellulose-based nanogenerators in energy harvesting.', 'Inspired by the desire to solve the energy-related issues in remote sensing applications, internet of things, wireless autonomous devices, and self-powered portable electronic devices, triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have been highly promoted. However, for use in the specified applications, especially in wearable and biomedical devices, environmental-friendly materials are required. Herein, an eco-friendly pectin polymer is used as a positive triboelectric material to fabricate a TENG with excellent output performance. Working in conjunction with a polyimide, the polyimide and microarchitected pectin (MA@pectin) polymer film-based TENG (PP-TENG) generated open circuit voltage (VOC), short circuit current (ISC), and charge density (QSC) of ∼300 V, 14 μA, and 70 μC cm−2, respectively, exhibiting remarkable enhancement compared to the TENG based on polyimide/pristine pectin polymer (VOC, ISC, and QSC of 170 V, 7.6 μA, and 47 μC cm−2, respectively) under similar operating conditions. The output performance of the PP-TENG is particularly reliant on the pectin concentration, indicating an optimum concentration of 9 wt%. The improved performance of the PP-TENG was systematically analyzed and explained in terms of pectin concentration, dielectric constant, and surface roughness. Furthermore, the PP-TENG can power portable electronic devices and light-emitting diodes to prove the capability of the TENG in practical applications. The fabricated PP-TENG is anticipated to be a sustainable energy harvester via a low-cost and facile approach. The choice of the active material plays a significant role in increasing the electrical performance of the TENGs. Typically, the materials utilized in the TENG charge generation layers are polydimethylsiloxane, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), polyamide, and other synthetic polymers.4,7-11 However, these materials are non-biodegradable and non-renewable, which restricts further advancement of environmental-friendly and cost-effective TENGs.12 Developing abundant, renewable, and eco-friendly materials for TENG manufacturing is one of the ongoing challenges. Recently, a few reports are available on fully biodegradable TENGs using silk fibroins, cellulose, sodium alginate, aloe vera, rice sheets, etc.12-14 In present, the usable positive triboelectric materials are still limited and there is a need to explore efficient positive triboelectric materials with an environmental-friendly nature, especially in easy and available manufacturing processes. On the other hand, existing positive triboelectric materials are mostly non-environmental-friendly, require complex fabrication, and are toxic due to the chemicals used in the preparation process such as nylon, butylated melamine-formaldehyde, etc.15,16 Therefore, investigating triboelectric materials with high performance is still a challenging task for the development of eco-friendly TENGs. Meanwhile, polysaccharides are biopolymers consisting of monosaccharides linked through glycoside bonds. They are important biological macromolecules in nature and are available mainly in plants, microorganisms, fungi, and seaweeds.12,17 In recent years, environmental-friendly and biodegradable triboelectric materials have been developed. The bio-TENGs have huge potential for energy harvesting applications and they can be used in wearable and implantable devices. Robert Ccorahua et al. reported a bio-TENG based on starch polymer electrolyte prepared from potato starch and glycerol to fabricate a dielectric biopolymer which was successfully used as a triboelectric positive material.18 Zhiqing Bai et al. successfully demonstrated a cellulose acetate-based porous nanocomposite positive triboelectric material and it was used in energy harvesting as well as motion-sensing applications.19 Nannan Wang et al. demonstrated a starch biofilm-based high-performance TENG.20 These investigations inspired us to fabricate an eco-friendly triboelectric polymer film with biodegradability. It is widely known that in cellulose-derived materials, pectin, also known as pectin polysaccharides, is rich in galacturonic acid and is soluble in water. The primary source of pectin is mainly extracted from fruits such as apples, oranges, lemons, and limes. Citrus fruits contain 0.5-3.5% pectin, which is mainly present in the peel portion of the fruit.21,22 Moreover, pectin-derived materials are now being examined and tested for controlled drug delivery because of their non-toxic nature and biodegradable properties.23-25 Furthermore, pectin polymer made from bio-based pectin powder and glycerol is an attractive feasible material with proven biodegradability and nontoxicity, and has been extensively used in biomedical engineering applications.26 Thus, encouraging high-performance environmental-friendly materials in TENGs can be employed as self-powered sources for electronic devices because of their improved properties. Moreover, biodegradable materials are a better choice than plastics and they can be easily metabolized.27-29 Producing pectin is environmental-friendly and it is abundantly available in nature; manufacturing pectin polymer film for TENGs is also inexpensive and facile. So, we chose a pectin source for producing a triboelectric polymer which could be used as a positive triboelectric material for energy harvesting applications. It is desirable to employ an eco-friendly pectin to fabricate TENGs. In this work, we developed an eco-friendly biodegradable pectin polymer-based TENG in the vertical separation working mode. Pectin polymer film was used as the positive triboelectric layer and polyimide as the negative triboelectric material. The structure, morphology, and dielectric constant of the polymers were studied systematically. The output performance was tested for the TENGs using different triboelectric materials and optimized with a polyimide layer to achieve maximum output. The polyimide and microarchitected pectin (MA@pectin) polymer film-based TENG (PP-TENG) delivered a better output performance. Finally, the PP-TENG was employed in practical applications to power portable electronic devices and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Our investigation on the pectin triboelectric layers will be useful for research on eco-friendly triboelectric materials for energy harvesting applications.', 'Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are regarded as a promising technology for energy conversion due to their light weight, easy integration, simple structure, and capability to harvest low-frequency energy from nature. (1−3) Among them, the selection of triboelectric materials is a key factor in determining the long-term use of TENGs. (4) Common triboelectric materials including polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), polystyrene (PS), and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) have favorable flexibility and strong hydrophobicity. (5−8) However, their inherent drawbacks, such as low dielectric constant, nonrenewability, and nondegradability, limit the further development of environmentally friendly TENGs. (9,10) Cellulose is the most abundant natural organic compound in nature. (11,12) The excellent biocompatibility of cellulose combined with its tunable surface chemical modification endows it with great potential for application in the field of TENGs. (13−15) Furthermore, its superior air permeability and flexibility provide it significant advantages for use in flexible wearable electronic devices. (8,16) However, natural cellulose as a triboelectric material still confronts numerous issues. (17,18) The surface of cellulose is enriched with a large number of hydroxyl groups, which combine with water molecules in the form of hydrogen bonds and accumulate on the cellulosic surface, augmenting the hygroscopicity of the cellulosic material and leading to a decline in its mechanical properties. (19−21) Moreover, electrostatic shielding is also generated, hindering the transmission of charges and circumscribing its application in flexible wearable, self-powered sensing fields and harsh environments. To enhance the output stability of cellulose-based TENGs in high-humidity environments, researchers customarily adopt encapsulation strategies to enhance the ability of cellulose to resist environmental interference. (22,23) However, traditional encapsulation materials are adverse to charge migration and severely impede the electrical signal output of TENGs. (20) Inspired by bionic structures, constructing micro/nanostructures and introducing low-surface-energy materials are also effective methods to achieve a superhydrophobic surface of cellulose. (24) By depositing the methylcellulose suspension into a sandpaper mold and capitalizing on the interaction of van der Waals force and hydrogen bonds, the methylcellulose suspension self-assembles to form a micro-peak structure, thus preparing a surface with excellent hydrophobicity and moisture resistance. (25) In addition, chemical modification and doping of hydrophobic nanoparticles can also enhance the superhydrophobic properties of cellulose. (26−28) For instance, when methyltrimethoxysilane and hexadecyltrimethoxysilane are used as hydrophobic modification reagents, silanols are formed through hydrolysis and then covalently cross-linked with cellulose nanofibers (CNF) and silica particles. The introduction of the electron-donating group (-CH3) significantly improves the output performance of TENGs. (29) Furthermore, spraying 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyltriethoxysilane onto the surface of the charge storage layer prepared from cellulose nanocrystals (CNC)and MXene can also reduce the surface free energy of the material, thus obtaining a triboelectric material CMF with both superhydrophobic and sensing capabilities (CA = 162 ± 2.5°). (30,31) Nonetheless, these methods still have some drawbacks, such as high cost, relatively complicated preparation processes, and difficulty in large-scale production. Additionally, many studies have focused more on solving the charge dissipation caused by cellulose moisture absorption, but the problem of mechanical property decline caused by it has not been considered and solved. This greatly limits the long-term use of cellulose as a wearable electronic material. Therefore, to address the aforementioned issues, this paper adopts a straightforward ″minimally invasive intervention″ strategy. While damage to the crystalline regions of cellulose is minimized as much as possible, transition metal ions Mx+ (Fe3+/Al3+), characterized by small ionic radii and high charge densities, are introduced into the amorphous regions of cellulose. It facilitates the formation of coordination bonds that are stronger than hydrogen bonds, restricts the free rotation of hydroxyl groups, decelerates the wetting rate of the cellulosic surface, and improves the mechanical properties of cellulose. Furthermore, the coordination with metal ions enhances the electron cloud density of cellulose and elevates its dipole moment (from 2.52 to 3.24 and 5.76 D), significantly increasing the open-circuit voltage of the Mx+-CNF films. Stable output can still be attained even at 90% RH. In this study, by harnessing the coordination effect between metal ions and the hydroxyl groups in the amorphous region, the problems of a reduction in the charge density and mechanical properties caused by moisture absorption of cellulose molecules have been simultaneously resolved. The Mx+-CNF films, utilized as triboelectric materials, are fabricated into self-powered pressure sensors for energy harvesting and self-powered sensing in challenging environments such as high-humidity ones.', "The triboelectric effect refers to the phenomenon where, when two different materials come into contact and rub against each other, equal amounts of opposite charges are generated on their surfaces. This further induces a potential difference on the upper and lower electrodes of the materials, and changes in physical quantities are sensed by detecting changes in this potential difference. Based on this mechanism, triboelectric sensors and triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have been developed [83]. The difference is that the former (triboelectric sensors) primarily focuses on using the potential difference generated by the triboelectrification effect for signal perception and detection, with sensing as its core function. In contrast, the latter (TENGs) emphasizes more on the efficient conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy. Beyond the sensing function, it places greater emphasis on energy harvesting and conversion to provide energy support for other electronic devices [148]. Many natural materials can generate charges when in contact with electron-complementary counter electrodes. Therefore, researchers have focused on developing triboelectric sensing devices based on natural materials. Skin compatibility is a non-negligible issue for wearable flexible sensing. Poor compatibility can lead to mechanical mismatch between the sensor and human tissues or robots, making it difficult to form stable interface connections and thus reducing sensing sensitivity and accuracy. Inspired by the natural biphasic structure of human subcutaneous tissue, Du et al. [171] developed an ion-electronic triboelectric gel based on cellulose. A competitive hydrogen bond system was constructed using solvent-nonsolvent interactions to trigger phase separation (Figure 13g). The resulting alternating hard-soft phase-locked structure endows the ion-electronic triboelectric gel with human skin-compatible Young's modulus (6.8-281.9 kPa), high stretchability (880%), and self-adhesiveness (peel strength >70 N·m−1). The flexible electronic skin prepared based on this gel has excellent stretchability and good conformal contact with the human body (Figure 13h). A stretchable single-electrode triboelectric nanogenerator was composed using the gel as the triboelectric layer and conductive silver paste as the electrode layer (Figure 13i). It can realize self-powered sensing of tactile signals through the coupling effect of contact electrification and electrostatic induction, and can withstand transient high stress. After enduring an instantaneous weight of up to 1.58 tons, its triboelectric output remains stable (Figure 13j). This innovative strategy based on the gel provides new ideas for the design of electronic skin, tactile sensors, and other fields. For on-demand adjustable adhesion performance, Zhang et al. [172] proposed a cellulose nanofiber-mediated dynamic synergistic strategy to construct a supramolecular hydrogel with both reversible strong adhesiveness and easily photodissociable properties. The coordination between the cellulose nanofiber-reinforced network and iron ions-polymer chains endows the supramolecular network with dynamic reconstruction ability and enables the regulation of hydrogel adhesion behavior. Based on this, a sticky and detachable triboelectric nanogenerator was developed, which can realize real-time collection of self-powered monitoring data and wireless transmission of whole-body motion signals. This opens up new possibilities for diverse applications in fields such as electronic skin and smart devices.
