Traditional hydrogels tend to freeze and lose their performance in low-temperature environments, which limits their application scope.", 'Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) represent a promising solution to mounting environmental concerns associated with battery disposal amid the escalating demand for portable electronics. However, prevailing TENG fabrication predominantly relies on nonbiodegradable, nonbiocompatible, and synthetic materials, posing a grave ecological threat. To mitigate this, there is a pressing need to develop eco-friendly and green TENGs leveraging sustainable, naturally occurring materials. This study pioneers the use of split black gram (SBG) as a tribo-positive material for TENGs. SBG’s effectiveness as a tribo-positive material stems from its abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups, as confirmed by FTIR analysis, facilitating electron donation during the triboelectric process. SBG offers compelling advantages, including widespread availability, cost-effectiveness, biodegradability, and hydrophobic and adhesive properties due to its richness in starch and protein, positioning it as an optimal choice for eco-conscious TENG manufacturing. The fabrication process of an SBG-TENG is not only economical and facile but also solvent-free, requiring no specialized tools. Demonstrating commendable performance, the SBG-TENG achieves a maximum power density of 15.36 μW/cm2 at 1 MΩ, with an open circuit voltage of 84 V and short circuit current of 28 μA, comparable to recent studies. In practical applications, the SBG-TENG seamlessly integrates with LEDs and portable electronic devices via a full bridge rectifier, successfully powering them postcapacitor charging. Moreover, an autonomous lighting system is developed by embedding the SBG-TENG in a foot mat, enabling wireless light control through human stepping on the mat, introducing power-saving functionality for residential and office environments. In essence, the introduction of the SBG-TENG not only delivers cost-effectiveness but also minimizes the environmental impact by harnessing sustainable energy from food sources. To ensure a sustainable green future, it is necessary to provide eco-friendly power to the rapidly increasing portable electronics market, which is projected to grow from USD 750 billion in 2023 to USD 810 billion by 2030, (1) as shown in Figure 1a. According to estimates, the global battery demand for consumer electronics is increasing rapidly and will reach 130 gigawatt-hours (GWh) by 2030, (2) as projected in Figure 1b. According to industry analysts, by 2030, global Li-ion battery waste will be 2 million metric tons per year. (3) These used batteries contain useful metals and materials that can be recycled, but due to various reasons, the recycling rates in the USA and the European Union are less than 5%. (3) Due to such low recycling rates, the majority of these used batteries and related metal and chemical wastes are ending up in the landfills, which are posing a threat to the life on earth and environment. (4,5)', 'Self-powered biopolymers-based hydrogel sensors that take advantage of the triboelectric effects have attracted increasing attention in wearable applications, (39,61−64) such as artificial skin, because they are capable of obtaining energy from circumambient surroundings and operating without an external power source. The triboelectric effect is the process in which two different materials acquire electrostatic charges upon contact due to friction. In contrast to piezoelectric nanogenerators to generate electricity by forming a dipole under mechanical deformation, (62) triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) that can tansduce mechanical energy into electrical energy based on the coupling between electrostatic induction and triboelectric effect are a more effective technology to collect ambient energy. The biopolymers-based hydrogel triboelectric nanogenerators enable the integration of ultrathin devices on the flexible textile or skin for wearable applications. Wearable hydrogel sensors mainly use two modes: single-electrode mode and vertical contact-separation mode, as shown in Figure 4a and b. For instance, Guan et al. (63) produced an environmentally friendly hydrogel-based self-healing and stretchable TENG (HS-TENG) (Figure 4d,e), which was achieved by incorporating photothermic-active polydopamine particle (PDAP) and multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT), and water-induced dynamic borate bond into poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/agarose hydrogel (Figure 4c). The HS-TENG was constructed to operate at the single-electrode mode (Figure 4a), which is more conducive to its practical applications. The rectified electricity could power commercial LEDs continuously by tapping the HS-TENG upon different mechanical deformations (Figure 4f,g). By harvesting mechanical energy from bodily motions, the HS-TENG was used as a soft self-powered energy equipment to sustainably supply electrical power for commercial LEDs and an electronic watch (Figure 4h). These outstanding features enabled the device to serve as a wearable energy sensor that monitors bodily movements in real-time. On the other hand, to fabricate a flexible, environment-friendly, and multifunctional self-powered sensor, fish gelatin (FG) film and poly(tetrafluoroethylene)/poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PTFE/PDMS) were used as the friction pairs to construct a typical contact-separation TENG (Figure 4b) for capturing mechanical energy and self-powered sensing of bodily biophysical and biochemical signals. (64) The open-circuit voltage (Voc), short-circuit current (Isc), and output power density of the obtained FG based TENG (FG-TENG) (Figure 4j) reached 130 V, 0.35 μA, and 45.8 μW cm-2, respectively. This was due to the strong electron-donating capability of the rough FG film (Figure 4i) in the triboelectric process. The FG-TENG could be used to charge a commercial capacitor for lighting 50 LEDs and driving an electronic calculator and a watch directly (Figure 4k). Additionally, the FG-TENG could function as a self-powered sensor fixed on bodily diverse positions to capture biochemical and biophysical signals in real time such as gentle fingers contact, joint motions, and breathing (Figure 4l). Importantly, a foldable and bag-mountable TENG fabricated through adopting the Miura folding could act as a self-powered sensor to detect bodily motions (walking and running) (Figure 4m). Polysaccharides consist of repeated units of monosaccharaides through different kinds of O-glycosidic linkage, representing a broad class of abundant and reproducible biopolymers that are biocompatible and biodegradable. (65) Polysaccharide and its derivatives possess distinctive properties such as hydrophilicity, mechanical stability, and tunable functionality. (67,68) Cellulose and chitosan/chitin are representative polysaccharides, and hydrogel networks obtained from these nature polymers exhibit high water-retaining capacity, renewability, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and nontoxicity. (65−71) Polysaccharide-based conductive hydrogels (CHs) can be constructed by introducing electronic or ionic conductors into the polysaccharide-based hydrogel substrate. (40,72) Electronic conductors contain three major type: metallic nanoparticles/nanowires (e.g., Ag and Cu), carbon nanomaterials (e.g., carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and reduced graphene oxide (RGO)), and conductive polymers (e.g., polyaniline (PANI) and polypyrrole (PPy)). Meanwhile, materials that can generate free ions in water mainly contain three categories: alkalis (e.g., NaOH), metallic salts (e.g., NaCl, KCl, LiCl, FeCl3, and CaCl2), and ionic liquids (e.g., benzyltrimethylammonium hydroxide (BzMe3NOH)). (72) Thus, polysaccharide-based conductive hydrogels (PCHs) are roughly classified into electronic conductive and ionic conductive hydrogels. In this section, some typical polysaccharide-based hydrogel sensors are summarized. Cellulose-based conductive hydrogels have been developed as robust platforms for sensor-related applications because of their good biocompatibility and biodegradability, renewability, and attractive and tailorable physiochemical properties (e.g., superior flexibility, tunable mechanical and electrical properties). (67−70) In this section, some typical wearable sensors based on cellulose-based conductive hydrogels are summarized including material and structural designs as well as properties to achieve high-performance wearable sensors including strain, pressure, temperature, and multifunctional sensors. (42,58,73−80,90−94,101,102,106)', 'Among biobased polymers, cellulose is the second most prevalent organic fuel after coal among organic compounds and is a relatively plentiful natural polymer. Cellulose is thought to be the most abundant biopolymer on earth, extracted directly from various natural resources, including wood pulp, cotton, or microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae. Cellulose fibers extracted from natural resources are categorized into cellulose nanocrystals (CNC) and cellulose nanofibers (CNF), collectively known as nanocellulose (NC). The NC offers prominent functional advantages such as easy chemical modifications, outstanding mechanical strength, low coefficient of thermal expansion, and high transparency, facilitating the fabrication of environment-friendly structures. (17−20) Therefore, much focus has been on fabricating cellulose-based TENGs since they are biodegradable and can meet net-zero emissions. Many research articles reported cellulose-based TENGs, which have merits in renewability, biodegradability, low cost, and biocompatibility. (21,22) However, it has been reported that pure cellulose, compared to typical synthetic polymers, has weak surface/friction polarity, preventing it from producing the requisite triboelectric performances. (23) Thus, researchers have altered surface morphologies of triboelectric materials through micro/nanopatterning, imprinting lithography, spin coating, electrospinning, and etching to improve charge production of TENGs through electrostatic induction and contact electrification. (24−29) All of these surface modification techniques effectively improved the triboelectric output performances of cellulose-based TENGs. Besides the improved triboelectric output performance of cellulose-based TENGs, the surface modification techniques increased the production cost and made the fabrication process more complex. Thus, exploring an economical way to fabricate environmentally friendly TENGs with high triboelectric performance is desirable. In this regard, 3D printing is a strong contender due to its economic, customizable, affordable, quick, efficient, robust, precise, and sustainable advantages. (30) 3D printing has shown remarkable potential in the creation of intricate TENG devices. Researchers have primarily used digital light processing and fused deposition modeling for TENG fabrication due to their low cost, rapid formation, and simplicity in manufacturing complicated designs. Since the first 3D-printed (3DP) TENG device was reported, (31) numerous research works have been reported on fabricating TENGs using 3DP technologies. (32) The 3DP structures significantly enhance the contact area, mechanical resilience, surface roughness, flexibility, reliability, and corresponding electrical properties. (33) Concerning the 3D printing of NC for TENGs, there is only one research article on printing NC where the printed samples were freeze-dried to form an aerogel and then further processed for TENGs applications. (34) However, to the best of our knowledge, no 3D printing of NC flexible films has been applied for TENGs. The 3D-printing method of NC flexible films is a more scalable and efficient approach in comparison to the solution casting method for TENG applications.', 'Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have emerged as a promising technology for harvesting mechanical energy from the ambient environment. However, developing tribopositive materials with strong piezoelectric effects and high electron-donating ability still remains a challenge. Herein, poly(ethylene glycol) monomethyl ether (mPEG) to soft poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is adopted, then PLA/mPEG nanofibers are fabricated under electrospinning and used as the tribopositive material for fabricating robust power density TENGs. The crystallinity and dynamic mechanical properties of PLA/mPEG nanofibers are investigated. The results revealed that the incorporation of mPEG provided an effective approach to elevate the electron-donating ability and charge transfer efficiency in PLA. The PLA/mPEG-based TENGs achieved a high open-circuit voltage of 342.8 V, a short-circuit current of 38.5 µA, and a maximum power density of 116.21 W m−2 over a 2 cm2 contact area at an external load of 106 Ω, respectively. Strikingly, excellent stability and durability are demonstrated after continuous cycles up to 104 cycles. Noteworthy, the TENGs are explored for self-powered sensing applications, with seven TENG units integrated to act as self-powered sensors playing music through buzzers when pressed by fingers. Eventually, this work provides new insights into tuning the structures and properties of electrospun polymers to reinforce the TENG output and self-powered systems. With the rapid advancement of flexible electronics in the fields of intelligence and portability, the development and utilization of sustainable and high-performance power supplies have become hot research topics.[1-4] As one of the novel energy harvesting devices, triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are capable of converting mechanical energy from the ambient environment to electricity and have become one of the ideal methods to realize self-powered and portable electronics with the advantages of flexibility, portability, and miniaturization.[5, 6] The electrical output performance of the TENGs primarily arises from charge transfer between tribopositive and tribonegative materials during contact and separation.[7-9] As the two friction materials come into contact, the difference in their triboelectric polarity affects the buildup of effective charges on the surfaces.[10-13] Therefore, improving the electron-donating/accepting ability and surface charge density of friction materials is critical for the electrical outputs of triboelectric nanogenerators.', 'Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have drawn much interest in self-powered sensors or wearable electronics, particularly those based on nanocellulose (NC) films fabricated by manual casting. Herein, we introduce the 3D-printing technique to directly 3D-print (3DP) NC suspension on polycarbonate substrates, followed by cleanroom drying (relative humidity: 45%; temperature 25 °C). The 3DP NC films show high flexibility, transparency, a tensile strength of 139.92 ± 5.3 MPa, a Young’s modulus of 5.74 ± 0.32 GPa, and a strain at break of 6.13 ± 0.15%, much higher than manually cast NC films (tensile strength: 66.29 ± 8.12 MPa; Young’s modulus: 4.02 ± 0.11 GPa; strain at break: 2.42 ± 0.09). When two different materials contact and separate, opposite charges are generated on their surfaces, creating a potential difference [4, 5]. TENGs harness this potential difference to generate electrical current. They emphasize **efficient conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy** for energy harvesting and powering devices [4, 5], beyond just sensing.

2.  **Why Biodegradable Polymers are Suitable for TENGs:**
    *   **Environmental Friendliness:** Prevailing TENG fabrication relies on non-biodegradable, non-biocompatible synthetic polymers (e.g., PTFE, PDMS, PVDF, PS), posing ecological threats upon disposal [2, 6, 8]. Biodegradable polymers offer a solution by being **sustainable, naturally occurring, renewable, biodegradable, biocompatible, and non-toxic** [1, 2, 6, 8, 11, 14].
    *   **Net-Zero Emissions Goal:** Cellulose-based TENGs, in particular, are biodegradable and can meet net-zero emissions targets [8].
    *   **Natural Electron-Donating Capacity:** Many biodegradable polymers like cellulose and pectin possess plentiful polar groups (e.g., hydroxyl groups in cellulose, oxygen-containing groups in SBG, amino groups in cationic cellulose/PEO composites) that endow them with strong **electron-donating capabilities**, making them promising **tribopositive materials** [1, 2, 6, 11, 13]. Pectin is highlighted as an effective positive triboelectric material [2].
    *   **Abundance and Low Cost:** Biodegradable polymers like cellulose (most abundant natural polymer), pectin (extracted from fruit peel), chitosan, and split black gram (SBG) are **abundant, widely available, and cost-effective** [1, 2, 6, 11, 13, 14].
    *   **Suitability for Wearable/Biomedical Applications:** Their **biocompatibility, flexibility, and biodegradability** make biodegradable polymers ideal for TENGs integrated into **wearable electronics, biomedical devices, implantable devices, and electronic skin**, where compatibility with human tissue is crucial [2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, 14]. Hydrogels based on biopolymers enhance flexibility and conformal contact [4, 5, 7, 12].
    *   **Facile Processing:** Some biodegradable polymer sources enable **solvent-free, low-cost, and simple fabrication processes** for TENGs (e.g., SBG-TENG) [6]. retrieved_contexts: ['Particulate leaching is a simple and popular technique to fabricate porous scaffolds. Using this approach, the pore size and porosity of the scaffold can be controlled by the size of the particulate (porogen) and particulate/polymer ratio, respectively. In this method, the particulates (sodium chloride, sodium citrate, gelatin, paraffin, etc) are dispersed in a polymer solution (in an organic solvent) and the dispersion is cast into a predefined 3D mold. The solvent is evaporated or lyophilized, and the entrapped particulates are eventually leached out to produce a defined pore structure. However, the residual organic solvents (may be harmful to cells, growth factors or nearby tissues) and a dense surface skin layer (usually formed during the solvent evaporation step), which can lead to the negative effect for in vitro cell culture or in vivo tissue regeneration in the scaffolds, are considered limitations of this approach. To complement these issues, melt-molding particulate leaching [51], which does not involve any organic solvents during the scaffold fabrication process and can prevent skin layer formation, was developed. Scaffolds fabricated using this approach exhibited highly porous and open-cellular pore structures with almost the same surface and interior porosities. 3D porous scaffolds of various shapes (disc, meniscus, or sphere shape) [51-53] have also been prepared using the melt-molding particulate leaching method for tissue engineering applications. Electrospinning is a widely used method to produce polymer meshes with fiber diameters in the range of nano to a few microns using an electrically driven jet of the polymer solution or melt [54, 55]. Various synthetic and natural polymers have been used to fabricate nanofiber meshes for tissue engineering applications [56, 57]. The electrospun nanofiber meshes have a high porosity, high surface area and flexibility, and therefore, they have been investigated in a wide variety of biomedical applications, including tissue engineering scaffolds, wound dressings, drug delivery carriers, and medical implants [58-60]. It is well known that the nanofibrous structure can closely mimic the natural ECM such as collagen, and thus can provide a good environment for cell adhesion and proliferation, which are deeply affected by surface structure and topography [61-63]. However, the difficulty of cells to infiltrate into the nanofibrous 3D structure due to the too small pore size compared to the cells still remains a challenge for tissue engineering applications. Recently, various efforts to overcome this limitation have been reported [64-66]. The solid free-form fabrication (SFF) technique, which has been used to fabricate highly reproducible scaffolds with fully interconnected porous structures based on computer aided design and manufacture (CAD/CAM), was initially introduced by Giordano et al [67]. For the fabrication of 3D porous scaffold using the SFF technique, 2D images obtained from computerized tomography (CT) scans or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the patient are converted to a 3D structure using CAD or other software, and an accurately designed 3D porous structure is fabricated by automated layer-by-layer construction through various SFF processes (for SFF scaffold fabrication reviews, see refs. [46-48, 68-70]).', 'Bone tissue engineering based on scaffolds aims to repair and regenerate bone defects, and ideal scaffolds should be composed of biocompatible and biodegradable materials, and also mimic the basic mechanical and biochemical properties of bone tissue. A three-dimensional (3D) porous structure is effective to achieve imitating bone tissue and facilitating cell differentiation, growth, and nutrient supply to cells.9 Methods for fabricating 3D porous scaffolds in the field of tissue engineering include textile technologies, phase separation processes, gas foaming, particle aggregation/solid freeform fabrication, and solvent casting/particulate leaching. Among them, the solvent casting/particulate leaching method involves mixing sodium chloride (NaCl) particles with a polymer solution, casting them in a 3D mold, and forming an interconnected porous network structure by evaporating the solvent and leaching of NaCl particles. The advantage of this method is that the porosity, shape, size, interconnection, and porosity of the pores can be effectively adjusted by modifying the shape, size, and amount of porogen. Several previous studies have produced porous scaffolds using solvent casting/particulate leaching methods, and the results have exhibited better interconnection, high porosity, and excellent mimicry of the bone microenvironment.10,11 Poly(glycolic acid), poly(lactic acid), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid), and polycaprolactone (PCL) are primarily used in solvent casting/particulate leaching methods and are extensively used as scaffold materials owing to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical strength. PCL is a useful polymer for bone tissue engineering because of its high crystallization rate and excellent mechanical strength.12 However, the inherent hydrophobicity and poor surface wetting properties of PCL limit its cell adhesion and proliferation.13 Therefore, when the PCL scaffold alone is used in the bone defect site, there is a limitation in that it is separated from the surrounding bone and recognized as a foreign material due to insufficient bioactivity.14 Several methods have been proposed in previous studies to compensate for the limitation, such as preparing scaffolds by mixing hydroxyapatite (HAp) with excellent osteoconductivity in PCL.15-17 HAp is a calcium phosphate bioceramic material that is synthesized from calcium and phosphate ions. The solution viscosity of macromer solutions used in the SCPL fabrication process was also examined and select compositions were used to fabricate scaffolds with larger dimensions.', '© 2019 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. The 'solvent casting and particulate leaching' method controls pore size in tissue scaffolds through the following mechanisms:  

1. **Porogen Size Selection**: The pore size is directly determined by the **size of the particulate porogen** (e.g., sodium chloride, gelatin, paraffin). Larger porogen particles result in larger pores, while smaller particles yield smaller pores. For example, NaCl particles sized 300–425 µm produced scaffolds with pores ranging from 290–346 µm ([5]).  

2. **Porogen Shape**: The **morphology of the porogen** influences pore uniformity. Spherical porogens (e.g., gelatin or paraffin microspheres) create more uniform and interconnected pores compared to cubic salt particles ([3], [10]).  

3. **Porogen/Polymer Ratio**: The **concentration of porogen** relative to the polymer adjusts **porosity** and interconnectivity. Higher porogen content increases porosity and pore interconnectivity but may reduce mechanical strength due to thinner pore walls ([1], [2], [5]).  

4. **Graded Pore Structures**: By **varying porogen size and content across layers**, gradients in pore size (e.g., 166–453 µm) can be achieved, enabling tailored scaffolds for specific tissue engineering applications ([4]).  

5. **Post-Leaching Effects**: After leaching, residual voids mirror the original porogen arrangement, with pore interconnectivity enhanced by closer particle proximity during casting ([12]).  

Thus, precise control over porogen parameters (size, shape, concentration) allows customization of scaffold pore architecture to mimic natural extracellular matrix requirements.

All reagents were used without further purification.', 'Recent advancements in alginate-based films have focused on developing active packaging solutions. This suggests that careful selection of additives is crucial to maintain the sustainability profile of alginate-based films.', 'The specific mineralization rate can be used to make an environmental fate prediction, and can be used in product design. A relevant characteristic of biodegradable plastics is the biodegradation rate because this is a parameter that is necessary to predict the environmental fate. The results suggest that biodegradable plastics do not generate persistent microplastics, because as erosion increases the surface area, this in turn increases the biodegradation rate to levels similar to those required, by the OECD, for chemicals to be defined as readily biodegradable.', "First published on 5th March 2024 To reduce global CO2 emissions in line with EU targets, it is essential that we replace fossil-derived plastics with renewable alternatives. However, contrary to what is often claimed, the biodegradation of such materials in the natural environment can be a very slow process, which has obvious implications for their actual environmental impact. It consists of an abiotic process, in which the ester bonds along the backbone of the PLA chain are hydrolytically cleaved to form lower molecular weight molecules, followed by a biotic degradation process, in which microorganisms assimilate and mineralize the degradation products, releasing elements such as carbon dioxide, water, and biomass into the environment [5,6]. Their true density, measured with a helium pycnometer (AccuPyc II 1340, Micromeritics-Alfatest, Italy), was ρf = 1.51 g/cm3.', 'Global plastic production is increasing yearly, with packaging materials and disposable plastics accounting for a sizable portion of the total. The environmental impact of greenwashing in the context of biodegradable plastics arises from misleading claims about their degradability, which can exacerbate pollution and hinder genuine sustainability efforts. Key points include:  

1. **Misleading Disposal Practices**: Biodegradable plastics often require specific conditions (e.g., high temperature, humidity, or industrial composting) for effective degradation. Greenwashing fosters public misconceptions, leading to improper disposal (e.g., littering or home composting), where these plastics persist like conventional plastics, contributing to environmental accumulation [[1], [4], [5]].  

2. **Persistent Pollution**: Studies show that biodegradable plastics (e.g., PBAT, PBS) may not degrade significantly in marine or soil environments over years, retaining mechanical strength and contributing to ghost fishing or microplastic formation if not properly managed [[1], [25]]. While some evidence suggests biodegradable plastics do not generate persistent microplastics due to accelerated biodegradation upon erosion, this depends on real-world conditions often not met [[3]].  

3. **Undermined Waste Management**: Greenwashing may reduce incentives to improve recycling infrastructure or develop truly effective biodegradable alternatives. For instance, polyesters like PLA require industrial composting, yet inadequate waste systems or consumer awareness limit their proper degradation [[4], [5]].  

4. **Carbon Footprint and Resource Misallocation**: While biodegradable plastics can lower CO₂ emissions compared to conventional plastics, greenwashing risks diverting attention from systemic issues like overconsumption or fossil fuel reliance. Misleading claims may also lead to increased production without proportional environmental benefits [[7], [8]].  

5. **Erosion of Trust**: Failed promises of biodegradability can erode public trust in eco-friendly solutions, slowing adoption of genuinely sustainable innovations and policies [[1], [4]].  

In summary, greenwashing in biodegradable plastics perpetuates environmental harm by fostering complacency in waste management, enabling pollution, and delaying critical systemic changes needed to address plastic waste.

This leads to the contamination of composting streams with non-compostable plastics, improper disposal in the environment (littering), and consumer confusion, ultimately hindering legitimate organic recycling efforts.

retrieved_contexts: ['However, PHB also has a number of drawbacks that make difficult to introduce it on an industrial scale. Moreover, PHB has a narrow processing window as its melting temperature (Tm) is close to its degradation onset temperature (Tonset) [40]. These technical disadvantages, together with its current high cost, due to its synthesis is based on a biotechnological routes, means that its use in food packaging is still limited. Therefore, the market penetration of PHB into the packaging sector is still far away the high expectations of the scientific community since it is not yet competitive with petrochemical derived plastics [41]. In this context, plasticizing by means of additives is one of the cheapest, simplest, and most effective methods to improve the ductile mechanical properties, such as impact strength or elongation at break [37], [50]. Natural and/or biodegradable additives, for instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG) [51], [52], [53], [54], glycerol [51], [55], chemically modified vegetable oils [32], [56], [57], citrates esters such as acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) and triethyl citrate (TEC) [50], [58], [59], [60], among others, have been successfully used as plasticizers for PHB. Moreover, the flexibility of PHAs can be improved by melt blending with more flexible biodegradable polymers, for example thermoplastic starch (TPS), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) or poly(butylene succinate-co-butylene adipate) (PBSA) [61], [62], [63], and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [37], [38], [39], [64] and its oligomers (oligomeric lactic acid, OLA) [38], [39], [64], [65]. This review aims to summarize the main applications of PHB for food packaging and food related disposable articles. With this propose, the synthesis and chemical aspects as well as the most emerging techniques for PHB recovery and/or end-life options are firstly described. Then, the most typical processing aspects of PHB at the industrial level are described, being particularly focused on the ageing phenomenon of PHB and its narrow processing window. Finally, some cutting-edge research works focused on enhancing the PHB stretchability by means of melt blending are described, considering both plasticizers and more flexible biodegradable polymers. Therefore, it gathers the most relevant information regarding the possibility to extend the industrial applications of PHB in the food packaging field.', "The excellent combination of its properties makes PHB ideal for biodegradable packing products and resorbable medical devices.21 Despite this, up to now there has not been a large production of PHB products because of its cost and some weaknesses in comparison with commodity and other technical plastics.22 One of the main drawbacks of PHB is its intrinsic fragility due to its high crystallinity, which can be higher than 55%. The melt temperature of PHB is located at about 180 °C and it can be processed at about 190 °C as higher temperatures (or longer residence times) promote chain scission with subsequent decrease in molecular weight.25 These problems can be overcome by using several techniques such as internal26 or external plasticization23, 25, 27 as well as physical blending with other polymers.28-30 Among the various options for preparing industrial PHB formulations, external plasticization represents an interesting, simple and cost-effective route to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of raw PHB.31 Generally, addition of plasticizers promotes a decrease in both the glass transition temperature (Tg) and the melt temperature (Tm), and this allows processing at lower temperatures thus reducing the risk of thermal degradation. It has been shown that epoxidized vegetable oils are a viable alternative to petroleum-based conventional plasticizers. These unsaturations appear in conventional fatty acids such as oleic (C18:1), linoleic (C18:2) and linolenic (C18: 3) acids with one, two and three carbon-carbon double bonds, respectively. On the other hand, Seydibeyoğlu et al.44 reported interesting results for intermediate plasticizer content with a different PHBV grade and different valerate content. The poor crystallizability and processability of PHB bacterial copolyesters have been the bottleneck for their large-scale commodity application.', 'Finally, optimized processing techniques, including controlled temperature, reduced residence time in the melt phase, lowering shear stress, and nitrogen purging, are crucial to mitigating thermal degradation during manufacturing. Moreover, the materials used in compounding were dry-blended with the same ratio and processed in laboratory- and pilot-scale extrusion lines to compare the properties and results of different blending methods.', 'Material scientists are interested in exploiting structural functionality and physical properties of polysaccharides for antioxidants (3) in multifunctional food applications; for films, coatings, emulsions, (4) additives, (5) and hydrogels in material applications; and for stretchable substrates in electronic devices. The melt processing of PHB is challenging without plasticizers due to two primary interrelated factors:  
1. **Narrow Processing Window**: PHB's melting temperature (Tm ≈ 170–180°C) is dangerously close to its thermal degradation onset temperature (Tonset ≈ 245–260°C). This narrow window forces processing near degradation conditions, risking chain scission, molecular weight reduction, and compromised mechanical properties (e.g., reduced tensile strength and elongation at break).  
2. **High Crystallinity and Brittleness**: PHB’s crystallinity (>55%) leads to rigidity and brittleness, hindering chain mobility during melting. This results in poor ductility, physical aging (secondary crystallization), and irregular pore formation, further limiting processability.  

Without plasticizers, PHB cannot be processed at lower temperatures safely, and its inherent brittleness exacerbates flow instability. Plasticizers address these issues by reducing crystallinity, lowering Tg and Tm, enhancing chain mobility, and widening the processing window to mitigate thermal degradation risks.

retrieved_contexts: ['In terms of chemical theory, both acids and alkalis can be used to deacetylate chitin. Chitin was converted into chitosan by chitin deacetylases, and the molecular chain was not degraded in the process of chitin deacetylation. (16)', "Chitosan is a naturally occurring linear amino polysaccharide biopolymer obtained from the crustacean’s exoskeletons, especially from shrimp, prawns, lobsters, and crabs as well as from fish scales [30,31,32,33,34]. Due to its strong hydrophobicity, chitin is insoluble in water and many other organic solvents. Chitin hydrolyzes with potent acids in a hostile environment to produce high-purity D-glucosamine [35]. Chemical structure of chitosan", 'Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide derived from chitin, the second most abundant organic compound next to cellulose in the nature. Chitin can be found in the shells of marine invertebrates (crabs, crustaceans, etc.), fungi, insects and yeasts. Depending on the source, it generally functions as an exoskeleton, providing structural integrity, commonly embedded in a matrix of proteins, minerals and at times various other polysaccharides. Chitin is a homopolymer comprised of 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-β-D-glucopyranose units; however, some units exist in the deacetylated form as 2-amino-2-deoxy-β-D-glucopyranose. When chitin is deacetylated to at least 50 %, it is referred to as chitosan, in other words this is essentially the N-deacetylated derivative of chitin. Chitosan has many interesting biological and chemical properties. The excellent features such as biocompatibility, ecologically safe biodegradability (degradation products of chitosan are non-toxic, non-immunogenic and non-carcinogenic) and low toxicity with versatile biological activities (chitosan has antimicrobial activity and low immunogenicity) recommends this biopolymer for applications in biomedicine [1-5]. The main advantage in the grafting efforts is the high degree of functionality of chitosan-the molecule backbone contains two hydroxyl groups and one primary amine group per repeat unit. The active primary amino groups on the molecule being reactive provide sites for the attachment of different side groups employing mild reaction conditions. In this way versatile materials based on chitosan with specific functionality can be obtained. Grafting vinyl monomers onto chitosan [10, 11] is one of the most effective methods to improve the performances of chitosan without sacrificing its properties and also is a challenging field of research with unlimited future prospects. Vinyl graft copolymerization can be described as the modification of a preexisting polymer chain (trunk polymer). Thus, from the trunk polymer backbone, polymer chains with structural units different from those of the trunk polymer are grown. The reaction begins by creating free radical sites on the trunk polymer chain whereby vinyl monomer can react with the radical to propagate into a new polymer chain that is covalently bonded to the trunk polymer. Radical chain growth mechanisms are important to polymer synthesis due to their greater versatility, relative to cationic and anionic methods, in regard to the wider range of vinyl monomers that are polymerizable by this method. This type of copolymerization offers the possibility of creating novel polymer systems that permanently combine the properties of both polymer chains.', "Chitin, one of Earth's most prevalent and renewable materials, serves as the primary source of chitosan. The former is majorly found in the cell walls of fungi, the outer coverings, or exoskeletons of arthropods like insects and crustaceans, the radulae of molluscs, the beaks of cephalopods, and the scales of fish and Lissamphibia. The deacetylation of chitin results in the linear polysaccharide called chitosan [32,33,34]. According to data from the Web of Science, there have been many patents and more than 167,000 articles about chitosan to date. As mentioned, conventionally chitosan is extracted from chitin by chemical route (Scheme. 1), which involves demineralisation, deproteinization and the key process of deacetylation [38, 39]. Enzyme-assisted extraction is specific, faster and utilizes a reduced amount of energy and water whereas microwave-assisted extraction increases the product yield and improves product purity [40,41,42,43,44,45].", 'Pyrazole is one of heterocyclic compounds that has two nitrogen atoms in five member ring [1], the presence of two nitrogen atoms in pyrazole nucleus exhibit its activity, while the nitrogen atom at position 1 can lose its proton during reaction with a base and nitrogen atom at position 2 is reactive towards electrophiles due to presence of a lone pair of electrons [2]. As discussed before, because of the biological activity of pyrazole, chitosan and Schiff base, we aimed to prepare new Schiff bases based on chitosan/pyrazole compounds and investigate the biological activities of the prepared compounds.', 'Chitosan (CH) is an amino polysaccharide obtained by the partial alkaline deacetylation (˃40%) or enzymatic degradation of chitin, which is the second naturally occurring and abundantly available polysaccharide in nature after cellulose. Chitin is extracted from the exoskeletons of marine crustaceans (such as crab and shrimp) and mollusks, the cuticles of insects and the cell walls of most fungi. CH is a linear polymer consisting predominantly (> 50%) glucosamine (2-amino-2-deoxy-β-D-glucopyranose) (GlCn; D) repeating units distributed randomly along with N-acetyl-glucosamine (2-acetamido-2-deoxy-β-D-glucopyranose) (GlcNAc;A) repeat units (< 50%) linked in a β (1,4) fashion [1, 2]. Chitin is a nitrogen-modified polysaccharide made up of N-acetylglucosamine, bound together in β-(1-4)-N-acetyl-d-glucosamine bonds. Structurally, it is very similar to cellulose, but it has an additional amine group and a hydroxyl substituent on each monomer. This limits its utilization and has led to several chemical modifications in an attempt to produce a more soluble and utilizable derivative such as chitosan. Chitin and chitosan have recently become the focus of researchers due to their beneficial biological properties, such as biocompatibility, biodegradability, non-toxigenicity, non-antigenicity, adsorption, ability to form films and to chelate metal ions (Rout 2001, Shahidi and Abuzaytoun 2005). Therefore, they have been applied in different industrial fields (Shahidi et al 1999, Ong et al 2008), as well as in poultry health and production in Malaysia (Kaikabo et al 2016a, 2016b). The aim of this study, therefore, is to isolate and study the chitin and chitosan structures of the house cricket (Brachytrupes portentosus) so as to reveal the differences between cricket chitin and chitosan and the commercial products by determining their physicochemical and nutritional properties.', 'Chitosan has been used as an effective food preservative, having the ability to form films, a biodegradable nature, and antioxidant and antimicrobial properties.1-3 This polysaccharide is a linear cationic (1→4)-2-amino-2-deoxy-β-D-glucan, produced commercially by partial deacetylation of chitin, which is the component of the exoskeletons of arthropods such as crustaceans (crabs, lobsters, and shrimps) and insects, the beaks and internal shells of cephalopods, including squid and octopuses, and fungi cell walls.4 Currently, nearly all chitosans produced commercially are chemically extracted from crab, shrimp and prawn exoskeleton waste. Shrimp is the most important commodity (4 million tons produced in 2012) by value (17 billion (1012) euros) in the international seafood trade, and it has grown exponentially in the last few decades.5 Shrimp industries generate approximately 45-55% of the weight of raw shrimp in waste, whose management is an extremely difficult and expensive process.6 This by-product yields 15-25% of chitosan.6,7 The main concern in chitosan uses for food and biomedical applications lies in its potential allergenicity for people with shellfish allergy. However, the purification of fungi chitosan is a costly process when compared to the seafood source, as it occurs in complexes with other polysaccharides, such as cellulose and β-glucans, thus limiting its wider food applications.9 The development of chitosan films with desirable properties sometimes requires chemical and/or physical modification. Recently, it was shown that skin test responses and oral challenges of wines containing chitosan-genipin films do not promote any adverse effect of chitosan in terms of allergy to shellfish allergic patients.19,20 Wine is one of the most consumed alcoholic beverages in the world, with a high economic impact. The world wine trade in 2013 was around 98 million hectolitres, representing 26 billion euros.21 Table wines still account for almost 71% of total wine sales, while sparkling wines have 20% of total revenues.21 SO2 is a preservative widely used in winemaking due to its antioxidant and antiseptic properties. Also, it is an anti-browning agent, inhibiting non-enzymatic browning reactions, including the Maillard reaction,22 and is a colour stabilizer, fixing, for example, the red colour of anthocyanins in red wines.22,23 In recognition of the potential health hazards to the population with sulphite hypersensitivity,24 indication of the presence of sulphites is mandatory on the wine labels. Accordingly, the International Organization of Vine and Wine (OIV) has progressively reduced the maximum concentration authorized in wines, which is currently 150 mg L−1 for table dry red wines, 200 mg L−1 for table dry white wines and 185 mg L−1 for sparkling wines.25 Also, according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, SO2 is one of the six greatest air pollutants, together with ozone, lead, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate matter.26 In this context, it is important to seek green methodologies capable of minimizing the use of SO2. Such a technology should be sufficiently simple, inexpensive and, when applied to winemaking, must not have adverse effects on the wine quality.', 'As most present-day polymers are synthetic materials, their biocompatibility and biodegradability are much more limited than those of natural polymers, such as cellulose, chitin, chitosan (CS), and their derivatives. In this respect, chitin and CS are recommended as suitable functional materials because these natural polymers have excellent properties, such as biocompatibility, biodegradability, nontoxicity, and adsorption properties. Chitin and CS are of commercial interest because of their high percentage of nitrogen (6.89%) compared to synthetically substituted cellulose (1.25%).1 Chitin is usually isolated from the exoskeletons of crustaceans and, more particularly, from shrimp and crabs where α chitin is produced.2, 3 Squid is another important source of chitin, in which it exists in the β form, which has been found to be more amenable for deacetylation. The extraction of chitin from its natural sources followed by its deacetylation to obtain the much more useful CS material has been studied by many authors.4-11', 'Biopolymers, in general, offer good properties and are available in abundance, whilst being biodegradable. Chitin is one such biopolymer, widely referred to as the “cellulose of the sea” [6]. Second only to cellulose in abundance, it is extracted from the exoskeleton of crustaceans such as crabs, prawns, lobsters, etc. and the cell-wall of few fungi [[7], [8], [9]]. Chemically, it is a polymer of N-acetyl D-glucosamine, with fewer units [10] of D-glucosamine (not more than 50%). The extensive intra and intermolecular H-bonding in chitin, prevent thermal transitions and solubility of the biopolymer in organic solvents, limiting the applications of this biomaterial [11]. However, when deacetylated to a degree greater than 50%, the copolymer becomes soluble in mildly acidic solutions (pH less than or equal to 6.5) [12]. This polymer, containing more than 50% of D-glucosamine fraction, is referred to as chitosan. Apart from being biocompatible, biodegradable and mechanically strong, the amine groups on chitosan make it haemostatic, antibacterial, antifungal, anticholesteremic and mucoadhesive in nature [13]. The chemical structures of chitin and chitosan are presented in Fig. 2. Due to its ability to be processed in solution form and the presence of amine and hydroxyl reactive “handles”, which allow easy modification, chitosan is widely used in many applications, unlike its acetylated counterpart. Having wound-healing and haemostatic properties, it has been used in biomedical sutures and bandages [11]. Also being bioresorbable and biocompatible, whilst having good mechanical properties, it has been used for making scaffolds for tissue engineering [14]. It is also used in cosmetics due to its biocompatibility, ability to hold moisture, whilst being non-allergenic and non-toxic in nature [10]. Being a polycation in its acidic solution, chitosan has also been used to flocculate or coagulate negatively-charged organic and inorganic impurities from wastewater. It has also been extensively studied to adsorb heavy metal ions from wastewater resources [15]. In the pharmaceutical domain, crosslinked chitosan particles and hydrogels have been used as targeted drug carriers, capable of controlled drug release [16,17]. Apart from usage as drug carriers, chitosan has also been suggested for use as an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) for the treatment of ulcers [18]. In agriculture, chitosan has been used as protective coatings for seeds and as foliar treatment agents, due to its antimicrobial nature [19]. Much research has also been done on using chitosan hydrogels in agriculture for the sustained release of water [10,20]. Clearly, hydrogels of chitosan hold the most commercial importance [21], among all other physical forms. This review sheds light on the three generations of chitosan-based hydrogels, distinguished on the basis of nature of crosslinks, environmental stability, mechanical strength and toxicity of the crosslinked systems. Applications of chitosan in various fields have been continuously, on the rise. This is reflected from the exponential increase in the number of patent applications published, relating to chitosan, in the preceding years. One aim of this review is to shed light on such most recent advances in the field of chitosan and more particularly in regard to chitosan-based hydrogels. In addition, given the widespread application of chitosan-based hydrogels in fields like biomedicine, agriculture and cosmetics, it becomes important to draw distinctions on the basis of nature of crosslinks (and thereby toxicity), mechanical and environmental-strength and stability, in light of which, this review become important. Furthermore, this review also dedicates much-needed attention to ionotropic, chitosan-based superabsorbents and how it has evolved from non-absorbing covalently crosslinked systems. The number of patent applications published yearly, relating to chitosan, is presented in Fig. 3.', 'Maillard reaction took place as storage time progressed. The employment of bio-based materials for the development of biodegradable films is considered a potential solution to face the serious environmental problems created by the huge use of conventional petroleum-based materials due to their prospective environmental benefits, mainly based in their renewable origin and biodegradability [1]. In this context, chitosan is a natural polymer derived by deacetylation of chitin, insoluble in water. When the degree of deacetylation is higher than 50%, it becomes soluble in acidic media and is called chitosan [2]. Tuning the biodegradability of biodegradable polymer films in soil for use as mulch films should be possible with chemistry tools and the existing know-how.', 'There are many different types of graphene-based materials, and they can be categorized by limiting them into groups of graphene, graphene oxide, graphite, expanded graphite, and graphite oxide. Polylactic acid (PLA)', "The intent of this review is to provide an original discussion of methods to accelerate the biodegradation process of biodegradable polymers from the perspective of differentiating them into abiotic and biotic methods. SAPs are usually made up of ionic monomers and have a low degree of crosslinking, which gives them the ability to absorb a much larger amount of fluid than normal hydrogels (up to 1000 times their weight)7 compared to traditional hydrogels (up to 10 times their weight).5 While this review covers literature on SAPs and hydrogels, the two terms will collectively be referred to as hydrogels hereafter since there has not yet been a definitive terminology in the literature.', 'One of the most heavily used commodity products world-wide are plastics. The terms 'bio-based' and 'biodegradable' in polymer classification differ in their fundamental definitions and scopes:  

1. **Bio-based**:  
   - Refers to polymers **derived from renewable biological resources** (e.g., plants, biomass, agricultural feedstocks). Examples include PLA (from corn starch) and bio-PE (from sugarcane).  
   - Focuses on the **origin of raw materials**, not the end-of-life behavior. A bio-based polymer may or may not be biodegradable. For instance, **bio-PE is bio-based but non-biodegradable**.  

2. **Biodegradable**:  
   - Indicates a polymer’s ability to **break down naturally via microorganisms** (e.g., bacteria, fungi) into water, carbon dioxide, and biomass under specific environmental conditions (e.g., composting, soil).  
   - Depends on the **chemical structure** (e.g., ester groups in polyesters like PBAT or PCL) and environmental factors (temperature, microbial activity), not the feedstock source. For example, **PBAT and PCL are fossil-based but biodegradable**, while bio-PE is bio-based but non-biodegradable.  

**Key Distinction**:  
- **Bio-based** addresses the **origin** (renewable vs. fossil resources).  
- **Biodegradable** addresses the **end-of-life degradation mechanism** (microbial decomposition).  
- These are independent attributes: A polymer can be bio-based and biodegradable (e.g., PLA), bio-based and non-biodegradable (e.g., bio-PE), or fossil-based and biodegradable (e.g., PBAT).  

**Standards**: Biodegradability requires compliance with certifications (e.g., ASTM D6400 for compostability), while bio-based status is verified by feedstock origin (e.g., ISO 16620 for bio-based carbon content).
reference: 'Bio-based' refers to the origin of the carbon source (derived from renewable biomass), whereas 'biodegradable' refers to the end-of-life capability to be microbial decomposed. A polymer can be bio-based but non-biodegradable (e.g., Bio-PE), or fossil-based but biodegradable (e.g., PBAT, PCL).

We have therefore tried to design various new monomer structures of TMC, that avoid ester groups for functionalization, because we recognized that no acid generation is one of the positive characteristics of conventional PTMC. It is therefore important to introduce functional groups without an ester strucure.', "Biodegradable polymers are degraded into natural metabolites by simple hydrolysis or enzyme action under physiological conditions.1, 2 Compared with metal materials and nondegradable polymer materials, biodegradable polymers have the advantage of not requiring secondary surgery.3 In recent decades, polylactic acid,4 polycaprolactone,5 polyglycolic acid,6 and other absorbable polymer materials are increasingly favored by researchers.7, 8 Poly (1,3-trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC) is an absorbable, flexible, and amorphous elastomer.9 Unlike other aliphatic polyesters, PTMC is degraded by enzymatic surface erosion.10 It can achieve zero-order release of drugs.11 PTMC hydrolyzes relatively stable in water or buffers solution (pH = 1-13) in vitro.12 There are no acidic products in the degradation process and should not cause serious inflammation.13 PTMC has great potential in biomedical applications, such as drug delivery systems,14-16 soft tissue engineering,17, 18 vascular prostheses,19, 20 or nerve regenerative systems.21-23 However, linear PTMC has very low modulus and low tensile strength.24 The amorphous structure and lower glass transition temperature result in poor dimensional stability of PTMC, and it is prone to creep at room temperature.25 This limits any practical application of PTMC. The free radicals generated during the irradiation can react with nearby oxygen, leading to autocatalytic oxidative degradation.30 The compressed molded films were vacuum-sealed and irradiated at room temperature.", 'Among the members of these biodegradable polymers, aliphatic polycarbonates have attracted much interest as a bioresorbable material in the design of implanted drug delivery systems due to their non-acidic degradated products [16], [17], [18] to avoid aseptic inflammation. Therefore, the best way to prepare the BCNs is to incorporate suitable reactive cross-linking agents into the polymer chain.', 'A recently developed viscous liquid aliphatic polycarbonate, poly(trimethylene carbonate-co-5-hydroxy trimethylene carbonate), has advantageous properties for the delivery of acid-sensitive drugs such as proteins and peptides. The enzymatic degradation mechanism of Poly(trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC) **in vivo** involves **surface erosion** driven by enzymes and reactive oxygen species (ROS) secreted by adherent macrophages. Specifically:  

1. **Surface Erosion Mechanism**: PTMC degradation occurs primarily via surface erosion rather than bulk erosion. This is attributed to the action of enzymes (e.g., cholesterol esterase, collagenase) and ROS produced by macrophages at the polymer-tissue interface, leading to gradual mass loss while maintaining structural integrity until late-stage degradation.  

2. **Key Enzymatic Actors**:  
   - **Macrophage-Derived Enzymes**: Enzymes such as cholesterol esterase and collagenase directly cleave the carbonate bonds in PTMC.  
   - **Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS)**: ROS generated by macrophages contribute to oxidative degradation of PTMC.  

3. **Degradation Products**: PTMC degradation does not generate acidic organic compounds (unlike polyesters like PLA or PCL), avoiding pH changes and inflammation. Instead, it produces **carbon dioxide** and **oligo(trimethylene carbonate)** residues, which are neutral and biocompatible.  

4. **Molecular Weight Dependency**: High-molecular-weight PTMC (>~457 kDa) exhibits pronounced surface erosion behavior, with studies showing ~60% mass loss in 8 weeks in vivo (e.g., in rabbit bone implants).  

This mechanism ensures controlled, localized degradation suitable for applications like vascular grafts, drug delivery systems, and tissue engineering scaffolds, where minimal inflammatory response and dimensional stability are critical.

This leads to linear mass loss with time while maintaining molecular weight, making it useful for drug delivery.

The adoption of biodegradable polymers is widely regarded as an effective solution to this issue.[8-11] Polylactic acid (PLA) and polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (PBAT) are two of the most widely studied biodegradable polymers due to their complementary properties. PLA, a bio-based polyester, is characterized by its high stiffness, strength, and biodegradability, but suffers from inherent brittleness and poor flexibility.[3, 12-15] In contrast, PBAT, a synthetic aliphatic-aromatic copolyester, exhibits excellent ductility and flexibility but lacks sufficient mechanical strength for high-performance applications. To overcome these individual limitations, blending PLA and PBAT has been explored as an effective approach to developing balanced biodegradable materials with improved mechanical properties, biodegradability, and processability.[9, 16-20] Despite the potential of PLA/PBAT blends, the inherent immiscibility between PLA and PBAT due to their different polarities and molecular structures results in poor interfacial adhesion, leading to phase-separated morphologies with compromised mechanical properties.[9, 21, 22] Therefore, compatibilization strategies have been widely investigated to enhance the interfacial interaction between these polymers, ensuring improved mechanical performance and structural stability.[23] Compatibilization affects polymer blends through two key mechanisms: i) preventing droplet coalescence and ii) lowering interfacial tension, both leading to reduced droplet sizes. These effects are most pronounced when the compatibilizer is located at the interface.[24, 25] In the absence of compatibilizers, polymer blend properties are notably inferior to those of the individual polymers. Common compatibilization strategies include i) non-reactive approaches using co-solvents or copolymers, ii) reactive methods that create copolymers in situ, and iii) nanofiller-assisted techniques incorporating small amounts of nanofillers. The selection of a method depends on factors such as cost, performance, recyclability, and biodegradability.[26-28] One common route involves the use of reactive compatibilizers, such as multifunctional chain extenders, which promote in situ reactions between PLA and PBAT to improve interfacial adhesion.[16, 29-31] Among these, epoxide-based chain extenders like Joncryl have been extensively studied for their ability to react with carboxyl (─COOH) and hydroxyl (─OH) groups, extending polymer chains and reducing phase separation.[16, 29, 32] Research has demonstrated that incorporating various types of Joncryl ADR, such as 4468, 4368, and 4370, into PLA/PBAT blends enhances tensile strength, elongation at break, and impact resistance. These improvements are attributed to better interfacial adhesion and an increase in molecular weight due to chain extension. For example, Wang et al.[33] developed high-strength, high-toughness PLA/PBAT (60/40) blends using a melt-reactive blending approach. By introducing Joncryl ADR-4370S as a compatibilizer through an in situ compatibilization reaction, its epoxy groups and the terminal carboxyl and hydroxyl groups of PLA and PBAT, forming a PLA-g-PBAT copolymer linking the two segments. This reaction notably reduced the interfacial tension between the phases. They achieved enhanced mechanical properties across all blends.[33] In another study, Al-Itry et al.[34] evaluated the effect of multifunctional epoxide (Joncryl;ADR-4368) on the interfacial properties of biopolymer blends based on PLA/PBAT. The results indicated a decrease in interfacial tension in the modified/compatibilized PLA/PBAT blend and the formation of the PLA-Joncryl-PBAT copolymer, leading to enhanced mechanical properties.[34] Arruda et al.[16] studied the influence of Joncryl ADR 4368 on PLA/PBAT blend and found that for the 60 PLA blend, the addition of a chain extender resulted in a 900% increase in elongation at break compared to the 60PLA blend without it. Additionally, it exhibited a 1200% increase relative to neat PLA, significantly enhancing ductility. Moreover, in the 60 PLA blends containing a chain extender, the dispersed phase was refined, transitioning from coarse sheets or platelets to elongated PBAT fibrils. This morphological transformation is likely responsible for the increased elongation at break. Additionally, a notable enhancement in stress at break was observed, rising from 22.3 MPa (without a chain extender) to 34-35 MPa with its addition.[16] However, the effectiveness of Joncryl in modifying PLA/PBAT blends is highly dependent on processing conditions. Previous research has primarily focused on single-step blending methods, where all components are processed simultaneously. In recent years, renewable resources and biodegradable materials have gotten more and more interest. Using “green-friendly” materials instead of traditional petroleum-based polymers as packaging materials is indispensable.1-3 Polylactide (PLA) is a biodegradable and biocompatible aliphatic polyester derived from lactic acid, which has comparable mechanical properties to those of some conventional polymers. To improve the compatibility between two immiscible components, a third component is added as a compatibilizer in most cases. The compatibilizer can be either premade or in situ formed during melt blending. One successful application of reactive blending is the addition of peroxides to several PLA blends, such as PLA/poly(ε-caprolactone),27, 28 PLA/PBS,29 PLA/poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBAT),17 by simultaneous melt blending. It was shown that the addition of peroxides to those polymer blends forms crosslinked and/or branched structures by heteroradical coupling reactions, which improve the compatibility of the polymer blends, the melt tensions and the extrusion stability. The other reactive application is principally based on the reactions between end functional groups (i.e., \uf8ffOH or \uf8ffCOOH) of PLA and other complementary functional groups (mainly epoxide groups) of the compatibilizers, for example, PLA/PBAT blend modified with glycidylmethacrylate (GMA),30, 31 PLA/poly(ethylene octane) (POE) blend with POE-g-GMA modifier,32 and chain extension of PLA with multifunctional epoxide.33 As a result, improved interfacial adhesion and hence fine dispersion were achieved. To enlarge its property (processing) window and thereby its applications field, PLA needs to be toughened and heat resistant. It has been demonstrated that reactive blending is an effective way in improving the toughness of PLA blends, particularly IS. In most of these blends, however, the achievement of superior impact relies on the addition of a large amount of nonbiodegradable petroleum-based polymers (>20 wt %), which is usually accompanied by a great loss in heat resistance and stiffness. Thus, how to enhance significantly toughness and heat resistance while minimizing the reductions in stiffness of the PLA materials, still remains a challenge. This work is based on two types of modifiers to modify the PLA/PC blend through twin-screw extrusion. We shall investigate improvement of the toughness and the heat resistance of PLA/PC blends by (1) balancing the toughness and thermal resistance of the ternary blends with EP or PBSL, (2) examining the morphological changes of the modified polymer blends, and (3) elucidating the mechanism for improvement of the physical properties of the blends. PBSL (GS Pla® AZ-type, lactate unit about 3 mol %, melt flow rate (190°C; 2.16 kg) 25 g/10 min, specific gravity 1.26, was supplied from Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation (Japan). The choice of these compatibilizers was based on requisites such as nontoxicity and biocompatibility. The catalyst tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB), analytical grade, was obtained from Acros. Reactive extrusion using peroxides like dicumyl peroxide (DCP) enhances PLA/PBAT blends through **crosslinking/branching** and **in situ compatibilization**. Here’s the mechanism based on the context:  

1. **Radical Formation**: DCP decomposes under heat during extrusion, generating free radicals (e.g., phenylisopropoxyl radicals).  
2. **Hydrogen Abstraction**: These radicals abstract hydrogen atoms from the polymer backbones of PLA and PBAT, creating reactive sites on both polymers.  
3. **Covalent Bond Formation**: The reactive sites facilitate **heterogeneous coupling** between PLA and PBAT chains, forming crosslinked or branched copolymer structures at the interface.  
4. **Compatibilization**: These copolymers act as **in situ compatibilizers**, reducing interfacial tension and improving adhesion between the immiscible PLA and PBAT phases. This results in a **finer dispersion** of PBAT droplets (e.g., reduced domain size to ~0.05–1 μm) and stabilized phase morphology.  
5. **Mechanical Improvements**: Enhanced interfacial adhesion enables efficient stress transfer, significantly boosting toughness (impact strength, elongation at break) while minimizing losses in stiffness and strength. Crosslinking also increases **melt strength** and extrusion stability, enabling applications like film blowing.  

**Key Outcomes**:  
- **Phase Morphology**: Smaller, stabilized dispersed phases (e.g., nanoscale PBAT domains) reduce stress concentration points.  
- **Thermal/Rheological Benefits**: Crosslinked/branched structures improve melt elasticity and processing stability.  
- **Balanced Properties**: Superior toughness (e.g., impact strength >53 kJ/m²) without sacrificing PLA’s inherent stiffness or biodegradability.  

This approach overcomes PLA’s brittleness and PBAT’s incompatibility, enabling high-performance blends for demanding applications.

Bio-PE is facing challenges on its production cost and the environmental impacts. Recycling can help reduce the virgin PE production, where mechanical or chemical pyrolysis are best beneficial option for the circular design.', 'Bio-PE production begins with the microbial fermentation of biomass-derived sugars (e.g., from sugarcane or corn) to generate ethanol. Recent research in sustainable polymer engineering is intensively focused on enhancing both the performance and ecological profile of Bio-PE. Several innovative methodologies are being employed to realize these enhancements:', 'Mechanical Recycling of New and Challenging Polymer Systems: A Brief Overview Biobased and biodegradable bioplastics provide several possibilities for an improved end-of-life with respect to fossil counterparts,[1-3] because in many cases they can be mechanically or chemically recycled[4-6] and, when it will be no more possible, they can be composted (organically recycled) contributing to soil fertility. Based solely on the provided contexts, the significance of contact angle in assessing biodegradable polymer films is:

1.  **Determining Hydrophobicity/Hydrophilicity:** The contact angle directly indicates whether the film surface is hydrophobic (contact angle >90°) or hydrophilic (contact angle <90°). This is explicitly stated in contexts [1], [2], [3], [6], [8], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], and [15]. For example:
    *   PBAT is hydrophobic (93.22°) [1].
    *   TPS films are hydrophilic (4°-13°) [1].
    *   PVA is hydrophilic (43°) [10], [11].
    *   F5%CNF is hydrophobic (101.1°) [12].
    *   PCL is hydrophobic (93°) [13], [14].

2.  **Predicting Water Sensitivity & Biodegradation Behavior:**
    *   Hydrophilic surfaces (low contact angle) absorb more water, which generally enhances susceptibility to biodegradation by microorganisms and enzymes in environments like soil or compost (evident in biodegradation studies in [1], [8], [15]). For instance, adding hydrophilic starch to hydrophobic polymers like PBAT or PCL lowers the contact angle and accelerates biodegradation ([1], [13], [14], [15]).
    *   Hydrophobic surfaces (high contact angle) resist water absorption, potentially slowing down biodegradation initially or making the material suitable for applications requiring moisture resistance ([1], [4], [5], [12]). The improved "water stability" and "superior and stable hydrophobicity" of the TPS-PBAT blend are highlighted as key findings for agricultural use ([4], [5]).

3.  **Evaluating the Effect of Additives/Modifications:**
    *   Contact angle measurements reveal how modifiers (like MA, TC, CNC, plasticizers, essential oils, compatibilizers) alter the film's surface properties:
        *   MA and TC lowered the contact angle of PBAT/TPS films, increasing hydrophilicity and water absorption [1].
        *   CNC fillers significantly increased the contact angle of SP films, enhancing hydrophobicity [2], [3].
        *   Cinnamaldehyde (hydrophobic) increased the contact angle of gelatin/PVA films [6].
        *   Plasticizers like glycerol, sorbitol, xylitol decreased the contact angle of hemicellulose/chitosan films, increasing hydrophilicity [12].
        *   Compatibilizers like St-g-PLLA *increased* the contact angle of starch/PCL blends, improving hydrophobicity and water resistance [13], [14].
        *   Adding starch decreased the contact angle of PMMA, increasing hydrophilicity and biodegradability [15].

4.  **Correlating with Other Functional Properties:**
    *   Surface hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity (indicated by contact angle) is intrinsically linked to water vapor barrier properties (WVP) and swelling behavior, as mentioned in contexts [6], [10], [11], [12]. Hydrophobic surfaces generally offer better moisture barriers.
    *   Changes in contact angle can reflect morphological changes or degradation state (e.g., oxidative degradation decreasing contact angle in rubber films [8]).

**In summary, within the provided contexts, the contact angle is a critical metric for characterizing the surface wettability (hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity) of biodegradable polymer films. This property directly influences water sensitivity, biodegradation kinetics, barrier performance, and is highly sensitive to compositional changes or modifications, making it essential for tailoring films for specific applications and understanding their environmental performance.**
reference: The contact angle measures the wettability of a surface. For biodegradable polymers, a lower contact angle (<90°) indicates hydrophilicity, which generally correlates with faster hydrolytic degradation onset and better cell adhesion. High contact angles (>90°) indicate hydrophobicity, often requiring surface modification for biomedical use.

retrieved_contexts: ["The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Therefore, performing an appropriate sterilization process for this new system will enable to use it in the clinic. The most widely used biodegradable polymers in medical applications are poly(hydroxy acid)s such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), and poly(caprolactone) (PCL). Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) containing polymers are also widely used.1, 2 Recently, several medical devices were commercialized that incorporate derivatives of the natural amino acid l-tyrosine.3-5 However, unlike devices made from metals and ceramics, devices made from polymers can undergo physicochemical changes during sterilization that could compromise their clinical performance. Materials and devices intended for in vivo applications are either aseptically processed or terminally sterilized before use to avoid any implant-related infection. Aseptic processing of medical devices is rarely practical or economical.6 Therefore, terminal sterilization, where a device is sterilized within its final sterile barrier package, is preferred for medical device sterilization.6 Clinical success of polymeric biomaterials thus depends on the ability of the polymers to be sterilized while retaining their essential physical and chemical characteristics.', 'A novel bioresorbable hybrid wound dressing which combines a poly(DL-lactic-co-glycolic acid) porous drug-loaded top layer with a spongy collagen sublayer was developed and studied. This hybrid wound dressing combines high strength with ductility and WVTR optimal for burn treatment. Therefore this new wound dressing is more suitable than other wound dressings for treatment severe burn. If a higher dose of 35 kGy is needed, the sterilization process can be safely performed in a L.N. environment, which practically does not change the structure of the PDLGA layer and even that of the more sensitive collagen layer. It should maintain a moist environment at the wound surface, allow gas exchange, act as a barrier to microorganisms, remove excess exudates and afford mechanical protection to the wound. A new bioresorbable hybrid wound dressing which combines a poly(DL-lactic-co-glycolic acid) porous top layer with a spongy collagen sublayer was developed and studied. The top layer contained the antibiotic drug gentamicin for controlled release to the wound site. It is of very high importance to use an appropriate sterilization process for this special new wound dressing, which will not have a deleterious effect on its function.
