Our research shows that gamma-sterilization process is feasible for our new concept of hybrid wound dressings and optimal conditions can be chosen. Copyright © 2016 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. A wide range of wound dressings has been developed over the years in order to cope with different kinds of wounds.1 Any wound dressing used in the clinic should be sterile according to appropriate standards. Gamma-irradiation is the most suitable sterilization method for dressings that contain natural and sensitive polymers. The current study describes the effect of gamma radiation doses and conditions on the physical and mechanical properties of a new wound dressing developed by us, in order to find an appropriate sterilization process for this wound dressing that will not have a deleterious effect on its function.', 'The influence of sterilization on the properties of titanium surfaces (wettability, protein interaction, in vitro bioactivity, mineralization ability and cell attachment) has been investigated [1-3]. Significant alteration in surface contact angle can be observed after sterilization, while mineralization is substantially unchanged [1, 2]. Moreover, variations of surface properties after sterilization affect cellular behavior [3]. As far as biological molecules are concerned, the effect of sterilization processes on proteins and drugs has been considered by a few authors in the literature, in particular the behavior of dry, frozen and aqueous solutions under sterilization has been analyzed [4, 5]. It has been observed that gamma irradiation (25 kGy) of dry or frozen commercial proteases, hybrid biomaterials (proteases-chitosan beads) [4] and drugs [5] can preserve their starting properties, while aqueous solutions were more sensitive to the same irradiation dose. This happens because in a dry material the effect of radiation is only ‘direct’ (due to the energy of the rays) while in aqueous solutions an additional stress induced by water-derived radiolytic free radicals must be considered. Freezing, however, should reduce this indirect effect since the diffusion of free radicals is hindered in ice. The effect of sterilization on allografts for bone and tissue regeneration has also been considered. It has been shown that gamma irradiation of bone allografts is safe for cells only after defatting procedures [6] while it induces heat denaturation (proportional to the irradiation dose) on Alloderm™ [7]. Several authors investigated the effect of sterilization on the osteoconductive properties of different bone demineralized matrices, conventional and innovative procedures have been explored. Different sterilization techniques, from the most commonly applied (ethanol, ethylene oxide, 25 kGy gamma irradiation and autoclaving) [8] to the more innovative ones (Clearant® technique using radioprotectants and cold temperature) [9] have been applied to partially demineralized bone matrix (PDBM) and the effect on the osteoconductive properties has been evaluated. It has been observed that autoclaving significantly damages PDBM, while ethanol, ethylene oxide and gamma irradiation allow the maintenance of bone forming properties. With the Clearant® procedure, the radiation-induced damage to the tissue is reduced by pretreating the tissue with radioprotectants that minimize the effects of free radicals that are generated and by performing the irradiation at dry ice temperature (as described before [4, 5]). Recently Seto et al [10] also showed that an optimized combination of a cross-linking protocol and a free radical scavenging mixture allows the assurance of sterility and the maintenance of both structure and mechanical properties of tendon allografts. Research in the biosensor field can offer interesting hints; in fact enzyme loaded biosensors must be effectively sterile and, at the same time, have to maintain their functional stability. The effect of different sterilization techniques has been explored [11] and it has been observed that both glutaraldehyde and conventional 25 kGy gamma irradiation irreparably damage the sensor while a combination of 0.6% hydrogen peroxide and 7 kGy gamma irradiation assures sterility without a significant alteration in sensor functionality.', 'Sterilization, aimed at minimizing the risk of the transmission of infection, comprises one of the essential steps in the preparation of medical devices (e.g. syringes, needles, probes, catheters, sutures, bandages, etc.), implants and pharmaceutical products, including those based on collagen [12]. The typical doses applied for the sterilization of medical devices range from around 25-30 kGy, concerning which the key issue is to choose the appropriate dose that provides for effective sterilization while not damaging the material [12]. Various sterilization methods are used in the food industry. Since ionizing radiation is known to eliminate microorganisms, it is tempting to believe that simply irradiating food results in its sterilization, the killing or reduction of pathogens and the enhancement of both safety and the shelf life [[12], [13], [14]]. However, as with medical devices, it is necessary to verify that the chosen radiation dose does not damage the product or even induce its radioactivity [12]. The doses of ionizing radiation used for food sterilization purposes vary widely over a range of between 0.05 and 50 kGy depending on the purpose [12], e.g. the inhibition of germination in vegetables (0.05-0.15 kGy), the retardation of the maturation of fruit and vegetables (0.5-1 kGy), the improvement of the technological properties of foodstuffs (2-10 kGy), the disinfection of food additives (10-50 kGy), the sterilization of meat and dietetic products (30-50 kGy), etc. [12,15]. However, some populations of microorganisms require the application of extremely high and lethal doses (e.g. 100-200 kGy for Penicillium expansum, 2 MGy for Pullularia pullulans) [12]. Biopolymers such as proteins and polysaccharides, which are two of the most popular components used in biomaterials and food additives [1], are often susceptible to standard sterilization techniques, and their sterilization is often problematic [2]. Ionizing irradiation influences both the structure of collagen and its mechanical properties [16] due to cross-linking [17], and may lead to the cleavage of collagen molecules [1]. Thus, the potential impact of ionizing irradiation on the cross-linking or cleavage of collagen molecules may have differing implications for biomedical devices and food products. In the case of biomedical applications, ionizing radiation can be applied, under the appropriate conditions, for their effective sterilization without affecting their properties, as well as to optimize the physical and mechanical properties of collagen-based materials, e.g. for the precise modification of the collagen and its combination with other polymers aimed at producing controllable systems [18] and the optimization of the mechanical and structural properties of the human cornea and cornea xenografts [19,20]. In contrast, radiation sterilization potentially adversely affects the properties of a range of biomedical applications, in particular bone tissue grafts. Evidence indicates that radiation doses exceeding 20 kGy lead to the degradation of bone matrix proteins and a decrease in bone strength [21]. Currey et al. reported the significantly reduced bending strength, work to fracture, and impact energy absorption of human allogenic bone grafts gamma irradiated with doses of 29.5 kGy (the tissue bank standard), 94.7 and 17 kGy [22]. Similarly, Cornu et al. determined a significant decrease in the ultimate strength and work to failure of a cancellous bone graft following gamma irradiation with a dose of 25 kGy [23]. Such adverse impacts on the mechanical properties of bone allografts can be attributed to the degradation of the collagen in the bone matrix (collagen-based) [24]. As with biomedical applications, ionizing radiation with the appropriate parameters is able to effectively sterilize food products without inducing significant changes in the physical and chemical properties, or it can be used to improve the performance thereof. The irradiation of hog and sheep natural casings via an electron beam with a dose of up to 3 kGy has been shown to effectively reduce the content of aerobic bacteria without affecting the physiochemical or sensorial properties of the casings [25]. Similarly, Trigo et al. reported that gamma radiation applying a dose of 5 kGy provides a suitable method for the substantial reduction of the microbial population in fresh pork casings [26]. Moreover, the appropriate selection of the irradiation parameters (whether it be gamma, UV, etc.) allows for the production of tailor-made and reproducible edible collagen casings with enhanced mechanical and structural properties [27,28]. A comprehensive review of the radiation processing of proteins is provided in Ref. [29]. The degree to which the various properties are affected does not depend solely on the dose or intensity of the radiation, it is also fundamentally influenced by the presence of water, the molecules of which are split into hydroxyl and proton radicals and hydrated electrons during irradiation, which ultimately leads to the scission or cross-linking of collagen, or even both phenomena simultaneously [1,30,31]. Although many papers have addressed the effects of the gamma and UV irradiation of collagen [[32], [33], [34]], only a small number of studies have considered the mechanical and structural properties of collagen following electron beam irradiation. Landfeld et al. [35] used oscillation rheology to characterize the mechanical properties of viscoelastic bovine collagen (type I) gel with a concentration of 7.7 wt% following electron beam irradiation at low doses of up to 500 Gy. They proved that although electron beam irradiation is capable of substantially influencing the rheological properties, the irradiation dose exerted practically no impact on the molecular mass fractions, whereas it did influence the percentage of the collagen content in the fractions. Chlup et al. [36] discovered the significantly enhanced modulus of elasticity of a bovine collagen (type I) gel with a collagen content of 8.0 wt% following electron beam irradiation (doses of 0, 250, 850 and 3300 Gy). The extruded material, with fibers oriented in the direction of flow, was observed to be non-isotropic and stiffer than untreated isotropic collagen. Their results confirmed that the electron beam irradiation of a water-collagen gel significantly enhanced the final stiffness. Riedel et al. [37], who studied collagen solutions (1, 2 and 3 mg/mL) of a rat tail collagen irradiated by doses of 0-100 kGy, proved the occurrence of network stiffening of over one order of magnitude, thus indicating an increase in the cross-linking density while preserving the secondary structure of the collagen. Demeter and colleagues [18] cross-linked 1 wt% collagen hydrogels via electron beam irradiation of up to 100 kGy and proved the formation of a strong hydrogel network, an up to seven times increase in the elastic modulus (100 kGy), no significant changes in the collagen secondary structure up to 25 kGy, but partial changes associated with the loss of the triple-helical structure following higher doses (50 and 100 kGy). Sharifi et al. using corneal tissue demonstrated the effect of the polarity of the medium used for the electron beam irradiation [38]. The mechanical, structural and optical properties of the cornea can be improved by using a medium with a low relative polarity, e.g. a solution of water and ethanol (up to 100 %), the increasing concentration of which correlates with the enhancement of the mechanical properties. In contrast, the high relative polarity of pure water acts to deteriorate the mechanical properties.', 'Autoclaving is a commonly used strategy in tissue engineering labs and is readily accessible to most laboratories interested in developing biomaterials for tissue engineering. However, in this study, autoclaving at the stage of freeze-dried powder form of GelMA (A-GelMAS1) or at UV-crosslinked hydrogel form of GelMA (A-GelMAS2) lowered the compressive moduli of the hydrogels compared to untreated GelMA. Autoclaving is a high temperature process that has previously been shown to cause thermal degradation in polymers [13, 46]. Thermal degradation can also occur when autoclaving is performed on the biopolymers submerged in buffer [46, 47]. We speculate that the loss in stiffness could be attributed to the thermal degradation of the freeze-dried GelMA or GelMA hydrogels. Similarly, EtO treated GelMA (E-GelMAS1) had lower compressive modulus compared to untreated GelMA, which could also be a result of chain degradation due to EtO treatment; this has been described in earlier studies [19]. However, more studies, such as size exclusion chromatography, shall be conducted in the future to understand the effect of polymer degradation due to sterilization and its effect on mechanical behavior of GelMA hydrogels. Meanwhile, gamma (γ) irradiation had inverse consequences on the stiffness of the GelMA depending on the stage of the treatment stage. The GelMA freeze dried polymer γ-irradiated at stage-1 could only form a very weak hydrogel. However, γ-irradiation at stage-2 (γ-GelMAS2) resulted in significantly stiffer GelMA compared to untreated GelMA (figure 1(b)). Previous studies have shown that the γ-irradiation could cause additional crosslinking in the hydrogels [29, 31]. It is likely than that the increased compressive modulus in γ-GelMAS2 is a result of γ-mediated crosslinking of gelatin chains, as noted in a previous study [30]. Biodegradation is a crucial parameter that could affect cellular functions such as cell migration in 3D through enzymatic cleavage of the extracellular environment, as well as drug release from drug-loaded scaffolds. Autoclaving and EtO treatment did not alter biodegradation properties; however, the γ-GelMAS2 biodegraded significantly slower than the rest of the groups (figure 1(c)). The slower biodegradation rate could be a result of increased crosslinking and smaller pore size, which would in turn reduce the swelling of γ-GelMAS2 [2]. Subsequently, this limited swelling would reduce enzyme diffusion into the matrix to degrade the scaffold. Another possible reason could be the oxidative damage of the protein, thereby changing the target site of the collagenase. Crosslinking of the collagenase-sensitive peptide sequences of the gelatin could potentially occur due to gamma irradiation; this could in turn slow down the degradation process. Further studies need to be conducted to verify this potential side-effect of gamma irradiation. Interestingly, γ-GelMAS1 had completely different properties. The γ-GelMAS1 was extremely fragile and weak, and disintegrated in the PBS when stored overnight, which made it practically unusable as a tissue engineering scaffold. Loss of methacryloyl groups of the GelMA, as observed in the NMR data, and fewer vinyl groups available following γ-sterilization for UV polymerization could explain extremely fragile γ-GelMAS1 hydrogel that was formed upon UV exposure. Previous studies have shown that gamma radiation produces free radicals [48]. Since the γ-GelMAS1 contains unreacted methacryloyl, we hypothesize that the generation of free radicals could initiate methacryloyl reaction with nearby methacryloyl moieties. This methacryloyl reaction could lead to a reduction in the available methacryloyl moieties for UV crosslinking of γ-GelMAS1 prepolymer. The result also highlights the importance of careful consideration of the stage at which GelMA hydrogel is sterilized. We characterized the bioactivity of the GelMA hydrogels with different sterilization treatments by using two different types of primary cells in 2D and 3D. The human dermal fibroblast cells (HDFs) as well as human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) surface attachment and density was comparable for untreated, autoclaved, EtO treated and γ-treated GelMA. The observations suggest that the cell adhesive RGD ligands representation is not affected by choice of the sterilization method. However, the cellular response was different when the cells were encapsulated in GelMA prepolymer solution prior to UV crosslinking. We chose Irgacure 2959 photoinitiator for UV curing of cell-laden GelMA because of its well-known cytocompatibility and applications in tissue engineering [1, 4, 39, 49]. A recent study has also demonstrated, with multiple cell types, that the exposure to low dose 365 nm wavelength UV light (such as the dose used in our study) does not induce changes in proliferation, apoptotic induction or proteome of the cells [50]. The 7 d HDF cell viability in A-GelMAS1 was similar to the untreated GelMA in 5% and 10% hydrogels, but it was significantly reduced in E-GelMAS1. EtO treatment is known to leave toxic residues in the scaffolds [10]. The slower cell growth in E-GelMAS1 observed in this study could be due to the presence of toxic residues. Interestingly, the cellular adhesion and density was not significantly different when the cells were seeded on the surface of E-GelMAS1. This could be due to the washing of the gels prior to cell seeding that removed the toxic residues. However, washing cannot be performed when the cells are encapsulated in the prepolymer. Therefore, such residue could have more deleterious effects in 3D culture of cells in EtO treated hydrogels compared to 2D culture. This highlights that the toxic effect of the sterilization treatment should be kept in mind when choosing a sterilization strategy, particularly for 3D cell culture. The selected duration of 3D cell culture study used is acceptable for long term 3D cell culture experiments. Gamma irradiation sterilization affects PLGA implants primarily through molecular weight reduction and alterations in physical-mechanical properties. Key effects include:  
1. **Molecular Weight Degradation**: Gamma irradiation induces **chain scission** in PLGA, reducing its molecular weight (Mw), which can accelerate degradation rates and compromise mechanical integrity. This effect is dose-dependent and exacerbated at higher doses (e.g., 35–50 kGy).  
2. **Mechanical Property Changes**: At standard doses (25 kGy, room temperature), PLGA implants exhibit **increased tensile strength and Young’s modulus** but become **more brittle** (reduced maximal strain) due to crosslinking, particularly in collagen-containing hybrid systems.  
3. **Temperature Sensitivity**: Elevated temperatures during irradiation exacerbate degradation. Cooling (e.g., to 0°C or in liquid nitrogen) minimizes thermal effects, preserving Mw and structural integrity, even at higher doses.  
4. **Functional Impact**: Doses ≤25 kGy at room temperature cause **manageable changes** (e.g., increased water vapor transmission rate, slight weight loss), maintaining functionality. Higher doses (e.g., 50 kGy) risk **microstructural collapse**, severely impairing performance unless cooling is applied.  

Optimal sterilization balances dose and temperature to achieve sterility (10⁻⁶ SAL) while minimizing adverse effects on PLGA’s properties.

retrieved_contexts: ['Effects of accelerated aging and compatibilizers on the mechanical and morphological properties of polypropylene and poly(acrylonitrile‐butadiene‐styrene) blends Starch materials have attracted considerable attention in the bioplastics field due to their abundance, biodegradability and low cost. The development of thermoplastic starch (TPS) from starch granules and plasticizer allows for the transformation of native starch into a fluid similar to other conventional thermoplastics.1, 2 This is achieved through the application of heat and in the presence of water and/or another plasticizer for starch. The advantage of TPS is that it can be processed using typical melt-processing equipment. Thermoplastic starch on its own, however, has certain critical weaknesses, namely poor mechanical strength and a susceptibility to pick up moisture. These failings can be overcome by blending thermoplastic starch with other polymers. The conversion of native starch into a fully plasticized thermoplastic starch using melt-extrusion processing is a complex operation and an understanding of the time/temperature boundaries ultimately required for the successful plasticization of starch on melt-processing equipment is critical.3 It is well known in polymer blends that the morphology control of the respective phases is a key factor in achieving the desired material properties. Typically, the morphology of polymer blends is strongly dependant on their composition, the viscoelastic properties of their components, the interfacial tension and the processing conditions. The phases in a polymer blend can be structured in droplet, fiber, laminated, and cocontinuous forms.4 Recently, even droplet-in-droplet and multiple percolated cocontinuous systems have been developed.5 A cocontinuous binary blend morphology is one in which neither of the blend phases can be defined as the matrix or the dispersed phase. It forms highly interconnected and intertwining structures and both the component phases remain fully continuous throughout the blend.', 'In this work, the processing and properties of blown films prepared from thermoplastic corn starch (TPS) and polycaprolactone (PCL) were studied, in particular at high TPS content. The influence of processing parameters and material moisture content on the tensile properties was also studied. The results show that final film properties are mainly controlled by the draw ratio, blow-up ratio and PCL concentration in the blends. The results also show that PCL/TPS films are less hydrophilic as PCL content increases. Finally, it was found that a very narrow processing window exists for this blend. © 2011 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J Appl Polym Sci, 2011. This results in an accumulation of material and leads to an environmental management control problem. One possible solution is the use of biodegradable polymers and their blends to produce films. However, there are some issues to be solved, such as lower mechanical properties, processing problems and higher cost of producing compared with conventional plastics.1-22 Starch is a low cost biodegradable polymer obtained from renewable resources, and it is considered a promising candidate for developing biodegradable materials.1-22 However, starch has poor mechanical properties and poor melt processability.5, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16 To be processed starch has been plasticized with water, glycerol and other agents, the obtained material is widely known as thermoplastic starch (TPS).2-4, 7, 8, 10-12, 14-16, 18-20, 22 A recent review on starch-based polymers processing was presented by Liu et al.20 The techniques used to produce starch-based materials include compression molding,3, 5, 9, 13, 19 injection molding,4, 7, 8, 14 extrusion,3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 14-16 and film casting1, 17, 19 and blowing.2, 7, 8, 18-20, 22 One of the most serious difficulties for production of starch-based films is poor melt strength, sticky film surface, and foaming.18 To improve melt strength and other properties, several methods have been proposed, including blending with biodegradable polymers such as polycaprolactone (PCL),3-8, 13, 14, 20, 21 poly(lactic acid),5, 15, 20, 21 or poly(vinyl alcohol).1, 20 Since starch is immiscible with these polymers, a compatibilization may be required to obtain a useful product.5, 7, 9, 14, 15 In addition, the mechanical properties of starch-based blends evolve with time through a series of complex processes like retrogradation and plasticization from environmental moisture.1, 9, 13, 16, 22', 'Thermoplastic starch (TPS) Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is a biodegradable biopolymer derived from starch-rich crops such as corn, wheat, and potatoes. Exhibiting thermoplastic behavior, TPS can be processed using conventional plastic manufacturing techniques, including extrusion, injection molding, and film blowing. Due to its renewable origin and inherent biodegradability, TPS has emerged as a promising material for environmentally sustainable packaging solutions [111]. TPS primarily consists of amylose and amylopectin, the two principal polysaccharides in starch. Amylose is a mostly linear polymer of glucose units linked via α−1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is a highly branched polymer featuring both α−1,4- and α−1,6-glycosidic linkages. To produce TPS, starch is plasticized using agents such as glycerol, sorbitol, or water, which enhance its processability and mechanical properties by disrupting inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonds [23]. The typical manufacturing process involves starch extraction through wet milling or enzymatic hydrolysis, followed by compounding with plasticizers under controlled heat and pressure to yield TPS in the form of films, sheets, or molded items [132]. TPS is widely utilized in producing biodegradable products such as bags, trays, containers, and agricultural mulch films. Its biodegradability, coupled with favorable water vapor barrier properties, makes it particularly attractive for food packaging applications [111]. By replacing conventional plastics with TPS-based materials, it is possible to substantially mitigate plastic waste accumulation and environmental pollution, thereby advancing sustainability in consumer and agricultural sectors. Nevertheless, TPS does present certain limitations, including lower mechanical strength, heightened sensitivity to moisture, and reduced processing compatibility compared to synthetic polymers [23]. Despite these challenges, TPS continues to gain prominence globally. According to Mordor Intelligence (2024), the thermoplastic starch market was valued at approximately 219.20 kilotons in 2024 and is projected to Reach 333.92 kilotons by 2029, reflecting a robust compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.79% over the forecast period.', '35% of isosorbide and MCC addition improved these properties in a greater extent. IntroductionThe replacement of conventional petroleum-based polymers by other more environmentally friendly polymers has been focused research in recent times. To this end, starch is one of the most promising biopolymers due to its natural origin from renewable sources, economically competitive and biodegradable. Native starch is not a thermoplastic polymer in a natural way, due to its degradation temperature is lower than the temperature required for plasticization. However, in the presence of a suitable plasticizer, under temperature and shear conditions, it is converted in a thermoplastic starch (TPS) able to be processed as the conventional thermoplastic polymers [1].Plasticizers for starches must be small molecules capable of diffusing between the starch molecules and they must own groups capable of forming hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups of starch molecules. Glycerol is, among the polyols, the most used plasticizer for starch due to its low cost, high boiling point and no toxicity. However, the interaction between glycerol and starch is not strong enough, so the starch often recrystallizes after being stored for a period of time. This undesirable process, very frequent in the TPS, is known as retrogradation [2,3]. Isosorbide is a bicyclic compound obtained from the glucose dehydration, characterized by having two OH groups and two oxygen atoms intercalated in the double carbon ring. Recently, isosorbide has been tested as a novel, effective and green plasticizer for starch due to its biodegradability and no toxicity, which prevents the starch retrogradation [4,5]. Although the studies about the use of isosorbide as a plasticizer for starches are scarce at the moment, its use is revealed as an interesting strategy to obtain more durable materials that do not present the disadvantages generated by retrogradation processes.The TPS have two main disadvantages compared to the common thermoplastic polymers including poor mechanical properties and a low moisture resistance. A strategy widely used in recent years to overcoming the TPS drawbacks consists of the incorporation of biodegradable micro or nanoparticles used as a filler in the TPS matrix. Some fillers used were clays and silicates [6], starch nanoparticles [7], talc nanoparticles [8], cellulose nanofibers [9] and cellulose nanocrystals [10].Microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) was revealed as a good candidate for the development of completely natural and biodegradable biocomposites, with significant improvements in the properties of TPS plasticized with glycerol [11,12]. However, there are no previous studies of starch-based materials plasticized with isosorbide, which have been reinforced, neither with microparticles nor with nanoparticles, in the bibliography consulted by the authors.Attending to the benefits described above, it is expected that the combination of both, the use of isosorbide as a plasticizer and the incorporation of MCC as a filler, leads to TPS materials with better mechanical and barrier properties, which are completely biodegradable and do not suffer retrogradation phenomena.Looking for this goal, we have studied recently novel biocomposites based on corn starch plasticized with isosorbide and filled with MCC (TPS/MCC biocomposites) prepared by melt processing. In that work, the effect of isosorbide as plasticizer, compared to the common glycerol, the plasticizer content and the MCC addition as filler were evaluated on processing properties, morphology, crystallinity and thermal stability. As a result, although the processing of materials with isosorbide needed higher shear and longer times to complete the plasticization compared to materials plasticized with glycerol, it could be carried out at lower temperatures. The thermal stability was enhanced with the use of isosorbide as plasticizer, attributed to a better starch-plasticizer interaction. The biocomposites showed a good filler-matrix adhesion attributed to the chemical similarity of starch and cellulose. Also, it was shown that isosorbide is adequate to prevent the retrogradation of starch, since the crystallinity remained constant along the time, while with glycerol the crystallinity increased [13].The improvements observed in these interesting green biocomposites places them as potential candidates for their use in specific applications as food packaging. In this field, the applications of the materials based on thermoplastic starches were, until now, restricted to short-time applications due to the retrogradation phenomena that they suffer. As isosorbide plasticized biocomposites have shown they do not suffer from this phenomena, they become a good option to be used even in food packaging applications for a longer time. Nevertheless, the study of other properties in a major extent is required to get usable materials. In this sense, new biocomposites, starting from the materials studied previously in the work described above, are developed in this work. Factors as the type and proportion of plasticizer used and the addition of MCC to the biocomposite, as well as the effect of the plasticizer in the function of MCC, were studied and related with the TPS properties. The structural interactions, the dynamomechanical properties and the behavior under environmental factors: water absorption and biodegradation by soil burial were analyzed more widely to check their use in food packaging industry, especially for their application during longer times. The analysis of the stability of the structure and the properties along the time, analyzing the retrogradation phenomenon was made to complete the study. The control of all these factors resulted to be crucial for the application of this new biocomposites in the food packaging industry. However, due to the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in starch molecules, the melting temperature of starch is higher than its decomposition temperature, rendering it unsuitable for melt processing. To address this, a substantial amount of plasticizer must be added to starch under high temperature and shear to facilitate plasticization, resulting in thermoplastic starch (TPS) with melt processability. Common plasticizers for TPS include glycerol,21 citric acid,22 glycerol triacetate,23 formamide, water and small molecules of poly(vinyl alcohol),24-27 with glycerol being the most commonly used and effective. However, the low mechanical strength of TPS and the issue of plasticizer migration and exudation contribute to a significant reduction in the mechanical strength of PBAT/TPS blend materials. Additionally, the strong hygroscopicity of glycerol leads to increased water absorption in PBAT/TPS blend materials. Therefore, improving the mechanical strength of TPS and addressing plasticizer migration and exudation are essential to effectively produce low-cost PBAT/TPS blend films with high starch content. Sorbitol, a commonly used sweetener in daily life, is obtained through glucose-catalyzed hydrogenation. Esmaeili et al. reported in 2017 that using sorbitol as a plasticizer for starch resulted in TPS with higher tensile strength and elastic modulus than when glycerol was used as the plasticizer.21 Sorbitol melts under TPS processing conditions, plasticizing starch by disrupting intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Excess sorbitol solidifies after processing, preventing plasticizer exudation and migration. However, using sorbitol alone as a plasticizer for starch requires a longer plasticization time and higher processing temperature, potentially causing starch coking issues during processing. Furthermore, ordinary starch can be modified to obtain hydroxypropyl starch by grafting epoxy propane, weakening the hydrogen bonds within starch molecules.28 This modification allows plasticizers to enter and plasticize the starch more effectively. Typically, after plasticization, the disrupted linear and branched starch chains can recrystallize into different ordered structures in a process known as regeneration.29 The regenerative capacity of hydroxypropyl starch decreases due to steric hindrance from hydroxypropyl groups,28 stabilizing the performance of plasticized starch and increasing the transparency of the resulting blend films.30 Therefore, the use of hydroxypropyl starch can not only reduce the amount of plasticizer used, increase plasticization efficiency and effectively avoid the transfer and precipitation of small-molecule plasticizers, but also reduce the impact of recrystallization of TPS on film properties.', 'There has been growing interest in development of bio-based thermoplastic products to reduce the environmental impact of plastic waste for the last two decades. Starch is one of the most abundant renewable resources on earth that attracts worldwide attention [1]. Native Starch itself cannot show thermoplastic behavior due to unusually low decomposition temperature, which is lower than its glass transition temperature (Tg). There are plenty intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen-bondings present in starches that interact with each other to form the complete microcrystalline structure in starch, which is the main reason for relatively high Tg of granular starches. The addition of plasticizers [2,3,4] and exposition to thermo-mechanical energy leads to disruption of the semicrystalline structure, resulting in an amorphous material termed thermoplastic starches (TPS). Its processing typically involves an irreversible order-disorder transition, which is the disruption of hydrogen-bondings and/or molecular organization within the starch granules. TPS products have being widely used in the plastic market [4,5,6,7], but the resistance of TPS to shock or moisture is significantly poorer than many other commodity resins [8]. TPS suffers from several limitations, such as poor mechanical strengths and moisture resistant properties during long-term storage. Rapid rise in moisture contents leads to significant reduction in mechanical retention strengths of hydrophilic TPS resins during storage [9,10,11,12,13]. “A”, “B” and “C” types of crystallinity are the mainly three types of starch crystals observed in the X-ray diffraction patterns of varying kinds of starches [8, 14,15,16]. Other amylose types of crystallinity were also found during thermomechanical processing of starches [16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23]. However, significant “retrogradation” effect was observed during conditioning processes of TPS resins, in which, the starch molecules reassociate in more ordered structures, such as, formation of new crystal structures [24,25,26]. In fact, recrystallization of starch molecules limits practical applications of starch and/or TPS based materials, since they become too fragile to use during long-term storage [27].', 'There is a growing interest nowadays in reducing the amount of waste which is caused by the disposable packaging mainly from petroleum-based plastics. Therefore, a large body of works has been already devoted to develop polymers from renewable resources. The related studies often addressed the development of fully bio-based and thus biodegradable packaging materials. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is considered as one of the most promising biomaterials for packaging purpose, mainly because of its low price and biodegradability.1-6 Note that starch is a renewable feedstock considering the fact that it can be recovered from numerous plants (potato, corn, sago, etc.).5 TPS may serve as a “green” packaging material, which can be produced using common thermoplastic processing technologies thereby considering some specific characteristics of starch.1 Starch itself is a polysaccharide having no thermoplastic feature; however, it can be brought into a “thermoplastic-like” state under specific conditions (using plasticizer and/or mechanical shear).7, 8 Melt compounding of thermoplastic materials is performed mostly in an internal mixer or in single- or twin-screw extruders. While internal mixing is a batch-type method, extrusion is a continuous process, which is not only a cost-efficient route but also allows for the combination of thermoplastics polymers with other polymers and/or reinforcements.2, 5, 9, 10 By using one- or two-step extrusion process the properties (mechanical, thermal, barrier…) of the TPS-based systems can be tuned to meet the application requirements. For TPS material development, however, other techniques such as dissolution followed by solution casting can also be used.3, 5, 11-13 Like any common thermoplastic polymer, starch can be processed via melt compounding techniques in presence of suitable plasticizers.2, 9, 14 Various plasticizers have been tried to convert starch into TPS but the most widely used ones are water, polyols (e.g., glycerol), vegetable oils, and sorbitol.9, 15-17 Being a by-product of biodiesel production glycerol is low priced and thus especially suited for mass production of TPS even if the mechanical properties of sorbitol plasticized TPS have been found to be slightly better.16 The amount of plasticizer used can be varied in certain limits to adjust the stiffness and strength of TPS to our needs. However, one has to bear in mind that if the plasticizer content in the mixture is not optimal, processing issues are often encountered,4, 18 also leading to the presence of residual granules (referred to “ghost granules” in the literature.1, 4). The presence of these ghost granules decreases the mechanical properties and gives a hazy appearance of the originally transparent material. This should be avoided in many cases, especially for selected packaging applications. Among the main disadvantages of TPS its hydrophilic character and poor mechanical properties should be mentioned. From this reason many studies have addressed the improvement of the properties of TPS.3, 9, 10, 12, 17, 19 Trials, done so far, include chemical modifications, grafting, blending with other biopolymers, and also the incorporation of a reinforcing particles.3, 5, 9, 11-13, 17, 20-24 Main goal of these studies was to improve the properties, while still preserving the biodegradability of the related TPS-based systems. These additives can improve the mechanical and barrier properties which are of great relevance for packaging. The dispersion of these particles and its effect on the properties of TPS were already topics of some publications.5, 9, 10, 13, 15, 17, 19, 25 Extensive kneading associated with melt shearing during extrusion support the disintegration of the entangled cellulose micro- and nanofibers when introduced in dry form. Extrusion melt compounding is also the right way when these cellulosic fillers are incorporated from a premix or aqueous dispersion.9, 26 In the latter case vent ports of the extruder may work for the evaporation of the excess water as discussed later.', 'Plasticization is often used for the modification of biopolymers to improve their processability and/or other properties demanded by a specific application. Plasticizers exchange the intermolecular bonds among polymer chains to bonds between the macromolecules and the small molecular weight compound thus promoting conformational changes resulting in increased deformability. Both the glass transition and the processing temperature of the material decrease, thus enabling the melt processing of heat-sensitive polymers, like poly(3-hydroxybutyrate), at lower temperatures [17]. The melt processing of starch is impossible without gelatinization, i.e. destroying the crystalline structure of native starch by the use of a plasticizer [18], [19]. The material obtained in this way is referred to as thermoplastic starch (TPS). The nature and concentration of the plasticizer strongly influence the rheological and mechanical properties of TPS. Neat starch has a high glass transition temperature, and its relative large modulus and strength is accompanied by poor deformability and impact resistance due to the limited conformational mobility of its stiff chains [20]. Elastomeric behavior would be advantageous for several applications, which can be achieved, among other methods, by decreasing Tg below ambient temperature via plasticization [21]. Numerous studies and patents describe the plasticization of starch using either low molecular weight or polymeric compounds [21], [22]. The plasticizers applied are mainly low molecular weight polar compounds such as water, glycerol, urea and formamide [22]. However, as in their elaborate work Lourdin et al. [21] point out, TPS is always a ternary system, since the water content of plasticized starch should always be taken into consideration. Recently, using state of the art visualization techniques Paes et al. have shown [23] that moisture content and interaction with water determines the fracture mechanism in cassava starch films as well as in gelatin and hydroxypropyl cellulose. Although water is a very efficient plasticizer for starch too, usually compounds with higher boiling point are preferred because they decrease water sensitivity and lead to more stable properties [19].', 'Disposal of enormous amounts of waste synthetic polymers pollutes the environment due to their high microbial resistance [1]. Raising this problem has led to growing attention to natural and biodegradable polymers such as starch from plants. Starch is a natural, renewable and inexpensive polymer, which can be decomposed with bacteria in the environments [2]. For processing starch it is necessary to destruct starch granules with addition of plasticizers (e.g. glycerol) under high temperature and extensive shear stress conditions, which results in the gel like material which is called thermoplastic starch (TPS) [3]. Since TPS is very moisture sensitive with poor mechanical properties [4], [5], blending with other polymer is recommended [6], [7]. The most studied polymer to be blended with TPS is polyethylene (PE), because of its widespread utilization for packaging and its strong resistance to biodegradation [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. However, in the case of composites of starch granules and polyethylene, starch granules behave as a stiff filler and increase the modulus [14], [15]. Because of high interfacial tension between starch and polyethylene [16], it is necessary to use a compatibilizer to increase the interfacial adhesion and enhance the mechanical properties of the blend [17], [18]. This improvement was attributed to the esterification reaction between maleic anhydride groups of PE-g-MA and hydroxyl groups of starch, and good interaction of its non-polar chain with the PE matrix [23]. Reactive compatibilization decreases the interfacial tension and leads to finer morphology [24]. Besides the interfacial tension, the morphological properties of the blends are affected by the rheological properties of the components, processing conditions and the component composition of the blends [25], [26], [27]. Rodriguez et al. showed that, by controlling the processing conditions, TPS and glycerol contents, a wide range of different morphologies such as spherical, fibrillar and even co-continuous can be formed [28]. The co-continuous morphology appears in a broad range, especially near the phase inversion point and usually at high concentrations of the minor phase [29], [30]. There are many empirical and semi-empirical models for describing the phase inversion composition. Although most of these models used the viscosity ratio of the components to predict the phase inversion point, there are some models which consider other properties such as elasticity or damping factor to fit experimental results. Since the phase inversion phenomenon is not as yet fully understood, there is no general model predicting the phase inversion composition [31]. Although many studies have been done on PE/TPS blends, most of these works were performed at relatively low TPS content where the PE is matrix. At high TPS content, the morphology of the starch blends changes significantly and phase inversion occurs. Above the phase inversion concentration, the TPS as a dispersed phase turns into the matrix which results in poor mechanical properties and high sensitivity to moisture of the blend [32], [33].', "Starch is a low cost biodegradable polymer obtained from renewable resources, and it is considered a promising candidate for developing biodegradable materials.1-22 However, starch has poor mechanical properties and poor melt processability.5, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16 To be processed starch has been plasticized with water, glycerol and other agents, the obtained material is widely known as thermoplastic starch (TPS).2-4, 7, 8, 10-12, 14-16, 18-20, 22 A recent review on starch-based polymers processing was presented by Liu et al.20 The techniques used to produce starch-based materials include compression molding,3, 5, 9, 13, 19 injection molding,4, 7, 8, 14 extrusion,3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 14-16 and film casting1, 17, 19 and blowing.2, 7, 8, 18-20, 22 One of the most serious difficulties for production of starch-based films is poor melt strength, sticky film surface, and foaming.18 To improve melt strength and other properties, several methods have been proposed, including blending with biodegradable polymers such as polycaprolactone (PCL),3-8, 13, 14, 20, 21 poly(lactic acid),5, 15, 20, 21 or poly(vinyl alcohol).1, 20 Since starch is immiscible with these polymers, a compatibilization may be required to obtain a useful product.5, 7, 9, 14, 15 In addition, the mechanical properties of starch-based blends evolve with time through a series of complex processes like retrogradation and plasticization from environmental moisture.1, 9, 13, 16, 22 There are reported some studies on TPS1, 18, 19, 22 and blends of TPS with other nonbiodegradable2 and biodegradable polymers6-8 films. The film blow processing of starch was first reported by Otey et al.2 using different ratio of polyethylene, poly (ethylene-co-acrylic acid) (PEAA), and starch. Good filmability was achieved by adding low amounts of ammonia and urea to improve starch-PEAA interactions. Thunwall et al.18 reported a processing window for the film blowing of TPS film as a function of water and glycerol content and processing temperature. Altskär et al.19 found that residual starch granules have a negative effect on the film blowing properties and could cause failure of the bi-axially stretched bubble. Kenley et al.28 decribed three major features of PLGA degradation curves: 1) Induction period where mass and molecular weight values are unchanged; 2) onset of molecular weight loss becoming exponential with time; and 3) erosion onset. Several factors contribute to the hydrolytic degradation (molecular weight loss) of aliphatic polyesters. Among these are molecular weight, composition (monomer selection, ratios for copolymers), initiator selection, and morphology. Hydrolytic degradation of biodegradable polyesters occurs by random or nonrandom chain scission. Hydrolysis of linear PLLA and PLGA is generally considered to proceed by random cleavage of ester bonds. However, nonrandom ester cleavage of PLGA arms from a PEG block has been observed in 2-arm PEG-PLGA.29, 30 The chain scission mechanism in multiarm PLLA and PLGA has been shown to be dependent on the backbone material.20, 29 Random chain scission of the PLLA and PLGA branches has been observed in polymers with a backbone of diethyaminoethyl dextran chloride20 and nonrandom chain scission when the backbone was dextran sulfate sodium,20 4-arm PEO, or 8-arm PEO.29 Cleavage of the branches from the core material was followed by the degradation of the resulting linear polyester fragments via the random scission mechanism until the molecular weight was low enough for the fragments to be water-soluble. When the polymer fragments are small enough to be water-soluble then erosion (mass loss) is observed. Polymer mass loss may occur via a surface or a bulk erosion mechanism. Polymers that undergo bulk erosion absorb water into the polymer matrix and undergo hydrolysis uniformly throughout the sample. Surface-eroding polymers do not absorb water into the matrix rather, erode from the outer layer in. Bulk erosion is considered to be the primary erosion mechanism for PLA and PLGA, however, it has been shown that PLA and PLGA erode in a nonuniform manner with faster degradation in the center of implants than at the surface.31 This heterogeneous bulk erosion is caused by autocatalysis, accelerated degradation inside the polymer matrix by trapped acidic degradation products. It is expected that the 2-arm PEG-polyesters and the multiarm PG-polyesters in this study demonstrate similar degradation behavior to the 2-arm, 4-arm, and 8-arm PEG/PEO polymers discussed above. Degradation and erosion behavior of linear and branched poly(L-lactide)s and poly(L-lactide-co-glycolide)s were investigated. Based solely on the provided context, the mechanism of chain scission in the hydrolysis of ester bonds involves the following:

1.  **Random cleavage of ester bonds**: Hydrolysis occurs by the cleavage of ester bonds along the polymer backbone. This cleavage is described as "random" for several polymers, including linear PLLA, PLGA, PCL, PLA, and PPDO ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [10], [12], [13], [15]).
2.  **Attack by water**: The hydrolysis reaction involves water molecules reacting with the ester bonds (C(=O)-O) in the polymer chain ([15]).
3.  **Formation of acidic end groups**: Chain scission generates carboxylic acid end groups (-COOH) on the resulting polymer fragments ([10], [11], [12], [13], [15]).
4.  **Autocatalysis**: The carboxylic acid end groups generated by the chain scission act catalytically, accelerating the hydrolysis of adjacent ester bonds. This leads to faster degradation, particularly within the bulk of the polymer matrix where acidic products can be trapped ([1], [2], [10], [12], [13], [15]).
5.  **Preferential attack in amorphous regions**: For semi-crystalline polymers (like PLA, PLLA, PCL), hydrolysis occurs preferentially in the amorphous regions due to better water permeability compared to the crystalline regions ([10], [12], [13]).

**In summary:** The mechanism involves water molecules randomly cleaving ester bonds along the polymer backbone (chain scission), breaking the long polymer chains into shorter fragments. This scission generates carboxylic acid end groups that catalyze further hydrolysis (autocatalysis), accelerating the degradation process. In semi-crystalline polymers, this process occurs more readily in the amorphous regions.

The water oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to the formation of a carboxylic acid end group and a hydroxyl end group. The reaction is often acid-catalyzed, meaning the generated carboxylic acid can accelerate further degradation (autocatalysis).

Zinc and magnesium alloys are grouped with biodegradable materials for implants due to their inherent ability to degrade in physiological environments, essential biocompatibility, and role as biologically vital elements. Here's the breakdown based on the context:

1. **Biodegradability**:  
   - Both metals corrode in the body, eliminating the need for secondary removal surgeries. Magnesium (Mg) degrades rapidly, often too quickly for clinical needs, while zinc (Zn) exhibits an intermediate corrosion rate closer to the ideal for bone or cardiovascular applications.  
   - Iron (Fe), another biodegradable metal, degrades too slowly, leading to complications akin to permanent implants. Zinc is highlighted as the most promising candidate due to its balanced degradation rate.  

2. **Biocompatibility and Biological Roles**:  
   - **Magnesium**: Essential for bone metabolism, promotes osteoblast activity, and mimics bone’s elastic modulus, reducing stress shielding. However, rapid Mg corrosion releases hydrogen gas, raising local pH and compromising mechanical integrity.  
   - **Zinc**: A critical nutrient for immune function, enzyme activity, and tissue repair. Its corrosion products (e.g., Zn²⁺ ions) are non-toxic and may enhance osteogenesis.  

3. **Mechanical Adjustability via Alloying**:  
   - Pure Zn and Mg lack sufficient mechanical strength for load-bearing applications. Alloying with elements like Mg (for Zn) or Zn, Ca, and rare earths (for Mg) improves tensile strength and ductility. For example, Zn-1%Mg alloys achieve a balance of strength and plasticity, while Mg-Zn-Ca alloys are clinically used in screws.  
   - Advanced processing methods (e.g., hydrostatic extrusion, hot rolling) further refine grain structures, enhancing mechanical properties without compromising biodegradation.  

4. **Clinical Necessity**:  
   - Permanent implants (e.g., titanium, stainless steel) risk long-term complications like inflammation, stress shielding, and secondary surgeries. Biodegradable Mg/Zn alloys address these by degrading *in situ* after fulfilling their mechanical role during healing.  

In summary, zinc and magnesium alloys are classified as biodegradable implant materials because they safely degrade *in vivo*, provide temporary mechanical support, and leverage their biological benefits, despite challenges in optimizing corrosion rates and mechanical properties through alloying and processing.
reference: Zinc and Magnesium alloys are biodegradable metals. They corrode/degrade in the physiological environment to form non-toxic ions ($Mg^{2+}$, $Zn^{2+}$) that are metabolized or excreted. They provide higher initial load-bearing capacity than polymers for orthopedic applications (bone screws) and degrade as the bone heals.

In PLA, common plasticizers include citrate esters like acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) and triethyl citrate (TEC), glycerides, polyethylene glycol (PEG), and lactic acid esters. While these plasticizers enhance flexibility, they present several disadvantages. They can migrate from the polymer to the surface or environment, reducing their effectiveness [11]. Certain plasticizers may have toxic or allergic effects on humans and animals, especially in medical or food packaging applications [12]. Additionally, not all plasticizers are fully compatible with PLA, possibly resulting in non-uniform distribution and adverse mechanical and optical properties [13]. Research focuses on bio-based plasticizers for PLA to find alternatives that offer better performance without the associated disadvantages of traditional plasticizers [14], [15]. Alternatively, blending PLA with other polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL) and polybutylene succinate (PBS) can enhance flexibility and processability but presents challenges. Incompatibility can cause phase separation, negatively affecting mechanical properties and appearance. Optimizing processing conditions for each polymer combination increases costs and manufacturing complexity. Adding certain polymers may also affect PLA's biodegradation rate and mode, undesirable for ecological applications [16], [17]. Phenethyl esters are compounds of great interest due to their unique chemical properties formed by esterification of carboxylic acids with different chain length with phenol [18]. Both products involved can be obtained from natural resources, a sustainable route for the obtention of biobased material with low impact for the environment [19]. The ideal plasticizer is proposed to possess a combination of structural features, including aliphatic chains that act as spacers to increase the free volume and consequently lower the glass transition temperature, ester groups that contribute to molecular cohesion, and aromatic rings that enhance compatibility with the polymer matrix, thereby promoting miscibility [20]. In this context, phenethyl esters represent a promising alternative, as they incorporate all the aforementioned functional groups, facilitating the development of an effective plasticizer. As part of the ongoing search for high-performance plasticizers, the use of naturally derived compounds containing ester functionalities has previously been explored [21]. Importantly, these phenethyl esters have not been previously used as plasticizers for PLA, confirming the novel opportunity to explore their potential in enhancing the mechanical and processing properties of the polymer. Phenethyl esters have diverse applications, due to their chemical and sensory properties [22]. Phenethyl propionate serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, including steroid hormones used in hormonal therapies [23]. As described, these esters generally have a favorable safety profile, making them suitable for use in products with direct skin, food, or medical contact.", 'Citrate esters triethyl citrate, tributyl citrate, and acetyl tributyl citrate were used as plasticizers for amorphous poly(D,L-lactide) (PDLLA). Nevertheless, phase separation was detected in plasticized PLA formulations with high MLO content (above 15-20 phr MLO), which had a negative effect on overall toughness. © 2017 Society of Chemical Industry The increasing concern about the environment and sustainable development is currently leading the search and development of new materials. Today, a wide variety of biobased and/or biodegradable polymers with potential use at an industrial scale can be obtained from renewable resources.1 These polymers could be used as environmentally friendly solutions as against conventional petroleum-based and non-biodegradable polymers in blend formulations,2 disposable products,3, 4 medical devices,5 packaging,6, 7 green composites,8-13 etc. It is worth noting the increasing use of aliphatic polyesters,14 polysaccharides15 and protein-derived polymers.16, 17 Despite the wide variety of biobased polymers, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most promising polymers due to its excellent balance between mechanical, barrier and processing properties, and an increasingly competitive price. It is obtained from lactic acid derived from several cereals and tubers, mainly from corn, wheat, beetroot, potato and other starch-rich products. Its biodegradability in natural media makes it the ideal choice for a wide range of disposable products that can undergo disintegration by hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation in controlled conditions (moisture, temperature, bacterial growth, etc.).18-20 Moreover, PLA is characterized by high biocompatibility and a good balance of mechanical properties, thus widening its uses in the medical sector,21 such as in resorbable interference screws and prostheses subjected to moderate mechanical stresses.22 In addition to this, its relatively good resistance to moisture and fats, together with overall balanced barrier properties to flavours and odours, makes PLA a good candidate for the food packaging industry. One important drawback of PLA is its extremely high stiffness, which leads to high fragility, and this fact restricts some engineering uses that require high toughness behaviour. To overcome this drawback, various approaches have been explored in the last few years. New flexible copolyesters have been investigated as toughened alternatives to brittle PLA formulations.23, 24 In these works, the results showed increased elongation at break values and a marked improvement in ductile properties. A wide variety of conventional plasticizers have been reported to greatly increase PLA ductility,25 but the potential toxic risks associated to some of these plasticizers restrict their use in some sectors such as food packaging, medical devices, toys, etc. For this reason, new plasticizers are continually being demanded by industry with the aim of reducing the toxic risk related to plasticizer migration.26, 27 Vegetable oils such as those obtained from linseed, rape, soybean and cottonseed, among others, offer a natural source of chemicals for the polymer industry.28, 29 They can readily be converted into their corresponding epoxidized oils by epoxidation, leading to materials with potential use as biobased plasticizers and matrices for green composites. Several epoxidized vegetable oils such as epoxidized linseed oil,30 epoxidized soybean oil (ESBO), epoxidized castor oil, epoxy octyl stearate31 and epoxidized cottonseed oil32-36 have been reported as environmentally friendly plasticizers for a wide variety of polymers.32, 37 The use of monomeric and polymeric plasticizers has also been reported in the last decade. Monomeric plasticizers such as acetylbutyl ricinoleate, acetyltributyl citrate, ricinoleic acid, adipate 2-ethylhexyl, diisodecyl adipate, octyl oleate, octyl trimellitate, methyl methacrylate, and glycidyl methacrylate, among others,14, 16, 38 have given interesting results in PLA plasticization. Also, several polymeric plasticizers such as aliphatic polyesters from dicarboxylic acids, polypropylene glycol adipate, thermoplastic starch, polycaprolactone, etc.,2, 39-44 have proved their efficiency in plasticizing PLA formulations.', 'Various changes of PLA packing structure to shift Tc have been reported. Conventionally, addition of a nucleating agent is the simplest way to induce crystallization. Several kinds of nucleating agents, such as talc [7], montmorillonite [8], and polysaccharides, e.g., chitosan, cellulose, starch [9], and nucleic bases [10] have been reported. A well-known example is the case of the stereocomplex between poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), which leads to an increase in the Tm of PLA to as high as 250 °C [11], [12]. It should be pointed out that although the stereocomplex successfully enhances the thermal stability, it has no effect on the Tg, and, as a consequence, the product obtained is still brittle. While crystallization is related to the chain packing, the lowering of Tg, in contrast, needs an initiation of chain mobility. Various types of compounds, such as tributyl citrate [13], [14], diethyl bishydroxymethylmalonate [13], and poly(ethylene glycol) [14], [15], [16], including partial fatty acid esters [14], have been reported as plasticizers to improve the flexibility of PLA. For example, in the case of 10 wt% poly(ethylene glycol) in PLA, the thermal characteristics of the product drastically changed, e.g., an increase in elongation at break of 10-15-fold and a decrease in Tg to 30 °C [16], [17]. In addition, the blending of PLA with biodegradable plasticizers such as poly(ε-caprolactone) [12], poly(butylene succinate) [18], [19], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) [20], and poly(hydroxy butyrate) [21], [22] to maintain the attractive attribute of biodegradability, have also been reported. Although the cases above showed changes in various parameters, such as the lowering of Tc and Tg, and an increase of crystallization rate and elongation at break, etc., at a certain level, the PLA products with those additives still exhibited a phase separation and, in some cases, the leaching of additives. In addition, obtaining both crystallization and plasticization, which are two different extremes, is still an unattained goal.']

Based solely on the provided context, the role of citrate ester plasticizers (like ATBC and TEC) in PLA formulations is:

1.  **Reduce the Glass Transition Temperature (Tg):** Citrate esters decrease the Tg of PLA, making the polymer less brittle and more flexible at room temperature and physiological conditions ([1], [2], [3], [8], [9]).
2.  **Increase Ductility and Elongation at Break:** Adding citrate esters significantly improves the elongation at break and ductility of PLA. For example, adding 20 wt% citrate ester increases elongation at break to approximately 300% ([8], [9]).
3.  **Enhance Processability:** The incorporation of plasticizers like citrate esters improves the processability of PLA ([7]).
4.  **Associated Disadvantages:**
    *   **Degrade Tensile Strength:** The addition of citrate esters reduces the tensile strength and modulus of PLA. A 10 wt% addition can decrease tensile strength by over 50% ([2]).
    *   **Potential Migration:** Citrate esters, being low molecular weight molecules, can migrate out of the PLA matrix over time, leading to a loss of plasticizing effect and potential brittleness, as well as possible environmental or health concerns ([1], [7], [8]).
    *   **Compatibility/Miscibility Issues:** At higher concentrations or with higher molecular weight citrate esters, phase separation and lack of miscibility with PLA can occur, negatively affecting mechanical properties and appearance ([1], [2]). Optimal performance is typically found at specific concentrations (e.g., around 20 wt%).
    *   **Potential Toxicity Concerns:** Certain citrate esters may have toxic or allergic effects, particularly relevant for medical or food packaging applications ([1]).
