retrieved_contexts: ['Research in polymer nanocomposites has been motivated by the opportunities to enhance or augment the physical properties of polymeric materials. Biomass-derived fillers, including cellulose nanofibers or lignin, have attracted particular interest in the context of ‘sustainable materials engineering’ as a means towards more benign (and low-energy) polymer materials. However, although the concept of reducing the environmental footprint of synthetic polymers by dilution with bio-sourced fillers appears to be straightforward, the loss of desirable physical properties, such as mechanical strength or optical clarity, that is often observed in biomass-based polymer composites limits the impact of the ‘nanocomposite approach’ for sustainable material engineering. The effect of filler addition on the physical properties of polymers sensitively depends on the morphology of the composite material and filler-matrix interactions. Aggregation of dispersed particle fillers is generally considered to be detrimental to physical properties of nanocomposites due to embrittlement of the material as well as the loss of optical clarity [1], [2], [3], [4]. This presents a particular challenge for biobased fillers - such as lignin - due their inherent chemical incompatibility with most engineering plastics [5], [6]. For example, blends of hydroxypropyl lignin in PMMA were found to exhibit a strain-to-fracture of less than 2% (about half of the value typically observed for pristine PMMA at moderate strain rates) - the embrittlement was attributed to weak polymer-filler interactions and the formation of micron-scale lignin aggregates [7]. A large number of studies involving both bio-sourced as well as inorganic particle fillers have corroborated the particular relevance of filler-matrix interactions as governing parameter that determines the physical properties of polymer nanocomposite materials [8]. A substantial amount of research - mostly on the phase behavior of inorganic particle-in-polymer dispersions - has established the sensitive relation between miscibility and architecture of polymer-tethered particle fillers (here the term architecture is used to describe the relevant structural parameters of polymer-tethered particle systems such as particle size, density as well as degree of polymerization and dispersity of grafted chains). For example, in the case of ‘neutral’ polymer grafts, in which the chemical composition of the grafted chains is identical to the matrix, miscibility has been shown to increase with the degree of polymerization of surface-tethered chains [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Parallel progress in surface-initiated controlled radical polymerization has established a range of synthetic methodologies to facilitate the tethering of polymer chains with precisely controlled degree of polymerization, grafting density and even modality of polymeric tethers [8], [13], [14]. Recently our group demonstrated that the application of surface-initiated atom transfer controlled radical polymerization (SI-ATRP) facilitates the efficient synthesis of polymer tethered kraft lignin with high molecular polymeric tethers [15]. SI-ATRP is a particularly interesting technique in the context of filler modification because of its applicability to a wide range of monomer chemistries, the high level of control over molecular characteristics of tethered chains as well as its proven economic efficacy and scalability [8], [16], [17]. Grafting of polymeric chains was shown to result in lignin-hybrid particles that could be assembled into ‘one-component lignin-hybrid materials’ with enhanced cohesive interactions as compared to the pristine lignin and polymer constituents - the latter was attributed to the occurrence of entanglements between tethered chains. The similarity of the effect of polymer-graft modification on the interaction between lignin fillers to those observed in inorganic particle brush analogs motivates the hypothesis that polymer-graft modification should be an effective method to facilitate the improved dispersion of lignin in polymer matrices and the fabrication of bio-sourced polymer composites with enhanced mechanical properties [18], [19].', 'Despite the potential benefits of incorporating lignin into traditional polymers to mitigate the shortcomings of composite materials, the utilization of lignin-based bioplastics is limited due to their inferior processability and mechanical properties [17]. The problem caused by poor processability of some types of lignin, such as Alkali lignin, can be solved by neutralization or acidification of lignin [18]. Moreover, it can only be blended in small amounts due to its immiscibility in the majority of polyesters. It was discovered that the organosolv lignin and its butyrate derivative were highly miscible with some polymers, such as PHB, and that lignin inhibits and delays the crystallization of PHB [19, 20]. Some researchers have tried synthesizing lignin copolymers, which is considered an effective approach to improve the compatibility of lignin and polymer matrix [21]. Moreover, using dicumyl peroxide as a crosslinker, which creates covalent bonds between lignin and polymer through reactive extrusion processing, and chemical modification of lignin through esterification are other techniques used to improve the compatibility of lignin into the polymer matrix [22, 23]. Organosolv lignin is a type of lignin extracted from biomass through the organosolv process. Lignin is a complex organic polymer found in the cell walls of plants, providing structural support. The organosolv process involves using organic solvents, such as ethanol, methanol, or a mixture of both, along with an acid or a base, to break down the lignin and separate it from the cellulose and hemicellulose components of biomass materials like wood, agricultural residues, or grasses. Organosolv lignin has been used by several researchers to address the poor properties of different polymers, especially polyesters [24,25,26]. Due to its structure, it can possess more complexity in the polymer matrix, resulting in higher resistance against biodegradation. Moreover, its low price, sustainability, and potential to be used as a reinforcing filler in polymer matrices make it a valuable additive [27, 28]. Since there is no discernible difference in the additive’s antibacterial and antioxidant activity between high and low lignin concentrations, the lower lignin concentration is seen to be ideal [29]. For example, based on phenolic chemicals in their structure, researchers found that 5% and 3% lignin in PLA-based composite may provide a high degree of antibacterial activity by inhibiting various bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli [30, 31]. However, a high lignin content would be more advantageous in terms of thermal and mechanical qualities like tensile strength; because of this aromatic polyester’s low aspect ratio, it can function as a filler.', 'A green, low-cost, and high-performance filler is a key factor in the development of the polymer industry. Although lignin is an abundant and sustainable biopolymer in nature with great potential as a filler, its applications are commonly limited by its heterogeneity. Here, a series of well-defined lignin-based fillers (lignin-graft-polymethyl methacrylate, L-g-PMMA) were synthesized by using a universal approach of the combination of chemical modification with lignin fractionation. The structural analysis of lignin fractions and tensile tests reveal that the strength and toughness of the lignin-filled polymer blends (PMMA/L-g-PMMA) can be well tuned by the molecular weights, kinds and contents of S/G units and flexible/rigid linkages in lignin macromolecules. This study not only provides a simple and effective strategy to overcome the heterogeneity of lignin but also paves the way towards high-value utilization of lignin on a broader scale. In the plant kingdom, lignin functions as a cellular glue and provides compressive strength to the cellulose structure.6,7 With the rocketing development of lignin chemistry, more unique and promising properties of lignin, including antioxidant and antimicrobial activities, anti-ultraviolet and fluorescence properties, and pH-sensitivity, are gradually unveiling.8,9 Among various applications, the lignin-based filler is still one of the most practical and efficient applications with good industrialization prospects. Some efforts are being made to use industrial lignins as low-cost eco-friendly fillers to prepare plastic and rubber blends.10-14 Although the strategies involved sacrificed some performance of polymer matrices, the cost can be reduced dramatically. Some researchers have made efforts to modify lignin by functional group modification and graft copolymerization in order to make it compatible and strengthened/toughened with polymer matrices.15-18 Some previous studies including ours showed that the significant heterogeneity of lignin (its molecular weight and the type, structure, and chemical composition in lignin macromolecules) has been linked with the performance of lignin-based materials and lignin/polymer blends.19-22 Until now, the fabrication of lignin/polymer blends to simultaneously achieve cost reduction and improvement and control of their performance still remained a challenge. Lignin fractionation, which was commonly utilized for the structural analysis of lignin, is an efficient upgrading process to obtain specific fractions with more homogeneous chemical and physical characteristics.23-25 Here, we innovatively combine the fractionation technique and chemical modification of lignin. The well-defined lignin-based fillers (lignin-graft-polymethyl methacrylate, L-g-PMMA) were prepared from lignin fractions via atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) grafting of methyl methacrylate (MMA) and blending with commercial polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). The molecular properties of lignin fractions and the mechanical properties of the resulting blends were systematically analyzed using gel permeation chromatography (GPC), two-dimensional heteronuclear single quantum coherence (2D HSQC) spectroscopy, quantitative phosphorous magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P NMR), tensile strength, and elongation at break. Furthermore, correlations of the properties of lignin/PMMA blends were obtained with the molecular properties of lignin fractions.', 'The aim of this work was to investigate the possibility of using cost-effective natural filler in a biodegradable polymer and find new set of materials for green biocomposites to be used in food packaging. In this regard, rice husk (RH) and bleached rice husk (BRH) have been used in the form of powder and the effect of lignin removal on mechanical and thermal properties of prepared composites with poly(l-lactide) and starch were studied. Using FTIR technique, the lignin removal from RH has been approved. The tensile, charpy impact, and hardness tests were implemented to investigate the mechanical properties. It was concluded that filler caused increase both in the toughness and the Young modulus of samples. It was also found that the lack of lignin in BRH samples improves the mechanical properties. It was clearly observed that the BRH samples show larger modulus, charpy impact strength, and hardness compared to those filled with RH. Despite larger values for the elongations at break of RH samples, the mechanical properties showed a significant improvement (between 25 and 50% improvements) on lignin removal. The differential scanning calorimetry thermograms revealed an improvement in crystallization behavior and reduction of Tg from 47 to 31°C in the case of BRH-filled samples. Finally, due to the removal of toxic lignin in the samples and modification of mechanical properties by this method, the BRH could have the ability of wide use in the bioplastics and food packaging industries. © 2014 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 2014, 131, 41095. Nowadays, environmental pollutions caused by the use of nonbiodegradable polymers have lured many researchers to use biodegradable polymers in their studies.1 However, biodegradable polymers cannot come to wide use as they are expensive and have physical and mechanical limitations such as their storage conditions, water absorption, interface adhesion, and brittleness observed in some polymers such as poly lactic acid (PLA).2 Starch is a potentially useful material for biodegradable plastics because of its low cost and natural abundance3; conversely, starch is a brittle biodegradable polymer, has strong water absorption, and is not good for practical applications.4 Thermoplastic starch that usually has been produced by conventional melt-processing has poor mechanical properties, which is mainly because of thermal degradation of starch before melting, the strong water absorption, and poor interfacial adhesion with other components.5-7 To settle these problems, starch granules were modified by the physical modification methods, such as blending and chemical modifications.8-10 Natural starch exists in a granular form. The granular shape and size are different in plants. Corn starch granules are mainly spherical, whereas wheat starch contains both spherical and disk shaped granules, and potato starch has a smooth granular surface, which is mainly oval.11, 12 In many investigations, starch is selected to fabricate biodegradable polymer blends. One of the most common bio-based polymers frequently studied is poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA). PLLA is attractive for disposable and biodegradable plastic substitutes because of its very good mechanical properties.13, 14 According to previous studies, this aliphatic polyester is a good choice for blending with starch to obtain a biodegradable blend with proper physical and mechanical properties.15-21', 'IntroductionRecently, the demand for bio-based and biodegradable plastics has been rapidly increasing due to concerns about the dangers of microplastics and the depletion of petroleum resources [[1], [2], [3]]. However, unlike non-degradable petroleum-based plastics, biodegradable plastics have weak mechanical properties, high prices, and difficulty predicting durability due to unwanted biodegradation [4]. To overcome the disadvantages of these biodegradable plastics, research on various composite materials using natural fillers that can reinforce mechanical strength, natural polymeric additives that can lower prices, and trigger functionalization agents to control biodegradation characteristics is constantly underway [5].Biomass-derived lignocellulose is the most abundant natural product on earth and has many potential applications as an additive for biodegradable plastics. Natural fibers have already been used as mechanical fillers for fiber-reinforced plastics (FRPs). With the recent introduction of nanocellulose, research on composite materials using nanocellulose as an eco-friendly binder or filler is being actively conducted [6,7]. On the other hand, lignin, a secondary component of lignocellulose, has recently been actively attempted to be used in the material industry based on its UV-blocking properties, antioxidant properties, and high organic carbon content [8]. However, when lignin is added to biodegradable plastics, it exhibits various disadvantages, such as self-aggregation of lignin occurring during the polymer melt process, low miscibility with the matrix polymer, and subsequent deterioration of the mechanical properties of the composite material strongly hindering its use [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. To overcome this problem, lignin fractionation, homogenization, and chemical modification have been proposed to increase the miscibility between lignin and a biodegradable polymer matrix [13]. A typical method for the chemical modification of lignin is acetylation, which has been reported to increase its hydrophobicity and compatibility with biodegradable polymers [14]. However, in the case of most biocomposites to which chemically modified lignin is added, the focus is on supplementing mechanical strength by enhancing the compatibility of the existing biodegradable matrix and demonstrating the UV-blocking effect of lignin [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. In particular, there are only a few studies reporting the effect of lignin addition on the biodegradation properties of manufactured biocomposites.Understanding the biodegradability and degradation mechanisms of bioplastics is important from an industrial and scientific point of view to predict their useful life and establish utilization plans. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the biodegradability of composite materials according to the addition of natural polymer fillers in biocomposite materials [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23]]. In fact, since general biopolymer fillers are hydrophilic, many studies have reported that most of them increase accessibility to the hydrolysis environment and accelerate biodegradation accordingly [24]. It has been also been reported that the addition of cellulose accelerated the biodegradation of PLA-based composites by 34 % and that the addition of microalgae-based biomass increases the degradation rate of PLA-based composites [[25], [26], [27]]. However, only a few additives have been designed to inhibit the degradation of these biodegradable plastics references [28].The main purpose of this study is to prepare chemically modified lignin, improve compatibility with PLA, and use it as a functional additive to control the biodegradation behavior of PLA-based biocomposites. Firstly, AL was prepared through chemical modification to improve the low compatibility and dispersibility with PLA, which are the shortcomings of commercial technical lignin KL, and incorporated as an additive in PLA biocomposites. Changes in the physicochemical properties of lignin due to acetylation were investigated through Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), gel permeation chromatography (GPC), phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance (31P NMR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). In addition, improved compatibility between PLA and AL was confirmed by observing the hygroscopic properties of AL, the dissolution and dispersion properties of AL in organic solvents, and the fracture surface morphology of the AL/PLA biocomposite. Ultimately, to investigate the effect of adding chemically modified lignin on the biodegradation characteristics of the lignin/PLA composite, a biodegradation experiment was performed for 45 days in a thermophilic composting environment above the glass transition temperature of PLA. Changes in physicochemical properties of lignin/PLA biocomposite according to biodegradation behavior were analyzed through GPC, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), TGA, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Recently, the demand for bio-based and biodegradable plastics has been rapidly increasing due to concerns about the dangers of microplastics and the depletion of petroleum resources [[1], [2], [3]]. However, unlike non-degradable petroleum-based plastics, biodegradable plastics have weak mechanical properties, high prices, and difficulty predicting durability due to unwanted biodegradation [4]. To overcome the disadvantages of these biodegradable plastics, research on various composite materials using natural fillers that can reinforce mechanical strength, natural polymeric additives that can lower prices, and trigger functionalization agents to control biodegradation characteristics is constantly underway [5]. Biomass-derived lignocellulose is the most abundant natural product on earth and has many potential applications as an additive for biodegradable plastics. Natural fibers have already been used as mechanical fillers for fiber-reinforced plastics (FRPs). With the recent introduction of nanocellulose, research on composite materials using nanocellulose as an eco-friendly binder or filler is being actively conducted [6,7]. On the other hand, lignin, a secondary component of lignocellulose, has recently been actively attempted to be used in the material industry based on its UV-blocking properties, antioxidant properties, and high organic carbon content [8]. However, when lignin is added to biodegradable plastics, it exhibits various disadvantages, such as self-aggregation of lignin occurring during the polymer melt process, low miscibility with the matrix polymer, and subsequent deterioration of the mechanical properties of the composite material strongly hindering its use [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. To overcome this problem, lignin fractionation, homogenization, and chemical modification have been proposed to increase the miscibility between lignin and a biodegradable polymer matrix [13]. A typical method for the chemical modification of lignin is acetylation, which has been reported to increase its hydrophobicity and compatibility with biodegradable polymers [14]. However, in the case of most biocomposites to which chemically modified lignin is added, the focus is on supplementing mechanical strength by enhancing the compatibility of the existing biodegradable matrix and demonstrating the UV-blocking effect of lignin [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. In particular, there are only a few studies reporting the effect of lignin addition on the biodegradation properties of manufactured biocomposites.', 'The main objective of the research is to use lignin and locally grown low cost biomass grass fiber in making injection mouldable materials with desirable properties combinations. It was targeted to achieve material with comparable or improved properties than the injection mouldable PBS (Bionolle 1020). PBS is a comparatively tough polymer as compared to other biopolymer such as PLA and PHAs. Investigating on several polymers it was found that PBS was quite compatible for lignin incorporation. Nearly 50 wt of filler incorporation was targeted in engineering a new biomaterial. Since PBS is an expensive biopolymer as compared to the petroleum based plastics in general, the idea here is to incorporate higher weight percentage of comparatively inexpensive filler thus to have a biomaterial with an affordable cost-performance attribute. Compared to other biopolymers, PBS allows high biomass incorporation. However, addition of filler drastically reduces the impact strength of polymer.3, 14, 16 Further, lignin is a brittle polymer and exhibits more reducing effect on the strength of composites compared to the switchgrass in the composite formulations. Consequently, incorporation of higher amount of lignin alone as filler was not possible in order to obtain a material with better material properties. Hence, after several studies, 1:4 ratios of lignin and switchgrass were selected as hybrid filler to fabricate 50 wt filler based PBS composites. As biofiller incorporation reduces the impact strength of polymer and our research objective was to obtain a material with nearly similar properties of PBS 1020, basing on our experimental results as discussed below a blend of PBS 1020 and PBS 1001 was selected as matrix polymer. Blending technology is often used to obtain materials with toughness and stiffness balance as well as to manipulate the properties of materials.18, 19 However, phase separation is an issue when two different polymers are used in the blend. Hence, blend of two different grades of PBS were taken as matrix polymer in our research. From Figure 1 it can be observed that, the tensile yield stress and flexural properties of two PBS grades and their 1:1 blend were nearly same. However, the impact strength of PBS 1001 was significantly higher than that of PBS 1020 and the blend obtained an intermediate value. Again, the processing of specimens with PBS 1001 was associated with a very high shear force. Based upon the properties comparison (Figure 1), processing suitability and concern for impact strength of biocomposite, a 1:1 blend of two PBS grades was selected as the matrix polymer. While all the properties of the resulted composites were compared with the properties of PBS blends, the impact strength was compared with both blend and the injection mouldable PBS 1020. The tensile strength and modulus of PBS 1020, PBS blend, and composites of PBS blend are shown in Figure 2. Incorporation of filler (1:4 lignin:switchgrass) into polymer resulted in 21% lower tensile strength compared to the matrix polymer (1:1 PBS blend). The tensile strength of material decreases with increasing agro filler content in polymers.16, 20, 21 This can be attributed to the poor interfacial adhesion between hydrophobic polymer and hydrophilic filler.21 Incorporation of 1% pMDI enhanced the tensile strength of material by about 25% compared to its counterpart without any chemical additives and obtained a value nearly the same as the that of matrix polymer. It can be attributed to the improved the interfacial adhesion in the material due to the formation of urethane (\uf8ffHN\uf8ffCOO\uf8ff) linkages (Figure 3) between the \uf8ffNCO groups of pMDI and \uf8ffOH groups of filler followed by the possible secondary intermolecular bonding between the N\uf8ffH group of the urethane linkages and the carbonyl groups of the polyester.3, 5, 22, 23 Significant improvement in the tensile modulus of composites (296 and 391%, respectively) was obtained by the incorporation of filler and pMDI. The addition of 5% ITPB into the pMDI compatibilized composite decreased the tensile strength which obtained nearly same value as obtained by the composites without any additive and was nearly 16% lower than that of PBS blend. Researchers5, 6, 23 have reported improvement in the tensile strength due to the incorporation of ITPB. Formation of urethane linkages between the \uf8ffOH group of biofiber and the \uf8ffNCO group of ITPB was considered as the cause of improvement in the reported literature. Incorporation of 2 and 4% ITPB has increased the tensile strength of the cellulose based polypropylene composites.5 The tensile strength of composites with ITPB increased with increasing filler content to 30 wt and then decreased when filler content reached 40 wt. However, the improvement at 30 wt filler was not very significant.5 None of these reports have explained the role of polybutadiene soft segments on the tensile properties of composites. In our study, 5 wt ITPB and 1% pMDI together were added to a blend that contained 50% filler content. In this case, phase separation due to presence of polybutadiene soft segments in the material,24 higher filler content and possible plasticization effect due to higher \uf8ffNCO content (in both pMDI and ITPB) could be the contributing factors for the decrease in the tensile properties. It is to be noted that phase separation due to the presence of butadiene soft segments was resulted in the reduction of the storage modulus of material.24 Incorporation of peroxide in the material obtained a tensile strength nearly 26% higher than the counterpart without peroxide and slightly (≈6%) higher than the tensile strength of PBS blend. It could be due to the peroxide initiated crosslinking and chain branching in the composite system. However, no significant effect on the modulus value was observed due to the peroxide addition. The schematics of the free radical reaction leading to crosslinking or chain branching, urethane formation and its hydrogen bonding with carbonyl group of polymer are shown in Figure 3a-c. Figure 3a shows the urethane formation followed by secondary hydrogen bonding between polyester group of polymer and urethane linkages. Introduction of polybutadiene segments into composite system is represented by Figure 3b. Figure 3c demonstrates peroxide catalyzed free radical reaction in the composite system. Peroxide (Luperox® 101) undergoes homolysis under blending conditions and forms tert-butoxy free radicals (tBuO•). These free radicals are prone to addition reaction with reactive species and to abstract hydrogen from C\uf8ffH bonds present in the constituents that forms carbon centered (C-centered) free radicals. The addition of these C-centered free radicals to C\uf8feC double bond present in ITPB forms new C-centered free radicals which undergo recombination with similar free radicals or other C-centered free radicals leading to crosslinking or chain branching of polybutadiene segments (Figure 3c). Furthermore, N\uf8ffH bond of urethane linkage involved in hydrogen bond formation with carbonyl group of PBS polymer provides further synergy to the crosslinking effect (Figure 3a and b). This crosslinking and compatibilization could significantly contribute to the tensile strength of the composites. Improvement in the tensile strength of the composites due to ITPB and peroxide in presence of MAPP was also reported by researchers.6 A reaction mechanism for the peroxide catalyzed free radical reaction between the polybutadiene and polyolefin polymers was reported in literature.7 The stress-strain curves of the composites are shown in Figure 4a and b. Although almost the same yield strain was observed for the PBS blend and PBS 1020, a significantly higher break strain was observed for the PBS blend. Brittle failure of composites can be observed from the figure. The strain at break of materials slightly improved by the pMDI and ITPB addition and no significant effect was observed due to the peroxide addition (Figure 4b). Composites exhibited significant higher flexural strength (nearly 65-140%) and modulus (283-395%) compared to the PBS blend (Figure 5). The addition of pMDI resulted in a 35% improvement in the flexural strength compared to the uncompatibilized composites. However, no change in the flexural modulus was noticed for this material which may be attributed to the effects, i.e., improved adhesion due to the compatibilization, and the plasticization that counterbalance each other. The above factors limit the usage of lignin as a “drop in” replacement for conventional fillers in development of compounds of polymers and elastomers.', 'Lignin is known as the most abundant aromatic polymer in nature, present in most terrestrial plants with weight percentages from 15 to 40%.1 Lignin was traditionally produced from pulp and paper industries as a byproduct. Based solely on the provided context, the primary challenge in using lignin as a filler in biodegradable polymers is:

1.  **Chemical incompatibility with the polymer matrix:** Lignin has an inherent chemical incompatibility with most engineering plastics and biodegradable polymers ([1], [5]).
2.  **Resulting in poor dispersion and aggregation:** This incompatibility leads to weak polymer-filler interactions, causing lignin to self-aggregate during processing (e.g., polymer melt process) and form micron-scale aggregates within the composite ([1], [5], [7]).
3.  **Leading to deterioration of mechanical properties:** This aggregation is detrimental, causing embrittlement and a significant loss of desirable physical properties, particularly mechanical strength ([1], [5], [7]). For example, lignin addition strongly hinders use due to the subsequent deterioration of mechanical properties ([5]).

**Key supporting evidence from the context:**
*   "[Lignin's] inherent chemical incompatibility with most engineering plastics" ([1]).
*   "weak polymer-filler interactions and the formation of micron-scale lignin aggregates" leading to embrittlement ([1]).
*   "self-aggregation of lignin occurring during the polymer melt process, low miscibility with the matrix polymer, and subsequent deterioration of the mechanical properties of the composite material strongly hindering its use" ([5]).
*   "lignin is a brittle polymer and exhibits more reducing effect on the strength of composites" ([7]).
*   "poor interfacial adhesion between hydrophobic polymer and hydrophilic filler" ([7]).

retrieved_contexts: ['GelMA, which is a derivative of gelatin, was first reported and synthesized by Van Den Bulcke et al [24]. Briefly, the reaction between the methacrylic anhydride (MA) and the primary amine groups of gelatin in the phosphate buffer (pH = 7.4) at 50 °C enables the methacrylate groups added onto the gelatin macromers to form GelMA. With the presence of a photoinitiator, GelMA can get photocrosslinked when exposed to a UV light. During the crosslinking process, the free radicals released from the photoinitiator upon absorption of the UV light polymerize GelMA. Currently, GelMA has wide applications in 3D bioprinting and tissue engineering fields. Gao et al [20] selected a 3D bioprinting platform to photopolymerize PEG-GelMA as a scaffold, and human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) were simultaneously printed using inkjet bioprinting. The scientific finding indicated its more prospective potentials in bone and cartilage engineering field. Zhou et al [25] used a tabletop SLA system to deposit bioink composed of GelMA, nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite (nHA), and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and found the micro-environment within GelMA and nHA was suitable for the cross-talk of multiple types of cells. Grogan et al [26] seeded human avascular zone meniscus cells on GelMA scaffolds fabricated with projection SLA. The GelMA scaffolds were used to mimic the meniscus collagen bundle, which was proved to promote meniscus regeneration. In GelMA-based 3D bioprinting, many parameters affect the cell viability, mechanical-physical properties, and microstructures such as UV light [27], GelMA concentration [28], photoinitiator concentration [29], GelMA degree of functionalization [30], and cell concentration [31]. Wadnap et al [32] utilized a dynamic optical projection SLA system to fabricate a tubular construct using bioink containing 5% (w/v) GelMA, 0.5% (w/v) Irgacure 2959, and a cell concentration of 2.5 × 106 cells ml−1. The post-printing cell viability measured immediately after printing was determined to be around 75%. It was found out that the mechanical properties including the ultimate tensile strength and the maximum strain decreased when the cells were encapsulated. Moreover, the swelling ratio and pore size of the GelMA hydrogels increased significantly within the first 24 h of incubation while they had no significant change from 24 to 72 h. Van Vlierberghe et al [33] successfully fabricated GelMA scaffolds with a gradient of pore size by controlling the temperature gradient during cooling. It was reported that the pore size of the GelMA samples decreased with the increase of gelatin solution and the cooling rate of gelatin hydrogel during the synthesis process of GelMA. Nichol et al [34] synthesized the GelMA with the methacrylation level from 20% to 80% by adding different percentages of MA during the synthesis process. The bioink containing human umbilical vein endothelial cells and GelMA with 0.5% (w/v) Irgacure 2959 was crosslinked to prepare the samples. They found out with the increase of the methacrylation level, the stiffness of 5%, 10%, and 15% (w/v) GelMA was enhanced while the swelling ratio was decreased. Moreover, the cell viability using different GelMA concentrations of 5%, 10%, and 15% (w/v) was 92%, 82%, and 75%, respectively. Based solely on the provided context, biodegradable hydrogels are essential components (bioinks) in 3D bioprinting, serving several key functions:

1.  **Cell Encapsulation:** Hydrogels provide a hydrated, biocompatible 3D environment that encapsulates living cells during the printing process and supports their viability, proliferation, and function (e.g., [1], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]).
2.  **Mimicking the Extracellular Matrix (ECM):** Natural hydrogels (e.g., gelatin, GelMA, collagen, alginate, agarose, silk fibroin) structurally and biologically mimic the native ECM, providing cues for cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation (e.g., [1], [6], [7], [8], [9], [12], [14], [15]).
3.  **Printability and Shape Fidelity:** Hydrogels must have suitable rheological properties (viscosity, yield stress) to be extruded or patterned during printing and rapidly stabilize (via crosslinking) to maintain the designed 3D structure. Biodegradability allows the scaffold to gradually remodel as new tissue forms.
    *   *Thermoresponsive gelation:* Agarose and gelatin solutions gel upon cooling ([2], [9], [10], [14], [15]).
    *   *Photocrosslinking:* GelMA, GelNB, SF-MA, PEGDA are crosslinked using UV/visible light and photoinitiators (e.g., Irgacure 2959, LAP) to form stable networks immediately after deposition ([1], [7], [8], [12], [13], [14], [15]).
    *   *Ionic crosslinking:* Alginate crosslinks with calcium ions ([6], [12]).
    *   *Chemical crosslinking:* GelNB uses thiol-ene click chemistry with PEGdiSH ([4], [13]).
    *   *Physical blending/composites:* Combining polymers (e.g., GelMA/HA, CMC/Agarose, ADA/GEL, GelNB/PEGdiSH, SF-MA blends, GelMA/mCMC/PEGDA, Agarose/Nanosilicates) enhances viscosity, mechanical strength, printability, or bioactivity ([4], [6], [9], [10], [11], [14], [15]).
4.  **Tunable Properties:** The biodegradation rate, mechanical strength (stiffness), porosity, and swelling of hydrogels can be modulated for specific tissue applications (e.g., bone, cartilage, skin, neural) by:
    *   Adjusting polymer concentration ([1], [8], [11], [14]).
    *   Varying the degree of functionalization (e.g., GelMA methacrylation level) ([1], [8]).
    *   Changing crosslinking density/duration ([1], [8], [14]).
    *   Incorporating additives (e.g., nanocrystalline HA for bone, nanosilicates for rheology/bioactivity) ([1], [10], [12]).
    *   Blending polymers ([6], [9], [10], [11], [14], [15]).
5.  **Supporting Tissue-Specific Regeneration:** Specific hydrogel formulations are engineered to promote the regeneration of target tissues:
    *   *Bone:* GelMA/nHA, SF-MA, GelMA/mCMC/PEGDA/nHAp ([1], [8], [11], [12]).
    *   *Cartilage:* GelMA, GelMA/HA, WPU-PCL/GelMA composites ([1], [3], [14], [15]).
    *   *Neural:* GelNB/PEGdiSH, tPU2, tPU2-Chitosan composites (PUC) ([4], [5]).
    *   *Skin:* CMC/Agarose ([9]).
    *   *Vascular:* GelNB/PEGdiSH (with QK peptide), GelMA constructs ([1], [13]).

**In essence, 3D bioprinting utilizes biodegradable hydrogels as the foundational "bioink" material to physically structure the printed construct, protect and nurture encapsulated cells, provide biologically relevant signals, and biodegrade at a controlled rate to be replaced by new tissue.** The choice of hydrogel and its formulation is critically tailored to the printing technology, the desired structural fidelity, and the specific biological requirements of the tissue being engineered.

For example, macrodiol containing acid-cleavable hydrazone was recruited to synthesize a kind of pH-sensitive PU, so that the drug carrier could quickly break down in tumor.20 PU micelles containing redox-sensitive disulfide bonds also demonstrated a rapid degradation process.21 Skarja and Woodhouse have reported a biodegradable polyurethane containing amino acid-based chain extender in hard segments to accelerate the degradation and improve the biocompatibility.22 These reports inspired us to design a stimulated degradable chain extender in hard segments to accelerate the degradation and simultaneously keep shape memory ability.', 'Shape memory polyurethane (SMPU) is a typical shape memory polymer widely used in biomaterials,1, 2 such as bone tissue engineering,3orthodontic,4 closure device,5 and self-expandable stents.6 The shape memory behavior, typically remembering a temporary shape and returning to its original shape, can be stimulated by pH, temperature, humidity, electricity, magnetism, electromagnetism, and so on.7 The most important specie among them is thermal responsive polyurethane.8, 9 The semicrystalline poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is popularly used as soft segments of SMPU because of its nontoxicity, low melting temperature, and biodegradability.10-13 The main aspect in designing PCL-based SMPU is the transition temperature of the soft segment, which controls the transition between temporary and permanent shape. Several attempts have been carried out in polyurethane modification to speed up the degradation. For example, macrodiol containing acid-cleavable hydrazone was recruited to synthesize a kind of pH-sensitive PU, so that the drug carrier could quickly break down in tumor.20 PU micelles containing redox-sensitive disulfide bonds also demonstrated a rapid degradation process.21 Skarja and Woodhouse have reported a biodegradable polyurethane containing amino acid-based chain extender in hard segments to accelerate the degradation and improve the biocompatibility.22 These reports inspired us to design a stimulated degradable chain extender in hard segments to accelerate the degradation and simultaneously keep shape memory ability.', 'In accordance with the development of science and technology, as well as the specific requirements for unique applications in the field of biomedical devices, aerospace, electronic engineering, etc, have accelerated the evolution of materials [1]. Shape memory polymers (SMPs) are polymeric materials with the capability to be fixed into a temporary shape by applying specific condition, and recover back their original shape upon the introduction of suitable external stimuli [2-5]. This behavior is also known as shape memory effect (SME) which is evaluated by shape fixity (SF) and shape recovery (SR) [6]. The switching segments play an important role in maintaining the temporary shape whereas the net points are responsible to retain the original shape [8, 9]. Bhd., (Malaysia), respectively. PKOp was supplied by Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (Malaysia). 4,4′-Methylenebis (cyclohexyl isocyanate) (HMDI or H12MDI), 1,4-Butanediol (BD, chain extender), and dibutyltin dilaurate (DBTDL, catalyst) were supplied by Sigma Aldrich (USA).', "As a popular kind of intelligent materials, shape memory polymers (SMPs) have the capacity to fix temporary shapes and recover to their original shapes on demand when exposed to an external stimulus, such as heat,1 moisture,2 pH,3 light,4 electricity,5 and alternating magnetic.6 In recent years, research about SMPs has gained an unexpected enthusiasm,[1, 7] mainly due to the vast potential applications in our lives and industries.8 Currently, thermoresponsive shape memory polyurethane/urea (SMPU) is one of the most common and studied SMPs. Although the carbamate bonds are exchangeable, the reprocessability of thermoset polyurethanes is rather poor.", "In principle, thermally induced SMPs consist of netpoints and switches. The netpoints determine the permanent shape of polymer network and can be of a chemical or physical nature. The switches are responsible for controlling the shape fixity and recovery.4,8 Generally, the material properties are mainly determined by their intrinsic structure. Consequently, SMPs with new macromolecular structures can be designed and synthesized based on their structural principles.14,15 And then their relationship between the structure and shape memory properties can be investigated so as to improve their relatively small recovery stresses, long response time, low achievable number of cycles and poor mechanical properties, which are some of the major drawbacks and the issues that remain challenging in the field of shape memory materials.16 A great deal of effort has been devoted to optimize the properties of SMPs through the reinforcement and molecular structure design of SMPs. First of all, incorporating small amounts of micro/nano-sized reinforcing fillers into SMPs significantly improved the mechanical performance and shape memory capabilities, especially, shape recovery stress levels.17-20 For instance, Miaudet et al. achieved the 150 MPa recovery stress in CNT/polyvinyl alcohol fiber, which is two orders of magnitude higher than that of neat SMPs.21 Recently, a novel family of organic-inorganic shape memory hybrids possessing high elastic modulus and excellent shape memory properties was developed by Agarwal et al.22 The hybrids called nanoscale ionic materials consist of SiO2 core and polyethylene glycol corona. And the detailed structure-property relationships for such systems have not been attempted, while the network properties are expected to play an important role in controlling the mechanical and shape memory performance and need to be addressed for the successful development of SMPs with the star-shaped structures.", 'Shape memory polymers (SMPs) are one set of very important smart materials that have the capability of rapidly recovering to their original shapes from a temporary shape upon application of appropriate stimulus such as temperature, light, electric field, magnetic field, pH, specific ions or enzyme [1-9]. Among them, thermally activated SMPs are the most common one [10]. Therefore, the thermo-responsive SMP in this work is meat for heating-responsive SMP only. Compared with shape memory metallic alloys and shape memory ceramics, SMPs possess the advantages of light weight, low cost, good processability, high shape recoverability and tailor-able switch temperature. Thus, SMPs can be used in a wide range of applications, including smart textiles and apparels, heat shrinkable packaging, intelligent biomedical materials and self-deployable structures in spacecrafts [11-15]. [16] filled shape memory polyurethane with cellulose nano-whiskers and concluded that the modulus of composites was higher than the pure polyurethane. Auad et al. [17] investigated the shape memory behavior of nano-cellulose reinforced polyurethanes. [18] prepared a self-deployable hinge using styrene-based SMP reinforced by carbon fiber fabrics and investigated the shape memory effect of self-deployable hinge. This study aims to develop a type of shape memory composite with good comprehensive performance to meet the needs of the aerospace industry. And shape memory glass fiber/SBS/LDPE composites were prepared with various weight fractions of short glass fiber (SGF). The thermo-mechanical properties and shape memory behaviors of the developed composites were fully characterized and systematically investigated.', 'Recently, the application of polyurethane-based SMPs in the medical field has been extensively investigated because a wide range of raw materials are available for the synthesis of polyurethanes (PUs), providing an opportunity to tailor the backbone structure to obtain polymers with different properties.2-4 Of these, the shape memory behaviour, the thermal responsibility, and the morphology of both hard segments (HS) and soft segments (SSs) of PU-based SMPs, such as poly(ether urethane) (PEU),5,6 segmented PU,7-9 and segmented polycaprolactone (PCL)-based PU,10 are well studied. Medical-grade commercial segment PUs are generally synthesized using 4,4′-methylenebis(phenyl isocyanate) (MDI).16 However, the aromatic diisocyanates release toxic degradation products such as carcinogenic and mutagenic aromatic amines, rendering them undesirable for use in the biomedical field. Biodegradable PU usually possess a segmented polymer network composed of soft segments comprising polyether or polyester crosslinked with urethane bonds and hard segments formed between isocyanate and chain extender [21]. Chitosan degradation undergoes through breakdown of the glycosidic bonds [40]. It was also recognized that degradation rate of chitosan is influenced by many factors such as deacetylation degree, crosslinking density, crosslinking agent, or molecular weight [41]. The Shape Memory Effect (SME) in biodegradable polyurethanes refers to their ability to retain a temporary shape under specific conditions and recover their original "memorized" shape upon exposure to an external stimulus, typically heat near body temperature. This behavior arises from their segmented structure:  
1. **Soft Segments (Reversible Phase):** Composed of biodegradable polymers like poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) or poly(lactic acid) (PLA), these segments undergo reversible phase transitions (melting or glass transition) at a defined temperature (Tₜᵣₐₙ). When heated above Tₜᵣₐₙ, the material becomes deformable and can be fixed into a temporary shape upon cooling.  
2. **Hard Segments (Frozen Phase):** Formed by urethane linkages from diisocyanates and chain extenders, these act as physical crosslinks or "net points," preserving the permanent shape. They provide structural integrity and enable recovery by elastic force when the soft segments are reheated.  

Key metrics include **shape fixity ratio** (ability to retain the temporary shape) and **shape recovery ratio** (ability to return to the original shape). For example, UPy-p-PDLLA-SMPUs achieve up to 98.6% fixity and 92.9% recovery near body temperature.  

Biodegradability is integrated through hydrolyzable soft segments (e.g., PCL, PLA), while crystallinity in these segments is critical for effective shape fixation. Challenges include balancing mechanical strength with degradation rates, often addressed by modifying hard segments or incorporating dynamic bonds. Applications span bone repair, biomedical implants, and smart textiles, where stimuli-responsive shape adaptation and biocompatibility are essential.
reference: The Shape Memory Effect allows the polymer to be deformed and fixed in a temporary shape and then recover its original permanent shape upon heating above a transition temperature (Ttrans, usually Tg or Tm). In biodegradable polyurethanes, this is driven by the phase separation between hard segments (permanent shape fixation) and soft segments (switching transition).

retrieved_contexts: ["Effect of biodegradation on PHAs-based blends and composites In general, stable composites are developed by shaping PHB polymers with suitable plasticizers, compatibilizers, stabilizers, fillers, and matrixes. PHB's functional group, crystallinity, hydrophobicity, and morphological characteristics all have an impact on how quickly it degrades in biological systems. Therefore, mcl-PHAs that has low crystallinity and low Tm degrades more rapidly than scl-PHAs that has higher crystallinity and Tm. The factors that affect the biodegradation of polymer blends include the blend's composition, surface roughness of the blend, miscibility between components, and phase structure (i.e., crystalline or amorphous) [89]. The entire biodegradability of the composite materials can be ensured by selecting a biodegradable polymer to be included with PHB in the blends. However, the second polymer's effects on the morphostructural, thermal, and mechanical characteristics of the PHB blends could potentially affect the degree of biodegradability [188]. The majority of biodegradable polymers break down into components that are safe for the environment, like biomass, CO2, CH4, and water. Nevertheless, this is only possible in controlled industrial composting environments or physiological settings [189]. In natural environments, a variety of chemical-physical (oxygen availability, temperature, pH, light, humidity), and biological (microbial population and enzyme types) factors influence the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers. Because of this, the rate of biodegradation and the profile of degradation might also differ greatly, possibly lasting a long time in the environment. As a result, biopolymers and their composites may weather and eventually generate biodegradable microplastics [190]. Furthermore, it has been noted that as blends' PCL content rises, biodegradation rates rise quickly. This acceleration could be triggered by surface alteration or a decrease in the samples' overall crystallinity [194].", 'Microfibrillar composites (MFC) are polymer-polymer systems prepared by melt- or cold-drawing of suitable polymer blends. The present work deals with a study of the thermal degradation of analogous PCL/PLA micro-fibrillated composites reinforced with unmodified halloysite nanotubes.', 'It has been declared in the literature that when the blends of PLA and PCL were prepared at different ratios, both polymers can be improved in the desired mechanical properties. There are studies in the literature that synthesized POSS cored star-shaped PCL or PLA via ring-opening polymerization [31], [32].', 'The aim and objectives of the study are to fabricate industrially valuable coated abrasive and paper based packaging products using bio-polymeric blends of PLA-PCL, which can replace the existing synthetic polymer based products causing pollution. Sources of financial funding and support', "Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) and poly(caprolactone) (PCL) are two prominent biopolymers widely studied for biomedical applications due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability. PLA, derived from renewable resources, is known for its high strength and stiffness but suffers from brittleness and slow degradation rates in biological environments. Conversely, PCL, a synthetic polymer, offers excellent flexibility and a slower degradation rate, which can enhance the mechanical properties and processability of PLA when blended [1]. The blend of PLA and PCL combines the advantageous properties of both polymers, such as improved toughness, tailored degradation rates, and better processing characteristics, making it an ideal candidate for various biomedical applications, including spinal cages [2-4]. In addition to PLA/PCL blends, other biopolymer combinations such as PLA/poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), PLA/thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), and PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) have been explored for biomedical and industrial applications. PLA/PBS blends are valued for their enhanced flexibility and biodegradability; however, they exhibit lower impact strength compared to PLA/PCL blends [5]. PLA/TPU blends offer significant improvements in toughness and elasticity, making them ideal for applications that require high flexibility and impact resistance, such as soft actuators and shape-memory devices [6]. Nevertheless, these blends lack the high stiffness that is characteristic of PLA/PCL blends [7]. PLA/PBAT blends are predominantly used in packaging applications due to their excellent flexibility and elongation at break [8]. However, PBAT's chemical structure can restrict PLA chain mobility, leading to reduced crystallinity in the blend [9]. Furthermore, PLA/PBAT blends often fall short in preserving the shape memory properties observed in other PLA-based blends [10]. Compared to these blends, PLA/PCL blends provide a unique balance of mechanical properties and shape memory effects (SMEs), making them particularly suitable for biomedical implants that must undergo programmed deformation and recovery. Spinal cages are medical devices used in spinal fusion surgeries to maintain disc space height and facilitate bone growth between vertebrae [11]. Traditionally, these cages have been made from metals such as titanium and stainless steel, which, while offering high strength and durability, lack the biodegradability and flexibility needed for tissue integration and growth. Furthermore, their rigidity can lead to stress shielding, where the metal bears most of the load, potentially inhibiting natural bone growth. In addition, metal implants can interfere with imaging techniques such as MRI and CT scans, complicating postoperative assessments, and they may require a second surgery for removal if complications arise [12, 13]. Polymeric materials, especially biodegradable ones like PLA/PCL blends, present significant advantages over traditional materials. Their ability to degrade within the body reduces the need for a second surgery to remove the device, and their mechanical properties can be tailored to mimic the natural spinal environment, promoting better patient outcomes [14-16]. This shift towards polymeric materials, combined with advancements in design, has enabled the development of more adaptable and innovative spinal cages that not only offer biodegradability but can also address specific surgical requirements, such as size, shape, and mechanical behavior tailored for individual patient needs. The dimensions of spinal cages play a crucial role in their performance and the success of the surgery. Among these, wider cages have gained attention for their ability to provide enhanced load distribution across a broader area of the spine, which is particularly beneficial in reducing the risk of vertebral collapse and ensuring long-term stability. This is especially crucial for patients with conditions such as osteoporosis, where the structural integrity of the vertebrae is compromised [17]. Wider cages also provide better mechanical support and increased resistance to collapse. However, narrower cages, like the standard 18 mm cages, are essential for minimally invasive procedures as they require smaller incisions and less tissue disruption. While narrower cages are important for these surgical approaches, wider cages could potentially offer better long-term outcomes by enhancing stability and reducing the likelihood of future complications [18, 19]. Therefore, self-expanding cage designs are highly advantageous as they combine the benefits of minimal invasiveness with the superior support of wider cages.", "The biodegradation test results demonstrate that all materials experienced mass loss over the 90-day period, with the rate of degradation varying based on the material composition. Pure PLA and PCL show different degradation profiles, with PLA degrading more rapidly than PCL over the same period. This can be attributed to the different chemical structures and properties of PLA and PCL, where PLA is known for its higher biodegradability due to its faster hydrolysis rate compared to PCL [44]. The addition of PCL to PLA blends influences the biodegradation rate. As the PCL content increases, the biodegradation rate of the blends also increases. This trend is evident in the results, with PLA/PCL60 showing the highest mass loss (18.21% at 90 days), followed by PLA/PCL50 (16.97%), PLA/PCL40 (15.89%), and so on. This suggests that PCL, although less biodegradable on its own, enhances the overall degradation rate of the blends when combined with PLA. This could be due to the phase separation that occurs within the material matrix of PLA/PCL blends. Phase separation can facilitate the easier penetration of water and enzymes into the material, leading to faster biodegradation [25]. PCL's aliphatic ester bonds are more susceptible to enzymatic hydrolysis by lipases and esterases compared to the ester bonds in PLA. This heightened enzymatic degradability accelerates the breakdown of PCL-rich regions within the blends, particularly in samples with higher PCL content, where a larger proportion of the material is prone to enzymatic attack. In addition, PCL typically has a more crystalline structure compared to PLA, as supported by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) results. In PLA/PCL blends, as the PCL content increases, a balance between amorphous and crystalline regions is established. The crystallinity of the blends plays a critical role in their degradation kinetics. While 20 wt% PCL content enhances crystallinity through a nucleating effect, higher PCL content disrupts polymer chain packing, reducing overall crystallinity. This reduction, as supported by DSC data, increases the accessibility of amorphous regions to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation, further accelerating the degradation rate. The crystalline regions of PCL are hydrolytically more stable than the amorphous regions, yet their interplay with PLA ensures a consistent degradation rate across the material [51]. Due to the increased presence of amorphous regions in the PLA/PCL50 and PLA/PCL60 blends, these regions are more susceptible to water and enzyme penetration, resulting in higher biodegradation rates [52]. The phase-separated morphology of PLA/PCL blends enhances this effect by creating localized PCL-rich domains that are more accessible to degradation agents. The interaction between amorphous and crystalline regions creates a dynamic system, where amorphous areas degrade faster while the crystalline structure provides stability over an extended period. retrieved_contexts: ['Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(trimethylene terephthalate) (PTT) are examples of polyesters with partial biobased content, produced by combining fossil-derived terephthalic acid (TA) with renewable components such as 1,3-propanediol (PDO) or ethylene glycol. This structural feature underlies the polyamides’ excellent mechanical properties, including strong impact resistance, high hardness, and good abrasion resistance.', 'Numerous studies and patents have been published on the enzymatic depolymerization of biodegradable aliphatic polyesters, often utilizing enzymes such as lipase or Proteinase K [120]. This process involves the initial breakdown of polymers into oligomers and further depolymerization into monomers. Lipases can increase the depolymerization rate by up to 30%, even at lower temperatures, thus reducing enzyme degradation. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that enzyme Immobilization on solid supports can enhance enzyme stability and recyclability, potentially increasing the number of recycling cycles from 3 to 10. Enzymes such as cutinase, lipases, and proteases, as well as specialized enzymes like PETase, play a crucial role in biodegradation by breaking down bioplastic polymers into simpler, eco-friendly monomers that microbes can metabolize. Microorganisms like Pseudomonas, Bacillus, Aspergillus, and Penicillium secrete these enzymes, driving the decomposition process, which typically takes three to six months to degrade substrates (Fig. 8). However entirely, challenges persist such as the enzyme instability under extreme conditions (temperature, pH), poor substrate binding affinity, and susceptibility to proteolytic degradation limit their efficiency in industrial settings [115]. Advancements in protein engineering and immobilization techniques have been pivotal. Protein engineering utilizes tools such as machine learning and artificial intelligence to optimize enzyme structures, thereby enhancing thermostability, substrate specificity, and catalytic efficiency. Complementary strategies include novel high-throughput screening methods to identify superior enzyme variants and reinforcement of enzyme surfaces to improve substrate binding (highlighted in the “Bioengineered proteins for bioplastic degradation” framework). Immobilization techniques further enable enzyme reuse and stability by anchoring enzymes to solid supports, mitigating degradation risks. Modern bioengineering methods, such as gene cloning and metagenomics (Fig. 8), have expanded the discovery of novel enzymes and microbial producers. For instance, microbial consortia exhibit synergistic effects by combining multiple species with complementary enzymatic activities, accelerating degradation kinetics. Species like Bacillus and Aspergillus are particularly promising due to their robust secretion of lipases and proteases, while Pseudomonas demonstrates versatility in degrading complex polymer blends. Despite progress, scaling up enzyme production while maintaining cost-effectiveness, ensuring long-term stability in industrial waste streams, and optimizing microbial co-cultures for consistent performance remain key hurdles. Continued innovation at the intersection of enzyme engineering, microbial ecology, and integrated waste management systems is essential to fully harness the potential of biodegradable plastics, aligning with the circular economy model depicted in the bioplastic lifecycle framework [115]. Enzymatic and microbial strategies targeting molecular interactions in polymeric structures for the degradation of bioplastics [115]', "First published on 17th May 2024 Polylactic acid (PLA) is attracting significant interest as a sustainable alternative to conventional plastics. However, its biodegradation rates vary across environments, and its integration into existing recycling infrastructure necessitates the development of complex end-of-life management strategies. Enzymatic depolymerization offers a promising pathway for closed-loop recycling and upcycling of waste plastics by recovering monomeric building blocks. Yet, few enzymes have been identified that exhibit PLA depolymerization efficiency comparable to those known for PET degradation. Here, we report the computational design of an esterase, RPA1511, from Rhodopseudomonas palustris, which exhibits hydrolytic activity against solid PLA but lacks thermal stability. Using a variety of computational enzyme stability design tools, a focused library was constructed for experimental validation. Further accumulation of beneficial mutations resulted in a five-point variant, R5, which showed an 8 °C increase in melting temperature (Tm) and a substantial 11.5-fold increase in relative enzyme activity at optimal temperatures. This variant achieved efficient PLA degradation, converting 85.38% of PDLLA powder into lactate monomers within 72 h at 65 °C, with a 3.3-fold enhancement compared to wild-type RPA1511. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that the V202 W mutation induced structural changes in the substrate binding pocket and potentially formed more productive complexes, while the remaining four mutations improved the variant's thermal stability. This combined approach through computational design yielded an efficient and thermostable PLA depolymerase, potentially facilitating PLA bio-recycling processes. Despite its biodegradability, PLA faces limitations. First, complete degradation requires specific industrial composting conditions, as PLA exhibits only minimal breakdown in natural environments such as soil and oceans after extended periods.6,7 Second, the integration of waste PLA into existing recycling infrastructure remains a challenge. Current systems designed for petroleum-based plastics view biodegradable plastics as contaminants because biodegradable plastics are not correctly sorted for recycling and are treated together.6,8 Additionally, consumer difficulty in differentiating plastic types leads to PLA also ending up in landfills or incineration, negating its biodegradability potential.", 'Despite these benefits, the expansion of bioplastic production must be matched with the development of effective end-of-life strategies for managing bioplastic waste. Without proper waste management systems, the environmental benefits of bioplastics could be compromised. It is crucial to implement comprehensive recycling and disposal methods tailored to the specific types of bioplastics, ensuring their environmental benefits are fully realized. This includes enhancing recycling technologies, developing standards for compostability, and increasing public awareness about the proper disposal of bioplastic products. As the bioplastics industry grows, these measures are crucial to prevent new forms of pollution and capitalize on the sustainable promise of bioplastics. Non-biodegradable bioplastics, such as bio-PET, bio-PE, and bio-PP, can be efficiently processed within existing recycling systems alongside conventional petrochemical plastics. However, the end-of-life treatment for biodegradable bioplastics, such as PLA and PHAs, is more complex. While biodegradation is often considered the standard disposal method, these materials can be processed through mechanical, enzymatic, and chemical recycling. These alternative recycling strategies not only help alleviate waste accumulation but also enable the recovery of valuable materials and molecular precursors. This approach conserves primary resources and may offer more favorable economic and environmental outcomes than biodegradation alone. By adopting these advanced recycling technologies, we can improve the sustainability of bioplastics and promote a more circular economy. PLA, one of the most widely used biodegradable bioplastics, degrades very slowly in natural and marine environments, potentially causing environmental pollution if not managed properly. Therefore, evaluating PLA’s recyclability is essential, starting with the development of an efficient waste collection strategy and considering the establishment of a dedicated recycling stream. This is crucial for maintaining the integrity of existing recycling systems for conventional plastics, such as PET. The choice of recycling method for PLA-mechanical, chemical, or enzymatic-depends on various factors, including the quality and condition of the PLA waste. This can be addressed by optimizing processing parameters and utilizing suitable compounding and additives, which enable the production of high-quality, marketable recycled PLA. Moreover, exploring advanced recycling technologies, such as catalytic depolymerization and AI-enhanced innovative sorting systems, can enhance recycling efficiency. In conclusion, a multi-faceted strategy that incorporates financial incentives, regulatory support, and technological innovation is necessary to optimize the recycling of bioplastics, thereby supporting the broader goal of sustainability in the plastics industry.', 'The escalating global reliance on petroleum resources has intensified research efforts toward renewable-processable bio-based polyesters as sustainable alternatives. FDCA-derived polyesters and copolyesters, leveraging their balanced physicochemical stability, tunable mechanical properties, and inherent sustainability, are positioned as leading candidates to displace conventional petroleum-derived plastics (e.g., PET) in diverse applications. However, industrial-scale deployment of FDCA-based polyesters remains confronted with critical barriers: (1) elevated FDCA feedstock costs; (2) undesirable decarboxylation side reactions during synthesis, inducing chromophore formation and product discoloration; (3) energy-intensive polymerization conditions; and (4) performance gaps in mechanical durability and processability compared to commercial counterparts like PET. Addressing these limitations requires synergistic advancements in three domains: strategic optimization of polymerization protocols, development of innovative catalytic systems, and implementation of advanced process engineering strategies. Such multidisciplinary integration is imperative to establish FDCA-based polyesters as industrially competitive materials for a sustainable plastic economy. Polyamides (PAs), characterized by backbone-repeating amide linkages (-NHCO-) [93], constitute a vital class of engineering thermoplastics classified into three structural categories: aliphatic, aliphatic-aromatic, and fully aromatic systems based on their molecular architectures. These versatile polymers have gained industrial prominence in textiles, automotive components, and electronic packaging applications owing to their exceptional mechanical robustness, thermal stability, wear resistance, superior gas barrier properties, and chemical durability [[94], [95], [96], [97]]. Despite being a top-tier engineering polymer, PA’s circular economy implementation remains underdeveloped, with incomplete understanding of degradation pathways and immature recycling infrastructure. The concurrent crises of fossil resource depletion and environmental degradation have driven a paradigm shift toward sustainable polymer design, prioritizing biodegradable systems and bio-based alternatives as critical research frontiers. This context underscores the strategic imperative to develop circular lifecycle solutions for PAs through innovative monomer sourcing, green synthesis protocols, and advanced recycling technologies. As non-food lignocellulosic feedstocks ubiquitous in plant cell walls, cellulose and hemicellulose offer strategic valorization pathways to decouple biomass utilization from food chain competition. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis/dehydration cascades convert these polysaccharides into platform chemicals (e.g., HMF), which can be further upgraded to diverse furanic monomers such as furanamine, FDCA, and 2,5-bis(aminomethyl)furan (BAMF) [98]. In light of the aforementioned context, bio-based polyamides have been initially industrialized as substitutes for petroleum-based materials, with products such as PA11 (castor oil-based) and PA610 (castor oil/sebacic acid-based) being introduced in succession. Although current market penetration remains limited, global R&D investments in bio-based polyamides maintain an upward trajectory, driven by advancements in biotechnological processing and green chemistry principles. Particularly noteworthy are FDCA-derived furanic polyamides that exhibit superior thermal resilience, enhanced mechanical integrity, and exceptional chemical resistance, positioning them as next-generation candidates to overcome critical performance limitations in bio-based polyamide systems.', 'The review paper explores the innovative utilization of recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste in synthesizing advanced polyester resin-based composites, particularly through integrating metallic nanofillers. PET, a highly durable and versatile polymer, poses significant environmental challenges due to its non-biodegradable nature and extensive use, especially in consumer packaging. The paper examines chemical recycling methods such as glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis, and aminolysis, which depolymerize PET into monomers that can be repolymerized into unsaturated polyester resins (UPRs). These UPRs, reinforced with metallic fillers like iron oxide, alumina, nickel, and copper, exhibit enhanced mechanical, thermal, and magnetic properties. The incorporation of these nanofillers significantly improves composite matrices, increasing tensile strength, thermal stability, conductivity, and magnetic responsiveness, thus making them suitable for applications in electronics, automotive, and structural industries. This study highlights the synergistic effects of multi-filler systems, which provide superior reinforcement by altering thermal conductivity and electromagnetic absorption properties. Furthermore, this review promotes the circular economy, demonstrating how PET waste can be transformed into high-performance, sustainable composites, thereby reducing environmental impact and conserving resources. Future research is directed toward optimizing nanoparticle dispersion and developing multi-functional composites tailored for specific high-performance applications. This paper contributes valuable insights into sustainable materials science by advancing Recycling Technologies and Hybrid Nanocomposites Development. Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) and Unsaturated Polyester Resins (UPRs) represent two pivotal categories of polymers with substantial applications across diverse industries, driven by their distinct properties and functionalities. However, the escalating production and consumption of PET have resulted in a corresponding increase in PET waste, presenting significant environmental and economic challenges. Efficient recycling methods exist for clear PET bottles, such as washing and remelting; yet contaminated or colored bottles pose greater difficulties. To address this issue, lower-quality PET can undergo chemical recycling processes that involve purification and conversion into new PET, thereby facilitating its reintroduction into the production cycle.', 'However, the exploitation of renewable feedstocks alone does not overcome the addressed issues and therefore the concept of the circular economy has been introduced [13, 14], where end-of-life materials are degraded either industrially or environmentally to be reintroduced into the value chain, contributing to a synergistic sustainability approach [15]. Specifically, FDCA-based polyesters are amenable to mechanical recycling or chemical depolymerization for the recovery of FDCA monomers or derivatives. While mechanical recycling often results in downcycling or blending with virgin materials [36], chemical methods offer a more promising route. For example, PEF can be efficiently degraded into its constituent FDCA monomers or derivatives via alcoholysis or hydrolysis, facilitating closed-loop recycling and decreasing dependence on fossil feedstocks, thereby contributing to sustainable material cycling [37,38]. [39] reported efficient methanolysis of waste PEF using zinc acetate catalysis under microwave irradiation, generating dimethyl 2,5-furandicarboxylate and ethylene glycol with a turnover frequency of 396 h-1.
