This review will guide researchers in selecting appropriate chemical technologies for BP upcycling, promote research on BP conversion, and facilitate the transformation of BPs into valuable resources with low carbon emissions. Biodegradable plastics (BPs) are defined as ester-based plastics that can degrade from the actions of naturally occurring microorganisms such as algae, bacteria and fungi.7 Under the current “plastic restriction” policies, BPs are becoming a crucial alternative to traditional plastics. In 2023, global BP production reached approximately 1.01 million tons, with projections estimating an increase to 1.95 million tons by 2029.8 Common BPs usually include polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT), and polycaprolactone (PCL). Due to their distinct properties, different BPs can be applied in various applications. PLA has favorable mechanical properties, making it ideal for blister products and injection-molded items. PHA exhibits significant potential to be applied in medicine and agriculture. Despite its excellent mechanical properties, PBS has limited aging resistance and is primarily used in agricultural films. PBAT is applied in packaging and food service utensils, while PCL is used in biomedical products and 3D printing materials.9,10 Chemical recycling of fossil-based polyurethanes has been successfully demonstrated at both laboratory and industrial scales over the past few decades. In contrast, BPs can undergo chain scission and chemical transformation under specific environmental conditions such as in soil and seawater, ultimately decomposing into CO2 and H2O.11 However, not all BPs are readily biodegradable in soil or seawater. If used in large quantities with the expectation of natural degradation, BPs may instead accumulate in ecosystems due to incomplete or slow degradation processes.12 Some have reported that PLA degradation in soil usually takes about 1 year.13 More importantly, the end product of the biodegradation process of polymers is CO2, which is essentially indistinguishable after incineration when assessing CO2 emission.14 In addition, the accumulation of BPs in the environment is partly attributable to insufficient public awareness and inadequate upcycling practices. Therefore, it is equally urgent to strengthen waste management systems and enhance civic education to ensure the sustainable disposal of BPs. The conversion of BPs not only recycles waste plastics but also advances the circular economy. Consequently, the treatment and disposal of BPs have received widespread attention. Current treatment and disposal methods for BPs include landfill, incineration, mechanical recycling, biological treatments, and chemical upcycling.15 Landfilling of BPs produces methane and carbon dioxide which can contribute to climate change.16 While incineration enables heat and power from waste BPs, it entails high costs and emission of volatile organic compounds and toxic pollutants.17 Mechanical recycling and biological treatments offer pathways for BP recovery. However, mechanical recycling is costly and end products may not be durable.18 Biological treatments which employ microorganisms or enzymes to enzymatically cleave polymers into constituent monomers, including enzymatic and anaerobic digestion, and composting. Biological treatments are considered as the most environmentally friendly methods for the treatment of BPs, showing great promise and attracting widespread research interest. However, they are hindered by higher operating cost and prolonged treatment cycles, restricting broad applications of biological treatments.19 In contrast, chemical upcycling enables the efficient depolymerization of BPs into monomers or oligomers under closed and controlled conditions, followed by the synthesis of high-performance recycled materials. The chemical upcycling approach not only retains the intrinsic carbon value of the polymers, but also offers broad adaptability and high conversion efficiency across diverse types of BPs through precise reaction condition optimization.20 Notably, photocatalytic and electrocatalytic approaches have recently gained attention as emerging strategies for high-value conversion in chemical upcycling. Photocatalysis converts BP hydrolysis products into value-added chemicals, such as converting PLA to alanine,21 by utilizing photogenerated electrons (e−) and holes (h+) on catalyst surfaces.22 Electrocatalysis utilizes redox reactions at electrodes under an applied voltage to produce valuable products, such as converting PLA to amino acids.23 Recent reviews have explored BP synthese,24 mechanical recycling,25 bio-recycling,18,26 partial chemical recycling methods, and the role of BPs in the circular economy.27 However, these studies provide insufficient analysis of the mechanisms and influencing factors of BP conversion technologies and fail to summarize emerging upcycling technologies. Moreover, the absence of systematic evaluations for advantages and limitations across various conversion methods hampers the selection of BP conversion technologies.', 'The depletion of fossil resources, as well as environmental issues, are serious problems and are the basis for the shift towards renewable sources for the production of materials. Plastics made from non-fossil sources such as polylactide (PLA) are an important part of ecological waste management, Circular Economy and carbon footprint reduction. It can be processed in many ways to create a full range of products such as films, fibres, injection molded details and preforms. Unfortunately, this material also has disadvantages. The main ones include the high cost of the material and some limitation in mechanical properties, which discourages manufacturers from using it [1]. One of the ways to reduce the cost of the material is to create a biocomposite with the addition of lignocellulosic filler. According to Mohanty et al. [2], adding a biodegradable filler to a biodegradable polymer matrix should allow for obtaining a biodegradable composite. Lignocellulose filler from agri-food waste allows the recycling of residue. All of this is in line with the EU Strategy for Plastics and Bioeconomy in the Circular Economy, encouraging sustainable waste management and the idea of „zero waste” [3]. Using agri-food waste as a plastic filler is a method used by scientists. Leszczyńska et al., used chokeberry pomace, raspberry seeds, hazelnut and walnut shells as a natural filler and natural blowing agent in rigid polyurethane foam composites [4]. Scafarro et al. used Posidonia oceanica dead leaves and as well as Botta et al., used artichoke stem as a PLA filler [5,6].', 'Non‐isothermal crystallization kinetics and melting behaviors of poly(butylene succinate) and its copolyester modified with trimellitic imide units Plastic waste has caused tremendous environmental problems. In particular, microplastic pollution has increased across the globe, including in remote areas with little to no human activity.1 Consequently, over the past decades, biodegradable plastics have received keen attention from both scientific and public communities as they offer a promising approach for coping with growing concerns over the potentially harmful impact of microplastics on various ecosystems. Among several categories of commercialized biodegradable polymers, poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) has gained intensive interest as a competitive candidate for a sustainable and circular economy.2-6 PBS is a bio-based aliphatic polyester that contains a hydrolyzable ester linkage in its main chain and is therefore susceptible to both abiotic and microbial attack.7 The polymer possesses desirable mechanical and thermal properties as well as processability comparable to those of conventional petroleum-based materials and is highly biodegradable.8 The biodegradation rate and physicochemical properties of PBS can be modified over a wide range through copolymerization with different comonomers and/or by adjusting their contents. Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) is an attractive PBS-based biodegradable copolymer that is commercially available for various applications.5, 6, 9-14 Its molecular structure differs from that of PBS only in the number of methylene groups in the diacid unit, as depicted in Scheme 1. The incorporation of the butylene adipate (BA) monomer in the copolymer led to lower crystallinity, resulting in improved biodegradability according to soil burial and enzymatic hydrolysis tests.2, 6 The biodegradation rates of polyesters depend on several parameters, including molecular weight, chemical structure, chain packing and mobility, and crystallinity.6, 7, 10 In addition to these intrinsic properties, environmental factors such as abiotic oxidation are also important. The **sol-gel transition** in injectable biodegradable hydrogels refers to a reversible phase change from a free-flowing liquid (**sol state**) to a semi-solid network (**gel state**) triggered by external stimuli, most commonly **temperature**. This transition is critical for applications requiring minimally invasive delivery, as the hydrogel can be injected as a low-viscosity solution and rapidly form a gel under physiological conditions (e.g., body temperature). Key aspects include:  

1. **Mechanism**:  
   - **Physical Crosslinking**: Driven by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, or micelle aggregation (e.g., in PEG/polyester copolymers like PLGA-PEG-PLGA or PCL-g-PEG). For example:  
     - In thermosensitive systems (e.g., chitosan/GP or SF/MC hydrogels), heating disrupts hydrophilic interactions (e.g., hydration shells), enabling hydrophobic domains to aggregate into a network.  
     - In star-shaped or graft copolymers (e.g., 3sPLGA-mPEG), micelle packing and partial crystallization of hydrophobic segments (e.g., PLGA, PCL) drive gelation.  

2. **Determination**:  
   - **Rheological Criteria**: The sol-gel transition temperature (\(T_{\text{gel}}\)) is identified when storage modulus (\(G'\)) surpasses loss modulus (\(G''\)) (**crossover point**) or when the phase angle (\(\tan \delta\)) becomes frequency-independent (**Winter-Chambon criterion**).  
   - \(T_{\text{gel}}\) depends on polymer concentration, heating rate, and molecular architecture. For instance, 2 wt% chitosan exhibits \(T_{\text{gel}} = 65.3^\circ\)C at 1°C/min, but extrapolates to an equilibrium \(T_{\text{gel}} = 46.7^\circ\)C at zero heating rate.  

3. **Key Features**:  
   - **Reversibility**: Physical hydrogels (e.g., SF, chitosan, PEG/polyester blends) undergo reversible gelation without chemical crosslinkers, avoiding toxicity or heat release.  
   - **Injectable Design**: Low viscosity at room temperature ensures injectability, while rapid gelation at physiological temperatures (e.g., 37°C) prevents leakage post-injection.  
   - **Biodegradability**: Degradation occurs via hydrolysis (e.g., PLGA, PCL) or enzymatic action (e.g., chitosan), matching tissue regeneration timelines.  

4. **Applications**:  
   - **Tissue Engineering**: Supports cell encapsulation (e.g., hDPSCs in HPCH/CW hydrogels) and mimics extracellular matrix stiffness (e.g., ~0.9 kPa for dental pulp regeneration).  
   - **Drug Delivery**: Sustained release of therapeutics (e.g., indomethacin in PNMHTI hydrogels) due to tunable mesh sizes and degradation rates.  

5. **Challenges**:  
   - **Mechanical Strength**: Enhanced via additives (e.g., laponite, Dex-PLA) or copolymer blending.  
   - **Gelation Kinetics**: Slow gelation at low concentrations or basic pH (e.g., SF) may require combinatorial methods (e.g., pH/temperature dual-responsive systems).  

In summary, the sol-gel transition enables injectable hydrogels to balance injectability, biocompatibility, and functional performance, making them indispensable for biomedical applications.

4.  **D-isomer incorporation disrupts stereoregularity and accelerates degradation:** Introducing D-lactide into L-lactide systems disrupts the stereoregularity of the resulting PLA chains. This reduces crystallinity, leading to completely amorphous, fragile materials that degrade rapidly (e.g., crumble in <24h in PBS) ([14]).

**In summary:** Stereochemistry primarily affects degradation rate indirectly via its profound impact on crystallinity. High stereoregularity (high L-content for PLLA or high D-content for PDLA) leads to higher crystallinity, which slows degradation. Racemic mixtures (D,L-content) or the intentional incorporation of the opposite isomer disrupt stereoregularity, resulting in amorphous PLA that degrades much faster.

Based solely on the provided context, the role of glycerol in the production of thermoplastic starch (TPS) is as follows:

1.  **Plasticizer:** Glycerol acts as a plasticizer for starch during the gelatinization process ([1], [2], [3], [6], [7], [8], [9], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]).
2.  **Mechanism:** It functions by creating hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl groups of starch molecules, replacing the strong starch-starch physical bonds with plasticizer-starch bonds. This disrupts the crystalline structure of native starch ([2], [3], [7], [8]).
3.  **Processability:** By disrupting the hydrogen bonding between starch chains, glycerol lowers the glass transition temperature (Tg) and makes the starch processable using conventional thermoplastic techniques like extrusion ([7], [8], [9]).
4.  **Common Choice:** It is the most common plasticizer used for TPS due to its high boiling point, low cost, high solubility in starch chains, and availability ([2], [3], [7], [8], [11], [15]).
5.  **Resulting Properties (Pros & Cons):**
    *   **Pros:** Imparts high flexibility and ductility to the TPS ([12], [13], [15]).
    *   **Cons:** Results in TPS with lower tensile modulus, lower thermal stability, higher moisture absorption, and poor resistance to retrogradation (recrystallization) compared to plasticizers like sorbitol. This is due to glycerol's relatively small molecular size, high vapor pressure, high hydrophilicity, and weaker interaction with starch chains ([2], [3], [7], [8], [11], [12], [13], [15]). Its high hydrophilicity also leads to sensitivity to water ([14]).
6.  **Co-plasticization:** Because of the drawbacks of using glycerol alone, it is often combined with other plasticizers (like sorbitol) in a co-plasticization strategy to achieve a balance of properties (e.g., flexibility, strength, thermal stability, retrogradation resistance) ([2], [3], [7], [8], [11], [12], [13], [15]).

The **lag phase** in the biodegradation of plastics in compost refers to the initial period during which **abiotic mechanisms** (primarily chemical hydrolysis) dominate over biotic (enzymatic) processes. This phase occurs because:  
1. **Microbial acclimatization**: Microorganisms require time to adapt to the presence of synthetic polymers (e.g., PLA, PBAT) that are not readily assimilable.  
2. **Polymer structure**: Synthetic polymers like semi-crystalline polyesters (e.g., PLA) resist microbial action initially. Hydrolysis first breaks down amorphous regions, generating smaller oligomers that microbes can later metabolize.  
3. **Environmental penetration**: Water and enzymes need time to diffuse into the polymer matrix to initiate depolymerization.  

**Key observations from the context**:  
- Natural polymers (e.g., cellulose, starch) exhibit **no lag phase** as they are immediately accessible to extracellular enzymes.  
- Synthetic polymers (e.g., PLA) show a lag phase (~10–20 days in compost) due to their resistance to hydrolysis and microbial assimilation.  
- Additives (e.g., graphene, GRH) or blending with biodegradable materials (e.g., thermoplastic starch) can **shorten the lag phase** by accelerating hydrolysis or improving microbial accessibility.  
- The lag phase ends when microbial enzymatic activity becomes dominant, marked by a rapid increase in CO₂ evolution during biodegradation.  

In summary, the lag phase reflects the time required for abiotic degradation to prepare synthetic polymers for microbial assimilation, influenced by material composition, crystallinity, and environmental conditions.
reference: The lag phase is the initial period where no significant mineralization (CO2 evolution) occurs. During this time, microorganisms colonize the surface and secrete extracellular enzymes to begin fragmenting the polymer chain. Only after the molecular weight drops sufficiently to produce water-soluble intermediates does rapid assimilation and mineralization begin.

retrieved_contexts: ["First, PHAs are very difficult to convert into packages with conventional plastic processing techniques. In addition to their low viscosity and melt strength, PHA thermal degradation occurs upon melting;5 this depresses the final structural and mechanical properties of the plastic part or package. In this respect, polyhydroxy(butyrate-co-valerate) (PHBV) is a microbial copolyester showing lower melting temperatures (Tm's) than polyhydroxybutyrate. This contributes to a reduced thermal degradation during melt processing.6 Second, PHA, and to a lesser extent PHBV, is a brittle material, which shows slow crystallization kinetics followed by secondary crystallization. Slow crystallization is a strong drawback in applications such as injection molding, as it significantly extends the cycle time. The secondary crystallization is also an issue as packages will show aging and, thus, properties evolving with time. The brittleness virtually casts away PHA and PHBV from film packaging applications. PHBV is preferred over pure PHB due to the incorporation of hydroxyvalerate (HV) units, which impart several key improvements:  
1. **Lower Melting Temperatures**: PHBV has a reduced melting point compared to PHB, minimizing thermal degradation during melt processing and preserving structural/mechanical properties ([1], [2]).  
2. **Reduced Brittleness**: PHBV exhibits lower crystallinity and slower secondary crystallization, leading to enhanced ductility and flexibility compared to the highly brittle PHB ([1], [3], [4]).  
3. **Improved Processability**: The lower melting temperature and reduced thermal degradation of PHBV widen the processing window, making it more compatible with conventional techniques like injection molding ([1], [5]).  
4. **Enhanced Mechanical Properties**: Higher HV content in PHBV increases elongation at break and toughness while maintaining strength, addressing PHB’s intrinsic brittleness and poor fracture resistance ([3], [7], [14]).  
5. **Favorable Crystallization Behavior**: PHBV’s slower crystallization kinetics and reduced crystallinity mitigate issues like aging and property evolution over time, which are pronounced in PHB ([1], [12]).  

These modifications make PHBV more viable for applications requiring flexibility, thermal stability, and processability, such as packaging and biomedical devices.

retrieved_contexts: ['Biodegradable materials based on magnesium alloys have a huge potential for bone fracture fixation devices due to their adequate mechanical properties and biocompatibility. However, their fast degradation and the consequent liberation of hydrogen gas at the initial stages of implantation is the major limitation for their use. In this study, the AZ91D magnesium alloy was surface treated by an environment-friendly, nontoxic, and low-cost anodizing process and the early in vivo response was studied in a rat transcortical model. Adequate maturation of woven bone around implants-detected at day 7 post implantation-to lamellar bone was observed from day 15. Lamellar bone after 15 and 30 days of implantation presented similar volume, mineralization pattern, mineral to protein content, and estimated bone maturity between anodized AZ91D and polylactic acid (control) implants. Histology observation showed neither release of hydrogen bubbles in the region closed to the anodized AZ91D implant nor systemic effects on liver, kidney, and spleen. Thus, anodizing of AZ91D in the conditions stated here induced an adequate short-term in vivo response, which postulates their use as potential biodegradable fracture fixation devices for bone healing. Bone fractures are commonly treated by the use of metallic devices, such as screws and plates, to stabilize the bone and allow their correct healing. These devices are typically made of titanium or stainless steel and require a second surgical intervention for implant removal once bone healing is completed. Currently, there is growing interest in the development of biodegradable materials for such application, which can provide temporary support for tissue regeneration and then completely degrade once the bone is restored. In this manner, biodegradable materials would eliminate the need of the second surgery, diminishing time of patient recovery, health care costs, and risks associated with a surgical intervention. Magnesium (Mg) based alloys are promising candidates for fracture fixation devices mainly due to their mechanical properties-density, elastic modulus, and yield strength-, which are similar to that of bone. (1) In addition, Mg is an element naturally present in the body, involved in several physiological processes, (2) and thus the degradation of a Mg based implant in the body is biocompatible. (3,4) The major limitation for the use of Mg based materials as implants is their fast degradation and the consequent liberation of hydrogen gas, a product of their corrosion in aqueous media. (5) Strategies of alloying with other elements such as aluminum, zinc, or rare earth elements, (6) and the surface protection with coatings (7) have been successful in retarding the corrosion rate of Mg. In some cases, promising uncoated or coated Mg alloys were studied in small (mice, rat, and rabbit) or large (guinea pig, goat, mini pig, and sheep) animal models (see Sekar et al. (8) for a review), which provide information regarding material safety, biodegradability, bone formation stimulation, and inflammatory response, among others. For example, fluoride, (9) calcium phosphate, (9,10) hydroxyapatite-MgO coatings, (11,12) aluminum, (13) and silicate oxides (14) coatings were demonstrated to increase corrosion resistance of Mg alloys in vivo and/or to favor bone formation. In spite of these favorable results, the use of Mg based materials in the orthopedic field is still scarce. Only one company is commercializing Mg based (Mg-Zn-Ca alloys) screws named MAGNEZIX since 2013, with good results in restoring motor function (15,16) and similar therapeutic efficiency than titanium screws. (17) On the basis of all this evidence, it is clear that Mg based implants have huge potential to replace inert permanent materials (e.g., titanium, stainless steel) for bone fracture fixation devices. Besides, when compared with other biodegradable materials as polymers (e.g., polylactic acid; PLA) Mg alloys present better and “close to bone” mechanical properties. However, although there is a profuse literature about the in vitro performance of the alloys, additional research is required to continue elucidating the in vivo corrosion process and to find surface treatments that could mitigate the hydrogen liberation during the first stage of implantation, which is still evidenced even in patients implanted with the new commercial Mg screws. (18)', 'Load-bearing biodegradable biocompatible materials are always needed for medical applications to serve mainly as osteoconductive implants [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. They may cause stress shielding accompanied by bone resorption and implant loosening due to high modulus implants. They showed a uniform degradation morphology, a sufficient bending force and an enhanced fracture healing with good osseointegration in the area surrounding the screws [25].', 'Surgeons often focus on residual volume ratio of magnesium-based alloy after implantation at specific time points due to concerns about the reliability of early fixation. Ultimately, the aim of this work is to facilitate the clinical promotion of well-established magnesium-based materials and the screening and improvement of newly developed materials and processing techniques for future investigators.', 'Degradation rate of Poly(l-lactide-co-glycolide) increased by ×22 at 47 °C compared to 37 °C. Traditionally, permanent metallic materials have been used in orthopaedic applications due to their high strength and inert nature. Moreover, the surfaces of the samples displayed apatite mineralization after 168 h of immersion in m-SBF solution, indicating that the welded samples, particularly the weld-coated samples, can be utilised as implant materials.', 'Magnesium possesses a modulus of elasticity similar to bone, and hence has been widely explored for orthopedic applications to avoid stress shielding. Challenges of utilizing magnesium alloys as an implant material are: (i) the substantial corrosion rate, which rapidly raises the local pH that harms the local tissue, (ii) the tendency for magnesium corrosion to produce hydrogen gas139 and form gas cavities next to the magnesium implant, which has induced mortality in rats,140 and (iii) the rapid decrease of mechanical strength due to the substantial corrosion.141 All these challenges could lead to premature failure of a magnesium implant. The substantial corrosion rate (and concomitant high pH values) can be obviated by the use of magnesium alloys with good corrosion performance, such as WE43, which has been used for applications such as bone screws47 and stents.142 Zinc has recently become of interest as a biodegradable metal. Zinc contributes to biological functions such as signal transduction and gene expression.143 The challenges for utilizing zinc for medical applications are the large creep strains, susceptibility to natural aging, and static recrystallization.137 Iron possesses the best mechanical properties and the slowest corrosion rate, slower than magnesium and zinc.144 Iron plays an essential role in red blood cells.145 However, iron can be lost through skin renewal, and especially by menstruation in pre-menopausal women.145 Therefore, a balanced iron diet is necessary to ensure adequate iron in the body (i.e. by eating plenty of green vegetables, particularly spinach). Thus, iron is indeed one of the essential elements, and this guarantees its safety when implanted in the body. However, the main challenges to utilizing iron for medical applications are: (i) the bulky non-soluble corrosion products (particularly those containing the oxidized ferric form Fe3+),32 which could disrupt the local tissue and (ii) the low corrosion rate, which may be too low for practical applications.146', 'The biocompatibility of the biomaterial is not compromise by the process. In terms of biodegradable materials for temporary implants, PLA/Mg composites have been developed in the last few years as new bioabsorbable biomaterials for several biomedical applications. These applications include dental [1], vascular stent [2], skin regeneration [3], bone repair [4], orthopedic [5] and tissue engineering [6]. Magnesium (Mg) is the fourth most abundant element in the human body, is essential in metabolism and is necessary in more than 300 biochemical reactions in the body [7]. Despite these benefits, before proposing Mg as a suitable temporary implant material, its degradation rate should be properly controlled, as Mg is one of the most reactive structural materials [8]. Several alloys and composites have been developed to control the degradation rate of Mg since uncontrolled degradation could result in loss of mechanical integrity, metal contamination in the body and intolerable hydrogen evolution by tissue [9]. A composite that combines Mg particles in a biopolymeric matrix, such as polylactic acid (PLA), could present similar properties to Mg but with a controlled degradation ratio. Additionally, PLA is a biocompatible and biodegradable polymeric biomaterial, approved by the FDA [10]. Nowadays, there are certain types of PLA polymer implants on the market, such as spinal implants, intramedullary plugs, artificial cartilage frames, screws, plates, meshes, tissue anchors, etc., offered by several companies [11]. PLA/Mg composites have been widely reported in the literature [12]. With regards to the neat polymer, Mg enhances its mechanical properties, particularly the compressive strength, and stiffness with a 15-30 vol% Mg loading [4]. The degradation of these composites in vitro has also been studied by several authors in several simulated media [13]. In PBS PLA/Mg experienced significantly higher weight loss compared to PLA scaffolds, and this weight loss increased proportionally with the addition of Mg. However, this degradation increase is also correlated with a trend towards higher alkalinity [14]. Conversely, in Simulated Body Fluid (SBF), it is revealed that PLA/Mg composites could effectively degrade in the medium, and the incorporation of Mg does not compromise the pH for 28 days [15]. The biological behaviour of PLA/Mg composites has been tested in vitro with several cellular lines such as pre-osteoblast cells [16], fibroblasts [3], [5], epithelial cells [14] and osteoblasts [17]. Additionally, PLA/Mg has been tested in vivo [18] showing that composites with a 10 % Mg loading exhibited optimal osteogenic properties, whereas a 20 % Mg composite group showed angiogenic effects and promising osteoinduction properties.', 'Titanium, nickel and cobalt based alloys are commonly used in osteosynthesis and healthcare systems as permanent bone fixation implants. However, they have some disadvantages, such as temperature and tactile sensitivity, growth restriction, and the possible dispersion of implant material particles within tissue, which may lead to the need for symptomatic removal. Therefore, alternative solutions are being sought [1]. In many countries, orthopedic practices use commercial fixation devices such as NOVAMag® (Botiss biomaterials GmbH, Germany) and MAGNEZIX® (Syntellix AG, Germany), which have been shown to perform equally well to Ti permanent implants [2], [3]. The biodegradable implants gradually dissolve as the healing process progresses, eliminating the need for secondary surgery to remove the implant and reducing healthcare costs [4], [5]. Magnesium alloys are attractive candidates for use in temporary fixation devices for osteosynthesis due to their acceptable biodegradation rate, suitable mechanical properties, and biocompatibility with human tissues [6], [7], [8]. Young’s modulus of Mg alloys is closer to that of cortical bone when compared to permanent Ti implants, which prevents the stress shielding effect [9], [10]. Various methods, such as hot extrusion, hot rolling, and equal channel angular pressing, are used to achieve the fine grain structure and high mechanical properties of magnesium alloys [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. The grain size has a significant impact on the mechanical properties of Mg alloys due to their high Hall-Petch strengthening coefficient (∼300 MPa·m1/2) [17]. In selecting the production route it is also important to maximize yield in order to reduce scrap and minimize environmental impact. These rods can be used to produce screws, nails, and other biodegradable devices.', 'Biodegradable Magnesium‐Based Implants in Orthopedics-A General Review and Perspectives Nowadays, biodegradable metal bone-implant materials are expected to be used as biomedical materials to promote bone tissue repair due to their good degradability, biocompatibility, and no need for secondary surgery. Therefore, improving the mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, biocompatibility, and antibacterial properties of degradable Mg alloys is a key issue to be urgently addressed.', 'Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Recently, biodegradable materials (BMs) have been needed to improve function and accomplish the target of tissue generation. The resorption time of Magnesium-based biodegradable screws is significantly shorter compared to polylactic acid (PLA). 

1. **Magnesium-based screws**:  
   - Magnesium alloys (e.g., AZ91D, Mg-YREZr) degrade within months to approximately **1 year** in vivo, depending on the alloy composition and surface treatments. For example, the commercial MAGNEZIX® Mg-YREZr screws degrade completely in rabbits within ~1 year [Context 2, 5]. Surface modifications, such as anodizing, can mitigate rapid hydrogen gas release while maintaining degradation rates compatible with bone healing (e.g., lamellar bone formation observed by 15–30 days post-implantation) [Context 1].  

2. **PLA**:  
   - PLA, particularly semi-crystalline poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), has a much slower resorption time, exceeding **5 years** in vivo due to its slow hydrolytic degradation [Context 4]. Even copolymers like PDLLA degrade faster but are unsuitable for load-bearing applications.  

**Conclusion**: Magnesium-based screws degrade **1–2 orders of magnitude faster** than PLA, making them more suitable for short- to medium-term fracture fixation without requiring secondary surgery. PLA’s prolonged resorption time limits its use to non-load-bearing applications or composites with faster-degrading materials.
reference: Magnesium-based screws typically degrade/corrode over a period of 1–2 years, depending on the alloy and coating. This is generally comparable to or slightly faster than high-molecular-weight PLLA (which can take 2–5 years for complete resorption), but Mg offers superior initial mechanical strength.

Efforts to enhance hydrogel functionality through biofunctionalization and biochemical cue incorporation could further enhance their relevance for organ-on-chip applications, ultimately advancing biomedical research and improving human health outcomes.', 'Much progress has been over the years, where glass compositions have been tailored with the aim to achieve controlled delivery of therapeutic ions, such as strontium (an anti-osteoporotic species),9,10 fluoride (for applications in dentistry),11 copper (to enhance angiogenesis), cobalt (to mimic hypoxia),12,13 magnesium (an important regulator of skeletal metabolism),14,15 silver (for antibacterial properties), etc. The physical form and composition of glasses and glass-ceramics may be further tailored to facilitate loading and controlled-release of therapeutic drugs. Based solely on the provided context, bioactive glass (BG) fillers enhance biodegradable bone scaffold function through several key mechanisms:

1.  **Enhanced Bioactivity and Bone Bonding:** BG releases soluble calcium (Ca²⁺) and silica (SiO₂) ions upon degradation (Context 1, 7, 14, 15). These ions promote the nucleation and growth of a hydroxycarbonate apatite (HCA) layer on the scaffold surface (Context 7, 9, 14, 15). This HCA layer is essential for forming a strong bond with host bone tissue (Context 7, 14, 15). BG exhibits superior bioactivity compared to other ceramics like hydroxyapatite (HA) or calcium phosphates (CaP) due to its high surface reactivity (Context 7, 14, 15).

2.  **Osteostimulation and Osteoinduction:** The ionic dissolution products (Ca²⁺, SiO₂) from BG stimulate osteogenic responses:
    *   They activate osteogenesis-related signaling pathways (Context 11).
    *   They stimulate gene expression in osteoblastic cells, enhancing osteogenesis and bone formation (Context 2).
    *   BG nanoparticles (BGn) exhibit osteoinductivity, modifying osteogenesis (Context 2).
    *   BG can induce angiogenesis and enhance osteogenic differentiation (Context 9, 14).

3.  **Improved Mechanical Properties:** Incorporating BG fillers into the polymer matrix:
    *   Increases compressive strength and stiffness of the scaffold/composite (Context 5, 7, 14, 15).
    *   Nanosized BG particles (nBG) provide a significantly greater enhancement in mechanical properties (e.g., Young's modulus) compared to micrometer-sized BG (μBG) due to higher specific surface area and interfacial bonding strength (Context 14, 15).
    *   Helps achieve mechanical properties suitable for bone tissue engineering applications, including potentially within the range of trabecular bone (Context 1, 5, 9, 11).

4.  **Controlled Degradation and Ion Release:** BG degradation contributes to the overall biodegradability of the composite scaffold. The formation of nanopores (e.g., inherent in sol-gel BG) increases surface area, tailoring the degradation rate and ion release profile (Context 1). In some systems (e.g., BG/alginate), the polymer matrix can temporarily store ions released rapidly from BG, achieving a more controlled release (Context 11).

5.  **Enhanced Cellular Interactions:** BG fillers improve the scaffold's ability to interact with cells:
    *   Provide cell adhesion sites facilitating integration with surrounding bone tissue (Context 7, 14).
    *   Promote osteoblast activity, bone integration, and resistance to implant failure (Context 6).
    *   Improve cell adhesion, migration, differentiation, and proliferation (Context 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 14).
    *   Nanostructured BG (inherent or as nanoparticles) guides cell attachment and migration due to increased surface area and nanotopography (Context 1, 14, 15).

6.  **Additional Functionalities:** BG fillers can impart specific beneficial properties:
    *   **Antibacterial Activity:** Addition of ions like silver (Ag⁺) or copper (Cu²⁺) to BG can provide antibacterial properties (Context 1, 13).
    *   **Drug Delivery:** Mesoporous BG (MBG) can be incorporated to enhance the drug delivery capacity of polymer scaffolds, enabling sustained release profiles (Context 5).
    *   **pH Stabilization:** BG ion release can stabilize the pH of the local environment, potentially benefiting cell behavior (Context 5).
    *   **Improved Hydrolytic Stability:** BG composites demonstrate enhanced stability in aqueous environments (Context 3).

In summary, bioactive glass fillers transform biodegradable polymer scaffolds into bioactive, osteostimulative composites with enhanced mechanical integrity, controlled degradation/ion release, and improved cellular responses, making them far more effective for bone regeneration than the pristine polymers alone.

These approaches can be roughly divided into synthetic approaches, i. e., chemical polymerization of low molecular weight monomers or exploiting bio-derived polymeric biomacromolecules (polysaccharides or proteins) from raw biomass, as well as biotechnological approaches involving genetic engineering for the production of mainly proteins.7-10 It is important to note that while the end-of-life aspects of bioplastics, i. e., their biodegradability, are often considered superior, many bioplastics are slowly to non-biodegradable, depending on the synthetic approach, such as chemical polymerizations11 or crosslinking reactions.12 Moreover, many bioplastics are not produced using green chemistry methodologies nor helping in lowering the carbon footprint of plastic. Similarly, within the OECD 302 guidelines there are multiple test systems; the most common for water-soluble materials is the OECD 302B or Zahn-Wellens test that measures biodegradation through the removal of dissolved organic carbon in the test medium through loss as carbon dioxide or conversion to biomass.', 'The log-of-slope (LOS) plots of the enzymatic degradation profile for the films with no retrogradation (M45MI, M23I, M23MI, GS70, GS30, GS15 and C0D) of the enzymatic degradation profile exhibit two first-order stages (as shown in Fig. 5A, which represents the degradation of M45MI and as such is an example of the films with no retrogradation), with two rate coefficients k1 and k2. It can be concluded from the above studies that most of the nanocomposites of starch have a reduced rate of overall degradation but still a border line conclusion about this is difficult to make because, very less studies have gone into the direct degradation of starch nanocomposites.', 'One of the most convenient way to reduce the usage of synthetic plastics is to blend them with renewable ones. The resultant nanocomposite film having intercalated clay layers, plasticized starch phase and compatibilizer exhibited superior physico-mechanical properties.', 'Summarizing, the thermo-kinetic analysis among copolymers indicates that the presence of the graft decreases the thermal stability and promotes the auto-catalytic degradation of the potato starch. Thus, it is concluded that the kinetic parameters, i.e. pre-exponential factor, activation energy and rate limiting step for a given conversion degree are dependent of the heating rate and temperature at which the conversion is reached.', 'As the consumption of single use plastic increases with increasing population, its disposal and treatment is major challenge and issue for manufacturers and researchers. Figure 1 shows the structure of PBS and its monomer.', "Biodegradable medical devices have attracted increasing attention owing to their safe resorbability, which eliminates device removal operations during secondary surgery28, 41, 72 and improves device biocompatibility. Based solely on the provided context, the enzymatic mechanism for starch degradation involves:

1.  **Extracellular Enzymes**: Enzymes like amylase are excreted to cleave the glycosidic bonds in the starch polymer backbone extracellularly ([4]).
2.  **Depolymerization**: Enzymes hydrolyze the α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds linking glucose units in amylose and amylopectin, releasing smaller molecules like glucose ([4], [9]). Glucose release is a measurable indicator of this hydrolysis ([9]).
3.  **Kinetics**: Degradation typically follows first-order kinetics. Films without retrogradation often show an initial fast degradation stage (rate coefficient k1) of easily accessible components, followed by a slower stage (k2) for the more resistant underlying structure. Retrograded starch, with higher crystallinity, shows only the slow degradation stage (k1), as crystallinity reduces enzyme accessibility ([5], [7]).
4.  **Susceptibility Factors**: Starch's inherent structure makes it highly susceptible to enzymatic cleavage compared to synthetic polyesters. Factors like molecular size (larger molecules degrade slower initially) and the presence of small soluble molecules influence the kinetics and extent of degradation ([5], [7]).
reference: Starch is degraded by amylases (alpha and beta). Alpha-amylase acts as an endo-enzyme, randomly cleaving alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in the interior of the chain. Beta-amylase acts as an exo-enzyme, removing maltose units from the non-reducing end. This synergistic action rapidly reduces molecular weight and produces metabolizable sugars.

retrieved_contexts: ['Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is considered one of the 3D printing techniques that can directly translate a computer-aided design into a 3D physical model of the required material through a layer-by-layer deposition process [6]. The main advantage of the FDM technique is the ability to accurately and rapidly fabricate 3D-designed scaffolds with complex porosity and pores interconnectivity [7]. Hence, the 3D-printed scaffolds by using the FDM technique show a 3D architecture that closely mimics the native cell environment. However, the FDM technique is restricted only to thermoplastic polymers [8]. Poly--caprolactone (PCL) is a thermoplastic, semi-crystalline, and biodegradable polyester polymer that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for biomedical applications [9]. It has good biocompatibility, appropriate mechanical properties, and unique viscoelastic properties; therefore, it is frequently used in the field of bone TE [10]. Also, the PCL has a low melting point at 60 °C and high thermal stability, which makes it an ideal thermoplastic polymer for 3D printing applications [11]. However, the PCL has a hydrophobic surface that impairs its cellular activity and makes its surface modification necessary to improve its surface properties and subsequent cellular behavior [12, 13]. Different surface modification techniques have been introduced to enhance the surface properties of biomaterials [14]. Of these methods, a plasma surface deposition can be effective in tailoring the surface properties, and subsequently improving and enhancing its interaction with cells [15, 16]. Plasma treatment shows a convenient method for modifying polymer surface properties in terms of hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, surface roughness, surface energy, and surface charge [15]. In addition to surface functionalization required for cell adhesion which could be tailored by the choice of the plasma gas [17, 18]. The plasma surface deposition can be performed using a non-thermal plasma focus (PF) device, where the ions and radicals have a temperature near room temperature which enables the use of plasma deposition for thermally sensitive polymers and reduces the risk of their thermal degradation [19, 20]. Also, the PF device can be used for the deposition of the nanoparticles on a substrate surface, which allows surface topography modification in addition to chemical modifications [18, 21].', 'Additive manufacturing (AM) is a new technique for building 3D parts with complex shapes layer by layer deposition to create a 3-dimensional object with the help of a computer-added model (CAD) [16,17,18]. Recently fused deposition modeling (FDM) or fused filament fabrication is the most widely used technique for the AM processing of thermoplastics [19, 20]. For illustration, thermoplastic polymers acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polyamide (PA), and PLA are the most frequently employed for 3D printing by FDM [21, 22]. Among all the thermoplastic polymers PLA is a more popular material used in the 3D printing technology owing to its excellent 3D printability, biodegradability as well as a non-toxic effect during the printing compared to ABS and polyamide (PA) [23, 24]. On the other hand, ABS originated from petroleum-based resources and requires complex FDM machinery and a heated bed. It also sometimes emits volatile components (e.g., styrene) leading to the warpage of desired product [25, 26]. Thus, PLA is a better alternative to petroleum-based thermoplastics due to its low melting point and low crystallization rate. Further, PLA does not require the employ of a heated bed and does not liberate any unpleasant odors which is the main advantage and require less energy for 3D printing technology compared to ABS [27]. The PLA revealed some limitations in its application owing to its brittleness characteristics. For that reason, PLA is blended with more flexible biodegradable polymers for instance poly (butylene succinate) (PBS) [27], poly(butylene-succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) [28], poly (propylene carbonate) (PPC) [29, 30], polyamide (PA11) [31, 32], and PBAT to improve the toughness properties and reduce the cost and expand its applications and can be used in 3D printing technology [33,34,35]. Amongst the entire polymer PBAT is the best biodegradable copolyester for the blending of PLA matrix and reducing the brittle nature and enhancing the ductile behaviour and toughening properties of the PLA. The toughness of the materials is defined in terms of impact strength, the ability to absorb sudden impact energy without breaking. The obtained blend system demonstrated good flexibility and high elongation (%) along with better hydrophilic and melt processing properties and easily degrades in a compostable environment in a few weeks [36,37,38,39]. The PLA/PBAT blend system revealed very good mechanical resistance and flexibility which is attributed to the PBAT without compromising their biodegradability. PLA/PBAT blend system manufactured by batch mixing method. As a result, it exhibited higher tensile and impact properties after being enhanced by PBAT loading (%) as well as the addition of glycidyl methacrylate (GMA) also improved the impact strength [40,41,42,43,44]. In the current study, we developed sustainable PBAT toughened PLA/PBAT blends 3D filament and its specimen by extrusion and micro compounder process respectively. We further investigated in detail the effect on PBAT loading wt% in the physicochemical, mechanical, thermal, and morphological properties of PLA/PBAT blend filament which provides reliable properties for PLA/PBAT blend filament and is used in various fields. Thus, PLA/PBAT 3D filament is great potential to replace the petroleum-based 3D filament in the additive manufacturing (AM) industries.', 'Three-dimensional (3D) printing, is one of a technique or method in additive manufacturing, produces objects with complex structures by depositing materials, such as metals, polymers, and ceramics, layer by layer [17, 18]. These fabrication techniques are widely used in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine to design patient-specific scaffolds with enhanced control properties [19, 20]. Three-dimensional (3D) printing technology is classified depending on the material and printing method used; fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most common method [21, 22]. In FDM, a thermoplastic material is placed into a nozzle, heated, melted, injected, and solidified in air. The advantage of FDM is that it can print a wide range of biodegradable and biocompatible materials without toxic organic solvents [23, 24]. However, the high temperature used to melt the material can change its physical properties, and high-resolution printing using FDM remains a challenge [23]. Currently, the materials used for alveolar bone regeneration include natural polymers, such as alginate, gelatin, collagen, chitosan, and fibrin, and synthetic polymers, such as polyethylene glycol, poly--caprolactone (PCL), and polylactic acid [25]. Natural and synthetic polymers have their advantages and disadvantages. For example, natural polymers have good biocompatibility but poor mechanical properties, and synthetic polymers largely have good mechanical properties but poor biocompatibility [25]. While some synthetic polymers show good biocompatibility, others fail to promote cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation because of low wettability and improper charge [26, 27]. Before these synthetic polymers are used as biocompatible materials, the properties of the transplant material must be changed to overcome the disadvantages and utilize the advantages [28, 29]. PCL, FDA, EDTA-approved synthetic and aliphatic linear polyester in nature, is emerging in tissue engineering for bone and cartilage regeneration because of its, low melting point, biocompatibility, biodegradability, controllable degradation kinetics, ease of handling, and suitable mechanical properties [30-33]. However, there is no biological recognition site on PCL surface, creating challenges in cell adhesion and proliferation [31]. Accordingly, current research projects aim to enhance cell adhesion and proliferation by binding various biologically active substances to PCL [34-37]. Leptin, a 16 kD-molecular-weight protein hormone secreted by adipocytes, not only controls appetite and metabolism [38-40] but also can induce the odontogenic differentiation and angiogenesis of human dental pulp cells (hDPCs) [41, 42].', 'Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is among the most commonly utilized 3D printing techniques, primarily due to its straightforward process to fabricate tissue engineering scaffolds [7]. This technique employs a temperature-regulated print head to deposit a thermoplastic material onto a platform, gradually constructing a 3D scaffold [8]. Serra et al. fabricated polylactic acid (PLA)-based composite scaffolds via 3D printing technique for tissue engineering applications [9]. Ceretti et al. prepared multi-layered polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffolds via FDM technique with high accuracy [10]. Kim et al. fabricated PCL-based composite scaffolds via FDM technique with great properties for bone regeneration [11]. The biomaterials for scaffold fabrication must also be carefully selected for biomedical applications. In other words, the designed scaffolds should be biodegradable, biocompatible and non-toxic. Appropriate biodegradable behavior of a scaffold allows for degradation along with the formation of natural tissue in a desired period of time. Therefore, choosing a biomaterial that has good biological properties and appropriate biodegradable behavior is an important issue in tissue engineering [12]. Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is a synthetic polymer and its monomers are not available. This polymer is usually obtained from the hydrolysis of polyvinyl acetate (PVAc). PVA polymer with many hydroxyl (OH) groups has been widely considered and used in medical and clinical fields due to its hydrophilicity and suitable mechanical, physical and chemical properties, as well as high resistance to tension and pressure. In addition, the biocompatibility properties of PVA polymer have encouraged biomedical engineering researchers to widely use it for biomedical applications and engineering various types of soft and hard tissues. Therefore, PVA is completely non-toxic and non-carcinogenic and does not stimulate the immune system and cells [13,14,15,16,17,18]. Acik et al. prepared electrospun PVA for drug delivery [19]. Mohammadi Tazehabadi et al. prepared pH-sensitive drug delivery systems based on PVA for drug delivery [20]. Ma et al. synthesized PVA/poly(vinyl pyrrolidone) (PVP) hydrogels for cartilage regeneration [21]. Babakhani et al. fabricated PVA-based scaffolds with great properties for bone tissue engineering [22]. PVA has high water absorption or swelling capacity and when placed in the moist biological environment of the body, it strongly absorbs the water of the environment and degrades in a very short time [23, 24]. Hence, the hydrophilicity of PVA limits its applications for hard tissue applications due to its weak stability. In other words, polymers such as PVA do not show suitable efficiency, so they are not used alone in tissue engineering applications. Therefore, other biomaterials such as bioceramics or other biopolymers are added to these polymers in order to improve their properties [25, 26]. Naebe et al. developed multi-wall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs)/PVA scaffolds via electrospinning technique for biomedical applications [27]. Chen et al. fabricated PVA/β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) composite scaffolds via FDM technique for bone tissue engineering [28]. Batool et al. fabricated PVA/whitlockite/gelatin scaffolds for bone tissue engineering with suitable properties [29]. Thus, the properties of biomaterials can always be improved in order to provide better results in biomedical applications [30].', 'Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most widely used 3D-printing technology due to its simplicity to operate and low cost. However, many engineering plastics such as polycarbonate (PC) with better properties cannot be applied in common FDM printer because of their poor processability and printability. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) as the most common printing material has the disadvantages of insufficient heat resistance and poor toughness, which limits the application of PLA-based FDM product in more potential fields. To develop new material available for FDM, PC/PLA blend was prepared by polymer blending and achieved essential printability for FDM. Ethylene-butyl acrylate-glycidyl methacrylate terpolymer (PTW) was introduced to PC/PLA blend as warpage modifier and also had a good toughening effect. The phase morphology of PLA changed from independent dispersed phase to semi-continuous phase with increasing PLA content. Different from the injection molding samples, the morphology of FDM-printed samples indicated that the PLA phase oriented in the same direction due to the tensile orientation of the filaments caused by nozzle scanning. The work provided some referential conclusions contributing to optimization of printing strategy. With the development of manufacturing technology, more and more companies begin to utilize additive manufacturing technology (also known as 3D printing) to assist in design and fabrication.1 3D-printing technology has unique advantages in complex shape forming, especially in the field of personalized customization, electronics, machinery and medical application.1, 2 Among all the 3D-printing technologies, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most widely used method due to its simplicity to operate and low cost, which attracts much attention both from industry and academia.2, 3 At present, the researches on FDM technology mainly focus on improvement of printing equipment, optimization of printing parameters, development of printing material and application, among which material development is an important research direction.1, 4-6 The feedstock material for FDM is required with suitable processability and good dimensional stability, such as acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) and poly(lactic acid) (PLA).7, 8 However, compared to the great variety of thermoplastic materials, few commercial materials are available for FDM on the market. Many engineering plastics with better properties cannot be applied in FDM because of their poor processability and printability, restricting the application of FDM in engineering field.9 For example, FDM products based on virgin polyamide-6 (PA6) are seriously warped during the printing process due to the serious shrinkage stress.10 Moreover, polycarbonate (PC) is a widely used engineering thermoplastic with excellent mechanical property and thermostability, but unmodified PC is hard to be used as FDM feedstock in common printer because its high processing and glass-transition temperatures raise stringent requirements to the equipment. Therefore, it is significative to develop a way to expand the range of materials available for FDM.', 'The shape of 3D printed products can be transformed over time, achieving 4D printing. In this work, poly(lactic acid) (PLA)/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) blends are fabricated via fused deposition modeling (FDM). The thermoresponsive shape memory effects (SMEs) of 3D printed blends are investigated by stress-controlled dynamic mechanical analysis in tension mode. The SME mechanism is clarified in detail, along with the crystallization and melting behaviors, dynamic mechanical properties, and morphologies of PLA/PCL blends. It is confirmed that the crystallinity of reversible phase PCL, the glass transition behavior of fixed phase PLA and the two-phase interfaces have important effects on the shape memory performance. In the field of advanced manufacturing industry, 3D printing is one of the most promising manufacturing techniques.[1] For manufacturing the products with complicated structures, 3D printing technologies have great advantages over traditional manufacturing processes.[2, 3] The selection of 3D printing techniques is based on the nature of raw materials and the performance requirements of final products.[4] Among the available 3D printing technologies, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most commonly used and cost-effective.[5, 6] However, the printing materials suitable for FDM are generally limited to thermoplastics. The printing anisotropy and printing orientation in FDM process attracted great interest. Chen et al. prepared thermoplastic polyurethane/poly(lactic acid) (PLA)/graphene oxide nanocomposites via FDM, and found that the mechanical properties of nanocomposites were highly dependent on printing direction.[7] Tekinalp et al. reported that acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS)/carbon fiber composites by FDM had both higher fiber orientation and higher molecular orientation compared to those by conventional techniques.[8] Jia et al. used FDM technology to make graphite sheets vertically oriented in polyamide 6 (PA6) polymer matrix, resulting in composites with high through-plane thermal conductivity.[9] It was reported that the performance of FDM products was closely related to their construction methods.', 'Nowadays, additive manufacturing (AM) technology, also known as three-dimensional printing, has drawn interests from various industries [1] because of its potential to produce complex structures with acceptable reproducibility and controllability [2]. Among different 3D printing methods, the fused deposition modeling (FDM) has become increasingly popular due to its ability to rapidly produce cost-effective objects with reasonable accuracy and quality [3]. FDM technology has many applications in medical, aerospace, and mechanical industries [4]. This process uses thermoplastic filaments extruded into hot dies where they melt [5]. Several ongoing researches are being conducted to extend the medical applications of 3D printing methods in the various fields, such as tissue engineering [6], surgical training equipment [7], and bone repairing [8] as well as the development of permanent non-biologic implants, bioactive scaffolds, and pathological organs [9]. For medical applications, polylactic acid (PLA) and polycaprolactone (PCL) have special significance as bio-resorbable thermoplastic polymers [10]. PLA is derived from the biological fermentation of green sources such as sugar cane or corn starch. As a semi-crystalline polyester, it can be used in various medical applications because of its biodegradability and preparation from natural resources [11]. Brittleness is a potent disadvantage for pragmatic applications of PLA [12]. Generally, one of the most effective ways to improve the toughness of brittle polymers is to blend them with ductile and soft polymers [13, 14]. The PLA/PCL blends also have a high level of biocompatibility and biodegradability, resulting in degrading into nontoxic substances. Moreover, their degradation rate may be modified after contacting with a living organism [20].', "Elastomers for Soft Electronics: A Review from the Material's Perspective Additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as an important manufacturing technology, and its application is found in various sectors.[1-3] AM is essentially a layer-by-layer manufacturing of a product with the aid of a computer-aided design (CAD) model.[4] AM offers the advantage of realizing complex shapes that are very difficult to fabricate using conventional fabrication techniques. It also aids product customization, making it suitable for producing customized medical instruments and biomedical implants.[5, 6] Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most widely used AM technique for polymeric materials. However, it is very difficult to process some polymeric materials with FDM, especially soft thermoplastic elastomeric (TPE) materials. However, they lack functional properties, which limits their applications in functional materials.", 'Currently, one of the most promising approaches in bone tissue engineering is the use of 3D-printed scaffolds; these scaffolds are manufactured with precisely controlled structure, porosity, and properties and can conform to specific bone defects (Tang et al 2021). Also, these scaffolds can act as carriers for the transfer of growth factors or small molecule agents to the transplant site, so that in addition to providing local strength, they release the factors needed for bone repair at the site (Ferracini et al 2018). Various 3D-printing techniques can be used for manufacturing bone tissue substitutes, including fused deposition modeling (FDM), low temperature deposition modeling, stereolithography, digital light processing, and jetting-based modeling (Ege and Hasirci 2023). Until recently, ‘immune-evasive’ biomaterials designed to be invisible to the immune system were favored, but current understanding suggests that the scaffold materials themselves could possess beneficial ‘immune-interacting’ or immune-regulatory properties that support tissue healing and regeneration (Vasconcelos et al 2019).', 'The main goal of this study is to develop PVA for 3-dimensional printing (3D printing). 3D printing is a rapidly developing technology that is quick inexpensive and can produce complex parts without geometry limitations.14 Fused deposition modeling (FDM), an important type of 3D printing that uses layer-by-layer deposition of extruded filament to build up a part, has been widely studied because it is fast, safe, inexpensive, and simple to operate.15 FDM has been utilized for tissue engineering such as fabricating scaffolds with controllable pore shapes and sizes.16-19 However, the multi-hydroxyl groups lead to strong inter and intra-molecular hydrogen bonding in PVA, narrowing the gap between the melting point of PVA and its decomposition temperature; thus, products fabricated from this material cannot be prepared by melt processing. Thus, PVA filament feedstock with appropriate properties and suitable for FDM processing can be successfully prepared. It is believed that this work will not only provide an effective strategy for thermally processing PVA but also a novel FDM-compatible material for use in the biomedical field.', 'The main goal of this study is to develop PVA for 3-dimensional printing (3D printing). 3D printing is a rapidly developing technology that is quick inexpensive and can produce complex parts without geometry limitations.14 Fused deposition modeling (FDM), an important type of 3D printing that uses layer-by-layer deposition of extruded filament to build up a part, has been widely studied because it is fast, safe, inexpensive, and simple to operate.15 FDM has been utilized for tissue engineering such as fabricating scaffolds with controllable pore shapes and sizes.16-19 However, the multi-hydroxyl groups lead to strong inter and intra-molecular hydrogen bonding in PVA, narrowing the gap between the melting point of PVA and its decomposition temperature; thus, products fabricated from this material cannot be prepared by melt processing. It is believed that this work will not only provide an effective strategy for thermally processing PVA but also a novel FDM-compatible material for use in the biomedical field.', "The research work aims to compare the physical and mechanical properties of biodegradable polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT), polycaprolactone (PCL), and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) fabricated via fused deposition modeling (FDM) and conventional compression molding (CM) method. Additive manufacturing (AM), which well-known as three-dimensional (3D) printing, is a computer-controlled process that creates 3D objects by depositing materials, basically layer-by-layer.1 Owing to its rapid prototyping, cost-effective, flexibility (personalized wide range of materials), competitive advantage (reduce product life cycle), as well as tangible design and product testing (hands-on), 3D printing technology is significantly improved human life.2 Apart from that, 3D printing is also benefited in terms of quality (step-by-step assembly), consistency (real time error detection), risk reduction (prototype verification), accessibility and sustainability (less waste/environmental impact).3 In recent years, the potential of 3D printing technology has gained immense research in numerous applications include medical, manufacturing, custom-design, and architecture.4", 'Fused deposition modelling (FDM) Fused Deposition modelling is another extrusion-based 3D printing technology, firstly presented by crump [94]. In FDM, melted thermoplastic materials are utilized and extruded through a nozzle with certain pressure in FDM. The fabrication process of FDM consists of several stages. Another challenge of FDM printing is to maintain the proper adhesion among the deposited layers. Schematic diagram of FDM printer', "With the development of manufacturing technology, more and more companies begin to utilize additive manufacturing technology (also known as 3D printing) to assist in design and fabrication.1 3D-printing technology has unique advantages in complex shape forming, especially in the field of personalized customization, electronics, machinery and medical application.1, 2 Among all the 3D-printing technologies, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most widely used method due to its simplicity to operate and low cost, which attracts much attention both from industry and academia.2, 3 At present, the researches on FDM technology mainly focus on improvement of printing equipment, optimization of printing parameters, development of printing material and application, among which material development is an important research direction.1, 4-6 The feedstock material for FDM is required with suitable processability and good dimensional stability, such as acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) and poly(lactic acid) (PLA).7, 8 However, compared to the great variety of thermoplastic materials, few commercial materials are available for FDM on the market. The 'printability' challenge of PCL in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is not explicitly highlighted in the provided contexts. Instead, PCL is described as **well-suited for FDM** due to its **low melting point (60°C) and high thermal stability**, which make it an ideal thermoplastic for 3D printing applications [1, 9]. However, **indirect challenges** related to FDM processes in general may apply:  

1. **Layer Adhesion and Structural Integrity**: While not specific to PCL, FDM inherently faces challenges in ensuring strong interlayer bonding and structural consistency due to cooling dynamics and material flow during deposition [13, 15]. For PCL, its semi-crystalline nature and ductility might influence layer adhesion if process parameters (e.g., temperature, cooling rate) are not optimized.  

2. **Mechanical Property Limitations**: PCL’s low stiffness and tensile strength [15] could affect the dimensional stability of printed structures during or post-printing, though this relates more to material performance than printability per se.  

3. **Post-Printing Modifications**: While PCL’s hydrophobicity necessitates surface modifications (e.g., plasma treatment) for biomedical applications [1], this does not directly impede printability but rather post-printing functionality.  

In summary, **the contexts emphasize PCL’s suitability for FDM** without explicitly citing printability challenges. Any inferred issues would align with general FDM limitations (e.g., resolution, warping) rather than material-specific drawbacks of PCL.

retrieved_contexts: ['Initiating a positive healing response from the vascular implant requires modification of the surface-binding peptide MP with bioactives that help guiding the regeneration process. An on-resin modification protocol combining the Diels-Alder reaction with inverse electron demand with the copper(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition was recently identified as an optimal strategy for the orthogonal introduction of two cell-adhesive peptides.11 The generated bifunctional coatings MP-RGD-HBP and iMP-RGD-HBP2 were tested for their ability to enhance the adhesion of HUVEC cells to PCLLC scaffolds. Under physiologic conditions, exposure to shear stress is a crucial factor in shaping endothelial morphology.44 During microfluidic culture, we observed dramatic changes in HUVEC morphology in comparison to static adhesion studies and the observed differences between coatings intensified. This is in agreement with literature, where a combination of integrin- and proteoglycan-binding peptides was identified to induce the alignment and spreading of endothelial cells under flow.31 Notably, collagen I, a standard coating in cell culture, was unable to promote spreading and cytoskeleton organization, even though it likewise displays both binding sites.45 This can be rationalized by the high affinity of the cyclic RGD peptide for integrin αVβ313 which results in an enhanced adhesion strength in comparison to linear sequences and the full-length protein.46 Additionally, anchor strength is enhanced in mussel-derived peptides compared to unspecific protein adsorption. Small peptides combine a number of advantages over structural proteins as they reach a higher packing density, provide receptor selectivity and display ligands in a defined orientation and spacing.47 Nevertheless, dynamic mediators like growth factors, cytokines and chemokines exert substantial roles in orchestrating cell recruitment, proliferation and matrix remodeling during wound healing. Incorporation of heparin-binding peptides into biomaterial coatings allow the immobilization of heparin and subsequent delivery of heparin-binding cytokines.17 Herein, the interaction between peptide and GAG is based on the electrostatic attraction of negatively-charged sulfate and carboxyl groups of the heparin with basic amino acids within the peptide. Consensus sequences include alternating motifs of basic and hydrophobic amino acids matching the charge density of heparan sulfates.48 Elongating the motif increases the number of potential ionic bonds and can, therefore, retain significantly more heparin. This, in turn, enables an adjustment of the amounts of chemokine bound and released by the implant.', 'Synthetic and functional grafts are a great alternative to conventional grafts. (2, 9, 36, 37) However, typical chemical conjugation methods that immobilize peptides, ligands, and growth factors require multistep, complicated procedures such as activation or functionalization steps that require additional chemical treatments. Surface modification with RGD peptides enhances synthetic biodegradable polymers by addressing their inherent limitations and improving bioactivity through the following mechanisms:

1. **Enhanced Cell Adhesion and Spreading**:  
   RGD peptides specifically bind to integrin receptors on cell membranes (e.g., αVβ3), forming stable anchor points that link the polymer surface to the cytoskeleton. This promotes organized actin fiber formation, cell spreading, and adhesion strength, as seen in HUVEC cells on modified PCLLC scaffolds ([1]) and mesenchymal stem cells on RGD-functionalized PEG-PLA-PGl polymers ([2]).

2. **Overcoming Hydrophobicity**:  
   Synthetic polymers like PCL, PLA, and PEEK are often hydrophobic, which impedes cell interaction. RGD modification, combined with hydrophilic components (e.g., PEG), reduces contact angles (e.g., from 114° to 74.8° in PLA-PGl-PLA scaffolds), improving wettability and media contact ([2], [9]).

3. **Synergy with Other Bioactive Elements**:  
   RGD cooperates with proteoglycan-binding peptides (e.g., HBPs) to enhance adhesion. Syndecans (via HBPs) mediate initial attachment, while integrins (via RGD) stabilize focal adhesions, synergistically modulating wound healing and angiogenesis ([1]).

4. **Improved Mechanical and Biological Signaling**:  
   RGD presentation (cyclic vs. linear) affects integrin affinity and adhesion strength. Cyclic RGD peptides exhibit higher integrin selectivity and stability than linear sequences, enhancing osteoblast adhesion on PEEK ([5]) and endothelial cell organization under shear stress ([1]). This is critical for directing adhesion-dependent processes like osteogenesis and angiogenesis.

5. **Biocompatibility and Functionalization Efficiency**:  
   Advanced conjugation methods (e.g., click chemistry, mussel-inspired catechol coupling) enable precise RGD immobilization on polymers like alginate, avoiding multistep protocols. This preserves peptide bioactivity, enhancing cell proliferation and differentiation in 3D hydrogels ([3], [8]).

6. **Facilitation of Tissue-Specific Regeneration**:

retrieved_contexts: ['PLGA copolymers can be prepared by either the direct polycondensation of lactic acid and glycolic acid or ring-opening copolymerization (ROCOP) of the related cyclic lactide (LA) and glycolide (GA). Compared to the step-growth polycondensation approach, in which only PLGA copolymers with low molar masses can be obtained,8 the ROCOP of LA and GA represents a more efficient strategy considering the advantages of atomic economy, controllable molar masses, low dispersities and well-defined chain-ends. The most widely investigated and used catalyst for the preparation of PLGA is stannous octanoate both in academia and industry.9-11 With the increasing concern about the health safety risk of stannous octanoate, some other low toxic metal-based catalysts were later developed for the ROCOP of LA and GA, including bismuth subsalicylate,12 zinc lactate,13 zirconium acetylacetonate14 and dimethyl(salicylaldiminato) aluminum compounds.15 Due to the much higher reactivity of GA compared to LA, PLGA copolymers with truly random microstructures were not directly achieved with the abovementioned organometallic catalysts.12-16 Although long glycolidyl blocks can be randomized to shorter ones by transesterification, product discoloration resulting from the high reaction temperature (typically above 140 °C) as well as metal residues still hamper the applications of resultant PLGA copolymers in biomedical technologies. Although it was reported that residual phosphazene catalysts also showed considerably cytotoxicity,17 organocatalysts have been intensively investigated as sustainable alternatives to metal-based catalysts in the past decades due to their easy preparation, easy manipulation, good stability and facile removal from products, especially for biomedical, electronic and food packaging applications, in which catalyst residues are undesired.18-23 A series of aliphatic polyesters, including poly(lactide), poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(δ-valerolactone) and poly(γ-butyrolactone), have been successfully achieved with organocatalysts.24-29 Despite the great successes achieved with organocatalysts in the ROP of cyclic lactones or lactides, the organocatalytic preparation of PLGA copolymers has been scarcely explored. Satoh and coworkers achieved the organocatalytic regioselective ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of optically active methylglycolides (MGs) to produce highly alternating PLGAs using an organophosphazene base tBu-P2 as the catalyst.30 But the MG monomers are not commercially available and the preparation needs several steps and tedious purification. To the best of our knowledge, the only organocatalytic ROCOP of lactide and glycolide was reported by Hoye and coworkers, in which GA was continuously added in a controlled manner to a mixing solution of LA, poly(ethylene glycol) macroinitiator and 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene (DBU) catalyst.31 Though PLGA copolymers with random microstructures were obtained with this semi-batch strategy, a sophisticated technique was necessary to control the addition rate of GA. This approach was also limited by the low LA conversion (ca. 50%) due to the much higher reactivity of GA relative to LA. The organocatalytic ROCOP of GA with LA needs to solve the dilemma that the reactivity of GA is generally much higher than LA. Otherwise, long glycolidyl blocks will form in the propagating chain due to the preferred incorporation of glycolyl units, resulting in the precipitation of the obtained PLGA copolymers in common solvents before full conversions of LA and GA monomers. In contrast to the previous catalytic systems, in which GA exhibited much higher reactivity than LA, the CTPB/urea binary catalyst herein led to similar reactivity of LA and GA, producing random PLGA copolymers with tunable monomer sequence lengths.', 'The commercial manufacture of poly (L-lactic acid) relies heavily on organometallic catalysts. Currently, enzymatic catalysis shows a great potential to substitute metal-based catalysts or toxic organo-catalysts and to limit final toxicity, environmental impacts and abiotic degradation of the polymer, in perfect agreement with a sustainable development and concepts of green chemistry [9].
