This disparity is ascribed to the different degrees of orientation of PHBHHx in the MD and TD. The reason might be that PHBHHx transferred into a continuous phase during the melt-blown film process, and the film primarily oriented in the MD. The activation of molecular chain mobility in PHBHHx during orientation, results in a brittle-ductile transition.49 After a 3-day aging test, numerous holes can be observed in surfaces of the films, the reason may be the detachment of abundant starch particles. The elongation at break of films decreased after the 3-day aging test, with a higher content of PHBHHx, the elongation at break decrease even more. Pan et al.50 considered that the decrease in ductility during physical aging is related to the rearrangement of PHBHHx chains from disordered to order. From Figure 6, the tensile strength of PBAT decreased by 66% after testing, some researchers reported that the esters groups in PBAT are easily hydrolyzed, the performance was significantly affected when in prolonged contact with water.51 In contrast to the highest tensile strength observed in films with 20 wt% PHBHHx content, after a 3-day aging test, the film with 50% PHBHHx content exhibited the highest tensile strength with 18.3 MPa. As shown in Figure 7, a large number of droplet-like morphology was observed on the film surface, indicating that the migration of TPS is the cause of the significant decline in mechanical properties. This is also consistent with the decrease in tensile strength values as the TPS content decreases. It is noteworthy that the elongation at break of PSH50 decreased from 493% to 10%, tensile strength increased from 17.8 to 18.3 MPa after a 3-day aging test. This phenomenon was also observed by Pan et al.,50 after aging at 40°C for 1008 h, the yield strength and tensile modulus of poly(L-lactide) increased by 18.8% and 23.1%, respectively. They considered that glassy polymers are in a nonequilibrium state after quenching, and these materials seek a state closer to equilibrium due to the interaction of polymer chains. This process leads to local rearrangement of chain segments, resulting in slow energy loss. Therefore, samples that were aged at higher temperatures have lower potential energy after a long time of aging. During tensile deformation, polymer chains are oriented, and free volume and potential energy increase. This evidently increases the tensile strength of the film. After 5 days of aging, the mechanical properties of all films further deteriorated. PBAT/TPS film mainly corresponded to a decrease in tensile strength, with almost no change in elongation at break. However, PBAT/TPS/PHBHHx films mainly corresponded to a decrease in elongation at break. As Figure 7 shown, it can be observed that the migration of TPS on the films became more obvious. Because PBAT/TPS contains a large amount of TPS (30 wt%), and even if a large amount of plasticizer migrates to the surface of film, water in the environment with high humidity (85%) of the experiment can also act as a plasticizer after being adsorbed by hydrophilic starch. With the reduction of TPS content in PBAT/TPS/PHBHHx system, the plasticizer migration ability reduced during aging. Moreover, the phase transition occurs after adding PHBHHx, PBAT/TPS gradually transformed dispersed phases and PHBHHx as a continuous phase was shown in films, it is more difficult for water to diffuse into TPS through PHBHHx. After 8 days of aging, due to poor compatibility, most films undergo cracking, forming a large number of brittle fragments. The mechanical performance of films cannot be tested. The experiment has demonstrated that PHBHHx has a significant impact on the aging properties of the film, and the film exhibits good resistance to hydrolysis.', 'Polylactic acid (PLA) is a typical biodegradable polymer material, which is mainly made from starch of entirely bio-based origin [8, 9]. Additionally, PLA exhibits excellent biocompatibility, mechanical strength, processing properties, and durability, making it one of the top choices for biodegradable materials [10]. Despite its great potential, the toughness of PLA is rather poor, with less than 10% elongation at break, which severely limits its use in some specific areas [11]. To improve the toughness of PLA, various strategies and technologies have been developed, including modification of PLA with plasticizers [12], blending with other biodegradable polymers [13] as well as copolymerization modifications [14]. Compared to the long reaction time and strict copolymerization conditions of copolymerization modifications, polymer blending is relatively simple, efficient and cost-effective [15], making it the most common method of toughening and modifying PLA [16]. Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), a biodegradable aliphatic-aromatic copolyester, exhibits excellent toughness with an elongation at break of more than 700% [17]. Due to its excellent toughness and extremely flexible with a higher elongating ability, to toughen PLA, a plenty of work on the melt blending of PLA with PBAT have been reported. Farselti et al. [18]. used different contents of PBAT blended with PLA. They found that when the PBAT content was 20 wt%,the elongation at break increased from 3%( neat PLA) to 45%, an improvement of about 15 times. Jiang et al. [19]. found that PLA and PBAT blends were incompatible two-phase systems. With the addition of 5% PBAT, the tensile toughness of PLA/PBAT blends could be greatly improved without loss of tensile strength and tensile modulus. Deng et al. [20]. prepared a series of melt blends with different PBAT/PLA mass ratios (0/100, 20/80, 40/60, 60/40, 80/20 and 100/0). They found that the toughening effect on PLA was best when the PBAT formed a co-continuous phase in the PLA matrix, at which point elongation at break increased dramatically from about 10% to 300%. In summary, it can be seen that biodegradable aliphatic-aromatic copolyester PBAT has a certain toughening effect on PLA, but the high price of PBAT, to some extent, limits its application [21]. In this study, the direct esterification method was used to synthesize another feasible highly flexible biodegradable aliphatic-aromatic copolyester: poly(ethylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PEAT). The lower cost of ethylene glycol (EG) compared to butanediol (BDO) gives PEAT a greater price advantage over PBAT. In addition, during the production process of PBAT, there is a high generation rate of tetrahydrofuran (THF) by-products, which results in significant energy consumption during their recovery and recycling, inadvertently increasing carbon dioxide emissions. PEAT, on the other hand, produces no tetrahydrofuran, making it more environmentally friendly and having a lower carbon footprint. Taking advantage of the excellent toughness and high elongation at break of PEAT, different mass fractions of PEAT were blended with PLA to prepare mechanically superior rigid-tough balanced biodegradable binary blends. The influence of the addition of PEAT on the mechanical properties, thermal performance, crystallization, phase morphology and rheological behavior of the blends was thoroughly investigated.', 'There are three ways to improve the compatibility between PLA and PBAT: reactive compatibilization, adding plasticizers and blending with a third polymer. Reactive compatibilization is mainly achieved through transesterification, chain extension or crosslinking reactions [9]. Coltelli et al. investigated the transesterification reaction occurring between PLA and PBAT during the melt blending with Ti(OBu)4 as a transesterification catalyst [10]. The results showed that improved compatibility of PLA and PBAT was attributed to the formation of a PLA-PBAT copolymer. Lin et al. prepared PLA/PBAT blends with various tetrabutyl titanate (TBT) concentrations by a twin-screw extruder. After the incorporation of 0.5% TBT, the tensile strength, elongation at break and impact strength of the blend reached 45 MPa, 298% and 9 kJ/m2, respectively, as the interfacial adhesion between PLA and PBAT was enhanced [11]. Lyu et al. prepared glycidyl methacrylate grafted poly(lactic acid) by melt grafting [12]. When the graft copolymer content reached 10%, the elongation at break of PLA/PBAT (70/30) blend reached 200%. Using a compound or polymer containing epoxy groups as a chain extender is also a kind of reactive compatibilization for PLA/PBAT blends [13,14,15]. Li et al. found that the addition of Joncryl ADR-4370F as an epoxy chain extender significantly increased the elongation at break and the notched Izod impact strength of the PLA/PBAT blend [16]. Racha et al. studied the thermal degradation and chain extension mechanism of PLA/PBAT blends modified by Joncryl ADR-4368 as an epoxy chain extender [17]. Crosslinking reaction is a useful method to tune the properties of PLA/PBAT blends. Ai et al. used bis(tert-butyl dioxy isopropyl) benzene as an crosslinking agent for PLA/PBAT film, thus improving the mechanical properties of the film such as tensile strength, elongation at break and sealing strength [18]. Signori et al. reported on the addition of the dicumyl peroxide to a PLA/PBAT blend, which increased the toughness and modulated crystalline content and thermal behavior of the blend [19]. Zhang et al. prepared the micro-crosslinking of PLA and PBAT with benzoyl peroxide, and the blend exhibited high complex viscosity and melt strength [20].', 'The findings of pristine PBAT and 80/20 (PBAT/TPS) are slightly higher than the result reported by Yi et al.5 By using cassava starch plasticized with 30% glycerine, they reported 16.8 and 7 MPa for tensile strength and 840% and 420% for elongation at break, respectively. Moreover, similar tensile properties had also been reported by Lendvai et al.19 by using maize starch mixed with glycerol (4:1), where the sample with pure PBAT had a tensile strength of 20.8 MPa and elongation at break of 1139%. As the TPS increased to 20%, 40%, 50%, and 60%, the tensile strength decreased to 11.7, 6.3, 5.8, and 6.6 MPa and 555%, 256%, 14.6%, and 4.6%, respectively for elongation at break, respectively. On the other hand, Pan et al.4 had determined the tensile strength of 23.5, 9, 5.3, and 4.4 MPa and elongation at break of 644%, 378%, 319%, and 256% when PBAT blended with 0%, 20%, 40%, 50% of thermoplastic corn starch, respectively. It is found that different types of starch affect the mechanical performance of the film due to different amounts of amylopectin and amylose. The films produced in this work had shown good tensile property and flexibility than other starches. Lackner et al.27 fabricated films with different PBAT/TPS contents. Pure PBAT had exhibited high tensile strength and elongation at break with 19.1 MPa and 985%, respectively. However, addition of 40% TPS had led to a significant reduction in tensile strength (4.6 MPa) and ℇb (8%). The findings from previous and present studies showed that the increase of PBAT content in the blend lead to the improvement of mechanical properties of the film, which is probably due to the formation of continuous PBAT phase in the blend (as shown by morphology in Figure 2A). The presence of starch domain in continuous PBAT phase resulted in the destruction of surface integrity and continuity of the pure PBAT film, which also partially explains the drop in the mechanical properties of PBAT films. The increase in TPS content generates larger defect due to starch agglomeration and thus forming a stress concentration point, which lead to tensile failure. Figure 2 shows the SEM morphology analysis of the PBAT and PBAT/TPS blends. Pure PBAT micrograph shows a smooth and well-defined fractured plane, which exhibits a ductile fracture surface. On the other hand, the presence of droplets in the PBAT/TPS micrographs correspond to the TPS domain. The tensile elongation (elongation at break) of PBAT varies depending on testing conditions and formulations, as reported in the provided contexts:  
- **250% in air** and **310% in water** (immersion) due to water acting as a plasticizer (Contexts 1 & 2).  
- **Close to 400%** for PBAT in packaging applications (Context 3).  
- **850% (machine direction)** and **809% (transverse direction)** for pure PBAT films (Contexts 5 & 6).  
- **Over 700%** in blends with PLA (Context 7).  
- Up to **985–1139%** in studies using thermoplastic starch blends (Contexts 9 & 10).  

These differences reflect variations in sample preparation, testing protocols (e.g., humidity, strain rate), and composite formulations.

retrieved_contexts: ['Buy this article in print Gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel scaffolds and GelMA-based bioinks are widely used in tissue engineering and bioprinting due to their ability to support cellular functions and new tissue development. Unfortunately, while terminal sterilization of the GelMA is a critical step for translational tissue engineering applications, it can potentially cause thermal or chemical modifications of GelMA. Thus, understanding the effect of terminal sterilization on GelMA properties is an important, though often overlooked, aspect of material design for translational tissue engineering applications. To this end, we characterized the effects of FDA-approved terminal sterilization methods (autoclaving, ethylene oxide treatment, and gamma (γ)-irradiation) on GelMA prepolymer (bioink) and GelMA hydrogels in terms of the relevant properties for biomedical applications, including mechanical strength, biodegradation rate, cell culture in 2D and 3D, and printability. Autoclaving and ethylene oxide treatment of the GelMA decreased the stiffness of the hydrogel, but the treatments did not modify the biodegradation rate of the hydrogel; meanwhile, γ-irradiation increased the stiffness, reduced the pore size and significantly slowed the biodegradation rate. None of the terminal sterilization methods changed the 2D fibroblast or endothelial cell adhesion and spreading. However, ethylene oxide treatment significantly lowered the fibroblast viability in 3D cell culture. Strikingly, γ-irradiation led to significantly reduced ability of the GelMA prepolymer to undergo sol-gel transition. Furthermore, printability studies showed that the bioinks prepared from γ-irradiated GelMA had significantly reduced printability as compared to the GelMA bioinks prepared from autoclaved or ethylene oxide treated GelMA. These results reveal that the choice of the terminal sterilization method can strongly influence important properties of GelMA bioink and hydrogel. Overall, this study provides further insight into GelMA-based material design with consideration of the effect of terminal sterilization. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS', "The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Therefore, performing an appropriate sterilization process for this new system will enable to use it in the clinic. It is of very high importance to use an appropriate sterilization process for this special new wound dressing, which will not have a deleterious effect on its function. The current study describes the effect of gamma radiation doses and conditions on the physical and mechanical properties of a new wound dressing developed by us, in order to find an appropriate sterilization process for this wound dressing that will not have a deleterious effect on its function.', 'Electrospinning (ES) was demonstrated as a facile manufacturing technique for nanofibrous biopolymer filters, whereby both the (99%) all-PLA and all-cellulosic filter composites achieved BR and FE requirements. It should be noted that the PLA composite did not quite reach the performance of a similar previously reported filter medium,[50] limited difference in technique (needleless ES), choice of a renewably-sourced PLA grade and solvent, as well as aim for lower BR. Nevertheless, both here reported filters were found to be suitable for reuse via alcohol sterilization and recharge based on ≈70% FE, even more so if tougher membrane composites were used. BR is reduced after sterilization, further improving the reuse potential. Since PP meltblown filters from medical masks did not prove reusable due to the significant drop in FE after both sterilization approaches, as well as are disqualified from recycling due to biological combination, ES nanofiber membranes stand out regarding sustainability, enabling bio-based manufacturing, disinfection and potential disposal via composting. Based on the energy-efficient one-step production and charging process with possibility for re-use, such membranes rival the mechanically superior but non-sustainable commercial ePTFE filters, but cannot compete in harsh (chemical) environments. The re-use strategy here employed based on alcohol sterilization and advanced recharge approach proved to be effective for all nanofibrous membranes in this study, recovering in FE to pre-sterilization levels. Mechanistically, an increase in chain mobility by diffusion of (non)solvent likely allows for alignment in a strong electric field and hence freezing of charges within the polymer matrix. A positive effect was also observed in another cellulose-based composite (PP-CO), which could be explained by a slight swelling analogous to the electrospun filters. PP is inert to the solvents (except superficially), and would likely require higher temperature for charges to be trapped as employed during the initial corona charge.[51] In contrast, no decrease in FE after alcohol treatment was observed in the ePTFE composite to begin with, likely due to the low-stress treatment and inertness/omniphobicity of the material. While it is not stated by the producer whether this membrane was additionally charged, PTFE is known to exhibit strong intrinsic electrical charges and is produced in a finer structure suitable for simple size exclusion effects. Silk fibroin sponges were cast from pre-sterilized silk fibroin solutions in sterile 24-well tissue culture plates in a laminar flow hood. Following freezing, scaffolds were placed in sterile autoclave bags and lyophilized. Scaffolds were water annealed in a glass desiccator, which was sterilized by autoclaving and placed inside a laminar flow hood. Finally, the mechanical properties of the silk fibroin scaffolds formed from 30-min boiling, 4 wt.-% silk fibroin solution that had been either sterile filtered or autoclaved were examined. This boil time and concentration was chosen as it is the commonly used to make silk fibroin scaffolds for tissue engineering applications. 54 Scaffolds were compressed under unconfined conditions using a 100 N load cell at physiological temperature and pH (37 °C, PBS). No difference in the shape of the strain-strain curve or compressive modulus was observed in scaffolds formed from filtered compared to unsterilized silk fibroin, but autoclaved silk fibroin resulted in significantly stiffer scaffolds compared to those formed from unsterilized or filter sterilized silk fibroin (Figure 2). Lower average molecular weight was expected to correlate with lower stiffness and strength; thus, it is possible that an increase in β-sheet content in the silk fibroin solution following autoclaving was responsible for these unexpected bulk material properties. The sterilization method of choice for heat-sensitive biodegradable polymers depends on the specific polymer and application, but **gamma (γ)-irradiation with controlled parameters** is often recommended. Key considerations from the context include:

1. **Gamma-Irradiation**:
   - Effective at standard doses (e.g., 25 kGy) but can cause chain scission or crosslinking, altering mechanical properties and degradation rates.
   - **Cooling during irradiation** (e.g., to 0°C or lower) minimizes thermal degradation, preserving molecular weight and structural integrity.
   - Lower doses (10–25 kGy) combined with cooling (e.g., liquid nitrogen) reduce adverse effects, making it suitable for polymers like PDLGA-collagen hybrids or silk fibroin.

2. **Ethylene Oxide (EtO)**:
   - Avoids heat but introduces toxicity concerns due to residual chemicals, requiring extensive degassing. This is impractical for clinical settings and may reduce cell viability in 3D cultures (e.g., GelMA).

3. **Hydrogen Peroxide Plasma (VHP)**:
   - A safer chemical alternative to EtO with minimal toxicity, though it may cause hydrolytic degradation in polymers with ester or amide groups.

4. **Autoclaving**:
   - Generally unsuitable for heat-sensitive polymers but viable for thermally stable materials like silk fibroin, where it enhances β-sheet content and stiffness.

In addition, chitosan (CS) has attracted considerable attention as a naturally occurring polymer with fascinating properties of biocompatibility, biodegradability, nontoxicity and cationic properties [14], [15], [16]. Accordingly, one smart strategy with merits of simplicity, celerity and high accuracy to prepare shape-controlled stimuli-responsive microgels is urgently required.', 'The synthesized PEG-PLGA-PNIPAM copolymer, commercially available ASP (Sigma, A2093, Darmstadt, Germany) and miR222/MSN complexes were used to fabricate the miR222/MSN and ASP co-embedded core-shell microspheres by a well-established double-emulsion method.61 To test the thermal responsiveness of the formed hydrogel, ASP and miR222/MSN co-embedded microsphere solution (30 wt%) was incubated at 37 °C and 25 °C respectively for 5 min (Fig. 3d). They have wide-range potential applications due to their employment as biomaterials, thermoresponsive materials, and carrier systems for active agents in drug delivery.1-3 Thermoresponsive polymers, undergoing changes in their properties (hydrophilic/hydrophobic) upon variation of temperature, have been widely studied as special class of stimuli-responsive polymers.4 The “gold standard” of thermoresponsive polymers is poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM),5 which exhibits lower critical solution behavior in water, meaning that it is soluble at low temperature and precipitates at higher temperature, with a cloud point or critical temperature [lower critical solution temperature (LCST)] of 32 °C. Likewise, poly(2-isopropyl-2-oxazoline) (PIPOX), which is a structural isomer of PNIPAM, shows a similar solution behavior with an LCST of about 36 °C.6, 7 The most thoroughly exploited smart property of poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazoline)s is thermoresponsiveness.1-7 Type of alkyl chain, concentration, molecular weight, additives, and surfactants considerably affect the cloud point temperature to be in a wide temperature range (≈5-95 °C).1, 3, 7-9 This property makes poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazoline)s usable in biomedical applications such as drug delivery, tissue engineering, and biofunctional molecular techniques.10 In addition, the type of alkyl side chain causes significant differences not only in solubility but also in thermal behaviors and chemically processing of poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazoline)s. Due to the variability of side chains, there have been substantially synthetic modifications to obtain polymers with different kinds of side chains to improve their chemical and physical properties such as stimuli-responsive properties, solubility, and thermal behavior.11-15 Especially, poly[2-(3-butenyl)-2-oxazoline] (PBOX), bearing a vinyl double bond in the side chain, can be modified with thiols applying thiol-ene “click” photochemistry.14 PBOX is more hydrophobic than PIPOX, thus it is not soluble in water but in common organic solvents such as tetrahydrofuran (THF) and chloroform. The energy density contribution of biodegradable separators in batteries is primarily achieved through enhanced ionic conductivity, improved electrolyte uptake, and superior cycle stability, which collectively optimize battery performance. Key factors include:

1. **High Porosity & Electrolyte Uptake**: Biodegradable separators like sulfonated cellulose (SC)/PLA-PBS blends (porosity up to 87.7%) and mesoporous cellulose nanocrystal (MCNC) membranes (porosity 75.3%) exhibit significantly higher porosity than commercial polyolefin separators (e.g., Celgard 2400: 42.1%) [1,3]. This enhances electrolyte retention, facilitating efficient ion transport and reducing interfacial resistance, thereby improving energy density.

2. **Ionic Conductivity**: SC/biomembranes and MCNC separators achieve ionic conductivities of ~2.7 mS/cm [1,3], surpassing conventional separators. Higher conductivity reduces internal resistance, enhancing rate capability and energy output.

3. **Capacity Retention**: Cells with SC/biomembranes (2 wt% SC) retained 106 mAh/g after 100 cycles at 1C, outperforming Celgard (81 mAh/g) [1]. Similarly, cellulose-reinforced separators in LiFePO₄/Li cells showed 160.6 mAh/g at 0.2C and 108.5 mAh/g after 1,000 cycles at 2C [7]. Sustained capacity retention directly supports stable energy density over cycles.

4. **Thermal & Mechanical Stability**: Cellulose-based separators (e.g., modified wood films, CNF composites) resist thermal shrinkage and mechanical degradation, enabling safer, thinner designs that maximize active material volume, indirectly boosting energy density [2,4,7,13].

5. **Sustainability-Driven Design**: Cellulose materials (e.g., TEMPO-oxidized nanofibrils) enable lightweight, eco-friendly separators with high tensile strength (227% improvement over commercial cellulose separators [4]), allowing efficient packing without compromising safety or performance [4,8,13].

In summary, biodegradable separators enhance energy density by optimizing ion transport, electrolyte compatibility, and long-term stability, while sustainable designs reduce inactive material bulk, aligning with high-performance and eco-efficient battery requirements.

They are especially appealing for temporary therapeutic applications [3], e.g. for the design of surgical implants or drug delivery vehicles [4], [5]. They remain inside of the body only temporarily but eventually are biodegraded. This degradation can happen either by hydrolytic or enzymatic degradation or a combination of both [6], [7]. The majority of biodegradable polymers is based on synthetic polyesters or modified biopolymers that are susceptible to enzymatic and/or hydrolytic cleavage [8]. The pre-evaluation of enzymatic degradation in vivo is difficult, due to varying enzyme concentrations at different sites in the body and often ex vivo investigations with purified enzymes or accelerated hydrolysis conditions are conducted [9]. In contrast, for synthetic PPEs, the potential biodegradability and biocompatibility are emphasized in most publications about PPEs, but only a few detailed studies of their degradation mechanism are available [15], [16]. Based solely on the provided context, the differences between alkaline and acid hydrolysis for polyesters are:

1.  **Reagents & Conditions:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Uses aqueous solutions of strong bases like KOH or NaOH (e.g., 4-20 wt% KOH, 18 wt% NaOH) [1, 3, 4].
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Uses concentrated strong acids like sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), nitric acid (HNO₃), or phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) [1, 3, 4].

2.  **Mechanism:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Involves nucleophilic attack by hydroxide ions (OH⁻) on the ester carbonyl carbon (saponification). This reaction yields a carboxylate salt and an alcohol [3, 4]. Hydroxyl anions act as a reagent rather than just a catalyst [4].
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Involves protonation (H⁺) of the ester carbonyl oxygen, making the carbonyl carbon more susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water. This reaction yields a carboxylic acid and an alcohol [3, 4]. Protons act as catalysts for both hydrolysis and the reverse esterification reaction [4].

3.  **By-products:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Produces carboxylate salts (e.g., terephthalate salts from PET) and alcohols (e.g., ethylene glycol from PET) [1, 3, 4].
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Produces carboxylic acids (e.g., terephthalic acid from PET, lactic acid from PLA) and alcohols (e.g., ethylene glycol from PET) [1, 3, 4].

4.  **Kinetics & Efficiency:**
    *   Polyesters generally undergo **faster hydrolytic degradation under alkaline (basic) conditions** compared to acidic conditions [2, 4].
    *   Hydroxyl anions (OH⁻) are reported to be more effective at targeting the polyester backbone and diminishing the energy barrier for ester bond breakage compared to protons (H⁺) under typical concentration ranges (e.g., 0.1-4 mol L⁻¹) [4].

5.  **Tolerance & Specificity:**
    *   The tolerance of polyesters to protons (H⁺) and hydroxyl anions (OH⁻) is "significantly different". For example, PHB monomeric hydrolysis is rare in 0.1-4 M acid solutions but occurs effectively in 0.1-4 M alkali solutions [4].
    *   Alkaline hydrolysis of PLLA can yield L-lactic acid without racemization (no D-lactic acid formation), suggesting control by dissolution kinetics [4].

6.  **Drawbacks (Commonly Cited):**
    *   Both methods require harsh conditions (high T, P, concentrated chemicals) and generate corrosive reaction systems [1, 3].
    *   Both generate large quantities of highly acidic or basic wastewater and, in the case of alkaline hydrolysis, inorganic salts [1, 3].

Continuous technological advancements and rapid obsolescence in the electronics industry compel both consumers and businesses to frequently update their electronic devices, resulting in a perpetual influx of discarded electronics. Consequently, electronic waste (e-waste) has emerged as a substantial global environmental pollution concern [1]. The important solution to addressing electronic waste is to effectively control environmental pollution at the source, including the management of materials within industry and related resources [2]. One of the essential raw materials for manufacturing electronic components is plastic. In 2014, the estimated global plastic production reached 0.27 billion tons, with approximately 0.0028 billion tons being used for electric and electronic equipment (EEE) [3]. The conventional plastics commonly used in electronic components are petroleum-derived, exacerbating challenges related to their disposal and degradation. Consequently, biodegradable plastics have emerged as a promising solution for tackling pollution linked with e-waste. These materials have the inherent ability to undergo natural decomposition through microbial action, ultimately converting into carbon dioxide and water within a timeframe of 20-45 days, contingent upon sufficient levels of humidity, oxygen, and microbial activity [4]. Polylactic acid (PLA) is highly notable for its biodegradability, synthesis from renewable resources, and classification as an aliphatic thermoplastic polyester [5, 6]. Additionally, it is extensively employed as one of the leading bioplastics in commercial applications, effectively replacing conventional non-biodegradable plastics [7]. In recent years, there has been a study of research focused on exploring the dielectric behavior of biodegradable polymers. For instance, Wu et al. investigated the dielectric properties of polylactic acid (PLA) were enhanced through the incorporation of titanium dioxide (TiO2) decorated carbon nanotubes. A significant challenge is their rapid corrosion rate in physiological environments, which can lead to premature failure and hydrogen gas release. Additionally, while Mg alloys have good mechanical properties, they may not always meet the strength requirements of certain applications, especially under load-bearing conditions. In fact, Bogyaa et al., [1] showed defects resulting in a significant reduction of the mechanical integrity before adequate tissue regeneration occurred. Li et al. [2] and Pana et al. [3] confirmed the existence of these limitations. They confirm that implants made from this alloy resulted in subcutaneous bloating. They attributed these side effects to the corrosion of the magnesium plate and the steel nail. This corrosion accelerates the degradation of the Mg plate and results in an accumulation of hydrogen within a short period. To overcome these issues, researchers have proposed the application of surface coatings [[4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]]. Sankar et al. [5] investigated the use of HAp coatings on WE43. Li et al. [6] applied hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) based silk fibroin (SF) coatings on AZ31 surface. Razavi et al. [7] used a nanostructured akermanite coating. Wang et al. [8] tried Polyp-xylene (PPX) coatings. Butt et al. [9] practiced direct immersion of AZ31 into molten PLA to coat its surface. In an exhaustive review article on the development of biodegradable magnesium coating-alloy systems, Zhang et al. [10] reported that the current focus of research in this field is the modification of HAp multifunctional composite coating on the surface of magnesium alloys. Kannan et al. [11] developed a three-layer hybrid coating on poly-L-lactic acid (PEO-CaP-PLLA). The three-layer hybrid coating reduced the degradation current density of pure magnesium. Then, Yu et al. [12] prepared a fluoride/polydopamine/sulfonated hyaluronic acid (MgF2/PDA/S-HA) composite coating on magnesium alloy ZE21B. The three-layer coating structure has great potential for controlling the biodegradation rate of magnesium alloy implants. Recently, graphene oxide has been strongly proposed as a coating to improve the mechanical strength of magnesium alloys [13]. However, graphene oxide coatings have several limitations, the main one being the difficulty in obtaining a uniform and consistent coating. In addition, the adhesion between the graphene oxide layer and the magnesium alloy may vary, which may cause the coating to delaminate or fail under stress. Li et al. [14] proposed the deposition of graphene oxide with hydroxyapatite (HA) as a composite coating. They found that the corrosion resistance of the HA/G/GO composite coating is 28.53 times greater than that of pure ZK60. Peng et al. [15] tested HAp-graphene oxide bilayer coating on magnesium alloy AZ31. They found that graphene oxide inhibits the formation and growth of degradation cracks on the HAp layer, thus showing higher biodegradation resistance. Tavakoli et al. [16] focused on using chitosan with the graphene oxide to create a chitosan/GO nanocomposite. They examined the mechanical, physical, biological, and degradation properties of the chitosan/GO nanocomposites and compared them to chitosan alone. They observed that the incorporation of 0.3 wt% graphene oxide into chitosan films increases the tensile strength by 296 % and the elastic modulus by 193 %. Despite the recorded improvements in reducing corrosion and slowing the biodegradation rate of the alloys, it seemed that there were no conclusive results. In their exhaustive review, Yang et al. [4] identified persistent shortcomings in the proposed coatings that concern the film adhesion. They consistently observed a loose interface between the film and its substrate which caused the film delamination after soaking in body fluid for a certain period. Yang et al. [4] criticized researchers for neglecting adhesion tests that are essential for evaluating the stability and feasibility of coatings. Other works focused on the use of Silane/Graphene Oxide coating to enhance the adhesion performance of the deposited film. Zhang et al. [17] studied the effect of graphene oxide (GO) combined with 3-Aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APT) on the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. The researchers found that the GO film exhibits a relatively low adhesion strength (~9.2 MPa) compared to GO-APS films (~20.4 MPa).”In summary, the use of graphene oxide (GO) coating on AZ31 presented significant challenges related to dispersion uniformity and particle agglomeration. Even with the addition of another organic phase to graphene oxide to create a binary composite coating, certain limitations persist. These include insufficient adhesion, reduced environmental stability in the case of chitosan/GO coatings [18]. In the case of Silane/GO coating, while silane can enhance adhesion, the compatibility between GO and silane may not always be optimal, potentially leading to inadequate bonding with the substrate. Silane coatings can be sensitive to moisture, which may affect the performance of the GO layer. In addition, despite the multiple of studies on various coatings for AZ31 and the significant progress made in terms of corrosion resistance, there is a lack of information in the literature regarding the simultaneous control of biodegradation and the mechanical behavior of films deposited on AZ31 alloys.For these reasons our paper proposes the combination of ternary composite coating consisting of graphene oxide (GO), chitosan (CS), and silane. This synergistic approach aims to enhance the overall performance of the coating by improving adhesion, mechanical strength, and environmental stability while mitigating the limitations associated with each individual component. To the best of our knowledge, the combined effects of incorporating both chitosan and silane polymers with graphene oxide have not been explored. In addition, the major challenge is to simultaneously control the biodegradation rate and ensure mechanical strength while guaranteeing strong adhesion at the film-substrate interface. Optimizing all these factors is essential to achieving optimal coating performance. retrieved_contexts: ['The LbL self-assembly method can be used to construct nanoscale ultra-thin films on solid substrates. This strategy is based on electrostatic interactions between polyelectrolytes or other ionic species with opposite charges, which promotes the deposition of materials via alternating adsorption. Specifically, the substrate is alternately exposed to solutions containing positively and negatively charged substances, leading to the spontaneous and orderly adsorption of these substances on the substrate surface to form a highly organized multilayer membrane structure [7] The LbL self-assembly technology applied in this study is characterized by precise microstructural control, high reproducibility, wide material adaptability, broad application prospects, and environmental friendliness [8]. Controllability is a particularly valuable advantage because it enables command over the structural and physicochemical properties of the obtained multilayer films according to the properties of the raw materials and the assembly conditions (e.g., pH, ionic strength, temperature) [9]. To date, the LbL self-assembly strategy has been applied in various fields, including the preparation of anti-corrosion films on the surface of magnesium alloys. For example, Xiao et al. [10] prepared polyelectrolyte-coated magnesium alloys using the LbL self-assembly method with polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) and sodium alginate (ALG), which increased the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Chen et al. [11] used phytic acid (PA), branched polyethylenimine (BPEI), and graphene oxide (GO) to prepare films on Mg-1Zn alloys via LbL self-assembly, thereby forming a physical barrier against corrosion. These studies demonstrated that an LbL self-assembled multilayer film can increase the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Despite these promising applications, existing LbL multilayer coatings for magnesium alloy protection still face several critical challenges that limit their practical implementation: (1) the hydrophilic nature of polyelectrolytes makes the coatings susceptible to delamination during prolonged immersion, (2) inadequate interfacial adhesion between the coating and magnesium substrate compromises long-term durability, and (3) the continued use of non-environmental solvent systems in some fabrication processes contradicts the sustainable advantages inherent to LbL technology. Urushiol, a naturally occurring phenolic compound extracted from lacquer trees (Toxicodendron spp.), has gained increasing attention as a sustainable and eco-friendly material for advanced coatings and functional applications [12, 13]. Notably, the catechol moieties mimic mussel-adhesive proteins, enabling urushiol to form robust chemical bonds with diverse substrates, including metals, polymers, and inorganic surfaces, thereby improving interfacial adhesion and long-term durability [15]. Beyond its protective capabilities, urushiol exhibits remarkable biological activity, such as antioxidant, antibacterial, and antitumor effects, making it a promising candidate for biomedical and environmental applications [16]. For instance, Fang et al. [17] demonstrated that urushiol-modified melamine sponges (UMS) exhibit excellent hydrophobicity and selective oil-adsorption capacity, while Jie et al. This strategy is expected to simultaneously overcome the challenges of weak interfacial adhesion and solvent sustainability, providing new insights for developing high-performance surface coatings for magnesium alloys.', 'Oxidation of alginate is a promising method that creates aldehyde groups, which can form stable cross-links with amine groups on chitosan. The films exhibit enhanced mechanical properties, UV-blocking ability, water resistance, and antioxidant as well as unique potential in preserving fresh fruits, thereby providing new strategies for the future development of food packaging.', 'The development of mussel-inspired materials with enhanced mechanical and physiological characteristics is fascinating due to the resulting structural properties. In this work, based on a chemical reaction, 3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)propionic acid and dopamine hydrochloride (DA), with a catechol group, were covalently grafted onto a bio-compatible polymer backbone of chitosan hydrochloride (CHI) and hyaluronic acid sodium (HA). In most work reported thus far, the controlling of viscosity of traditional glue for fluid flow during device fabrication remains challenging, especially when dispensing through a capillary using a thin film deposition processes.20-24 An adhesive with a special shape to fit the substrate has been used instead.22-24 Generally, there are three types of medical adhesives based on their physical form: powder, gel and film.24 Adhesive films with water resistance capacity are currently popular because of their great potential and existing applications, such as for closing wounds in tissue and surgical repair.21-25 Among water-resistant adhesives, adhesive films have a unique two-dimensional structure, which is thought to provide unique advantages for biomedical applications.23,26-28 Additionally, the curing conditions of conventional biomedical adhesives are usually extreme and unfriendly to organs.6,29 Therefore, new methods are being developed to fabricate water-resistant adhesive films with the following characteristics: (a) several micrometre thickness; (b) convenient to control; (c) operational and curable in aqueous solution; (d) facile and environmentally friendly processing; (e) stable mechanical connection; and (f) biocompatibility and biodegradability. Then, the physicochemical properties of the NPs are presented and finally, the results of the release behavior of an entrapped lipophilic molecule, BP, are discussed.", "Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a versatile technique based initially on the adsorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (PELs) on a substrate.1 LbL assembly was designed in the first place for macroscopic surfaces.2 Recently, coating of nanoparticles (NPs) with PELs using the LbL technique has received great interest due to the advantage of obtaining NPs with controlled surface properties. Then, the physicochemical properties of the NPs are presented and finally, the results of the release behavior of an entrapped lipophilic molecule, BP, are discussed.", 'Research and development of smart nanostructured materials governed by their surface properties is a rapidly growing field [1]. Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a simple bottom-up technique to modify surfaces, synthesize nanocomposites and thin films of different materials [2,3]. This method consists of alternating physisorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes, whereby electrostatic is one of the most critical interactions between molecules [4]. [32] analyzed carboxymethylcellulose (CMC)/CHI films. In that sense, this work deals with the fractal analysis of polyelectrolytes assembled by LbL into nanofilms. In that sense, this work is useful for the understanding of the driving force behind nanofilm formation.', 'Electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding coating materials with thicknesses in the microscale are required in many sectors, including communications, medical, aerospace, and electronics, to isolate the electromagnetic radiation emitted from electronic equipment. (2−5) Electrically conductive polymer composites can be used for EMI shielding (6−17) because of their lightweight, resistance to corrosion, flexibility, good processability, and low cost compared to conventional metal-based materials. (28) Graphene papers with thicknesses between 12.5 and 470 μm (23,24) and ∼30-60 μm thick graphene/polymer composites (25,26) were also investigated as EMI shielding materials. Thus, a detailed evaluation of how the microstructure and electronic properties develop in LbL multilayered structures with increasing amounts of graphene is needed to optimize the properties of the coatings, while minimizing thickness, weight, and amount of graphene.', 'Nanogels were prepared by ionotropic gelation of chitosan (CS) with tripolyphosphate (TPP). A pKa ∼ 3.5 was reported for alginate (3.38 and 3.65 for guluronic acid and mannuronic acid, respectively).44', 'The LbL technique as a classical bottom-up technique has emerged recently as widely used method to design material coatings with different molecules, mostly polyelectrolytes (PEL).29 With this technique, chemical cues can be introduced to biomaterial surfaces that address cell receptors.30,31 Moreover, parameters like wetting properties, surface potential, topography, thickness, and viscoelasticity can be regulated by selection of PEL and by control of process parameters during multilayer formation.31-33 In case proteins and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) were used for multilayer assembly, the structure and composition of ECM could be mimicked.33,34 Moreover, the rather high water content of such multilayer systems offers specific viscoelastic properties that can be tailored either by the complexation conditions or by chemical cross-linking.35,36 In previous studies we could show that LIL can be used to design defect-free structures of gold of different size and periodicity on silicon as model surface.24 We could demonstrate further that spreading of human adipose-derived stem cells (hADSC) decreased with increasing feature dimensions, which had an effect on cell differentiation.24 In another study we studied how polyelectrolyte multilayers (PEM) made of hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly-L-lysine (PLL), either as native or cross-linked system varying in elastic modulus, guide hADSC adhesion, growth, and differentiation.37 We found that hADSC spread and grew more on stiffer, highly cross-linked than on soft native PLL/HA multilayers. The layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly technique constructs functional coatings on biodegradable films through sequential adsorption of oppositely charged materials, primarily leveraging electrostatic interactions. Here's a stepwise breakdown of the process and its functional outcomes:

1. **Alternating Deposition**:  
   - Oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (e.g., chitosan [CHI, cationic] and alginate [ALG, anionic]) or functionalized molecules (e.g., urushiol, graphene oxide) are alternately deposited on a substrate. This creates a stratified, nanoscale multilayer structure with controlled thickness and composition.

2. **Microstructural Control**:  
   - Parameters like pH, ionic strength, and temperature are adjusted to tune charge density, layer interpenetration, and film stability. For example, oxidized alginate forms aldehyde groups that cross-link with chitosan’s amines, enhancing mechanical robustness and reducing pH-dependent dissolution.

3. **Functional Enhancements**:  
   - **Anticorrosion/Barrier Properties**: Layers like branched polyethylenimine (BPEI) and graphene oxide (GO) form dense, impermeable coatings on magnesium alloys, acting as physical barriers against corrosion.  
   - **Antibacterial Activity**: Incorporation of agents like l-cysteine or catechol-modified polymers (e.g., dopamine-grafted hyaluronic acid) imparts antimicrobial effects. Chitosan’s inherent antibacterial properties are amplified in multilayer systems.  
   - **Drug Delivery**: Encapsulation of therapeutic proteins (e.g., TGF-β3) within CS-TPP nanogels or DNA in cationic starch/alginate films enables controlled, enzyme-triggered release.  
   - **Adhesion and Water Resistance**: Mussel-inspired catechol groups (e.g., in urushiol or dopamine-modified polymers) form covalent bonds with substrates, enhancing underwater adhesion and coating durability.

4. **Crosslinking and Stability**:  
   - Chemical crosslinking (e.g., via Schiff base formation between oxidized ALG and CHI) or physical interactions (hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic effects) improves mechanical strength and resistance to delamination. For instance, urushiol’s crosslinked networks enhance hydrophobicity and corrosion resistance.

5. **Biocompatibility and Biodegradability**:  
   - Natural polymers (chitosan, alginate, cellulose) and eco-friendly components (tannic acid, starch) ensure the coatings remain biodegradable and cytocompatible. Enzymatic degradation (e.g., α-amylase for starch-based films) allows programmed dissolution in biological environments.

6. **Multifunctional Applications**:  
   - **Food Packaging**: LbL coatings with anthocyanins and carboxylated graphene oxide improve UV-blocking, hydrophobicity, and antioxidant activity.  
   - **Biomedical Implants**: Graded coatings on PCL fiber mats enable localized drug delivery for tissue engineering.  
   - **EMI Shielding**: Conductive graphene/PEI layers deposited via spray-LbL create micrometer-thick coatings with high electromagnetic interference shielding.

In summary, LbL assembly leverages electrostatic and chemical interactions to build tailored, multifunctional coatings on biodegradable substrates. By selecting materials and tuning assembly conditions, the technique addresses challenges like corrosion, microbial growth, and controlled release while maintaining environmental sustainability.

This creates a nanostructured, ultra-thin coating. retrieved_contexts: ['According to ASTM-D-6400, a biodegradable plastic is “a material whose decomposition is caused by naturally occurring microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae”. This material, under certain environmental conditions, is designed to suffer a significant change in its chemical makeup. This leads to a loss of properties over a specific time frame that can be measurable by standard test methods that are appropriate for proper classification. To satisfy these conditions, a biodegradable plastic must demonstrate a satisfactory rate of biodegradation where at least 90% w/w of (i) the organic carbon in the whole component or (ii) each constituent making up more than 1% weight by dry mass is converted to carbon dioxide within 180 days, and other constituents making up less than 1% by mass but less than 5% summative, do not necessarily biodegrade. Composting (home or industrial) is one common pathway for biodegradation. The remains of these naturally aged materials remained intact after 8.5 years in the soil, even though they were further degraded.28", 'Flow behavior of LDPE and its blends with LLDPE I and II: A comparative study Packaging polymers, particularly polyethylene films, have been considered to be the major culprit for causing the rising environmental pollution problem. These polymers, after completing their useful short lifecycle as packaging films, find their way to constitute the major fraction of solid municipal waste, where they refuse to degrade because of their hydrophobic nature. The problem aggravates due to the high molecular weight associated with these polymers. An acceptable solution to this problem is the use of oxo-degradable polyethylene, which first disintegrates to small pieces, thereby reducing their ubiquitous visual presence. In the process, their molecular weight is reduced and these become potentially biodegradable organics, which can be subsequently consumed by the microorganism to form biomass.1-3 Major strategies to facilitate the disintegration and subsequent biodegradation of polyethylene are mainly focused on the direct incorporation of carbonyl groups within the backbone of the polymer (ethylene \uf8ffCO copolymer)4 or by addition of certain pro-oxidants (Scott-Gilead Process) during the processing stage.5, 6 These pro-oxidants, in the presence of either light or heat lead to the generation of free radicals on the polymer chain, which further react with oxygen to form carbonyl groups through a series of reactions. These carbonyl groups, then undergo photochemical reactions (Norrish Type I, II, and III) to finally lead to chain scission and physical embrittlement.4 In the recent years, linear low density polyethylene (LLDPE) is fast replacing low density polyethylene (LDPE) as packaging films, because of its better mechanical properties and comparable cost. Keeping in mind the increased use of LLDPE, we felt the need of performing accelerated degradation studies on LDPE, LLDPE, and LLDPE -LDPE blends. As a part of our ongoing efforts towards development of oxo-degradable polyethylene, we have reported the pro-oxidative action of cobalt stearate on LDPE,7, 8 which first leads to the abiotic disintegration of the matrix. The degradation of these disintegrated films by bacterial consortium has also been reported.9 The effect of such pro-oxidants is expected to be less pronounced for LLDPE because of the lesser degree of branching in the polymer chain, therefore requiring higher concentrations of the pro-oxidant to reach the same level of degradation, which has been confirmed by our investigations.10 To avoid the slight bluish tinge in the films containing higher concentrations of cobalt stearate, the present investigation was performed on films containing manganese stearate which also belong to the broad category of pro-oxidants.11', 'It can be noted from observing the results of the literature surveyed in the aforementioned table that biodegradation is typically reached within a minimum period of 90 days in controlled aerobic conditions measuring CO2 evolution. It can also be withdrawn in parallel to the previous conclusion that the standard test method of ASTM D 5988-18 [33] ‘Standard Test Method for Determining Aerobic Biodegradation of Plastic Materials in Soil’ is the most common accepted method for determining the biodegradability of biodegradable polymers. Other studies have also reported the response of various oxo and hydro-degradable materials using various analytical characterisation techniques. Yashchuk et al. [34] have studied commercial grades of polyethylene (PE) based oxo-biodegradable plastic films using infrared-spectroscopy (IR) and monitoring their CO2 release. During the first 20 days, the biodegradation rate was faster for the oxo-biodegradable PE in comparison to virgin PE. Furthermore, the oxo-biodegradable samples reached a 10-day period plateau and by the end of the test timeframe of 90 days, the biodegradation rate was slightly lower than the virgin PE one (24%). This was attributed to the amount of additives present in the virgin specimens which acted as a source of nutrients to microorganism in the soil as shown previously by Davis [35] and confirmed by IR analysis on the studied materials. Sera et al. [36] tested various biodegradable synthetic polyesters and cellulose (as a reference material) using ASTM D5988-18 [33] whereby they have shown that an increase from laboratory temperature (25 °C) to 37 °C will increase the mineralisation rate due to increase in microorganism activity. Rosa et al. [37] compounded hydro-biodegradable polymers consisting of polymer waste consisting of HDPE/PP blends with corn starch and glycerin as a thermoplastic starch (TPS). The addition of TPS has reduced the melt flow of the materials tested which compromises their integrity as a plastic product suitable for the market. Recently, Guras et al. studied the effect of the addition of TPS and plasticiser to PCL which showed a negligible effect on its thermal stability. PCL and starch blends were also noted to be higher in biodegradation rate in comparison to neat PCL by Mariani et al. [38] due to the increase in the blends crystallinity enhancing preferential attack of microorganism on the starch content. In this work, we report for the first time the biodegradation extent determined as per ASTM D5988-18 [33] for polymer waste blends that incorporate oxo-prodegradant additives, in addition to thermoplastic starch compounded and tested in the form of film specimens. The samples were compounded and prepared in accordance to industrial protocols for plastic films processing, and were characterised for their thermal stability and chemical nature at first. Furthermore, the aerobic degradation conditions were chosen (namely soil used) to represent a local landfill site in the State of Kuwait. This will determine the optimal fate for polymer waste and the best route to treat in future ventures, and whether it is suitable to compound biodegradable blends out of which that could be mineralised with time. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to report the fate of polymer waste biodegradation after following a similar workflow. This work aims to demonstrate the fate of polymer waste after inducing its biodegradation by compounding it as either oxo or hydro-biodegradable plastics that could be used on the market. Materials and methods', 'Development of degradable polyolefin has attracted increasing interest due to their low price, useful properties, broad suppliers, and mature processing facilities and techniques. UV-oxidative degradation and blending with natural polymers can enhance their biodegradability.1-6 Oxo-degradation incorporates oxygen into the carbon chain and results in the formation of functional groups such as carboxylic or hydro-carboxylic acids, esters, aldehydes, and alcohols. This process can be accelerated by exposure of samples to ultraviolet (UV) light or heating. It is suggested that once the molecular weight of a polymer is significantly reduced during oxo-degradation, the oxidized products are deemed susceptible to further degradation by various micro-organisms, which assimilate the oxidized fragments and convert them into CO2, H2O, and biomass.7, 8 Photo-oxidative degradation is the process of degradation of the material by the action of light and the free radical chain degradation.9-11 Rate of abiotic oxidation of polyolefins is important as it determines the rate of subsequent biodegradation process. It has been reported that to achieve significant biodegradation in a reasonable time period, the average molecular weight of oxidized polyolefin should be less than 5000 Da.7, 8, 12-19 Transition metal salts and transition metal free systems have been widely used as prodegradants to accelerate the oxidation process of polyolefins, as the metal ions can absorb some of radiant energy and transform it to the polymer chain to accelerate its fragmentation. Various Fe and Co-based pre-degradants are commercial available in the market.4 Recently, it was found that hydrophilic polymers such as starch20-22 and cellulose23 play an important role in accelerating the degradation of polyolefin in a photo-degrading environment. It has been reported that addition of starch influence the molecule weight of low-density polyethylene (LDPE), resulting into significant reduction in the molecular weight of starch/LDPE blends on exposure to UV radiations.21 Raquez et al.22 studied degradability of LDPE using thermal analysis and scanning electron microscope (SEM) and found that oxidative degradations of oxo-degradable LDPE was enhanced with thermoplastic pea starch (TPPS) under UV-condition. Previous studies1, 24-26 have also shown that starch can accelerate the oxidative degradation of polyolefin blends and encourage their biodegradation by micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, and algae)1, 24-27. However, there is no clear understanding of the mechanism by which starch influences degradation process of polyolefin-starch blends. To further explore the degradation mechanisms, it is important to study both chemical and physical changes in the interface between starch and polyolefin, and identify the stage at which acceleration starts.', 'Some critics claim that biodegradable plastics may not be the best solution for mitigating environmental burdens [23]. In 2019, Greenpeace argued that the natural decomposition of biodegradable plastics requires high temperature and humidity conditions, which are rarely found in natural environments [24]. Napper and Thompson (2019) reported that oxo-biodegradable and biodegradable bags that had been submerged in a marine environment or buried in soil for >3 years were not conspicuously degraded and exhibited load-bearing performance similar to that of conventional non-degradable bags [25]. Similarly, the public expresses concern that biodegradable plastics may not be effectively degraded unless specific environmental conditions are present. Unfortunately, they believe that biodegradable plastics are not a viable solution to address plastic waste issues. To clarify negative greenwashing and public misconceptions regarding biodegradable plastics, researchers have studied their biodegradation under various environmental conditions in compost, soil, and aquatic systems [[26], [27], [28], [29]]. These studies indicated that degradation is possible, although the rate might be slow. Moreover, accelerating biodegradation while maintaining excellent load-bearing properties by engineering the polymer structure and whiskers was recently reported, to emphasize industrial applicability in the service, agricultural, and fishing industries [[30], [31], [32]]. To-date, there has been no in-depth study on the fate of biodegradable plastics or microbial analysis in the real world. In this study, we investigated the decomposition of biodegradable plastics, including polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), and PBAT, mimicking real-field conditions as follows: fertile soil prepared by replenishing vermicompost with horticultural topsoil, thereby simulating an agricultural setting, and live marine ecosystems prepared in an artificial aquarium, thereby simulating a fisheries setting. Seawater degradation in a coastal marine environment was also examined for comparison. Concomitant microbial analysis demonstrated that the mechanical properties of PCL weakened over time, thereby reducing the probabilities of ghost fishing. In particular, we utilized 3D printing to fabricate fishing gear using PCL, which exhibited the most rapid rate of decomposition among the three biodegradable plastics tested [[33], [34], [35]]. Our results demonstrated that biodegradable plastics have sufficient functionality (mechanical strength and formability through 3D printing) as substitutes for traditional non-degradable plastics. Therefore, non-degradable plastics, which are widely used in agriculture and fisheries, can be replaced with biodegradable plastics and are anticipated to provide a solution to address problems associated with ghost fishing and plastic waste in the environment (Fig. 1a). Again and by comparison with the literature, the process is more faster as compared with the photo-oxidation degradation of LDPE in this stage.24 The obtained results showed that there is a synergistic effect on the oxidation process of the oxodegradable LDPE/TTPS blends when exposed to UV-sunlight. This means that photo-radiation could induce oxidation reaction enhanced and could accelerate the biodegradability rate of LDPE/starch blends by creating oxodegradable LDPE/starch that is more susceptible to biotic reactions. This article was devoted to highlight the synergistic association of oxodegradable LDPE with thermoplasticized pea starch under UV-ageing. Melt-blends between thermoplasticized pea starch and oxo-degradable LDPE, compatibilized or not with maleic anhydride-grafted polyethylene (MA-g-PE), were prepared using an internal mixing chamber. Tensile properties, morphology, and thermomechanical properties of resulting melt-blends were studied. Tensile properties show that oxodegradable LDPE and TPPS have some affinity, as evidenced by the smooth decrease of ultimate properties for the resulting melt-blends at different TPPS content. When MA-g-PE is used as a compatibilizer, the tensile properties of the resulting melt-blends were significantly enhanced up to a high content of TPPS close to 40 wt %. This allows valorizing pea starch (plasticized or not) as a biosourced material at high content in polymeric compositions. DMTA and DSC studies were performed on oxodegradable LDPE and compatibilized oxodegradable LDPE/TPPS melt-blends (30 wt % TPPS) after a 25-week UV-ageing study to clearly distinguish the contribution of both polymeric partners in the oxodegradable LDPE/TPPS melt-blends. It results that oxodegradable LDPE or in combination with TPPS underwent photo-oxidative degradations as promoted by prooxidant added into LDPE. During the first weeks, the thermomechanical properties of oxo-degradable LDPE show that the crystallinity of the olefinic matrix increases with UV-irradiation time, due to the preferential cleavage of branching points of LDPE. After 13 weeks, the UV-degradation proceeds directly through the main backbone, leading to a decrease of crystallinity degree. When TPPS is added, starch is also subject to degradations as some preferential cleavages of these α (1-4) and α (1-6) bonds. This leads to a decrease in amplitude and intensity according to the glass transition of plasticized starch fraction. Note to reader: R; Radical, PD; Prodegradant Oxo-biodegradable plastics have to be viewed from various angels; namely environmental and performance integrity ones, to be able to pass them of as acceptable products on local markets. There exist various governing bodies that have adopted (or developed) standards to make such products a mandatory on local plastic dealers for commercial markets. Oxo-biodegradable plastics have to pass various ecotoxicity and standard biodegradation tests as well. Enigmatically, very scant literature exist as to the real performance of such commercial products with respect to their biodegradation rate. In addition, very little effort has been devoted to study the biodegradation rate of compounded plastics in general whether they were claimed to be oxo-biodegradable or hydro-biodegradable (i.e. plastics with natural resources prompting their fragmentation such as starch) using standard test methods. Readers are referred to Table S1 in the Supplementary Materials File for a review on main biodegradation test results disseminated in technical literature. Research in biodegradable polymers is also receiving renewed attention nowadays with emphasis on their properties and performance post exposure to various environments. Suresh et al. [9] studied PE compounded with pro-oxidant additives and determined that oxidation occurred on the blends as a result of the additive content. Al-Salem et al. [10] characterised thermoplastic starch (TPS) blends and determined their thermal stability. The degradation kinetics estimated were comparable to those of virgin polyolefin resin. Lai and Lee [11] have recently investigated biodegradable poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) with 1,3:2,4-dibenzylidene-D-sorbitol (DBS) prepared by melt blending. It was confirmed that presence of DBS interfered with the crystallization rates of PLLA. Petchwattana et al. [12] determined the effect of natural (outdoor) weathering on rice hull composites with PE. Silica rich rice hull content improved the mechanical, properties examined in their work. The standard test method of ASTM D 5988 ‘Standard Test Method for Determining Aerobic Biodegradation of Plastic Materials in Soil’ is among those certified procedures for determining the rate of biodegradation of biodegradable plastics. Table S2 depicts the main test methods used in determining the rate of biodegradation of plastics and other major biodegradability test procedures. Major dispute also exist as to the applicability of oxo-biodegradable products to fit various standards and harsh climatic conditions. In this communication, three commercial grade oxo-biodegradable plastic PE film products were tested using the standard test method of ASTM D 5988 [13]. The materials were sourced from local dealers in the State of Kuwait where governmental authorities have taken the initiative to start developing standards to govern the use of biodegradable products locally. This is due to the fact that PSW has been accumulating in landfill sites for the past thirty years and majority of what is claimed to be biodegradable plastics has been noted to neither degrade nor fragment when exposed to aerobic conditions in landfills. The materials tested were firstly verified for their biodegradable nature. The second stage of the work encompassed the activities associated with the determination of their actual biodegradation arte. To the best of our knowledge, the work shown in this communication reveals the first attempt of determining biodegradation rate in the Middle-East region.', 'Products made from natural rubber are often vulcanized during the production to improve their strength and durability. Vulcanization improves the mechanical properties of the rubber at the expense of its biodegradability [4], [5]. Sulfur vulcanization and the presence of certain additives (such as antioxidants) in some of these products extend the duration needed for decomposition in the natural environment [5], [6]. Polyolefin plastics and metal complexes (such as Fe, Co, and Mn stearates) that serve as pro-degradant additives (PDA) or catalysts are frequently used to accelerate the natural degradation process of polymers [7]. The mechanism involved includes the absorption of UV light and oxidation, followed by the generation of unstable hydroperoxide that will subsequently dissociate to form a pair of free radicals responsible for the eventual disintegration of the polymer [8], [9]. The oxidation of the polymer also results in the formation of carbonyl groups in the hydrocarbon chain (Fig. 1A), making it more vulnerable to further degradation since these groups are photolabile and easily undergo photolysis via Norrish I and Norrish II reactions (Fig. 1B) [10], [11]. Given the current enormous volume of rubber usage, there is a need to consider the end-of-life treatment of rubber products, including ways to hasten its biodegradation in the environment. One viable strategy is the enhancement of oxo-biodegradable properties of natural rubber [4]. The introduction of oxo-biodegradable properties has been extensively studied in the plastics industry, evidenced by the high volume of patents and successful commercial products in the market with many positive results [12], [13], [14]. The most common approach to improving oxo-biodegradability is introducing a PDA in the polymers. The oxo-biodegradation of a polymer refers to a two-stage degradation process that begins with the oxidation of the carbon backbone of the polymer to form smaller fragments containing carboxyl, ester, aldehyde, and/or alcohol groups, followed by bio-assimilation of the oxidation products by microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), and biomass. In the first stage of degradation, the oxidative breakdown of polymer to produce smaller and hydrophilic fragments is crucial to improve water wettability of the substrate, and molecules of the material must be sufficiently small for microflora, such as bacteria and fungi to assimilate carbon source in the substrate [15], [16]. This explains why most hydrocarbon thermoplastics, which are hydrophobic and usually produced with very high molecular weight, are bioinert. This could also explain the persistency observed in vulcanized natural rubber which is composed of poly(isoprene) chains connected by sulfur linkages [4], [5]. Over the past ten years, there have been reports of successful improvements in the oxo-biodegradability of plastics, particularly through the use of various PDA [17], [18]. Although a similar approach can be applied to rubber and may work equally well, little research has been done to develop oxo-biodegradable rubber, and its potential impact on plant and soil health remain unclear. The objectives of the present study were to develop and characterize oxo-biodegradable rubber through the incorporation of two metal stearates as PDA, namely iron (III) stearate (FeSt) and cobalt (II) stearate (CoSt), as well as to assess the effects of the oxo-biodegradable rubber on plant and soil health. The development of novel and safe oxo-biodegradable rubbers is vital to ensure sustainable development in the rubber industry, and securing a greener future that supports sustainable living, which is in line with the targets of the global sustainable development goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 12 Responsible Consumption and Production, and SDG 15 Life on Land.', 'Copyright © 2011 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Synthetic polymers (plastics) are widely used in industry and agriculture. Because of their high durability, they accumulate in the environment at a rate of 25 million tons per year.1 Plastics are not normally biodegradable until they are degraded into low molecular products which can be assimilated by micro-organisms.2, 3 This shows that biodegradation must be preceded by an abiotic treatment that produces monomeric and oligomeric products. It has been shown that alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, etc., which are generated by oxo-biodegradation, can be utilized by the micro-organisms as nutrients for their growth.4 In a study, it has been reported that linear paraffin molecules having a molecular weight below 500 Daltons,5 or n-alkanes upto C44H90,6 can be utilized as a carbon source by micro-organisms. Commercial polyethylenes, which are widely used, are very much resistant to oxidation and biodegradation because they contain antioxidants and stabilizers. However, they can be made oxo-biodegradable by the use of pro-degradant additives.7, 8 The most active pro-degradants are those based on metal combinations capable of yielding two metal ions of similar stability and with an oxidation number differing by one unit, e.g., Mn2+/Mn3+.9 Thus, the material degrades via a free radical chain reaction involving oxygen from atmosphere. The primary products are hydro peroxides, which can either thermolyse or photolyse under the catalytic action of a pro-degradant, leading to chain scission and the production of low molecular mass oxidation products, such as carboxylic acids, alcohols, ketones, and low molecular mass hydrocarbons.10 Peroxidation also leads to hydrophilic surface modification, which is favorable to micro-organisms.11 In a study of a commercial photo biodegradable polyethylene12 that low molar mass products are removed from the surface of the polymer by bio erosion without significant effect on the molar mass of the bulk polymer. The microplastic generation risk of oxo-degradable plastics is **high** due to their reliance on abiotic degradation mechanisms (e.g., UV light, heat, or oxidation) rather than true biodegradation. Key findings from the context include:  

1. **Physical Fragmentation**: Oxo-degradable plastics fragment into microplastics through chemical reactions (abiotic degradation), which do not produce CO₂ or achieve full mineralization. These microplastics persist in the environment, posing risks to wildlife and water systems ([1], [2], [3]).  

2. **Failure to Meet Biodegradation Standards**: Independent testing (e.g., ASTM D5338, ISO 14855) confirms that oxo-degradable plastics fail biodegradability norms (ASTM 6400, ISO 17088). Even after 8.5 years in soil, fragments remain intact, demonstrating no significant biodegradation ([2], [3], [9]).  

3. **Environmental Persistence**: Studies show that oxo-degradable plastics degrade into smaller particles but retain their polymeric structure, with molecular weight reductions insufficient for microbial assimilation (typically requiring <5000 Da). This results in long-term accumulation of microplastics in terrestrial and aquatic environments ([6], [7], [14]).  

4. **Regulatory and Ecological Concerns**: Laws (e.g., in California) restrict claims about oxo-degradable plastics due to unverified biodegradation. The persistence of microplastics raises concerns about chemical leaching, physical ingestion by organisms, and ecosystem disruption ([2], [3], [12]).  

In summary, oxo-degradable plastics primarily generate microplastics through abiotic fragmentation, lacking subsequent biodegradation under real-world conditions, thereby posing significant environmental risks.

This leads to the accumulation of persistent microplastics in the environment, which is why the EU and other jurisdictions have moved to ban them.
